en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuyi:
Within the Great Radiance, there is nothing that does not exist, and there is nothing that is not empty. The two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—manifest as reflections therein.
A single point of luminous clarity becomes muddled by conceptual knowledge and views; a fleeting thought arises and is taken as the place where one establishes a dwelling and sustains one's life.
Sometimes it shifts and changes without ceasing; sometimes it solidifies and does not dissolve. Whether rising or sinking, it is left entirely to the whims of the Creator.
A great man holds the universe in his hand; he creates transformation within his own mind. Alas, how can one listen to the mechanisms of destiny and submit willingly to servitude?
Is it not for this reason that those who guide me do so not in vain? At the age of childhood, I already contemplated in secret the way to transcendence.

This remained vividly in my mind. I presented myself at the Imperial Examination several times, yet it was difficult for me to attain even a single degree. By a stroke of misfortune, I received an imperial decree appointing me as a Magistrate of Xin Prefecture.
There, I heard that from the time National Teacher Shao of Tiantai first opened the path at Boshan, the transmission of the lamp had never been interrupted;
now, Master Wuyi has succeeded to the Patriarchal lineage and established a distinct branch, propagating the school’s style by teaching according to the capacities of his followers. I read...
For four years he first engaged in its creation and requested instruction. Beholding his spirit and demeanor, they were transcendent and clear, like a solitary crane soaring through the sky;
yet he was imbued with a profound kindness and harmony, never seeking to distinguish himself. When one probes his inner core, it is deep and unfathomable.

Since the Way resides within what is witnessed before the eyes, we cast aside our parasols without further words. Sitting together upon a rush mat, we consult one another to resolve doubts regarding the mind. Your younger brother...
The disciple brought out the casket and showed it to me; it was the Master’s discourse from his ascent to the hall. On this day, the heat was great, and sweat fell like rain.
While I was reading through it, suddenly, as if stirred by a gentle breeze, the trees in the courtyard and the mountain mists all gave rise to a coolness that permeated my body;
the stifling heat vanished in an instant. At that moment, the Master rose and asked, "Do you understand yet? At that time, I remained silent, feeling a sense of regret.
Separate. Alas! When the flower was plucked and transmitted, who could have known the wind of that smile? With nostrils reaching toward heaven, who is truly skilled at grasping the clouds?
This serves as the preface. Disciple Zhao Shizhen, with humble obeisance, inscribes this preface on the *Faxian* (Dharma-Almsgiving) for the Transmission of the Lineage.
Ordinary people of the world are unable to practice supramundane filial piety, yet those who have transcended the world are able to fulfill even mundane filial duties.
As I observe Master Boshan’s chapter on "The Dharma-Almsgiving of Extending Kindness," none can compare to him.

To provide for one’s parents while they live and to offer them remembrance after their passing is worldly filial piety; the Master has practiced this. To bring forth the depths of emotion and to pervade one’s very nature is world-transcending filial piety;
the Master has perfected this. When young, he grieved for his mother; as he grew up and pursued his studies in official service, he subsequently heard of the death of his compassionate father.
Bearing these two in his heart, he was moved by the decline of the age and was dyed by it; such were the great matters of the ancients.
Not yet enlightened, he was as if mourning for his parents. At this juncture, the Master was truly not as the records describe: he was full of vigor yet felt as if he were at an end;

he was majestic yet felt as if he were searching for something and failing to find it. With this profound mind, he turned toward the boatman on the other side of the hidden shore, piercing through the nostrils of his father’s Dharma-body.
The six-year dream was shattered, and the ice of kalpas melted away. He reached out and grasped the clouds.
At the crag, a precious mirror hangs high; the sacred robe is not yet hung. Filial piety fills Mount Cao; we meet suddenly as if it were but yesterday.
The field of merit is vast, the waters of compassion flow deep—the Three Dukes are far removed. Encourage yourselves in the waves of Chan for the Pure Land—strive for the nine grades!
Having journeyed westward, he has now set out eastward. The sun shines upon the lofty mountain; the rain nourishes the small grasses. A few stumps of the funeral trees cast down their wondrous shade.

To Tongqing: With a single incense offering from a devoted heart, may auspicious mists entwine upon Fudu. Having been liberated from the long fetters of a layman’s home, there was no need for the array of tripods and heavy carpets.
Yet, lingering alone within the gates of the Dharma, how could one behold the old village of Xinfeng?

Returning my gaze to Zhendan, before the curtains of the Jade Palace and beneath the hem of the water-field robe—how could there be such a thing as "passing the examination" through the emptiness of mind? With no fixed means of providing for one's parents, the ocean of sorrow is brewed.
It is the very essence of ghee; it is the lush fatness of Mount Compassion. Filial piety, both mundane and supramundane, is perfectly cultivated in a single thought-moment.

Is this not like our Great Master acting as the sovereign who extends his influence to all? For we have heard that when an echo transmits sound in a hollow valley, the call and response arise together;

when the blossoms of awakening scatter their radiance, cause and effect are simultaneous. To seal mind with mind, where one seed gives rise to a corresponding seed—this is precisely the meaning of "extending influence."
Alas! We of our kind desire to become followers of the Great Master, yet have not yet received the Great Master’s seal of approval;

we gaze with focused intensity like a blind turtle awaiting a floating log, finally entrusting ourselves to the compassionate vessel. Having received the Great Master’s seal of approval, yet failing to become one of his kind, is like a blind turtle losing its floating log;
in a single instant, three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas pass, and one sinks forever into the ocean of *kalpas*. May you attain [liberation].
Not a single person did not feel heartache and distress. They drew near to the fundamental inquiry entrusted by the Dharma-donor, contemplating it day and night.
Letting go of their hands over the precipice, they suddenly encountered their own mother; after death, they were revived once more, returning their whole body to the Father.

In the kingdom, they brandished their swords and slaughtered all who dwelt in peace. The quail’s egg cried out at night; the crane’s feathers fell at dawn. At such a time as this, is there anyone who can match Mount Bo? Who will pay their respects?
Is there no place for reverent dedication? Is there no place where Boshan responds to conditions and manifests transformation?
Is there no place where Boshan puts on Touzi’s cassock and beats Fushan’s Dharma drum? It is such that, within the flash of a stone-light, [all is realized].

Busily chasing the shadow of the whip; vainly plucking at the branches of empty flowers. Idly gathering the pearl from within one’s robes. Once the phoenixes have soared into the clouds, the wild sheep hangs its horns there.
Simply realize that white clouds always lean against the peaks; do not ask about the green mountains, for they remain unknowable. The passions of birth and death are hollowed out.
Mind and mind do not touch; the nature of nirvana is all-pervasive. Step by step, one returns home. The toil of beginningless time is fully repaid in a single instant.
Great filial piety is inexhaustible—yet it is still but a single drop in the ocean; how much more so the rest?

If this is not yet the case, then for now, become a wood-eating insect within the *Xilei* (Categorizing Analogies) section, and according to your capacity, gnaw upon even a single character or half a character. In future lives and subsequent worlds...
"The day for returning the throw is at hand. Disciple Guangyue and Wu Yingbin pay their respects with *vaṃdana* and respectfully provide this preface to the *Shenglù*.
Formerly, during a time when the Dharma-gate was desolate, Shouchang’s words resonated with inner sound and his conduct was free from self-interest, causing the [Linji] tradition to...

The former lineage was once again revitalized; how magnificent was his achievement! When Yushan bestowed his instructions, he overthrew Boshan; when the water arrives, the channel is naturally formed.
His entire being is a mouth, like a multi-storied pavilion in the sky, with every side exquisitely clear.
The light of his Dharma-sound shines universally throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The world unanimously took him as their master. I visited Boshan at Shouchang once more.
Having been specially granted a seal of transmission, he subsequently served Master Shouchang.

Last winter, while traveling through Huaiyu, he met Master Liusue Yin at Yingshan, who presented him with a manuscript of the *Shenglü* (Record of the Remaining). Beholding it once more was like seeing a familiar face;

it was as if splitting a sandalwood tree—every fragment is fragrant—and it is truly a standard within the Buddha-dharma. As for the profound mechanism of the ultimate path, it transcends words and letters.
[The] Characteristics. Now tell me: did my late teacher, Boshan, have any superfluous words? "Since the time of disorder thirty years ago, I have never lacked salt or sauce.
Written by the disciple Huang Duanduo, prostrating in homage, as a preface to the *Chan Jingyu* (Admonitions on Zen).
"Jing" (警) carries the meaning of awakening or alertness; it may also be interpreted as "startle. For example, suppose there is a thief eyeing a grand mansion.
The master sits upon the hall at night with lamps lit, coughing and clearing his throat to make a sound. The thief, fearing discovery, cannot act immediately.

However, if the master should fall into a slight slumber, the thief seizes the opportunity to enter and overturns the master's treasury. Therefore, walled cities strike the wooden clappers (*tuoluo*), and sentries ring the *diaodou* gongs at their chariots; yet, should a sudden change occur—

Yet there is no cause for alarm, because one remains vigilant before the trigger of circumstance. Human beings face the great affliction of birth and death—a long dream from which they do not awaken for ten thousand kalpas.
Moreover, this state serves as a medium for thieves who daily plunder the treasures of the household.

Were it not for the piercing words of awakening from a great hero of supreme enlightenment, one would remain forever drunk in a dream, with no day of realization in sight. It is not merely that one cannot act while asleep; [one is likewise incapable of acting while under the influence of ignorance].

The Master [Zongze] said: "At night, his eyes remain open and his delirious muttering is even more severe. Therefore, Great Master Bosha, riding upon the power of his compassionate vows, has come to act as a Great Physician King.
Using a single-flavored gāthā, he universally treats the karmic diseases of madness and recklessness.

Thus, there are these 'Warning Words on Zen Sickness,' which are direct, concise, and appropriate; they grasp the very marrow of the sicknesses inherent in practicing Zen and explain them through to their end. Regarding this instruction:
The language of practicing the Way is the most urgent and vital matter; it is truly a new essential manual for the Zen school, and also a ninefold elixir for saving the world.
As for Zen itself, it is a provisional name without substance—how could there be any illness? This is because those who investigate Zen...

They frequently give rise to clinging emotions and erroneous understandings, being deceitfully slain by the mind, intellect, and consciousness. Instead of seeking within the realm of the immediate occasion, they instead search for it within intellectual learning.
They are either obstructed by the words and phrases of the ancients, or they are drowned in stagnant water, or they sit entrenched in the armor of "nothingness.
This is not because their vital intelligence has died out; rather, it is because their minds have become either deludedly attached or merely revolving in circles.

It cannot be severed; thus, the life-faculty is difficult to cut off, and birth and cessation remain vividly present. To perceive one’s entire body as being entirely one's own illness is for Zen to have fallen ill.
In extreme cases, this leads to madness or possession by demons, such that even the Buddha could not save them; this is called a karmic illness, not an illness of Zen.
Even if one were to die, if various states of mind arise and one is willing to apply oneself to practice, it will accord with the principle of the Dharma-body.
They have never stepped upon the pivotal mechanism for ascending; they sit within a basket of rice, feeling light and at ease.

Yet this very state of light ease is precisely a sickness of Zen. Thus, when a monk asked an ancient master, "What is the pure Dharma-body? the master replied, "The source of immeasurable great illnesses.
These words are like a chestnut burr; truly difficult to swallow or spit out. The ancients engaged in authentic inquiry and genuine practice...
Regarding "Awakening": having passed through an episode of illness, when it comes to extending one's hand [to treat others], one must naturally apply the needle and probe without confusion.

One requires a person who has completely severed the breath and knows both pain and itchiness before being willing to examine them. Thus, only by recognizing the illness can one eliminate the illness; only after regulating oneself can one regulate others.
Can this not be called "one who has broken three arm-bones becomes a skilled physician"? Master Boshan himself has come from such a background.
Investigating this Way reaches the ultimate in integration; every word and phrase strikes the very core of the matter.

This is not an intentional fabrication of lofty, subtle, or mysterious discourse intended to leave others ignorant. Rather, it is the state realized through personal experience and practice, what has been seen, spoken, enacted, and applied.
Its principles are lucid and its eloquence unimpeded; thus, he speaks of Chan with such ease.
Regarding illness: it is like grasping the jade mirror of the Qin palace; it reflects the livers and gallbladders of all officials so that not even a single hair’s breadth of concealment can remain.
Among those throughout antiquity who sat upon the curved *lu* bed, claiming to be "good knowledge-holders" (*shanzhishi*) and preaching Chan, few have been able to match your Master’s subtlety.

Yet, the illnesses of Chan are most difficult to speak of, and even if spoken of, they cannot be fully exhausted. Why is this? Illness is the illness of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The Dharma-body has no...
How many illnesses can there possibly be? For one who skillfully heals the illness of the *dharmakāya*, illness becomes a wondrous medicine;
illness becomes their daily sustenance; illness becomes a sweatshirt pressed against the skin. It is simply a matter of preserving it well.

When the ancients were in the midst of illness, they engaged in the Buddha-work of playful sport. This was because they had seen through the fact that the *dharmakāya* has no master; thus, the illness cleared away of its own accord. Therefore—
Dongshan said: "When I, this old monk, look at it, I do not see any illness; it arises solely because of deluded thoughts and attachment, whereby 'Zen illnesses' compete to manifest.
In the past, the Buddha spoke of the demonic activities regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the biased calculations of external paths (*tīrthika*);

these are precisely the matters found within the Zen illnesses of people today. However, if one becomes attached, it constitutes a demon; if one calculates, it is called an external path. If one neither attaches nor calculates, it is also called [the Way]."

This is the illness. Therefore it is said: "To not give rise to thoughts of superiority is called a 'wholesome state'; if one takes this as a realization of sainthood, one immediately succumbs to various devils.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "There was a guide who well knew the roads—whether passable or blocked, dangerous or difficult—and was thus able to lead those people forward to the place of treasure.
Thus, this treatise by the Great Master is precisely the vessel for the final age and the direct path for those with the initial resolve.
It will not only be beneficial for today, but will also provide assistance for the future.

For those who resolutely desire to engage in Chan practice and apply themselves to the work, seeking the gate of great awakening—if they are willing to examine this book closely, it will serve as a great strategic aid.

It can cause the state of doubt to arise where it had not yet arisen, and it can penetrate the root of the illness where it could not yet be pierced, like sifting through sand to reveal the treasure. It requires that you...
Take it up yourself. It is like seeing the sky when the mist clears, causing people not to become lost. Within the path that cuts off all ways, there is a path for emerging;
within the phrase of death, there is the phrase of life. Like a perfect sphere rolling upon a tray, one does not linger on a single word. Such is its wondrous function.
If everyone knew how to apply their mind in this way, they could see the Way while sitting or sleeping, without wasting the price of so many straw sandals.
Until one reaches the field of great peace and bliss, where one breathes through the same nostrils as the Buddhas and Patriarchs—
those who can use this to admonish themselves and thereby admonish others, and who use this to heal themselves and thereby heal others, may also be called "Living Medicine Kings" (Vaidyarāja).
By causing the life-vein of the Patriarchs to flow unceasingly, and ensuring that the national pulse and the pulse of wisdom are both firmly established, one will not fail the Great Master.
Such is the power of the expedient means revealed by his compassionate descent. This serves as the preface.
Written in the first month of autumn in the Xinhai year of the Wanli era, by the disciple Liu Chongqing, in humble salutation.
Preface to the *Religious Teachings: Echoes in Response*.
One who asks questions well is like one carving hard wood: first attack what is easy, then the knots and joints. After a long time, they will explain themselves through mutual understanding.
One who receives questions well is like striking a bell: strike it lightly and it rings softly; strike it heavily and it rings loudly.
Wait for its resonance to settle, and only then will it exhaust its full sound. One who is unskilled at answering questions is the opposite of this.
This is true for the way of learning in all its aspects; how much more so for the Dharma-gate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and this great matter of birth and death!
How could one allow it to be obscured and muddled, as if grasping at shadows or catching the wind, or merely speculating and conjecturing like one divining by tortoise-shell or pottery shards?
Now, as for what is called an "inadequate response to a question," does it necessarily mean that the answer itself was inherently bad?

It may well be that there are those who call themselves "men of knowledge" (jñānin) yet fall into the unwholesome; why is this? Because when there is a deliberate intention to do good, that very intention has already become unwholesome.

Having read the *Chongjiao dahan* (Echoes of the Religious Teachings), I have analyzed its subtle details and synthesized its systematic threads, thereby enabling the tips of its arrows to be sharp and piercing.

The target is hit; the edge of the sword is transformed into a level path. The questioner addresses his own fundamental share, and the respondent meets the immediate occasion—this is the most excellent of the good.
Beyond this, perhaps the layman should have further explanations to offer, and the Great Master should have further words of composure.
As for that which severs the path of thought and cuts off the way of speech, though I am not quick-witted, I still...
May you hear this. Recorded by the disciple Zhang Rui on the wuchen day of the autumn month at the Boshan Monastery.

The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume One.
Compiled by the Dharma-grandson from Boshan, Honghan;
and jointly collected by the Chief Seat Dharma-grandson, Hongyu.
The Discourse Record of Master [Zhaojue] Residing at Nengren Chan Monastery in Boshan, Xinzhou.
The Master had resided at Boshan for many years; although monks gathered there in great numbers, he had never yet opened the Dharma. This was because Shouchang sent him five letters.
They proceeded toward the world-transcending [state]. Thereupon, he ascended the seat and offered incense, saying: "This single portion of incense:

its branches and trunk are adorned by clouds of golden treasuries; its roots and stem are nourished by the ocean of fragrant waters. Auspicious signs are welcomed at the dragon pavilion as purple qi surges upward;
the jeweled hall is shrouded in mist as auspicious clouds spread everywhere. I burn this within the burner specifically to offer prayers for the long life and prosperity of the Emperor."
May the present Emperor’s sacred life be ten thousand years of peace.

May the Empress live as long as the heavens. May the Crown Prince enjoy a thousand autumns. May the foundation of his blessings be adorned like the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka), and may his lifespan be equal in measure to Vairocana.
Furthermore, we pray for the expansion of the patron’s auspicious celebrations, and that the ocean-like assembly be peaceful and harmonious. This single incense offering is pure and bright.

The sun and moon illuminate the vast expanse of heaven and earth; within the empty nature of awakening, there is neither Buddha nor birth. Yet, as it perfumes the myriad phenomena, there arise causes and effects.
I now offer this incense into the burner, single-mindedly extending this offering.
In the hall of Shouchang, the Abbot, the Great Monk Wuming, sat upon his seat to repay the grace of the Dharma-milk.

After the mallet was struck to signal the assembly, the Master spoke: "The Buddha does not seek the Buddha; the mind does not transmit the mind. It is like water meeting water, or gold being traded for gold.
If you understand this, it is wrapped up right before your eyes: the mountains are vast and the monkeys let out long cries. If you do not understand..."
Wrapped in the past; the forest is sparse, yet the birds are not startled. Whether they meet or part, all is wrapped before one’s eyes.
One emptily proclaims verses on formlessness; this very wrapping must also be wrapped.

Playing a stringless lute upon the water—when you brothers penetrate this point, take Mount Sumeru to be the four great oceans with white waves flooding the heavens, and take the four great oceans to be Mount Sumeru.
Mountains: red dust fills the ground. One boils the marrow of empty space, yet its flavor is ever fresh;

one picks out the lamp from the bottom of the water, yet its radiance extends throughout the great universe. Here there is no need for a sharp needle; within this, what use is a golden needle? Therefore it is said:
Following this single path, the wise know it to be remote. This ultimate pivot of the teaching is where the stone man claps his hands.
Opening the pavilions of Maitreya, one’s vows and practices unfold in successive layers; treading upon the crown of Vairocana, the radiance of his white tuft blazes forth.
Reaching this point, every step penetrates the profound mystery—what wisdom cannot know and what consciousness cannot perceive. Brothers, this is your native home.
This is the scene. If you are willing to follow the path back home, you will immediately be able to turn yourself around and return to your father. Are you willing?
"From this point on, if one does not go out, returning is attained; who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Grasping the bones of empty space, swallowing the thorny *liji* fruit, he cleaves open the realm of dust and wondrously maneuvers within the world.
Seven clouds and eight clouds; a cluster of chrysanthemums here, two clusters there. Clearly revealing the meaning of the Westward Journey—how many eyes and ears remain blind and deaf?
Brothers, investigate this thoroughly! Furthermore, there is the earthen ox bellowing at the moon and the wooden horse neighing in the wind."
I have clearly explained it to you: upon this lump of red flesh, there is a tawny-tailed tiger.
Heh! Do not mistake gold for copper.
[Ascending the hall: "This very mind is Buddha"—Master Mazu’s teeth grew hair. "Neither mind nor Buddha"—Master Mazu...
The gaze falls to the ground. It is not mind, not Buddha, and not an object. Master Wáng follows along. Bóshān does not act in this way at all:
"White duckweed and green feathers—the village elder smiles as he draws near.
Bóshān acts in this way at all: "The Emperor’s decree within the realm; the General’s command beyond the passes. Do you understand Bóshān’s intent? If you do...
If you understand the meaning of Boshan, you will understand the meaning of the Patriarchs. If you understand the meaning of the Patriarchs, you will understand the meaning of all Buddhas.
If you understand the meaning of all Buddhas, you will understand your own original nature. Brothers, do not let the months and years slip by in vain, nor waste your time in aimless wandering.
Rouse your spirit with vigor and bring this Way to clear illumination; only then will you not be obstructed by the tongues of the old monks throughout the land.
You should know that the old monks of the world all look upon people with a single pair of eyes; they all breathe from a single mouth.
Brothers, do you understand? Clouds come to the green peaks as mountains don their faces; the moon reaches the clear pool as waters paint their brows.
Ascending the hall: Tipping the pools and overturning the peaks—the entire great earth is gathered up. Stirring up dust and scattering ashes—not even a hair’s breadth is established.

When gathered up, it encompasses all in vast breadth; you must know that this is like a chick crying out in broad daylight. When not established, it is tranquil and luminous; who understands the barking of a dog in the red dust?
Whether it be a Buddha, strike him! Whether it be a Mara, strike him! Who cares whether it comes by boat or by land? Even when hungry...
One meal is enough; another meal for satiety. For now, I am glad the firewood is dry and the water is convenient. No trace where to hide the body;
with a pair of bare hands, beg but a single coin from those one meets. Where the body is hidden, there is no trace; two brows knit together.
Meeting a Buddha, one may offer three prostrations. I was at Yaoshan for over twenty years before I finally clarified this matter; these are the words of my own experience.
[Pause. Do not let outsiders hear this. Where all people hide their bodies, Bo Shan knows it all;
where Bo Shan hides his body, no one knows. Brothers, today here at this Dharma assembly, we cannot help but present ourselves face-to-face.
If you go to other places, do not mistakenly mention this when meeting people. Take care.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Winter is not yet cold; wait until after the winter solstice to see. This old fellow does not care for the snow; it is only the young child who weeps at his thin clothing.
There is only that one fellow from the eastern village, a man without a shred of refinement: with disheveled hair and a grime-stained face, bare hands and empty fists, he is not afraid of the cold."
In the heat, he does not fear the heat; in the coldest weather, he sings a song of snow. When most hungry, he acts as a rice-seller.
Without a single coin, he wishes to compete in wealth with all people under heaven; without a fraction of beauty, he wishes to vie in loveliness with all beings upon the earth.
Sometimes he rides an iron horse backward at a crossroads; sometimes he ascends Mount Sumeru against the current in the vast Western Ocean;
sometimes amidst blazing flames, he chews ice and bites snow; and sometimes within the thick dust of the mundane world.
"Plucking grass and picking out a lamp, sometimes pointing east while speaking of the west, sometimes calling south by the name of north;
taking the ditches of the Three Vehicles as one's gate and walls, and designating the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages as one’s kin.
Brothers, would such a person be fit for companionship or not? He laughed again and said, "He has already been taken in by Boshan."
Ascending the hall, Guo-hu said: "With eyes wide open and eyebrows raised, look back and forth; who is this person? Dong-shan said:
"This person is now truly me, but I am not now this person. Shi-shuang said: "He has no land;
where could one meet him? Some say: "He is without birth and death. Others say: "He has attained freedom. Or some say: [He is...]
It is said: "He does not form such an understanding. Brothers, what is this "he"? Does he face the eye, or does he not face the eye?
If he faces the eye, he becomes two things; if he does not face the eye, why do you look at him again and again?
If you can see through this directly, you will realize that he is precisely you and you are not he.
If you can realize that you are not he, you will be able to tread alone upon the Great Way, standing solitary on the peak of a lone mountain. Being correct, you do not establish the mysterious;
being partial, you do not attach to things. Then you will realize that since he has no land, where could one meet him? Since there is no land, throughout immeasurable kalpas—
If you seek the characteristic of birth, it is utterly unobtainable; if you seek the characteristic of death, it is utterly unobtainable. Then you will realize that he has neither birth nor death.
Indeed, being without birth or death, there is a thousandfold self-liberation and a hundredfold sovereignty; then you will realize that he has attained this very freedom.
When you reach such a state, the path of words is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases; then you will realize that he does not constitute a thing.
Understanding. This saying of Boshan is like waves striking a silver mountain, flowers blooming on a green peak, a stone woman raising her eyebrows, and a dark monkey chasing shadows.
"A three-year-old child with hair like snow; the fish swimming at the bottom of the ravine are never done with their busyness.
When you unfold them, they are like eyebrows—how so? "The matter that is clear is spoken with earnestness. Brothers, tell me: what is this matter of earnest speech?
"How is it? [The Master] claps his hands twice, opening wide the world of silver. "Who can distinguish its source, whether traversed or coming?
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ultimate principle does not change; the ultimate function does not preside; the ultimate Way has no form; the ultimate realization is not contrived.
If you can correspond with these four phrases, you will become a liberated monk—eyes unstained by black or yellow, feet unsoiled by mud."

Water. When the mind does not take all phenomena as its object and the tongue does not grasp the profound essence, one reaches the state where the perfect capacity universally responds and the profound realization is all-pervasive and unobstructed.
The pure substance has no dependence; the numinous clarity is beyond all relativity. Thus, the Great Master Xuansha said: "He will not stay when ensnared; he does not turn his head when called.
The ancient sages made no arrangements, and to this day there is no fixed location. Brothers, [consider this].
In the present age, practitioners of meditation do not believe that their own minds are Buddha, but seek Buddha outwardly;

they do not believe that their own minds are fully endowed with all dharmas, but seek dharmas outwardly. Since they are ignorant of their own minds, even if they engage in extensive practice, it is all merely karma of birth and death.
Furthermore, you should know that seeking the Buddha and seeking the Dharma constitutes having a point of reliance. Once there is a point of reliance, one cannot attain mastery over one's own mind.
It is like a destitute son who wanders about in hardship, sustaining himself by begging for food, yet remains oblivious to the priceless jewel within his garment;
how could such a person be considered wise? As Master Jia Shan said in verse: "Toiling to uphold the laws of birth and death, one only turns toward the Buddha..."
Seeking at the periphery, one is currently deluded regarding the correct principle; it is like extinguishing a fire to search for bubbles on the water.
There is no need to stand here long; take care. Ascending the hall on his birthday: That which was originally non-existent now exists—look with a smile at the wild flowers in the mirror.

That which was originally existent is now non-existent—stirring up the still waters before the cliff. A single sheet of white clouds spreads vast and wide; how many birds and flowers lose their tracks therein? Pressing through and shattering empty space.
The furnace and bellows smelt and refined the Buddhas and Patriarchs; they brandished the precious sword aloft.

With straw sandals, they rescued the cat and restored it its skin-sack, winning the bright moon over the Five Lakes. Therefore, the World-Honored One of Great Enlightenment abandoned the royal palace and entered the Snowy Mountains.
Beholding the morning star, he opened the Eye of the Path. During the three weeks that followed, he contemplated this matter;

thereafter, he revealed the provisional to manifest the ultimate and preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. Finally, at the very end, he held up a flower to show the assembly and said, "There is a separate transmission outside the teachings."
To examine the future, it is like a dream. Bo-shan was born among the common people; there was no royal palace to abandon.
He traveled and transformed beings in the Eastern Land; there was no Snowy Mountain to enter. The great earth is dark; there is no bright star to behold.
Slaves and masters cannot be distinguished; there is no eye of the Way to open. Thus, though noble and base differ, fundamentally their heads and brains are alike. From—
In youth, one is pitiable; before the age of twenty, one establishes a household and prospers in one's career. After twenty, one squanders family wealth.
Before thirty, one goes north to Uttarakuru to master the tridents and armor of the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan).
After thirty, one goes south to Jambudvīpa to shatter the spears and banners of the Five Ranks (Wuwe). Before forty, if you wish to go, I have my hook.

I hook you. But Boshan does not hook you. No matter how many thousands or tens of thousands of miles away you may be, once you are past forty, if you wish to dwell [in the Way], I have a gong to strike you;
yet Boshan does not strike you. Even if you are inside the eye of a tiny gnat, it is the same.
Today marks my fortieth year. The hook and the mallet have both been set aside; Bo Shan is not here.
Bo Shan possesses a plot of ancient ground that has existed for over a thousand years, ever since it was first established by National Teacher Shao of Tiantai.
The Chan master Yunfeng has succeeded his predecessors for over several decades, and today he preaches the Dharma here.
Is this something that originally existed and is now absent? Do not speak of dreams before these people. Or is it something that originally did not exist and is now present?
"One must not speak of dreams in the presence of others. When you have thoroughly seen through the dream-state, how is it?
"One must not speak of dreams in the presence of others. Why is this? Within this, one cannot find birth or non-birth; one cannot find cessation or non-cessation;
one cannot find existence or non-existence; one cannot find being or non-being. Furthermore, by what means could there be a lifespan?"
Furthermore, taking the bodies of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings as their life-span, they cannot be increased or diminished by the holy or the mundane;
taking past kalpas and future kalpas as their life-span, the sun and moon cannot displace them; taking Mount Sumeru and the Saṃkhya Ocean as their life-span.
It cannot be damaged by dryness or moisture; it takes as its life-span the entirety of empty space and the pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm. Heaven and earth cannot conceal it.
And yet, although this is so, for what reason today do you call it forty years? After a long silence, he said: "Before the Phoenix-Resting Cliff, the clouds and mist roll away;
beneath Mount Bowing-Ox, its fame is passed down through antiquity and today."
Ascending the hall on New Year’s Eve: "Brothers, the months and years have come to an end; the ten-day period has concluded.
Regarding this great matter beneath the patched robe—do you understand it yet? If one speaks of practicing Zen, one must establish a true mind;

then the beginning and the end will be upright, and there will be no inversion in between. Furthermore, one must recognize the root of the illness before success can be achieved. There are many varieties of this Zen."
Illness must be understood. If you do not recognize the root of the illness, even if you are diligent, it will all be the work of Māra.
What constitutes the root of the illness? Listen as I, Boshan, shall explain it from the beginning, so that you may avoid wounding yourself or committing a blunder.
First, do not calculate time or count days. Second, do not bathe by striking ice. Third, do not huddle around a fire.
1. Do not play with fire. 2. Fourth, do not steal light from within the darkness. 3. Fifth, do not keep your eyes open while dreaming.
4. Sixth, do not touch trees or obstruct the flow. 5. Seventh, do not steer against the wind. 6. Eighth, do not mistake the short for the long.
7. Ninth, do not expose your bones to the wind. 8. Tenth, do not strike a stake and shake the oars. 9. Eleventh...
One must not ascend higher step by step. Twelfth, one must not let go from the void.
If you do not fall into these twelve kinds of illnesses, you can become a pure and white monk; you can take soil and turn it into gold, and call an ox a horse.
Even the Elder Śākyamuni could do nothing against you, let alone anyone else. Nevertheless, even so, there is more.

One Matter. [The Master] asked the assembly: "Suppose you resolve your mind on the first day of the first month; look, as you pass the time until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how will you settle the account?
After a long silence, he said: "Discussions of the profound and explanations of the wondrous are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
"That fellow walks along feeling the wall.
Entering the hall, he said: Master Shenzang said, "Knowing while being without knowing; it is not that there is no knowing, but rather speaking of 'no knowing'.
Master Liangsui said, "The place where Liangsui knows, you all do not know; the place where you all know, Liangsui knows it all."
Chan Master Heze said, "The single word 'knowing' is the gateway to all wonders. Chan Master Gaofeng said, "The single word 'knowing' is the gateway to all calamities.
These great elders each possessed a single eye, striking from the side and lifting up from the flank.
Today, Boshan will not begrudge his lips and teeth as he provides a commentary from beginning to end; it is simply to inform you all that there is knowing without knowing.
Their mental capacities are similar; it is not that he lacks knowledge. Yet, when it is said that "ignorance burns the eyebrows," one must save what remains.
That which Liangshui knows, others do not know—this is much like "suppressing the noble to make them base.
That which all of you know, Liangshui knows entirely; such a "knowledgeable old man" should not be encountered. The single word "knowing" is the gateway to all wonders. [He] takes the hand...
"Dragging one in. This single word "knowing" is the gateway to all calamities. At the head of the feet and at the bottom of the feet, even the word "knowing" is not evil.
Brothers, when Boshan provides such an interpretation, do you understand Boshan’s meaning? Although it is thus, Boshan certainly does not speak in this way:
"To know through non-knowing is called 'knowing by knowing'; to know as knowing is non-knowing."
"I do not know. Brothers, is there anyone who does not make their livelihood based on 'knowing,' yet is instead someone who transcends the crowd and stands out?
You should know that the sound of a water-lute and the resonance of pines can transmit the heart of an infant; the red-tailed golden-scaled fish does not fall into the hands of the fisherman.
Tell me, is this the same as the ancients, or is it different? He spoke again: "East, west, south, and north."
108,000 [people were present].

On the eighth day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall. The *vinaya-dhara* struck the mallet and said: "In this Dharma assembly of dragons and elephants, you should contemplate the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
The Master said: "How does one contemplate the primary truth? To look upon it is to go blind; to smell it is to split one's brain. He raised his staff.
Walking, the traces of movement vanish; a stirring thought is neither born nor extinguished. Eye and form, ear and sound—the mind forgets, and the path of thought is cut off.
The sages and worthies of past and present share the same road yet take different tracks.

Zhongfeng’s lute beneath the water, Mazu’s moon in the heavens, Touzi’s oil in his hand, and Zhaozhou’s cypress before the courtyard—Bo Shan has nothing to show, yet it leaks forth upon the plum branches. It is spat out.
Emerald green mingles with contained fragrance; in the intense cold, it defies frost and snow. Its pure scent fills the ten directions;
to touch it is to have one's whole body drenched in blood. I clap my hands and weep for the blue heavens; Old Fubei’s tongue is tied.

Brothers, at that time on the eighth day of the twelfth month, Śākyamuni Buddha shattered the void into seven pieces and eight fragments. Throughout the entire world, not a single person could understand it.
"Using the Jewel Monastery as a cloud," he said, "if it were not for Old Woman Lingxing, how could she have untied the heart-knot?
At the request of Layman Xu Weiming, he ascended the hall and said: "The Great Way has no boundaries; how could the numinous clarity wait to be sought?
From the beginning it has always been thus—how could there be distance or intimacy? With ash on the head and dirt on the face, when has it ever been covered over? [With] sharp teeth..."
Fierce teeth. Ultimately, the sound accords with the echo. This is why Ruiyan would constantly call out "The Host" upon the rock, and then respond himself, saying, "Stay alert!
Do not let others deceive you on some future day. Ruiyan was much like one who invites a thief to plunder his house;
yet, even so, the bystander is the one who looks ugly. Today, Boshan cannot help but set the whole tray out for you—upside down.
"The granary is emptied and the storehouse is overturned; let me explain this to the great assembly. He then pointed with his finger and said: "Outside the gate are tens of thousands of white clouds;
by the hedge are two or three branches of red apricot."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In delusion, there is awakening; in awakening, there is delusion. From the beginning, delusion and awakening have been like delusion;
today, awakening and delusion are not awakening. Having severed both ends of delusion and awakening, what more need be said of sages and ordinary people?
Raise your eyebrows! Cherish the pupils in your eyes. Unravel the seam of your robe! Reveal your iron-and-stone heart and liver. The lantern and the pillar..."
Interconnected. The Buddha Hall shares its three gates with the eaves-beams. A ball of mud formed by bare hands; an iron steamed bun forged in a red furnace.
Let it be tossed east and west as one pleases; in the end, it buries its light and shrouds its brilliance.

Even if a wild fox spirit were to shed its shell within the crags, turning after turning without error, it would only bring laughter to the Red-Bearded Old Barbarian. If you wish to know the water buffalo, look for it at the foot of the mountain.
Entering the womb—this is entirely and perfectly so. It must be the Great Being of Mount Huai. O brothers, the Great Being of Mount Huai has acted as an ox;
the horns on the head of Bo Shan have long since grown. Is there anyone yet who can bear witness? After a long silence, he said:
"Even if the Great Being Bodhidharma were to come, I would let him pass with one stroke."
Ascending the hall on New Year’s Day: The spring breeze has just stirred and the spring flowers bloom; The spring rain urges them on and the spring waters flow.
Only the stone at the summit of Tongxuan Peak Remains as before, covered with white lichen and green moss.
"Great assembly, what is the Buddha-dharma of the new year? He spoke again: "The birds beneath the eastern and western groves Add to their melodious songs."
Ascending the hall upon the conclusion of the retreat: Who says that after the retreat is closed, it must be reopened?
Even established rules are all not [ultimately] so. Into the void he hurls Yunmen’s firewood; snow-waves and silver flowers bloom across the earth.
Having found an old, worn wooden ladle, the hawk flies off to Silla. Since you have no mind, I too shall rest; future descendants will laugh at the wine shop.
The long-term practitioner Xiangyan, who once struck a bamboo until it made a sound that deafened both his ears, now reflects back upon the old Lingyun of yore:
"Upon seeing a single peach blossom, my eyes were blinded. Who is deluded and who is awakened?
When the spring breeze touches the coral tree—Who is awakened and who is deluded? All is complete within one's own original nature; mind is neither mind nor non-mind.
"Things are not things. [The Master] wrote several characters in the air and shouted, "Hmph! "Venerable brothers, why did he write several characters in the air and shout 'Hmph'?
He then joined his palms and said, "I do not dare slight you; you shall all become Buddhas."
On the day of the birthday celebration, [the Master] ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time are born together with Boshan;

beneath the shadowless tree, the sun and moon hang suspended. The twelve classes of living beings share the same longevity as Boshan; upon the sproutless branch, the seasons of spring and autumn are discerned.
The world is a dry city, a mirage; the Buddha’s birth is a dream, a phantom, a bubble, or a flower. In a dry city or a mirage, the world is such that every form and color is empty. A dream..."
Like illusions, bubbles, and flowers, the minds of both sages and ordinary people are profoundly still; every form is empty, and the face one was born with stands out clearly.

With mind after mind in profound stillness, it pervades the breast of every patch-robed monk. When asked how many springs and autumns have passed, he simply says, "The flowers fall and the flowers bloom.
When further inquired about the brevity or length of kalpas, who would say that emptiness is formed or emptiness is destroyed? If you can grasp this at such a moment, then you are an ancient.
Now, it is not a matter of successive generations, yet extension and brevity occur simultaneously; a single thought-moment is ten thousand years, and ten thousand years are a single thought-moment.

How could this be discussed in terms of calculation, numbers, years, months, days, or hours? Even if one were able to observe the waters of the vast ocean, how many times have they become shallow and clear?
He is still but a hired laborer. Even if Baozhang were to remain in this world for one thousand seventy-two years, how could that be anything more than fleeting?
Brothers, tell me: how many autumns and springs has Boshan lived until now?
If you understand, speak from this very point. If not, you must count backward forty years; at that time, Boshan and...
The Great Assembly. Meeting at Biepeak.

Ascending the Hall, he said: "Brothers, whenever the ordinary mind enters into awakening, you must skillfully apply your mind. If you do not skillfully apply your mind, demons will find their opportunity.
Thus, a single word of 'calculation' gives rise to the ninety-six kinds of external paths; a single word of 'attachment' gives rise to the five [hindrances]."
The ten aggregates as Māras, as well as the Māra-kings and their retinues, are fully detailed in the scriptural vehicles and must not remain unknown. As the Sūtra says:
"For example, wherever there are openings and crevices, wind can enter, causing objects to shake and making them unstable. It is the same for the Bodhisattva:
if the mind has intervals or gaps, the mind will then be shaken and lack mastery. This continues until the point where all such states are considered Māras.
It is merely karma. What is meant by "Māra"? Delight is Māra; affliction is Māra; torpor is Māra;
restlessness is Māra; fear and agitation are Māra; aversion to stillness is Māra; delighting in talk is Māra;
loving to wander about is Māra; even down to disparaging images, destroying sutras, breaking the Vinaya, violating the precepts, and engaging in [frivolous] verses and gāthās.
To take advantage of karmic conditions to propound heterodox interpretations; to pursue poetry, prose, literary composition, and miscellaneous arts;

and to greedily seek out discourses on the Dharma—all such things are demonic. Therefore, Boshan instructed his fellow practitioners to hold a single "meaningless" koan within the field of the eighth consciousness, so that they might immediately lose all awareness of their physical body and mind, and no longer perceive mountains as external objects before them.
The great earth and the rivers are neither internal nor external; they roll together into a single mass of doubt. Walking, one does not know that one walks; sitting, one does not know that one sits.
It is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies, or like a mind constantly feeling as if crossing a bridge.
You must illuminate this matter until, by encountering it head-on and striking against it, you shatter the mass of doubt. Then your entire being will be eyes, even if you encounter Śākyamuni himself.
"Great Master, having received the prediction upon the crowning of my head, even a Buddha could not act against me; how much less could an army of Māras enter?
O brothers, if you understand it in this way, who among you would not be a true man? Nevertheless, though it be so, one must fear those with a calculating mind.
You must directly, in a single thought-moment, realize non-arising and transcend the provisional views of the three vehicles. If you attempt to use the mind to make the mind mindless,"
Yet it becomes existent. You must directly seek the mind; when it cannot be found, you will realize the Dharma-gate that transcends magic.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Water wets by its nature; fire dries through its conditions. Where there is water, there are fish; where there is a forest, there are birds.
When eating rice, one bites one's own tongue, yet can say: 'The blue sky requires no sweeping. Brothers, you must settle this for yourselves. Under the same night..."
A single awakening. Try taking this saying and broadcasting it throughout all quarters. Do not say that a wasteland does not discriminate between weeds;
look further at Yunmen’s staff, which has transformed into a dragon and swallowed up the mountains, rivers, and the great earth. Brothers, tell me: where is Boshan right now?
After a long silence, he said: "Profound, firm, secluded, and remote; no one can reach it. He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall for the ceremony of opening the light and concluding the retreat: The ninety-day period is now concluded; who among the hundreds of thousands can know the samādhis?
A painted dragon may not necessarily ride upon the clouds; alas, for the twelve hours of the human world! The twelve hours pass with a mere snap of the fingers;
even to raise one’s eyebrows is already a mistake. Tossing aside the patched robe, one sleeps with the clouds; upon the flat rock, the pine...

The flower falls; hearing and seeing are pure, yet purity itself is not real. The Dharma-body is without illness, so there is no need to seek a physician. From the crown of the head, the eye of Maheśvara protrudes;
at midnight, the black hen flies with snow. "Flying with snow" is precious for its mutual interplay; the golden phoenix does not perch upon the shadowless tree.
When the cross-pattern of the ten directions is reckoned, one cannot remain within the rank of Buddhas and Patriarchs. One cannot remain.
Abiding, it strikes one across the face. Rabbit horns and tortoise hair are planted within the eyes. Today, I carry this staff out across my shoulder;
what man would consent to be buried alive? Brothers, today is the day of releasing the retreat.
We encounter Amitābha Tathāgata, who performs universal Buddha-work for all of you, emitting great radiance that illuminates the lands of the ten directions without limit.
Obstruction! Furthermore, by means of unimpeded spiritual power, he merges the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the Sahā world into a single realm.
If one says it is the Pure Land, it is yet the Sahā world; if one says it is the Sahā world, it is precisely the Pure Land.
Now tell me: in which land does the Tathāgata Amitāyus ultimately reside? Today, Boshan personally points it out: clearly, it is this very seat.
The Central Circle.
Ascending the hall: "All you practitioners of Zen, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are themselves the Buddha-dharma; the Buddha-dharma is itself seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Fundamental ignorance is itself the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas; the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas is itself the sense-faculties."
Fundamentally, ignorance is itself lust, anger, and delusion; precept, concentration, and wisdom are themselves lust, anger, and delusion.

If one perceives this clearly within, one will finally know that when the Great Master Bodhidharma came across the sea, he was merely pointing out the principle of what is already manifest and complete.
Furthermore, what is this principle of what is already manifest and complete? A wooden man.
To dance upon rising is not extraordinary; a barren woman combing her hair is exceptionally new.
At the summit of the peak, having finished citing the Ten Wholesome Paths, he further cited Master Jiantong Ji.

Having lived in the mountains for twenty years, he attained sudden and great enlightenment upon seeing a felled tree fall. Later, the Governor of Jiujiang invited him to preside over the seat at Yuantong. Thereupon...
Carrying his staff and wearing straw sandals, he ascended the platform and spoke a verse: "The Perfect Penetration opens no pharmacy for the living; It sells nothing but the head of a dead cat.
I know not which one among those lacking discernment Will eat it and have cold sweat pour down their entire body. The Master said: "How shameful!
This ancient man lived in the mountains for twenty years and realized nothing more than the head of a dead cat. If it were Boshan, however—"
Not so. Boshan wishes to open a pharmacy for the living; he sells, according to conditions, a "living cat's head.
Who knows which one will have the wit to realize that upon consuming it, their entire body will flow with fresh blood? Brothers, tell me: is this the same as the ancients, or is it different?
After a long silence, he said: "If you attempt to understand through conceptual consciousness, you bury the mind of the Patriarch."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Śākyamuni Tathāgata was born in the Western Regions; he opened his stage for forty-nine years and delivered over three hundred assemblies of sutras.
At the very end, he held up a flower to show the assembly and further declared that there was a 'separate transmission outside the teachings.

This has brought trouble upon all the sages of antiquity and today, who have done nothing but explain worldly dharmas to the people. What are called worldly dharmas? Clarifying the mind and seeing one's nature—this is a worldly dharma."
The categories of precepts, concentration, and wisdom are worldly dharmas. The three bodies and four wisdoms are worldly dharmas. The five eyes and six supernormal powers are worldly dharmas.
The three vehicles and ten stages are worldly dharmas. The eighteen unique qualities are worldly dharmas. The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are worldly dharmas.
The six perfections and myriad practices are worldly dharmas. Even the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood is a worldly dharma. —Bo Shan.
It is not so. Now, I shall speak briefly of the Buddha-dharma for this great assembly. What is called the Buddha-dharma? The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the Buddha-dharma.
The sun, moon, and the constellations are the Buddha-dharma. The chirping of magpies and the cawing of crows are the Buddha-dharma.
Even when you, my brothers, laugh and sing together, that is the Buddha-dharma. Does the assembly understand? If you can understand, this is the Dharma abiding in the Dharma.
The position is that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. Should this not yet be so, you may enjoy the beautiful scenery of the conjured city as you wish;
yet it is a pity that you wear the jewel within your robe while chasing after the moon. Descend from the seat.

The Ancestor-Seal Master ascended the hall for the formal address: "It is easy for humans and devas to assemble, yet a Pure Land is rarely encountered. Today, as we welcome [the assembly], it is just like a Buddha-land.
Great assembly, the Buddha-land has already arrived; do you hear Amitābha preaching the Dharma? After a long silence, he said:
"One must know that the Buddha pervades the three thousandfold world-system, and the Pure Land is entirely spread within eight characters."

Village relatives have arrived for the ascent to the hall. The wise moon in the jade sky illuminates both antiquity and the present; the awakening flowers of the Buddha-nature perfume the fields and the inner chambers.
You all have long been away from your hometowns, wandering in solitude; today, sitting together at this banquet, you are fortunate to meet these old acquaintances.
Brothers, let us set aside for a moment the meeting of kinsmen and old friends; I dare ask: have you received any news from home?
There is none. If there were anything to present, Boshan would have personally opened and examined it with you.
If this is not yet so, I entrust Baiyun to constantly guard the door, listening by its side for the wild geese to bring news of a messenger.
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth Festival: The season meets the midsummer heat, and the holiday arrives at the Dragon Boat. In the city wards, men sip the potent yellow wine;

in the river villages, one hears the sound of the "kuan-nai" chant. While people say that the mundane world is a realm of chaotic confusion, Bo Shan declares that the Wheel of Dharma is turning in great force.
Mugwort leaves serve as a standard to sweep away the ninety-six kinds of external paths; sweet flag serves as a sharp sword to shatter the fifty-fold army of the *skandha*-demons.
Yet when the ancients spoke of "awakening to the Way upon hearing sound" and "clarifying the mind upon seeing form," Bozan observes with cold eyes that this still amounts to a dull impediment.

Birth is this Way. Behold now the crimson pomegranates and the green willows; these are form (*rūpa*). What do you call "mind" (*citta*)?

If you can understand it clearly within this, you are just right to buy straw sandals and travel as a pilgrim. If you have not yet understood it within this, you must feel dread. Look at the midst of these playful sensory realms:
a boat drifting on green water, brocade surpassing the pavilions by the fishing weir—like a shuttle threading through jade-patterned silk. It is like...

"It is only when it reaches the hand that it is truly obtained. At this very moment, is there anyone who can cast aside the boat and lay down the oar to play together with Boshan?

Having finished offering incense to pray for the longevity of the Emperor on the New Year’s Day, he then held up the incense and said:

"This single portion of incense cannot be contained by empty space, nor can it be supported by the great earth. I burn it before you all, yet you do not recognize it. [The Master] descended from the seat.
When Mahākāśyapa attained it, he said: "All sentient beings universally possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata;
it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they are unable to realize it. Upon attaining it, Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
He then said: "That which seeks me is my self; Ānanda has attained it. He transmitted it to the compilers who heard and upheld it, and to his successor to propagate the teaching.

Śāṇakavāsin attained it and said: "The body is seventeen, but its nature is not seventeen," and so on, until Dharmatrāta attained it and spoke to the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, saying: "This is a worldly treasure, yet it is not sufficient to be supreme among all treasures."
Among these, the Dharma Jewel is supreme; yet this is but the light of the world and is not yet the ultimate. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme;

Perfectly clear and aware, it does not depend on mental activity. Take care!"
Ascending the Dharma Hall on New Year’s Day: What omen precedes this auspicious beginning of the year? The long days and clear skies shine with brilliant light.
Awakening and delusion, heterodoxy and orthodoxy—let us discuss them in vain. Who can clearly distinguish the sage from the ordinary? The realm manifest before us is not distant at all;

Yet if one speaks of it as being in the West, the path is obscure. Within a single mote of dust, the total function is revealed: The mountains, rivers, and great earth are but a single blade of grass.
Look with fixed eyes into the field of illusory transformations; among the myriad dharmas, there is no fault—simply accord with conditions as they arise.
Even so, may you receive blessings in accordance with the times. But how about this? [He plants his staff. Do not say that the *kāṣāya* was originally old;
the spring breeze arrives first at the tip of the staff.
Gu Yu of Changqing Temple on Fodian Mountain in Duchang, having prepared a vegetarian feast to offer merit for his deceased father, requested the Master to ascend the hall. The Master said:
"For over twenty years, Boshan has preached the Dharma; why is it that he now refuses to ascend the hall?

It is because the Dharma-gate has become muddled and corrupted, with many who are reckless and incompetent treating the ascent of the hall as a mere game. Therefore, Boshan limps along and drags himself about, simply passing the time in this manner."
At that time, the Elder Yuguo, out of filial devotion for his deceased father, repeatedly and earnestly entreated [Bo Shan] without ceasing. Yet once again, he could not avoid it.
Brothers, within the three realms of saṃsāra, one cannot abandon the bonds of affection; to cast aside such affection and enter the state of non-action is truly to repay one's debt of gratitude.
Master Śākyamuni should not have taught people to ruin their families. Today, Bo Shan follows this path.

Seeing this injustice, I could not help but draw my sword to assist him. Wandering through the three realms of saṃsāra, following the crowd and joining the ranks, one remains no different from others.

Unable to cast off the bonds of affection, one seeks instead to laugh and sing praises to proclaim Prajñāpāramitā. Abandoning such attachments to enter the state of non-action—amidst the simple offering of beans and water to bring joy to one’s parents—who am I?

Truly, I am one who repays their kindness. Even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the seven obstructions may be known as those worthy of ritual courtesy. This is not the way of Boshan.
This indeed contradicts worldly conventions and even brings reproach upon the Sangha; yet, though their transgressions may fill the heavens, their gratitude must still have its rightful place.

Long ago, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, five hundred bhikṣus had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernatural powers, yet they had not yet realized the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).

By means of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna), each of them individually beheld their own past deeds: having murdered their fathers and harmed their mothers, as well as other grave offenses.
Within their own minds, each harbored doubts and was unable to penetrate the profound Dharma.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, took up a sharp sword in his hand and pressed it against the Tathāgata. The World-Honored One then said to Mañjuśrī:
"Stop, stop! You must not commit an act of parricide; do not seek to harm me. It is I who will surely harm him.
To be harmed for the sake of doing good—Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning you have had no self or person; it is only because of your inner mind that you perceive a self or person.
When the inner mind arises, I am inevitably harmed, and this is precisely what is called 'harming. At these words, all five hundred bhikṣus attained awakening."
The Way. Brothers, if you can understand it at the point where Mañjuśrī brandishes his sword, the debt of the Buddha’s grace and your parents’ kindness will be repaid all at once.
If you do not understand it here, then even if you were to grind your bones to powder, the profound kindness of your parents could never be fully requited.
Even had Maudgalyāyana possessed the power of spiritual penetrations to save his kin from within hell, it would have been too late. When Xuansha [pointed] toward the jeweled stupa—

To recognize one's father as a mere relative—how could this be consistent with the rites of gods and men? To have Xinghua command others to assist in mourning—this is contrary to the reputation of filial piety.
Muzhou’s making straw sandals for his mother—his reward for the field of merit was largely stingy.

Although these venerable masters were said to be supremely filial, they still belonged to the realm of conditioned arising; when examined by both monastics and laypeople, they are not without flaws. How can they compare to the Ancient Fool (Gu Yu)?
The Master sat and converted both his father and younger brother, causing them to leave the household life together and become monks. He guided them with pure karma.

His father composed songs of self-reproach and self-reflection, as well as verses on the non-substantiality of the stupa and the non-true nature of reality. At the time of his death, he knew in advance that the end had come; his right mindfulness was clear and distinct.
It can be known that his father attained great peace and happiness. That the ancient master Guyu repaid his debt of gratitude and requited his virtue can likewise be known. O brothers, each of you...
Each possesses their own biological parents. As for what it is like within the realm of the person themselves—how so? [He] strikes the meditation staff and says:
"To grind one's bones and crush one's body would not suffice as recompense; a single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds. Adieu.
The newly constructed Dharma Hall was inaugurated at the request of the Honorable Governor Xiao. Ascending the seat, he said: Beside the Dragon-Bathing Pond, auspicious clouds part;
In this chamber of ten feet, he knew the noble guest was coming. Suddenly realizing the affairs of the Patriarch’s gate, His tongue within his mouth is as slippery as moss.
Master Yunmen said: "With a single glance, high and low, the ten thousand phenomena are simultaneously revealed. In the mere interval of deliberation, one lies dead ten thousand *li* away.
Boshan, however, is not like this. With a single glance at high and low, he sees his own nose; it fills the void. From within this, breathe forth!
Brothers, if you can bring this to a conclusion through discussion, the Great Layman Commissioner Xiao will act as your advocate.
Proof. If this were not so, I would have the staff break it open for the sake of the assembly. (He strikes the staff once.
The Head Seat asks, "Just now we heard the Master take a single glance at all things high and low;
with eyes seeing the bridge of the nose, how can one turn the body and breathe freely when completely filling empty space? The Master strikes the staff and says, "No trace, no effort."
"A thousand mountains add their verdant hues. The student said, "If that is so, then the void is shattered and one's entire being is possessed of living eyes.
The Master said, "Before the gate, one stream gathers three; behind the house, a thousand pines cover ten thousand.

The student said, "As for what Commissioner Xiao said—that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all entirely a dream—tell me, is this a true dream or a floating dream? The Master said, "Directly..."
"Look down. The student said, "In that case, the spring wind stirs the whisk made of tortoise hair; the staff moves freely, gathering all within the Dharma-realm.
The Master said, "For now, let this point pass. The assembly leader led the multitude in prostration.
At the request of the Venerable Dharma Master, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "Brothers, the ancients said, 'This matter does not accord with the scriptural teachings.

This, too, is but a provisional expression. Furthermore, how could one know that throughout the entire Tripitaka, there is not a single word or character that does not trigger the awakening to this very matter?
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: 'The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; having no gate is the dharma-gate. Since it says this..."

Taking the mind as the fundamental principle, the three vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all merely extensions of the mind. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "How marvelous, how marvelous!
All sentient beings are fully endowed with the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata. This may be called the opening up of the source of one's nature. It further says:
"If there are those who see that the essence-nature of the Tathāgata is non-existent, they shall attain clear realization through cultivation. This...
A person immediately becomes a Buddha. If one knows that the essential nature is non-existent, even the single word "Buddha" is a superfluous expression.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "The Great Luminous Treasury of the Tathāgata is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings;

the ground of pure awakening for sentient beings is precisely the Great Luminous Treasury of the Tathāgata. This may be called the common source of ordinary beings and sages; there is no need for further pointing or directing.
It is further said: "When a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Enlightenment on the causal ground, he knows it to be like a flower in the sky;

thus there is no cyclic existence, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death. This is because, within the stage of cultivation, one realizes that the deluded body and deluded mind are like the appearance of flowers in the sky."
This is truly effortless. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions completely vanishes.
If one truly knows that empty space can vanish, then the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang Shijie*) will be so densely packed that not even a hair’s breadth of leakage remains.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "These dharmas abide in their dharma-positions; the characteristics of the world are eternally present. If one truly knows this...
The Dharma abides in its place and the Dharma remains in its station; one may call this an immeasurable treasury of jewels whose source can be known in an instant.
Brothers, this is the ultimate standard of the Teaching. To attempt to fathom it with a conceptualizing mind is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow—it will never succeed.
Nevertheless, you must further understand that there is a superior dimension within the Gate of the Patriarchs before you can truly attain it. (He strikes the meditation staff.)
It is said: This staff—within the domain of Mazu, it walks like an ox and strides like a tiger; grass bows and wind blows before it;

Within the domain of Shitou, it is called "the mind of the Great Immortal of Zhutu," transmitted secretly from east to west. Within the domain of Pang Jushi, it is the bamboo pole and wooden staff carried along with one, encountered wherever one goes.
On the stage of performance: in the lineage of Linji, he drives the plowman’s ox and snatches the hungry man’s food;

In the lineage of Yunmen, the seal covers heaven and earth, following the waves and drifting with the current; a single glance doubles the phrase, and a raised brow drops two or three.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The Buddha-dharma is neither dharma nor non-dharma; even 'neither' and 'not-neither' are negated. When both 'neither' and 'not-neither' have left no trace, only then can one speak of the subtle and the profound.
Brothers, if you wish to resolve the matter of right and wrong, you must first distinguish between the clear and the turbid within the scriptural teachings;

Delusion and craving, the afflictions and ignorance—these are the dharmas that obstruct the Path; this is the teaching of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, spoken from the perspective of the turbid current.
There is no Buddha to be realized, and no birth to be delivered from; the nature and characteristics of the sentient and the insentient are equal;

this is the teaching of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, spoken from the perspective of the pure current. Reaching the essence where there is no name, the holy function shines alone; this is the "Medicinal Word."
One must not speak of medicine before one who is not ill. To speak of cultivation and realization, and to establish cause and effect—this is the teaching of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;

it is the discourse of those on the margins of the turbid stream. To speak of neither cultivation nor realization, yet not being oblivious to cause and effect—this is the teaching of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;

it is the discourse of those on the margins of the clear stream. Both "cultivation" and "non-cultivation" are superfluous words; these are the words of medicine for one who is ill. For one who is not ill, they are unnecessary.
One must not speak of medicine in the presence of others. To speak of the "position of existence" or the "position of non-existence" is the teaching of the heterodox;

to speak of the "position of both existence and non-existence" or the "position of neither existence nor non-existence" is likewise the teaching of the heterodox. To transcend the four positions and sever the hundred negations—this is the discourse on medicine.

One must not speak of medicine in the presence of those who are not ill. If one is greedily attached to worldly toil and thereby violates and damages the True Dharma, [one is not fit for this medicine].
"This is the speech of Pāpīyas; it is one who has lost right concentration and delights in attachment to various sensations—this too is the speech of Pāpīyas.
"The mountains crumble and the oceans dry up, yet his mind remains unmoved"—this is the word of the Medicine King. One must not speak of medicine before those who are not ill.
O brothers, when all that is wrong is cast aside, the heart of an infant is restored in its entirety. When the single Way is level and even, one suddenly emerges as Maheśvara.
The Eye. Take heed. Entering the hall, the late Master Shouchang said: "Treading upon the first peak of the clouds, the eye perceives a vast and small void.

The fundamental tenets of the Caodong school are clearly set forth for you all; there is not the slightest bit of concealment.

A single peak: the ravines and precipices must be scrutinized with care. Within the eye is the vast, subtle void; the eye is within the void, and the void is within the eye.
Try to settle this and observe it. At first, when you wished to see, there was no way to see; facing one another, you did not recognize each other.
A thousand miles apart, yet the wind is the same. Today we meet, everywhere the same—what kind of face is this? Point!

To take east as west, or to call south north—would that be possible? If you understand this through the lens of Boshan’s commentary, then the late Master Shouchang is emitting light and shaking the earth beneath the very feet of all of you, having entered the *Ratnādarśa-samādhi*.
Nevertheless, although it is so, it is not fitting for Boshan to scatter the private property enjoyed by the Elder Shouchang before you all.
"Under the heels of people—do you not see that 'the father conceals for the son, and the son conceals for the father; uprightness lies therein'? Adieu.

Xie bowed and offered a response. The Master said, "Tell me then: what was the scene before the clouds of kalpas? Xie replied, "There is no need for further pursuit today;

Through the conditions of non-birth, there is birth; through the conditions of birth, there is non-birth. One who realizes this..."
This principle of arising does not obstruct further arising; therefore it is said: "Arising within arising is called the Way. For ten thousand ages the emerald pool’s light is bright and clear;
in all four directions and eight points there is no obstruction. Whether called 'sage' or 'ordinary,' none can comprehend it.
Master Ciming said: "With my hands I melt the Yellow River until it dries up; with my feet I tread upon Mount Sumeru until it collapses. Both heaven and hell are produced solely by the mind."
He struck the meditation platform with his staff and said: "If one is a true lion cub, one does not seek it elsewhere.

Take heed, brothers. If you wish to realize the truth beneath your own heels, you must first see through both the primary and secondary retributions, as well as the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence—all of which arise from causes and conditions and likewise perish due to causes and conditions.

For forty-nine years, the Elder Śākyamuni spoke horizontally and vertically; all were but the Dharma of dependent origination. Have you not seen that the retribution-body and transformation-bodies are not...?
