Jian said, "In the future, you shall realize this for yourself. Xiu said, "I am only like this; what about you, Reverend? Jian said, [and remained silent].
"This is the Director’s quarters; that is the Head Cook’s quarters. Regarding the phrase "Practicing prostrations," [Zhaozhou] remarked:
"Turn the tip of the nose around; flip open the lips and teeth. To trim the long and patch the short, there is naturally a specific occasion.
These words were intended not only to cut off Master Xiu’s tongue, but also to open the eyes of future generations. It can truly be said that they sever the entanglements.
Wandering along the elephant path, one clears away the thorns and brambles to reveal the jade branches.
Such is the "live word. It is said that Cuiyan addressed the assembly, saying: "Throughout this summer retreat, I have been speaking for you, my brothers.
Look—do Cuiyan’s eyebrows still remain? Baofu said: "The heart of a thief is always apprehensive. Changqing said: "They grow! Yunmen said: "The barrier."
The Master holds up his whisk and says: "Spinning fine silk from a spring silkworm; growing thick fur from a winter marten.
Each of the great masters has extended their single hand. But tell me, what matter does this pertain to? Take care of your eyebrows!"
Case: Yangshan asked Zhongyi, "What is the meaning of Buddha-nature? Zhongyi said, "I will give you a parable.
Suppose there is a room with six windows and a monkey is placed inside. Outside, a monkey calls out from the east, 'O gibbon!'"
The monkey immediately responded. When he called out to all six windows in this manner, they all responded simultaneously.
Yangshan said, "Suppose the monkey inside has fallen asleep while the monkey outside wishes to meet him; how would you deal with that?
Daoyi took Yangshan’s hand and danced on the meditation seat, saying, "The langur has already met you."
The Master holds up the verse and says: Zhongyi laid out the text and expounded its meaning with such refined metaphors that even the venerable Yangshan had to concede his respect;
how could he have let him slip? But tell me, does this man possess the Buddha-nature or not? With hair white as frost, he dwells in mountain valleys;
at midnight, he puts on his boots and enters the marketplace.
Case: A monk asked Caoshan, "What is it like when the spirit-clothes are not yet hung? Caoshan said, "Today is the completion of the mourning period for Caoshan.
The monk asked, "After the mourning period is over, what then? Caoshan said, "Caoshan loves to get drunk on wine."

The Master holds up the whisk and says: "The pines return the wind of a thousand ages; the numinous robe sheds its physical form. The dew wets the moon of the midnight hour; one strolls and sings wildly.
It requires such a drunken madman as this to act thus. As for the primordial chaos of heaven and earth, he does not recognize anyone he encounters."
Caoshan’s heels are still stained with mud and water.
[Case] A monk asked Fayan: "The teachings state that 'from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. What is this root of non-abiding?
Fayan said: "The form has not yet arisen; the substance is not yet there. The name has not yet emerged; the name is not yet there."
The Master picks up the case and says: "Before forms arose and names were established, tell me: from where did the myriad phenomena of the universe come?
To let this matter pass here would not do."
Case: Ruigan asked Yantou, "What is the fundamental, eternal principle? Yantou said, "Movement. Ruigan said, "What is it when there is movement?
Yantou said, "One does not recognize the fundamental, eternal principle. Ruigan paused in thought. Yantou said, "If you accept this, you have not yet escaped the root and the dust."
"Unwilling to sink forever into birth and death.

[The Master] picked up the case and said: "When the sound of the virtuous decree resounds, the earth cracks and the rivers part; without exhausting one's spiritual effort, one transforms into a *kūṇ* or a *jīng*.
This is not without its significance for Yantou, yet I, Boshan, must ask him: Since this is the fundamental, eternal principle, why is there 'willing' and 'unwilling'?"
Vague is the kingdom of Yue; faint is Yangzhou.
[The Master] raised his head and addressed the assembly, saying: "If you can realize the first phrase, you may become a teacher to the Buddhas and patriarchs.

If you can realize the second phrase, you may become a teacher to humans and devas. If you can realize the third phrase, you will not even be able to save yourself. A monk asked, "What about you, Master?"
"Which phrase did he realize? Shanshan said, "The moon has fallen; at the third watch, it passes through the marketplace.
[The Commentator] says: Having swallowed all Buddhas and Patriarchs, they take Buddhas and Patriarchs as their teachers; having exhorted humans and devas, humans and devas follow their example.
Yet, in a place where there are no tracks or traces, one establishes names, titles, and numerical divisions, calling them "the first" or "the second"—this is already like adding legs to a snake.
Yet, in its unfolding and exposition, its withholding and bestowing are adapted to the moment. On the tip of Shoushan’s tongue there is a blade; his throat is like the sea.
Do you still know the phrase, "The moon falls in the third watch"? To those who are unconditioned and without affairs, there is a distinct set of leisurely implements.
Case: A monk asked Yangshan, "Does the Master know how to read characters? Yangshan replied, "I do so to a certain extent. The monk then circled him once clockwise and asked, "What character is this?
Yangshan wrote the character for "ten" (十) on the ground. The monk then circled him once counter-clockwise and said:
"What character is this? Shanshan changed the character for "ten" (十) into the *svastika* (卍).
A monk drew a circle and held it with both hands, like the posture of an asura grasping the sun and moon, saying, "What character is this? Shanshan drew a circle surrounding the *svastika*.
The monk assumed the posture of Lohitya (Louti). Shanshan said, "So it is, so it is. Guard and uphold it well."
The Master held up his whisk and said: "This monk turned his body and struck at smokeless fire; Yangshan drew lines on the ground and picked out a lamp from the bottom of the sea.
The heavens of meaning shone brightly; both were masters of the craft. They cannot be contained within the six scripts—tell me, what kind of character is this?"
The great earth has no blind people; who is there to appreciate and discern? Case:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? Yunmen said, "A steamed bun."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "To employ incense and rice from beyond the kalpas and to arouse offerings in the present—this talk of 'sticking to the dough' (huping) blocks people's mouths.
Its pure resonance is like jade; even if one possesses eloquence like a cascading torrent, one cannot match it in discourse. Why is this?"
It is like wild oats and rice porridge for the hungry: one eats until satisfied and then stops. As for discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs, wait for another time;
only then shall I provide you with its commentary.
Case: A monk asked Master Hui of Changsha, "How was it before you had seen Nanquan? Hui remained silent for a long while. The monk said, "And how was it after you saw him?

Hui replied, "It cannot be anything else. When the monk returned and related this to Changsha, Changsha said, "The person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole—though they have gained entry, it is not yet the ultimate reality. One must advance further from the top of that hundred-foot pole."
"The sands of the worlds in the ten directions are my entire body. The monk asked, "How does one advance further from the top of a hundred-foot pole?

Sandokai said, "The mountains of Langzhou; the waters of Lingshou. The monk said, "I do not understand. Sandokai said, "The four seas and five lakes are within the realm of the King's transformation."

The Master picks up the case and says: "Master Hui sits and kills the Dharmakāya, allowing neither ordinary people nor sages passage. Old Cen is beyond the blue sky and outside the clouds, yet he vies for even more essence and brilliance.
The white ox goring the buffalo is managed through many methods; the dead cat knows how to play—it is alive!
He applies medicine to the eyes of the blind and opens the ears of the deaf. But does Master Hui still recognize pain and itch?"
Case: Longya asked Cuibei, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Cuiwei said, "Give me the meditation board.
Longya took the meditation board and gave it to him. Cuiwei took it and struck him. Longya said, "I am willing to be struck, but there is still no meaning to the Patriarch’s coming from the West.
He then asked Linji, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Linji—
Jiashan said, "Give me the meditation cushion. Yanguan took the cushion and gave it to Linji. As soon as Linji received it, he struck him. Jiashan said, "Strike, you may strike;
however, this still does not capture the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West."
The Master held up the staff and said: "This fellow Longya has a back made of solid iron, straight and rigid to the very end.
Even if he were to shatter the Great Tang Empire, it would be difficult to find anyone whose head and tail are so perfectly aligned."
Case: When Xuansha arrived at Putian, a hundred entertainments were staged to welcome him. The following day, he asked the Elder Xiaotang, "Where did all that commotion go yesterday?
Xiaotang lifted the corner of his *kāṣāya*. Xuansha said, "I suspect it has nothing to do with it."
The Master held up his staff and said: "A person probes with words; water probes with a staff.

To distinguish true gold amidst a blazing fire, to recognize the Son of Heaven in the midst of a bustling marketplace, and to identify this old monk beneath his monastic robe—this is the man of Xuan Sha’s small pond.
Even if he were to cover it all over, his mouth is bitter while his heart is sweet. Yet there is more to come."

Case: Yunmen said, "To awaken to the Way upon hearing a sound, and to clarify the mind upon seeing a form: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva came with money to buy a sesame cake, but when he let it go, it turned out to be a steamed bun."
The Master held up his whisk and said: "To awaken to the Way upon hearing a sound—the void does not ring when struck. How so?
To clarify the mind through seeing form—the pure breeze has no physical substance. How so? It is not that speaking in barbarian tongues or Chinese is impossible;
yet, when Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva enters the Samādhi of the Universal Door, where can this fellow Yunmen go to search for him?"
Case: Guishan asked Wuduo, "Where have you come from? Wuduo said, "I have come to visit the sick. Guishan said, "How many people are sick?
Wuduo said, "There are those who are sick and those who are not. Guishan said, "Is the one who is not sick the Venerable Zhi?"
Wuye said, "Whether one is ill or not ill, it has nothing to do with others' affairs. Shanshan said, "Not even a single word has anything to do with it;
speak quickly, speak quickly! Wuye said, "Even if you could speak it, it would have no connection to him."

The Master held up the whisk and said: "Huishan Huiran valued benevolence; Daowu Shangyi valued righteousness. Although these two elders did not expose even the point of a needle, they were nonetheless exceedingly clever.
But tell me: who is the sick person? Who is the one who is not sick? Who is the one who is not involved? Try to point them out."
Case: Master Juzhi. Whenever he was asked anything, he would simply raise a single finger.

The commentary says: "The more it is hidden, the more it is revealed; the more clumsy it is, the more skillful it becomes. Letting go and gathering together, empty space is completely filled. Now tell me: [what is this?]
"What is this? He then held up one finger and said, "The gaze of ten eyes. [The Master] raised [his hand].
Emperor Suzong asked National Teacher Huizhong, "What do you require after a hundred years? The Master said, "Make a seamless stupa for this old monk.
The Emperor said, "I ask the Master for the model of the stupa. The Master remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand."
The Master said, "I have a Dharma-heir disciple named Danyuan who understands this matter thoroughly; I request that you summon him to question him.
After the Master passed away, the Emperor summoned Danyuan and asked, "What is the meaning of this? Danyuan replied: "To the south of Xiang and north of Tan, Within lies gold filling the entire land.
Beneath the shadowless tree, the boat is joined; Upon the crystal palace, there is no one with knowledge."
The Master held up the staff and said: "The ancient hall is sealed with moss; it does not reach those who meet it. Deeply locked by white clouds, even where there is a path, one remains lost.
The green mountains press close, revealing their towering majesty; yet at the edge of the ten-thousand-fathom cliff, the summit is never revealed.
Through all time, how many people have tried to capture this within the shadow of the stupa, yet failed to depict it? Only Tiantong and Xuedou have managed to approximate it slightly."
Case: Linji asked Huangbo, “What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Huangbo struck him. This occurred three times.
Thereupon, Linji took his leave of Huangbo and went to see Dayu. Dayu asked, “Where have you come from? Linji said, “From Huangbo.
Dayu asked, “What words did Huangbo say to you? Linji said, “I asked three times about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and each time—”

He was struck with a staff; he did not know whether he had committed a fault or not. Yunju said, "Huangbo was so compassionate for your sake that he exhausted himself on your account, yet you still come to ask whether you have committed a fault or not. At these words, Linji attained great enlightenment.
The Master held up the whisk and said: "Three years without opening his mouth—what a poisonous breath he emits! Three times he was struck with painful blows, like being brushed by a *gaozhi* staff.
He was caught at Huangbo’s place and had his roots pulled out by Dayu. In the end, whenever he meets someone, he shouts wildly and indiscriminately.
What kind of principle is this? It is not as if he were scattering pearls from within a purple silk curtain; in the end, he is merely a shrimp that cannot leap out of its basket."
Case: Shushan arrived at Weishan and asked, "I have heard your teacher say: 'The phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning are like a vine leaning against a tree.
Suddenly, when the tree falls, the vine withers. Where does the phrase return? Weishan laughed heartily. Shushan said, "I have traveled four thousand *li* to sell my cotton robe;
why do you, Master, deceive me? Weishan called to his attendant, "Give this man some money. The attendant brought it forward. Shushan took it and left.

Xuanshu sat down and instructed him, saying, "In the future, there will be the 'One-Eyed Dragon'; he shall be the one to pierce through your understanding for you. Later, Xuanshu went to Mingzhao and brought up the previous conversation.
Mingzhao said, "Touzi was truly head-to-tail upright, yet he simply did not meet a true知音 (one who understands).
Shu asked again, "When the tree falls and the vines wither, where do the words return? Mingzhao said, "This would make Touzi’s laughter even fresher. Only then did Shu [attain realization].
Wuyu said, "Tiaoshan originally has a blade within his smile.
[The Master] took up the case and said: "The One-Eyed Dragon and Zizai share in the profound transformation; the Short Uncle smashes through the ball of doubt.
Tell me, where does the ultimate phrase finally reside? In vain he makes Tiaoshan’s smile ever more fresh."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see?

If you see this 'not seeing,' it is naturally not the characteristic of that 'not seeing. If you do not see the ground of my not seeing, it is naturally not a material object; how could it not be you?"
The Master picks up the topic, saying: "The entire earth is this Śākyamuni; Ānanda is plugged into Śākyamuni’s nostrils. The entire earth is this Ānanda;
the World-Honored One tears open Ānanda’s chest. Now tell me, where do you see him? Where do you not see him?
If you can fix a single eye here, then the Yellow-Faced Gautama has deceived not only others, but himself as well."
This is merely self-deception. [Case] presented.
Dongshan, upon concluding the summer retreat, ascended the hall and said: "At the beginning of autumn and the end of the summer, you brothers may go east or west;

you must head toward a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not even an inch of grass. After a long silence, he said: "As for that place ten thousand *li* away where there is not even an inch of grass..."
"How is it? He looked around left and right and said, "If you wish to know this matter, you must have flowers grow upon withered wood;

only then will you be in accord with it. Shishuang said, "Stepping out the door is already walking on weeds. Ming'an said, "Even if one does not step out the door, it is still a vast expanse of weeds."

The Master picks up the case and says: "Dongshan’s set of teeth rings when struck and resounds when tapped. He speaks in barbarian tongues and Chinese alike; he scatters them wide and gathers them back together.
Truly, this can be called 'the profound guidance in the dim light. These two old fellows ride upon the tiger's head and grasp its tail."
Their mouths are as sweet as honey, yet their hearts are like the venom of a *he-chen* bird. Do you know where they fall? It is said:
Once Master Yangshan dreamed that he went to the abode of Maitreya and occupied the second seat. The Venerable One (Maitreya) said, "Today, the one on the second seat shall preach the Dharma.
Yangshan rose and struck the gavel, saying: "The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations. I respectfully..."
[The Master] says:

"Yangshan was wide awake even in his dreams; he startled the multitude and moved the assembly by preaching the Mahāyāna Dharma—transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations.
Have you ever penetrated this thoroughly? You must quickly cast away the wooden gong before you can succeed."
Case: Grand Master Lu Xun said to Nanquan, "Dharma Master Zhao is truly extraordinary;
he explains that 'Heaven and earth share the same root as I, and the myriad things are one body with me. Nanquan pointed to the peony flowers in front of the courtyard and said, 'Grand Master...'"
People of that time saw this single stalk of flowers as being like a dream.

[The Master] picked it up and said: "The Great Official traces the current back to its source; Nanquan’s clouds move and rain falls. Viewed through the True Eye, it is all merely a dream within a dream."
Case: Yunmen gave this teaching, saying: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form.
Take the lantern into the Buddha hall; bring the triple gate onto the lantern.
The Master held up his staff and said: "To trace it through all states of mind is like pointing to one's own palm; to manifest its benevolence is to conceal its function.

To develop the source of one's nature—how ultimate this is! To take the lantern and bring it into the Buddha Hall, to take the triple gate and place it upon the lantern—Master Yunmen has let this matter pass by one stroke."
Case: Master Zu asked Nanquan, “The mani-jewel no one recognizes; it is personally held within the Tathāgata-garbha. What is this ‘garbha’?
Nanquan said, “That which comes and goes with you, Old Teacher Wang, is it. Zu said, “What about that which does not come and go?
Nanquan said, “That too is the garbha. Zu said, “What is the jewel? Nanquan called out to Zu. Zu responded, “Yes? Nanquan—
[The Master] said, "Go! You do not understand my words.

[Bozan] picked it up and said: "Old Man Nanquan was fortunate to have encountered our Patriarchal Master. Had Boshan been present at that time, as soon as Nanquan’s call had not yet ceased, I would have responded, saying:
'There is no need to pick out rubble. I would have ensured that Nanquan would have been left speechless."
Case: Dongshan was unwell. A monk asked, "When the Master is ill, is there one who is not ill? Dongshan said, "There is.
The monk asked, "Does the one who is not ill look after the Master? Dongshan said, "The old monk has a share in looking after him.
The monk asked, "How is it when the Master looks after him? Dongshan said, "Then one does not see the illness."
The Master held up the whisk and said: "The Gate of Non-duality opens; the face of the sun, the face of the moon—none of these resemble Dongshan’s peculiar ailment.
They cannot be mixed, nor can they be made uniform. This is skillfully observing the illness within the illness. This monk has sinews in his eyes and blood beneath his skin;
if he wishes to see Dongshan, it will not be difficult."
Case: Linji asked the Hall Master, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come from selling yellow rice in the prefectural city.
Linji said, "Have you sold it all? The Master said, "I have sold it all. Linji drew a line with his staff and said, "Can you sell this too? The Master then shouted, and Linji struck him.
Next, the Head Cook arrived. Linji brought up the previous conversation. The Cook said, "The Hall Master did not—"
He grasped the Master’s meaning. Linji said, "And what about you? The Head Cook bowed, and Linji struck him as well. [The Master] commented: "Linji’s staff has eyes;
he skillfully examines the capacity of those who come before him. It is not that he does not know their origin, but he wishes for the Head Cook to recognize the 'painful staff' (the blow).
The Head Cook then shouted, and the Steward bowed. This is "emerging from within the gate"—a matter of both firmness and flexibility.
They assist one another. If you can penetrate through the state of exhaustion, it may be said that "a single drop of ink forms two dragons.
Case: When Shishuang passed away, the assembly requested the head seat of the hall to succeed him as abbot. Jiufeng was unwilling and said, "Wait until I have questioned him;
if he understands the meaning of our former master, he shall serve him just as the former master did. He then asked the head seat: "The former..."
The Master said: "Rest! Cease! A single thought for ten thousand years! Cold ashes and withered wood! An incense burner in an ancient temple!
A single length of white silk! Now tell me, what matter does this clarify? A monk said, "It clarifies the matter of the 'one color' (monochromatic) realm."
Feng said, "If that is so, then you have not yet grasped the meaning of our former teacher. Zuo said, "Do you not approve of me? He then had incense prepared.
Zuo burned the incense and said, "If I have not grasped the meaning of our former teacher, I shall not be able to cast off my body once this smoke rises.
Having spoken, he sat down and passed away. Feng then patted his back and said, "To die while sitting or standing is certainly possible, but as for our former teacher—"
The meaning has not yet been grasped.
[The Master] held up [the staff] and said: "He who establishes well does not pull out; he who debates well appears as if mute. The Head Seat damaged its flower but filled its fruit.
To purify one's conduct and take it as a model for others—how could such things apply to the affairs of a monastic abbot?
Jiufeng was extremely stubborn and unconventional; do you understand Shishuang’s meaning yet? In short, he deserves thirty strokes of the broomstick.
Case: Emperor Tongguang said to Xinghua, "I have acquired a treasure from the Central Plains, yet there is no one to appraise its value.
Xinghua said, "Lend me your Majesty’s treasure for a moment. The Emperor held up his *fuhou* (a head-wrap) with both hands.
Xinghua said, "Who would dare to appraise the treasure of a sovereign?"

The Master picks up the topic, saying: "A jade disc of one inch in diameter, a pearl that illuminates a carriage—compared to the radiance of the Central Plains, these might not even equal a ten-thousandth part.
Mañjuśrī’s jeweled crown cannot conceal it; Vimalakīrti’s room of ten feet cannot contain its manifestation.
Yet, even so, Xinghua ultimately finds no price with which to repay it. Nevertheless, who says that gold is like dung?"
Case: A monk asked Dongshan, “Among the three bodies, which one does not fall into any numerical category? Dongshan said, “I have often been pressed on this point.
[The Master] comments: It cannot be leaned upon when near; it cannot be carried away when far. Pushed forward, it does not move ahead; pulled back, it does not retreat. Dongshan—

In this regard, it is like an iron stake. As for those who discern rare treasures, gather the black pearls of Li, seek the unpolished jade of Hua, or pursue the lapis lazuli of Lan—how could they possibly speak of this?
One must depart from words and phrases; only then can one be close to it.
Case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the samādhi of every particle of dust? Yunmen said, "The rice in the bowl; the water in the bucket. [The Master] comments:
In my ordinary daily life, I use withered wood for fuel and wild greens to make my soup.
If someone were to ask me, "What is the samādhi of every particle of dust? I would simply say: "Be careful not to seek rice within the bowl, nor look for water within the bucket. And so it is.
"How far apart are the Way and Yunmen? [The Master] raised his staff.
A monk asked Master Langye Huijue: "If the fundamental nature is pure and still, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?"
Jueyun said: "It is fundamentally pure and serene; how could it suddenly give rise to mountains, rivers, and the great earth?
[The Master] picked up the point and said: "It is fundamentally pure and serene; from where did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come?
How could they have suddenly arisen? This is yet another layer. One who has a cataract cannot be spoken of in terms of pure simplicity; one with blue eyes cannot be dazzled.
That "dark and yellow" is what the Celestial Youth referred to as "seeing existence and non-existence.
If one were to awaken in this very way upon hearing Langya’s response, who could it be? I do not know.
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Ten;
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Eleven.
Compiled by Honghan, Dharma-grandson residing at Boshan.
The Head Seat and Dharma-grandson Hongyu, together with the assembly,
composed verses on the ancient precedent of the Flower and the Smile.
Auspicious petals and numinous branches—a spring beyond kalpas. Picked up, they stir the clouds over the seas and mountains. How vast is this compassionate heart, like the heavens!
Who is the person who drags through the mud and carries water?
The Gandharva King presented music; Kāśyapa rose to dance, with the corner of his *kāṣāya* robe trailing slightly.
Scattered toward Jambudvīpa, they sowed the seeds of sprouts. Most delightful was the sound of the lute, penetrating the very marrow of the bones;
in every mountain and stream, the *dharma*-flower blossomed.
When the World-Honored One, because of the seer with five supernormal powers, was asked about the meaning of the six supernormal powers, his responsive "Amen" caused one power to vanish.
Mountains collapsed and oceans dried up as all traces of his form were severed; though the seer had a mouth, he could not analyze or explain it.
His double ears were keen and clear, yet seemed as if they were deaf.

The Universal Eye desires to see Samantabhadra and three times earnestly surveys the entire realm; the great trichiliocosm fits upon the tip of a single hair. The six-tusked white elephant was never far away;
it is mostly because we fail to see that we are deceived by our own eyes.
When the woman emerged from samādhi, she falsely claimed it was but the blink of an eye; her display of supernatural power was in vain, for it did not concern [the matter].
Now, accustomed to eating *harā* rice, she remains idle after three meals a day, satisfied.
Venerable Ānanda asked: "Apart from the golden robe, what else is transmitted?
Having already donned the golden robe, it is already late. When sound and resonance correspond, one should know the proper time. The banner-pole has been overturned at the gate;
which branch of the empty flowers has been blown down?"
The Second Patriarch requested the Great Being Bodhidharma to settle his mind;

seeking the mind, he could not find it, and thus his mind was settled. The moon reflects upon the clear pool, its depths utterly cold. Do not pursue sense-bases and objects to give rise to inferiority;
all you people, look at this golden-maned lion!
The Third Patriarch repents his sins;
ten thousand li of sky open up, and a gust of wind blows. Pushing the moon’s carriage from behind the clouds, it emerges veiled in mist. Deep autumn, deep river—how clear that reflection!
Dewdrops fall upon the lotuses, crimson on both banks.
Beating the ox, beating the cart, people say the cart moves because it is the ox that moves. I would rather plan for the ox’s transport and let the beating of the cart cease.
Suddenly, when the cart is broken and the ox has perished, there remains only a single head, covering the earth and reaching to the heavens.
A monk sent by Nanyue went to ask Mazu. Mazu said: "Since the chaos first broke out, the smoke of war has been swept away, yet my resolve does not rest.
On a clear, white day, it makes people sorrowful. In the Great Peace, the general does not hang his seal;
only when he casts aside his blade and hangs up his spear has he reached the ultimate."
Master Pang asked Mazu: "The mountains form the painting, the waters form the lute;
who can understand the wondrous sound arising from within? This is what Master Ma can play, yet its notes are so clear and piercing that they are difficult to endure."

When Mazu was unwell, Ciyun responded with "the jade returns and the pearl turns," manifesting the true mechanism. They cannot be mixed; their types are not the same. Do not say that this old fellow lacks strength;
he rides a stone tiger backward across Liaoxi.
Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu:
Holding up his whisk, he displayed the ancestral majesty before all eyes. It is difficult to discuss the subtle nuances of this moment in words.
Clearly, he thrust forth a firebrand that illuminates the void; this one is truly a golden-haired lion cub.

Baizhang’s wild fox burned away hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies; who was he, and who was the person? If you attempt to communicate through the obscurity of falling into delusion, the principle of ignorance throughout vast kalpas will not be extended.
Nanquan asked a monk, "The night brought a fine breeze;
try asking whether the wind in the pines is with or against you. In vain he attempts to clear his eyes of gain and loss; the venomous dragon refuses to lightly open its mouth.

A monk asked Nanquan, "Where will you go after a hundred years?

The Abbot of Yanguan called to his attendant:
"It is evident the fan is broken; bring me an ox. A tree without roots planted upon a rock—then and there the *yuanxiang* (perfect circle) was cast forth.

While Guizong was weeding grass, one stroke of his hoe split two segments; blood flowed profusely. When the mountains and rivers of the great earth begged for their lives, they recognized this old man’s true countenance;

Zhaozhou asked Daci: "What is the essence of Prajñā?

Zhaozhou’s interrogation of the old woman and the discourse on the path to Mount Tai:
beneath the feet of the path to Mount Tai, no one from ancient times to the present has been able to distinguish right from wrong. Having been interrogated, she still goes straight ahead as before;

Zhaozhou went to great lengths to act out a bout of madness, laboring his four elements with the harmonious wind until he provoked the old woman to say, "It is not yet complete."

From the beginning, the Great Way has penetrated Chang'an; answering him from outside the wall makes the dialogue increasingly difficult.

Deshan’s begging bowl brought his lineage to prosperity;

the silken decree responds to the signs before they have yet been born.

Regarding the enshrinement of the stupa for Master Shouchang:
What is the Buddha? A magnificent mountain. His white curl is like flowing silk; his aura is like indigo.
The clouds of compassion transform into the eyes of heaven and earth, left for gods and humans to behold forever.

The Archang Tai Zhashuo is over seventy years old, yet he has added eight more years to his life; among those of the monastic order, he stands at the very forefront. Why wait for rebirth in the Pure Land?
This morning, we have personally beheld a lotus flower within the flames.

Chan Master Guangfu, setting fire to two thousand li away—what business could he possibly have in mind? Casting off his hometown, he walks straight ahead. Today, observe the transformations within the flames:
lotus flowers grow upon dry land, bearing clouds.
The Chan master Bianci, whose single-mindedness pervades all, takes the three realms as his home. Like a purple *zhizi* fungus nurtured in excellence, he is as flawless as white jade.
Today, as this spiritual sprout flourishes, let us await and behold the lotus blooming amidst the flames.
"Mind is always meditating": how is this mind?
"The green mountains rise high where white clouds dwell deep. "How is 'always'? "The ancient road is grand and level as a plain.
Now it is cast upon the summit of a solitary peak; thus one walks amidst the blazing flames of a torch. [He strikes with the torch.]
A single circle says: Where is the constant mind? It radiates light throughout all realms.
When a practitioner shaves their head, rice inevitably becomes cooked rice; the monk was originally a layperson. Śākyamuni propagated the sutras from this very principle, and Mazu took this to heart.
Sumo wrestling! Three thousand miles away, I rejoice that you have sinews beneath your feet; five hundred years hence, they will laugh that my tongue has no bone.
Heh! Eradicate the delusive causes and conditions of beginningless time, and for now, take up lodging within the palace of Brahmā.
Praise of Amitābha Buddha (II): His vows are vast and his practices are great;
his compassion is profound and his wisdom is deep. Thus he adorns the realm of transformation and truly purifies the minds of ordinary beings.
One must know that through the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), one will ultimately attain Buddhahood; it has never been heard that a peak can suddenly arise where there was no foundation.
Coming by the power of vows to repay the debts owed to sentient beings, it is said that this Sahā world is itself the realm of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

This is universally called "transforming iron into gold. Within this, however, there is both benefit and harm. Why is this? If you perceive Amitābha merely upon paper, you have already lost out to me.
One should engage in virtuous commerce.

Śākyamuni Buddha praised this Compassionate Honored One, who, by the power of his compassionate vows, transforms those with karmic affinity. Their right faith becomes harmonized and upright; they do not know me.
I do not recognize him. Piercing through his skull, it is clearly a thief. If I miss this moment again, I shall simply wait for the future to question Maitreya.

Eulogy on Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (II) I prostrate to the Great Compassionate One, seated upon the Paṇḍaka Rock. His countenance is revealed here and now; why speak of him as being in the past? When sentient beings possess a pure mind, [he appears].

The wondrous wisdom of all Buddhas is like jade teeth, resonant and clear. They do not recognize the character "Universal" (Pu), for the nature of seeing is not illumination, and the nature of hearing is not acuity.

Turning toward the Buddha is turning toward birth; it is the fragrant countenance in a precious mirror. Its name is Great Compassion, and it is also called Great Kindness. Who would say that the wondrous function of the Universal Gate (Pumen) resides here?
The Flower Treasury World is entirely within the space of a single meditation cushion. Bearing an unpayable debt, one relies upon sentient beings to repay it.

Exercising compassion while mobilizing pity, one assists those in suffering to await peace. Manifesting in the five realms of existence—what a multitude of affairs! Yet, witnessing the clear sky, one remains tranquil throughout the day.
He covers the groves of purple bamboo while harboring profound sorrow; he sits upon the stone of *pantala* while silently manifesting deep compassion.
He rescues sentient beings from their suffering and distress, acting as a substitute for the conduct and rituals of all Buddhas.
Some call this the "Universal Gateway Manifestation," yet he does not abandon those amidst the howling winds and surging waves. Aha! Now is precisely the time.
In the realm of the West, the Buddha resides upon a ground of lapis lazuli; flowers bloom within a pond of eight virtues; railings and pavilions rise high and far;
and pearl groves and jeweled nets are layered one upon another. One must by no means dismiss this as a mere mental construct. Since it is not a mere construct, Amitābha is present right now.
Where is it? Alas! An Inscription for the Śarīra Stūpa of Fushan (with Preface).

When the Buddha was cremated in the past, stūpas flourished in the ten directions. The eight kings requested portions of the śarīras; as for those that entered Zhendan (China), they were indeed innumerable.
This is the account. When Venerable Yasas first came from the Western Regions, there were two instances where he enshrined śarīra relics at Mount Lu.

It has emitted light that filled the mountains and valleys, and numerous auspicious and extraordinary manifestations have appeared, which cannot be fully recounted. This is indeed due to the pure and profound realization of the Elder Qingzhan and the Elder Zibai.

He was the Son of Heaven. Through the power of causes and conditions, after years of accumulation and repair, it was opened and inspected, whereupon three vases were found filled with gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.

The Grand Historian of Wu, Guan, obtained twenty-two grains from me. After a long time, he opened and inspected them again, and they were full.

Thereupon, the Grand Astrologer, with a heart of reverence and in union of compassion and wisdom, desiring that all who saw, heard, praised, or prostrated before them might plant seeds of supreme merit, planned [the event] atop Mount Fu.
He constructed a stūpa to emulate the Golden Wheel. Formerly, there was a person who entered hell and saw Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, who said to him:
"Your transgressions are deep and heavy; you ought to fall into hell. Hasten to Mount Mao to pay homage at the Śarīra Stūpa, and you may escape this suffering.

Considering that a single prostration and a single bow can immediately effect liberation from hell, it is clear that the eminent causes planted by the Grand Astrologer [are such that they will surely lead to deliverance].
All you faithful ones, there is no doubt that you shall swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi. While traveling to Fudu, I was able to behold and pay homage to it;
with palms joined in praise, I spoke these verses:

Extensively cultivating myriad wondrous practices, he brought the *pāramitās* to perfection; his inconceivable merit he dedicated entirely to the Buddha-wisdom.
Dharma Master’s Praise (IV):
To call you "this very Bodhidharma" is to be swindled by others. To call you "this very Boshan" is to be bewildered face-to-face.

Facing the wall for nine years, gouging out people’s hearts, severing people’s elbows—how many times did he nearly bring about ruin? Yet the earth turned and the heavens revolved;
with a single stroke of true mechanism, the elephant leaps and the lion roars. Still, with but a single sandal, he returned to the West. Truly, he was but a shrimp.
One cannot leap out of the measure.
Looking up, no heaven is seen; looking down, no earth is seen. A pair of large ears with rings; two nostrils breathing air.

Purple qi and auspicious clouds swirl and cover the riverbank. Who is it that breaks the reeds? It is the Iron-Faced Man.
To draw near is truly difficult; why then do you offer praise? Two lines of ink remain far beyond contemplation; a single bright pearl shines with radiant splendor.

Face-to-face is a green ox, its four hooves treading the earth. Face-to-face is this Old Master, his beard and hair white as snow.

The green peach blossoms cluster thickly; the shadows of the jade grasses deepen. Yet there is further the meaning of the West—do not seek it recklessly upon these high mountains.

This old man of Mount E is admirable for his earnest practice. His form is no form; it is difficult to capture in paint or ink. With ash on his head and dust on his face, he is beyond representation.
The Laughing God’s radiant light bows to the snow; his heart is of copper and his gallbladder of iron. He punishes the World-Honored One for holding up the flower;

he takes a worn-out meditation cushion as his seat and a tattered straw raincoat as his *kāṣāya*. Resting his head on stones and rinsing his mouth with springs, he clings to the clouds and wears the rosy mists.
A man of such refined elegance cannot be surpassed—even thirty years among these magnificent mountains, the handle of his hoe has become his living livelihood.
I prostrate to my Master, the compassionate father of the four modes of birth. His words enter the profound mystery; his pedagogical skill prizes indirect response.
At the seven sites of enlightenment, surrounded by a thousand fingers, he cast forth the wish-fulfilling jewel and emptied out the basket—this single phrase has been displayed for all morning.
Taking right for wrong, and treating the light as heavy, I entered the tiger’s den and personally encountered its venomous claws;

having died and returned to life, it was like drinking fine wine. From my prime until old age, I have remained singular and peerless. Now, departing from the assembly with serenity, I clearly point the way.
When the world heard of this, they called him "The Extinction of Ambrosia. His descendants and lineage carry on his legacy, their fragrant influence remaining stern and formidable.
This monk is half-hidden and half-manifest; he treats the high as low and makes the deep seem shallow. At times, he is compassionate, quelling the anger of the asuras;

A eulogy for Master Fengding by Master Zhe:

His appearance was not handsome; he mixed the black with the white and took the hour of *yin* for the hour of *mao*. He broke the water-drawing pole—this has already been seen in the case of Master Bian.

Eulogy for Dharma Master Tian’an of Mount Hongtao (With Preface) I have been hanging my staff at Boshan for many years.
I have often worried that my native village lacks anyone to bring about spiritual transformation. As for the monastics who come and go...
It is recorded that the Dharma Master T'ian'an propagated the teachings of the Vehicle and served as a *karmācārya*.

I have long held him in high esteem, yet I had not yet found the opportunity to meet him. In the spring of the Dingmao year, I returned to my native village; by then, Master An had already passed away.
Upon entering the mountains, I saw his stupa standing majestically, and thus composed a eulogy to fulfill my long-held aspiration.

The world is without reliance; the faculties and their objects are empty and quiescent. With compassion and wisdom forming his body, he brings forth the benefit of wisdom. His virtue of precepts is inconceivable; his practice is free from self-interest.
Through the vast embrace of compassionate conditions, he first attended to his native village. There, the Dharma arose like clouds, and his instruction of others flowed like water from a pitcher.

The benefits of his giving did not remain localized; those both near and far were all transformed by him. When his mission of conversion was complete, he was enshrined in a stupa upon this mountain. His Dharma voice wondrously resounded, and even the birds sang in harmonious chatter.
Clouds disperse across the vast sky;
the Yang-spring returns to the great earth. All sentient beings within the Flower Treasury World breathe forth from the tip of the staff.
—Inscription by Master Kongyin.

This old, weather-beaten fellow—amidst a biting, piercing cold, now dying and now reviving—at what season does this occur? Surveying the past and encompassing the present, it is like thunder crashing and lightning flashing.
His conduct in action and withdrawal is distinct from that of others; yet it is not distinct. Thus he wins for himself the legacy passed down by people as "the Extinction of Ambrosia" (Ganlu Mie).
In praise of Chan Master Gao: Who is this person? It is my elder brother Gao. He has stored and preserved his wisdom like the sun and his compassion like the wind.

With surplus funds, he supported the monastic community; with no remaining dharma, he guided the masses of the ignorant. For a thousand years, the color of the pine trees remains unchanged; the clear stream flows on.
Clouds penetrate the vast void;

even the Dharma Master of the Single Hermitage cannot be apprehended. Where, then, can the traces of the hermitage remain? The jewel pond is clear of great waves, and a lotus-picking boat is moored across it.

The Ancient Master of the Mind-Dharma praises the ancient Buddhas for transmitting the lamp long ago; the Teacher of the Mind continues the flame far and wide. If you wish to know his whereabouts, he lies amidst the fragrant grasses in the slanting sun.
As clumsy as this praise.
Seeking skillfulness, it cannot be found; from where would clumsiness come? Like a *maṇi* jewel cast into the fire-womb of a stone—when there is a sudden flash of insight, upon what can one rely?
Deep within the mists and clouds lies the Terrace of Gusu.
Understanding deeply, one praises the profound Dharma; the caverns of affliction are shattered. Iron walls become transparent; silver mountains stand towering.
At the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, look with a sidelong glance; keep your heels firmly planted and do not be deluded.
The true portrait of Longfeng, eighty-one years old, was produced when he was over eighty.

His conduct of precepts was like empty space; the Flower Treasury World was his dwelling place. His distinct title was Longfeng (Dragon Peak). He has inspired me to personally compose this eulogy for him. Aha!
Suddenly beholding the pearl upon one’s own head, the vast ocean is made to dry up to its very bottom.

Let the ten fascicles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* circulate as you please; let the single pulse of Bodhi be subject to praise or slander. He is like one who has vanished.
The old dhūta who makes use of these things has been exiled into this most evil world of Jambudvīpa, leaving behind a model for gods and humans.
Wang Xuanshi of Wanling composed a shadow eulogy:
"Sparse pines and bamboos; pure and fitting tea along with wine. Among them is one who finds delight, facing south to gaze at the Northern Dipper."
Today we have met amidst the mountains and waters. Upon this unrolled plain silk, what indeed shall there be? By the rocks of Kongtong, the fragrance of *zhī* and *lán* blooms;
beneath the brush, wind and clouds move like dragons and snakes. Clad in Daoist robes and wearing a woodcutter’s cap, with brows arched and mouth agape, he fashions these refined verses anew.
Extraordinary compositions were produced on the spot. He boiled spring water with the help of a servant and gathered *zhī* fungi by borrowing another’s hand.
Within these acts lay boundless elegance, never falling into the common molds of his contemporaries. Throughout the Five Lakes, everyone recognized him as Master Xuánshí;
for all eternity, he shall be hailed as a fellow member of the Bóshān Society.
In the great circle of light within this portrait eulogy for the lay devotee Liu Longtian:

Proclaiming the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they hasten toward both the mundane and supramundane realms, coming and going in playful mastery. How is this known? Mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees;

Praise! How marvelous!

I now append this preface to serve as a genealogy for Jambudvīpa.
From where do the three-in-one nest originate? If one were to recognize them, it would not be by much. Since time immemorial, they have had no face or features;
today, this hair-tied *dhūta* monk further transmits the true and the false through ink and water. This shall put to laughter the old woman who pointed the way in years past.
A Self-Eulogy for the Layman Yü Jisheng. The Master painted his own likeness and that of the layman; they sat facing one another, and the layman requested a eulogy.

Dipped in golden dust, only at fifty does one realize that four times nine is not thirty-six. Capturing the hare and the elephant alive reveals his full majesty;
with earnest devotion, he treats state affairs as if they were the Buddha’s work, offering his single heart of loyalty like the brilliance of the rising sun.
This fellow has eyes of purity and brows of noble bearing; most malicious and poisonous, feigning compassion. When preaching the Dharma, he does not reflect;
he reviles all quarters with agonizing needles and awls. He drags people to stand on the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff and exerts his full strength to give them a single shove.

Throughout his life, he never sought instruction from others; he merely probed and felt within his own mind. Suddenly, he shattered the lacquer bucket, causing people everywhere to be struck with amazement.

Born in the north of the river, grown in the south of the river—there is clearly a reason for this. He possesses no skillful means whatsoever;

his mouth is constantly dripping all day long, and his mind has not a single moment of still contemplation. Yet, wherever he goes, he forms many joyful affinities, leaving them for all people to enjoy as pure appreciation.
Painting me on paper does not capture my likeness; truly, he is difficult to approach. He has a whole body, yet lacks the five viscera.
Having shaken off all traces of the Buddha-dharma, there is not even a hair’s breadth remaining. How could he dare to receive the offerings of all people? (At the request of Chan Master Chuan-shi).
This fellow Laozi fabricates much emptiness; he craves sleep and is constantly dreaming. Entering the marketplace, he passes by the qilin and the phoenix;
yet when he comes near another's eyebrows, it causes them pain. Floating and drifting, he is as light as five *liang*; yet looming and heavy, he weighs more than a thousand *jin*.
This fellow has neither gain nor loss; having resolved this single condition, all matters are finished. With little artifice, he is most simple and sincere; he loves to proclaim secrets to others.
Sometimes he sits alone upon the peaks of chaotic crags, pointing at the winds and clouds as he plays the *bīlù* flute. *Du!* (Hark!)
This old, freezing beggar calls himself a hero, yet he possesses not a shred of merit.

For the sake of the Dharma, his tongue is as humble as a thread, while his backbone is as rigid as iron. All day long he prattles on with millions of words, only adding a few more flakes of snow to his head.
This fellow has no length [of stature]. He is content only to acknowledge his own faults. He is supple when meeting the firm, and majestic when encountering the compassionate.
He carries his path along with him; he knows the manifest and the subtle. Within his belly there is not the slightest thing; in a lifetime, he has won nothing but a fat mouth.
Heh! The entire body is in disarray; the face is covered in dust. Joy does not cloud the mind; anger does not provoke resentment.

He reviles Panshan for being "faceless," and laughs at Chuanzhi for his skill in "concealing the body. Amidst drifting clouds and ancient trees in the deepest recesses, auspicious birds and wondrous flowers shine with fresh brilliance. Heh! Who are you?

As solemn as the clarity of the moon and as compassionate as the brilliance of the sun, his conduct and withdrawal do not flow along with the common crowd, making it difficult to distinguish between his goodness and evil.
Black and white. Because the Zen practitioner Tanhui has pressured me to produce this, I cannot help but write it down to temporarily serve as a defense.

Today I have inscribed this painting. Let it be at the mercy of others' ridicule.

Verses on the Teaching for Collection by the Head Seat and Dharma Grandson Hongyu (2): For Imperial Censor Wu Guanjiao The world is like a dream; Birth and death are illusory. If you wish to transcend them, Seek the Way within yourself. The mind is originally empty and still; Sentient beings are fundamentally non-existent. When delusion ceases, wisdom appears; When wisdom arises, delusion vanishes. Do not seek outside of yourself; Seeking is itself a hindrance. If you can awaken to this principle, You will see the Buddha-nature clearly. The myriad phenomena are all empty; There is neither subject nor object. If you can realize this in an instant, You will attain the unconditioned fruit. The great matter of birth and death Is not something to be feared. Only when you have severed the root of delusion Will you be free from the cycle of suffering. Do not cling to appearances; Appearances are but fleeting shadows. If you can let go of all attachments, You will dwell in the realm of liberation. The Dharma is beyond words and speech; It cannot be grasped by the intellect. Transmit it directly from mind to mind; This is the true lineage of the Buddhas. Do not seek for it in scriptures; Scriptures are merely pointers. If you can recognize your own nature, You will be a true heir of the Buddhas. I offer these verses to you, To encourage your resolve. May you practice with diligence, And together realize the Way.
