If you turn back to look at your own mind, You will find the Buddha-nature immediately. Do not wait for a future life; Do not seek it in some distant land. Right now, in this very moment, Awaken to the truth of non-arising. [Verse] The myriad phenomena are all empty and false; They are like dreams and illusions. If you can realize they are empty, You will be free from all attachments. Do not cling to appearances; Do not pursue forms. Detach from both subject and object, And you will attain liberation. [Verse] The Bodhisattva path is vast and deep; It requires great courage and resolve. Do not fear the cycle of birth and death; Do not shrink from the suffering of the world. With compassion as your heart and wisdom as your eye, Benefit all sentient beings without limit. This is the true practice of the Mahayana; This is the way to fulfill the Bodhisattva vows. [Verse] To study the Way is to study the self; To study the self is to forget the self. When the self is forgotten, the Way is found; When the Way is found, the self is realized. This is the teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; This is the instruction of the ancient sages. If you can practice this with diligence, You will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

Sudden awakening to the source of the mind opens the precious treasury; one finds joy in leisure amidst the clusters of ten-thousand flowers. Even the spring breeze understands the meaning of *dhyāna*;
it blows away the withered red petals to accompany the flowing water.
To Layman Liu Zidu:
Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Treasury. The bell tolls and the drum resounds; test them within the sensory dust.
Since you have recognized the dharma of the conditional mind, You are but a single carefree man of no-mind.
Showing Layman Baoming that he has suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the treasure storehouse: From others' afflictions and bodhi, he passes his three meals at any time;
with nothing to do, he listens to the birds singing in the deep mountains.

To Layman Deng Jiuru, he demonstrated the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury. With a piercing laugh, he pointed out Mazu’s circle. Truly, the crown of his head possesses the eye of Maheśvara;
black and white ultimately return to perfection beneath the phrase.
To Layman He Shi: Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. Rubbing my sleepy eyes, I see the blue sky.
This ready-made koan is brought forth once more: three monkeys tossing coins at night.
To show Layman Fu Yuandu how he suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury: There is a provenance for this matter of the patched robe;
he swallowed the whole Qizhou date at once, and even until now, he remains satiated without ceasing.

The lay practitioner Yu Xiong of Shifang was shown the source of the mind through sudden awakening, opening the precious treasury; where the rooster crows and the dog barks, the True Vehicle is proclaimed.
Although he busies himself day after day with his affairs, eating and wearing clothes as if they were never his concern.
To Layman Liu Jindu:

Sudden awakening to the source of the mind opens the precious treasury. The story of the cypress tree in the courtyard is particularly long. This Daoist does not understand the meaning of the Westward Coming;
with each gust of clear wind, there is a fresh coolness.
To Layman Yang Zhongyi:
Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. Gold, sand, and stones need not be discussed; With both hands spread wide, there is nothing to grasp.
The myriad phenomena of the universe are swallowed in a single gulp.

To Layman Yao Linqing, he showed the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury. The children of the Pang family are those who truly know this. Transcending the mundane, he allowed nothing to remain;
casting aside his home and garden, he sank away into the world.
To Layman Deng Zhique:
Sudden Awakening to the Source of Mind and Opening the Treasure Treasury. His family style is not the same as that of worldly people;
hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of samādhis reside solely within ordinary speech and silence.
To Layman Liu Wenchang:

To reveal the source of the mind and open the precious treasury is a matter of sudden awakening; yet even one who fully accepts and bears this burden does so with lingering hesitation. Only when one further intends to swallow up the surging waves to their depths will they laugh the Great Master Mazu of Jiangxi right off his feet.
To the lay practitioner Wang Yuanchun, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury: the ancestral fields have never been moved.
If one seeks them through calculation and deliberation, it is much like pouring from a full cup into a leaking vessel.

To the Layman Wujian, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury. Within this very place, not even a speck of dust is established. Who says that rare treasures are inferior to sand and stones?
Yet one still laughs at one's former poverty to the bone.

Showing Chen Feibai, the Layman, the Sudden Awakening to the Source of Mind and the Opening of the Treasure Trove: The moon glows softly upon the coral branches; This pure and void realm is not of the human world.
The wind of the evening trees blows away the floating clouds.
To Layman Xiong Feiqing, who has suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury: "The yellow chrysanthemums and green bamboos are all True Suchness.
If you were to give rise to conceptual understanding regarding these flowers and bamboos, you would be laughed at by the blue-eyed barbarian of old."
Shiye reveals to Layman Duiyu the sudden awakening to the source of the mind, opening the precious treasury: the numinous talisman behind the elbow, the pearl within the robe.
How many abstruse wonders have been cast aside; simply recognize Yangqi’s three-legged donkey.
I show you that the layman has attained it:
he has suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury. Upon the main thoroughfare, he rides crosswise upon a white ox-cart;
the infinite ornaments upon its horns are all contained within the home of the Elder of Profound Compassion.
I have not yet shown you the rest, Layman.
You have suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury; the sutra-scrolls of the great trichiliocosm need not be sought elsewhere.
Clearly, you are one true simpleton, whose capacity for holding has from the start been as deep as the sea.

To Layman Chang of Juyan, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury. When meeting people, I am too weary to discuss mere "mouth Zen. Pearls are gathered within the leather bag;
both the staff and the shout are altogether not it.
To Layman Deng Lusheng:
Revealing the Source of Mind through Sudden Enlightenment, Opening the Treasure Treasury. Fine mountains and fine waters are gathered all at once; from of old, he has never stepped outside the gate.
He has attained freedom within the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas.

Showing Layman Zhang Ne the Sudden Enlightenment of the Source of the Mind and Opening the Precious Treasury: The skull has no consciousness, yet the eyes are first made clear; One further knows the state where mind and objects are as they are (*tathatā*);
Even when flowers and birds encounter a person, they are not startled.

Showing the King his dream, Layman Lan attained sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury. The ancient path of many years has become as slippery as moss; the pure vase was shattered and then picked up once more.
Having returned to Jambudvīpa, he shall come here again.
To Layman Yao Danying:
Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. Drinking dry the Western River is no marvel;
Performing a somersault in the presence of the sun, One blows the iron flute—a poem beyond the kalpas.
To Layman Wu Shuda:
Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. Following sounds and chasing forms through morning and night, one wanders through the clouds with a single staff;
gain and loss, intimacy and estrangement, are all left unconsidered.
To the Layman Wang Junhan:
Sudden awakening to the source of the mind opens the precious treasury; falling flowers and flowing water are all the family treasures. The old woman of Mount Tai labored in vain;
once you have reached the shore, there is no need to ask for the ferry crossing again.

To the lay practitioner Wang Hongqing, he showed the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury. Why labor to ask separately about the wind and the banner? The hunter’s alarm shattered the dream of the third watch;
only then did he realize that all previous affairs had been but vexations.
Showing Layman Xu Zhenke the Sudden Awakening to the Source of Mind and Opening the Treasure Treasury: Within the Great Tang Empire there is no Zen Master;
the void performs a somersault, clapping its hands and strolling about, asking, "Who am I?"
To the Layman Zheng Tuchen:
You have suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury; picking up incense and selecting firewood is now but a mundane task.
Now that you have recognized this bit of leisure, you laugh at how busy your hands and feet were before.

To Layman Cai Yuyuan, he showed the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury; with a raised brow and a blink of the eye, he revealed the full functioning of his total capacity. How many jars of salt and vinegar have been poured out!
Now he gathers them up and dwells in a thatched door in the deep mountains.
Showing the Layman Baisheng how to suddenly awaken to the source of the mind and open the precious treasury: Deep within the white clouds lies a family tradition;
clearly extending a hand that grasps the clouds, one should skillfully steer an iron ship through the void.
To Layman Luo Yuanqing, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury: wearing robes and eating rice, one sees the Tathāgata;
there is no need to ask further about the Southern Mountain path—just laugh and point to the moss upon the stone in the courtyard.

To the Layman Zhengsheng, I show how he has suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury: Upon the coral branches, the sea breeze is clear; what present matter could serve as an obstruction?
As soon as one engages in thought, it is already ten thousand eight thousand leagues away.

To the Zen practitioner Bi-hui, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury; from beneath the jaws of the black dragon, I pluck the pearl and bring it forth. Now I am too weary to discuss the mass of radiance;
I shall simply wrap myself in this skin-sack and learn to be a fool.

Manifesting auspicious signs for Chan practitioner Ruiya, he suddenly awakens to the source of the mind and opens the precious treasury: "The Land of the Rising Sun has always been to the east of the Sea Gate; the monk’s robe is often patched with clouds and mists.
There is no need to trouble Master Zhigong with questions about shears and rulers."

To Layman Sheyufu, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury; yet one must further smile to manifest the tradition of the Buddhas. The face given by one's mother is recognized through conditions;
the waterbirds and mountain flowers are the same everywhere.
I show the layman Kuíwú that he has suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury. Jīnlíng was originally Shítóuchéng;
ten thousand years pass without change, like the long river, where all people may at their leisure wash their own ceremonial cords.
To the Layman Huayu, he reveals the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opens the precious treasury: where one’s feet tread, all is pure gold.
Furthermore, knowing the news of spring within the brocade curtains, the stone maiden weaves flowers without using a needle.

Showing Layman Hongyu the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opening the precious treasury: coming from the Qiantang River to play with the tide, he returns without a thought for his clothes getting wet;
suddenly meeting someone on the way, a smile fills his cheeks.

To the Layman Zhenyu, he showed the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury: "Meeting face-to-face, a mere movement of the eyebrows reveals the知音 (zhīyīn—those who understand). Do not seek the realm of non-arising before you;
the flowing spring in the deep ravine is the zither of antiquity."

To Layman Lianxi, he showed the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury: "With a hundred thousand pieces of gold girded at his waist, he went down to Yangzhou;
from of old accustomed to indolence, he had no other intent—when the wind is naturally clear, the waters flow of their own accord."

To the Chan practitioner Chongxuan, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury: the retinues of the Mara-king are all one’s own kin; the bright mirror facing the courtyard leaves no shadow unreflected;
ultimately, there is no room for even a single speck of dust.
To Layman Chen Haopu:
Sudden Enlightenment into the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. True light is fundamentally identical to worldly light;
the infinite fragrant cloud-canopies of the Avataṃsaka all return, through a mere gesture, within the range of one’s gaze.
To the Layman Jikang of Shifang:
Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. Within the City of Vaiśālī lies my own home; from within the palm of the great trichiliocosm, I lightly extract it.
The mark between the brows radiates brilliance as the shadow of the stupa slants away.
Showing Master Zhuo Wuliang the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opening the precious treasury: the golden needle piercing the hole is no difficult task.
At the depth of night, weary of listening to the fishermen’s songs, he rides the clouds with the moon and descends upon the green sands.

Showing Layman Xiong □□ his sudden awakening to the source of the mind and opening the treasure storehouse: neither honor nor disgrace belong to the home of the Way-man. A single length of white silk follows him;
stir it even slightly and it becomes as tangled as hemp.
To Layman Xu □□: Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. Wherever one’s feet tread, every place is green mountains.
If you would not give rise to intellectual interpretations of the Buddha-dharma, shatter your worldly toil and learn how to be at ease.

To Layman Guo Xuanlang, I show the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury. After the meal, he takes up his staff and joyfully practices walking meditation. He has plucked all the willow branches hanging by the stream;
how can you compare this to the eyebrows? What do you say?
I show you, Layman Shen-er, the sudden awakening to the source of the mind and the opening of the precious treasury. Through the conditions of arising consciousness, one realizes the primordial body;
like the lotus root sprouting from within the mud, one smiles at dwelling in the dust yet remaining unstained by it.

Showing the Elder Duanyu the Sudden Enlightenment of the Source of Mind and the Opening of the Treasure Store: Whether south of the Yangtze or north of it, there is no need to distinguish. The sound of the stream and the color of the mountains are the meaning of the West;
Ten thousand miles of blue sky, ten thousand miles of clouds.
The Venerable Shiyingshi suddenly awakened to the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury. A clear, piercing breeze comes from the river;
having attained the phrase of resonance through conditions, he has trampled the moss upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
He showed the Three Pitaka Hall, where the Chief Administrator suddenly realized the source of the mind and opened the precious treasury. Picking up rubble and stones, they surpassed gold;
having traveled throughout Jambudvīpa to seek a kindred spirit, he finally returned to the Jetavana Grove upon attaining his heart's desire.
To Qixia’s Chief Administrator:
Sudden Enlightenment to the Source of Mind, Opening the Treasure Trove. After the fragrance of the osmanthus comes the fragrance of the chrysanthemum;
at dawn, facing the mirror and scrutinizing one's features, one finds they are originally Zhao Dalar of the Eastern Village.
For the sake of the Chan practitioner Sixxue entering retreat, I reflect back upon the old Yunmen of former days; his "Guān" (Gate/Retreat) character was a response to the most supreme capacity.
He entrusted it to the practitioner Bo-shan Yin, lest he should fail to honor the brow of Cuiyan.
For the sake of the Chan practitioner Six Snows as he leaves the cloister to begin the Great Matter: For six years, Six Snows entered sudden, perfect clarity like a single sheet of ice;
today, fortunately, he has personally encountered the seamless stupa, wrenching open thousands upon thousands of layers of locks.
The Four Public Cases, presented by the Seat-Holder Six-Snow (Liu Xue):
No trace, no place to hide the body. Where the body is hidden, there is no trace. Swallowing the waters of the sea, the golden-scaled leviathan leaps forth;
only then, upon the clear river, do the flowers appear in profusion.
What object comes in such a manner? The waves on the road to Caoxi roar like thunder. To describe it as a single thing is not the point;
at Mount Dayu, the net is spread wide to turn back [delusions].
Do not dwell where there is a Buddha; run swiftly past where there is no Buddha. Three thousand miles away, pluck the willow blossoms;
when meeting people, do not speak of the worn-out meditation cushion.
Three catties of hemp, a dried piece of excrement—no sooner grasped than the pathways of the mind are exhausted. You have torn through the Chan master’s iron mask;
the meditation seat is as bright as the moonlight at the third watch.
To Layman Fang Shixiong (Three Poems) The thousands of sages and myriad saints have taught that all is but mind;
If you recognize this, you should sing and chant in joy. Within, it is clear and bright—there is not a single thing;
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all pure gold.
Neither Buddha, nor mind, nor any material thing—your weary body has labored in vain, tasting only bitterness and hardship. The sensory objects appearing before you are as clear as if washed;
I shall point each one out to you in detail.
A single drop of the spiritual source never changes its color; it is neither of the present, nor of the past, nor is it new.
Cutting off the ten directions and shifting one’s step once more—it is not the Xiang River, nor is it Qin.

I show my thanks to Layman Zai zhi, who has recognized Yunmen’s "One-Character Chan. Sentient beings and all Buddhas are fundamentally of the same marketplace; when the occasion arises, he further asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey:
"The lotus flowers on dry land, each and every one, are fresh."
To show that Master Wang Xinjing responds immediately to the occasion is not difficult; yet, when neither "contrary" nor "touching" applies, it lies within the subtle interval of the essential pivot.
To observe these transformations amidst a great mass of fire, the True Text does not wish to reveal its full markings.
To the Layman Wu Dingfu:
Wherever you turn your head, there is no place without green mountains. The ancestral meaning lies within a single glance;
if you recognize where the flower was not yet plucked, neither right nor wrong shall reach the countenance of Kāśyapa.
Showing the Monk Xuánjīng’s Cutting of His Thigh to Heal His Mother (Two Verses):
Born from the essence of the father and the blood of the mother, One must believe that from the start one has been utterly destitute to the bone.
If this skin-sack were to be cut away entirely, Who would be "I," and who would be "another"?
In this world, there is no one as filially devoted as the Buddha. A youth’s heart should also emulate him. At the gateway of illusion, open a single eye;
you must also remember the moment the sword was drawn.
To Shi He Zhiyue, Minister of Rites (Two Poems):
The Way is attained when the stream is deep and the ladle’s handle is long; Forget all deliberation regarding empty flowers and mirages. Cast east and west this treasure within your robes;
Though your tongue reaches the three thousand worlds, do not vainly raise it in praise.

How could worldly truths ever fetter the conditions for transcending the world? Chasing the wind and pursuing the sun, arrows fly from the bowstring. When the occasion arises, meeting face-to-face is like receiving a direct transmission;
the pact is sealed and the oath sworn, with no need to count the years.
To Mr. Yuan Danyu, District Magistrate:
In autumn, the leaves of Jambudvīpa have fallen away; why then do the yellow chrysanthemums bloom in the ninth month? Only consciousness persists, following its transformations;
observe with cool detachment as it swirls away and returns.
To Chan Master Xuehang:
Having traversed ten thousand peaks and myriad mountains, you met people and deliberately displayed your folly and simplicity.
Once you saw through the moon upon the branches, you first realized that the clear pool is cold to its very bottom.
To Chan practitioner Chang’an:
Once you have recognized true permanence, then dwell in the hermitage. Let your *kāṣāya* robe be as tattered and frayed as you please; take tangerine-peel tea for your midnight snack;
gaze at the moon while singing by the cup, and descend into the emerald depths.
To Zen practitioner Zhuan:
A single sheet of idle clouds returns to the ridge; three thatched huts nestle by a mountain bend. The universe is wrapped within the folds of the *kāṣāya*.
Today, it is clearly entrusted to Damei.
To Zen practitioner Bin-ying:
Dwell as you please in this three-room thatched hut; let your two eyebrows unfold by themselves. Truly exhaust the thieving mind until it is utterly dead;
only then will you know that this cloth bag is as alive as a deity.
Showing Chan Practitioners Beyond the Mundane (Two Poems) The waters flow on as I see off the departing boat; Only the remaining journey through Jiangnan remains for this fine excursion.
Having traversed every inch of my native land, I shall surely laugh upon my return from atop the chaotic peaks.
A truly wondrous matter beneath the heels: how can one shake off worldly conditions to transcend them?
If a Chan practitioner truly knows that the lamp is fire, why would Niaoke need to use a blade?
Showing the Floating Chan Practitioner Shizhao on His Pilgrimage (Two Poems) I ask you, have you ever read the five-carriage library?
Your writings, composed with brush and inkstone, seem to be more than sufficient. I have already shaken my whip—do you believe me?
Upon returning home, you shall surely laugh at yourself for riding a donkey backward.
Riding backward upon a donkey toward Yangzhou, it surpasses the crane-riding excursions of yore. What a realm lies by the Shaopo River?
Amidst the depths of mist and clouds, the waters flow on endlessly.
To Chan practitioner Hanchen:
Several times you have dreamed of entering your old hometown. You needlessly speculate about barley rice and leek soup. Having traversed mountains and rivers, what is the point?
You simply must personally see your own father and mother.

Shown to the Zen Practitioner Xizhi (Three Poems) The essential matter of the Zen school is as bright as snow; It is soft as a diamond and hard as mud. Walking at night without cause, one must surely hold a torch;
One must know that there are heights and depths beneath one's feet.
Clearly two mouths, yet not a single tongue; tossing soil and raising dust without ceasing. Suddenly emerging from the sea gate is the great sun-disk;
it turns out, after all, to be the moon of Silla.
When one strides freely across the clay ox, One blows the iron flute crosswise and sings new verses.
Though it may press out sweat from every pore, To whom shall this load of pure wind be entrusted?
To Zen practitioner Hengyi:
For many years you have maintained a single, earnest heart in seeking your kin; regardless of the distance traveled, you have reached the highest peak.
Today, you return by the same path you came, and upon your arrival, you shall behold your own father and mother face to face.
Jiurú, the Head of the Monastery, bears this burden with extraordinary resolve. With iron brows and copper heads, he is truly a match for the task.
Having exhausted many bitter and sour flavors, only now does he perceive the fragrance of the vegetable root.
A Parting Gift for Chan Practitioner Zhizhi, Sending the Master Back to Zhejiang:
With sincere and special devotion, I see you off as you return to Zhejiang. When you go from here, may you return on this very day. Do not say that the scenery by the river is different;
every year in the ninth month, the chrysanthemums bloom.
To Chan practitioner Pomi:
Carrying his mendicant’s staff across your shoulder, you enter Mount Jing; how could you fail to believe that the skull is cold amidst the wind and frost? Gather it securely atop the thousand peaks;
if you say the rugged path makes each step more difficult, you have not yet seen the true way.

I observe that the practitioner of the first dhyāna who enters the mountain pass returns just as he did when leaving it. His *kāṣāya* tightly wraps his belly, yet he is hungry; today he has not prepared offerings for the mountain peak.
Amidst the lingering clouds and trees, he goes wherever he pleases.
To Zen practitioner Baoyan:
Why do you hasten only toward the west of Yuzhang? Let not your iron staff complain of the mud beneath your feet. Cast your gaze far out over the banks of the River Bi;
the crimson disk rises in a swirl, accompanied by the cry of a single cock.

When the Chan practitioner who demonstrates self-mastery hears the heavenly flowers falling in profusion, the essential matter of the Zen school must be known through personal realization. With a single turn of the body, he brushes past the crown of Vairocana;
such a one is a true cub of the golden-maned lion.
To Zen Practitioner Yinwen (Three Poems) Recognizing the Seal-Text Face-to-Face at the Critical Moment,
One Resolutely Refuses to Let Worldly Thoughts Disturb the Mind. Simply let the frost and snow melt away,
And there will naturally be the spring of a single branch of spiritual life.
The supreme treasure has never been contained within the six sense-faculties; it roams freely within the realm of the faculties and their objects.
One morning, when the entire framework is overturned, both the middle and the two ends are shattered asunder.
Dreams, illusions, bubbles, and flowers are easy for people to understand; do not harbor doubts regarding these bubbles, flowers, dreams, and illusions.
At the point where worldly conditions are thoroughly integrated, they are as soft as diamond and as hard as mud.
To Shi Yin and others, attendant Kun said:
"The blue mists hang upon the layered cliffs of the Azure Stone; this exquisite adornment adds flowers upon brocade. Turning my head, I suddenly see the road to Mount Kuang;
before the Five Elders' Peak lies a living snake."
For the Zen practitioner Xiao Yu:
The watchman’s calls and the dripping water are quite in harmony; yet in the blink of an eye, one becomes a common "Old Eight.
When one awakens to the clarity of day, there is nothing else—this Dharmakāya is originally but a stinking skin-sack.
To Zen student Shilang:

On the stone cliffs of the Long River, waves surge toward the heavens; the willows on the banks and the flowers upon the crags are likewise dazzling. I am most pleased by the moon at the bottom of the clear pool;
to open one’s eyes costs nothing of straw sandals.
To Chan practitioner Mu:
When encountering conditions, do not feign exhaustion by saying "enough. Examine closely the Five-Character Ox of Mount Guishan.
If you can truly believe that empty space can be ground into powder, where will you go when you have no body beyond the kalpas?
To the Zen practitioner Xuanchuan:
The profound path does not involve verbal explanation; having crossed over, one still boards the bottomless boat. How could the other shore admit even a trace of dharma?
When meeting people, one simply exchanges greetings of "How are you? and "Are you well?"
Showing the Way to Zen Practitioners (Three Poems) The road traveled on foot these past years has grown ever longer; amidst the drifting white clouds, do not let your progress falter.
The robe and bowl remain at Dayu Pass even now—can you bear their weight with all your strength? Can you move them?
Having traversed ten thousand mountains and myriad peaks, the skin of one’s feet is worn while the skin of one’s mouth remains calloused.
Not a trace of warmth is found throughout the entire body; the torch is clearly seen face-to-face.
The attendant has not yet grown weary after three years; his heels have been shaken much by the evil winds. No one here recognizes the Buddha-dharma;
who would be willing to move the tuft of cloth at this very moment?
The Zen practitioner at the ordination ceremony cuts off their natural hair as the occasion demands; the *maṇi* jewel atop the crown is revealed. I entrust this to all people:
look up with eyes wide open! This time, you see the Red-Bearded Barbarian face-to-face.
To Chan practitioner Fuzhong:
Fuzhong has completely eradicated all views and knowledge. This fierce man has never kept books; every single word and phrase has been cast out.
Turning his body around, he laughs at Zhaozhou for being "without."

To the Chan practitioner Yin Zong, I show the seal that shatters the school’s tenets and strengthens the iron ox. Roaming freely south and north of the stream, one day it suddenly breaks through the nose-ring and returns;
there stands a single beast, covering the earth and obscuring the heavens.
Clouds arise from the valley as the first dhyāna is shown;
the valley gives birth to clouds. Amidst the gathering masses, Jetavana possesses a spring of its own. As the precious incense seals vanish, the monks rise from their meditative absorption;
Before the steps, the rain of flowers falls in profusion.
To Layman Chen Zhiwang:
You must cultivate the field of your own home; diligently tend the oxen and sheep, lest they stray from the herd. Within, the sacred sprouts must be sown early;
when the time comes, the rain of flowers will fall in profusion.

Demonstrating that departure is not for those who lack meditative concentration, one naturally ceases to crave the flavor of fragrant bait. Three meals of tea and rice are as sweet as honey. When the blood in the tongue-organ is exhausted, the light of the sūtras appears;
one should then head toward the deep mountains to cultivate purple mushrooms.
The precious mirror displayed before the hall—how can it contain anything? Within its gaze, all images have completely vanished. Its wondrous embrace is total and without leakage;
do not vainly mix this precious treasure with empty voidness.
To the Chan practitioner Yin Kong, he showed that the four great elements are fundamentally not the self; he broke through the mother-born iron mask.
When the discourse reached the point where celestial flowers fall in disarray, the stone woman before the cliff gives birth to a child at night.
Shown to Imperial Commissioner Shen Donghua:
After finishing a single meal of vegetarian fasting, drink a cup of tea; sweep the floor, burn incense, and recite the Lotus Sūtra.
It is fortunate that within this there is nothing else; do not let the black bean sprout again.
To Layman Zhizhuan: When hungry, eat your rice;
when cold, add a layer of clothing. This is precisely the time for Vimalakīrti to maintain his silence. Do not say that the north wind cannot blow through;
though the weather is freezing, it is precious that everyone knows this.
To the Layman Gubang:

Raise your eyebrows and do not be indolent; you must diligently shoulder the matters of the Dharma-gate. When the day comes that you strike through the tip of your finger, you will realize for the first time that everything prior was entirely mistaken.
To the Layman Qiaoyang, I show that the ancestral wind of Shaoshi has no separate dharma: from of old, the mountain stream has been as blue as indigo;
atop Mount Wutai, the golden-haired lion appears—look through and see through both the three before and the three after.
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Nineteen;
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Twenty.
Compiled by Honghan, Dharma Grandson of [Chan Master] Boshan.
Verses on the Teaching for the Assembly, by the Senior Seat and Dharma Grandson Hongyu (6).
When the lay practitioner Liu Hehe was departing for the imperial examinations, [the Master] sent him off with straw sandals and simultaneously presented these four verses.
A verse once heard: "Barefoot, he descended upon Tongcheng; this morning the layman walks thus. His straw sandals are fastened tight, yet both toes are exposed;
he shall surely cause the sound of thunder to be heard upon level ground."
Where the osmanthus fragrance lingers, the true mechanism is revealed; this is precisely the moment of passing the imperial examination with an empty mind.
If there is a wild goose in the high winds north of Yan, ask the idle one to send a poem to Boshan early.
Straw sandals tread upon the roads of Chang’an; straight ahead, one enters the highest tier of the Golden Terrace. Upon the wall, a monk looks up with keen eyes;
he shall well carry on the transmission of the Dharma lamp.
The heels touch the ground as auspicious lotuses bloom; atop the ten-thousand-fathom peak, one returns with realization attained.
When asked, "Where can one find these straw sandals? he replies, "I have been to Bo Shan."
Showing Zhou Kencheng, the lay practitioner, playing with a fishing rod while adrift in the midst of the sea of suffering: let him follow the eddies and currents without interference.
Though he might swallow every drop of the Western River, the entirety of the sand-grained worlds remains within a single sitting-cave.
I show Layman Faya Hu:
shaking out his body, not even a trace of Dharma remains. His wild nature is biased toward worldly entanglements;
had he recognized the Great Way at the outset, he would have put to shame the old woman of Mount Tai who points the way.

Showing that Layman Pingzai treats all things with an even mind is his constant practice; yet he governs heaven and earth with extraordinary novelty. The pearl in his robe stands out like common rubble;
it does not hinder him from finding the thoroughfare wherever he may be.

I show you that for Governor Yu, the crane is long and the duck is short—this is all natural. How does this compare to your family’s ability to sleep through the day? Though all the people in the world search for it, they do not find it;
the seal of the stars breaks through the moon in the midst of heaven.
**Parting from Peng Zhixian, the Xuebo:
Two Poems** When one dharma is empty, all dharmas are empty; where the myriad conditions are empty, their essence is identical.
In the grandeur of daily life there is nothing else—pointing it out, it is fully manifest within a single glance.
When walking freely atop the rain-swept mountains, I report to you that my mind has attained the highest rank. Who will shoulder the Buddha-dharma before our eyes?
Jade trees and pearl flowers reflect the green vines.
Beholding this portrait, the spirit of Layman Baolin as he grasps the brush is exceptionally wondrous. This sentiment can only be known by one's own mind. It truly captures his natural countenance;
for a thousand ages, people shall long for the times of antiquity.

The lay practitioner Huang Ziyi requested scriptures in order to seek a single half-verse and was willing to sacrifice his entire body. Today, as this lay practitioner walks in such a manner, who can testify that he has kicked his own finger through?
Upon ten thousand sheets of paper, the discourse on non-arising remains.

The Layman Sùzhēn requests scriptures and returns to gouge out his own flesh to light a lamp for the Dharma; his heels have trodden through many patches of moss. When the helm is firmly grasped, one travels through the swift current;
atop the mountain of shoes, upon the mountain peak, auspicious lotuses bloom.
A heart of iron is forged; fierce waves and wild winds clash against it. Today, looking back at the moon upon the mountain peak, who would say its feet are in a hurry?
Splitting open the dust of phenomena, I desire straightway to see the entire scripture; how could I refuse the boat and oars to sail across the distant ocean?
With strange rocks and wild winds piercing beneath me as I pass, only now do I truly say that the Buddha’s teaching is peaceful.

Traveling by both water and land, my mind is at ease; beyond the city walls of Shitou, I hasten toward Changgan. Amidst the boundless shadows of stupas and the seeds of radiant light, only today do I realize how difficult it was to encounter such a moment.
Chan Master Yue Shan shows that one does not traverse stages along the path; one simply desires to walk upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
If you should personally encounter Kāśyapa Muni face-to-face, ask him: "Where is the place of dependent origination?"
Shown to the Disciples of Qinglin on the Banks of the Jian’an River (Three Poems) We have met but suddenly half a year has passed;
With hair in twin-tails like young girls, you have skillfully grasped the primordial [truth]. The precious seals have long been submerged as the palace drips grow cold;
I pray you take this fragrant water to offer to Vairocana.
Against the current lie tier upon tier of rapids; meeting after a thousand li, parting is difficult. On the return journey, stone horses seem to collide;
deep gorges and secluded forests lie within a mere glance.

Coming, it brings coolness; departing, it dispels the sultry heat. It has earned for itself a reputation that the mountains loathe as rank and foul. Today, by the riverbank, where can one find solace?
There remains only the lightness of a single leaf-like skiff.
To the Assembly of Zen Practitioners (Two Poems) On a single blade of grass, a jade tower appears;
It sucks dry the four hundred prefectures of China. Having won the pure breeze that dries one’s white sweat, What need is there to specially bestow anything that would cause others to grieve?
The heavens are high and the earth deep; I ask for the origin of this matter. Staff and shout fly back and forth, never ceasing.
Even changing one's bones and washing one's entrails is still not it—Who knows that within the house one is peddling Yangzhou?
To Layman Yang Lansi:
At the peak of Mount Touzi, years are not recorded; Zhaozhou turns back the "old woman’s Chan. One must go there in person at night;
only now is this public case brought to completion.
To Zen Practitioner Longquan of Fuhu Monastery (Two Poems) One snake and one tiger always follow him;
When confronted face-to-face, he does not yield. When he cannot let go, he carries them away;
Thus he wins the clouds atop the ridge for his *kāṣāya*.

When Jinxi was engaged in combat in his prime, the spiritual nature of a beast was already somewhat known. Now that he has realized the matter of Gehu, his conduct through a thousand years of tradition shall not waver from its course.
The boat-dwelling on Shan Water and the traces of horses—how could these dusty footprints not be possible? Joyfully following upon the water’s surface, he accompanies the Chan monks;
his rope bed is settled amidst the horns of the black dragon, and beneath the long embankment of slender willows, he continues the ancestral lamp.
To the Chan practitioner Sizong, who has abandoned his mountain hermitage to wander as a cloud-dwelling traveler: with satchel, gourd, and straw hat, you joyfully seek rest from toil.
Although you have pointed out the path facing the sun, one must remain cautious of slippery stones at the fork in the road.
A Memorial for Laywoman Jiang Yige’s Mother (Two Poems) Chastise away the clay ox and wooden horse;
Horizontally hold the jade thread and golden needle. Stitching out the brocade of ultimate emptiness— Why need one seek it elsewhere?
From the beginning, you have never been a sentient being; what need is there to further seek a living Buddha? Who is it that emits light and shakes the earth?
It is called the single thing of true nature.
To the Layman Lianmaoyu (Four Poems).
A human life lasts a hundred years; the workings of destiny are like drifting clouds. A priceless pearl lies within one’s robes—I point it out clearly to you.
How long can this world endure? Examine your worldly attachments with care. There is no end to rising and falling; as they revolve in turn, one’s very pores grow cold.
When desire is few, the spirit is tranquil; when there is no anger, the breath is naturally pure. If one practices with this understanding, what need is there to ask about longevity?
What is essential is only compassion and forgiveness; a compassionate heart is the Buddha-mind. To realize that compassion is the Buddha is to not seek it elsewhere.
Pointing out the Way and Opening Zen:
People gather to drink tea; these people transcend by one grade. There is no need for all-night practice. The dew wets their robes, cold.
Pointing out the one who releases living beings (two stanzas).
I contemplate the thoughts of those that fly and those that hide; their craving for life is the same as mine. Yet they harbor no karma of enmity; why, then, are they trapped in nets and cages?

When they turn their heads toward the sun upon the water, or when they beat their wings in the air—could it ever have been their intention to seek glory and rank? Moved by compassion, I report this to you, Your Majesty, so that you may know.
To Magistrate Huang Hai'an (Four Poems):
The people’s wealth is my own wealth; the people’s flesh is my own flesh. I drink no wine and eat no meat—this is the stipend of a high minister.
He practices objectless compassion and exercises coessential pity. Whether to nurture or to punish, he must consider who is involved.
He regulates through legal codes and sustains through ritual propriety; regarding good and evil, the worthy and the foolish, he treats them as if they were his own self.
One should take the seashore as one's object of focus. Raise the great banner of the Dharma. From every pore of the body, let the fragrance of sandalwood be emitted.

With a mind of pure faith in cause and effect, do not harbor even a single grain of rice for oneself; do not maintain distinctions between self and others. [This is the teaching for escaping] the seven hells of fruit.

Two hungry ghosts with cakes; even the slightest deception is worse than poisoned water. A single bolt of silk or a single coin; a pig’s head and a donkey’s feet—these are the signs of one’s sins and blessings.
Observe the Tathāgata’s injunctions; selling precious longevity-ginger; lighting a lamp at a stone window—a pungent sharpness that lasts for a thousand years.
Eternal radiance throughout the ten thousand ages!

We address you, O Master of Transformation and Field of Merit for all sentient beings. Before the Wheel of Dharma has yet been turned, sustenance must first be provided. Be it a single grain of rice or an inch of silk—each is essential.

The wise can be intimidated. Brick money, tile money—throughout antiquity and today, these have been called strange and marveled at. Holding Linji’s bowl and tallying Dahui’s ledger, they come along together.
They laugh the Great Enlightenment (Yuánwù) to a standstill; the ancient mirror has not yet been polished. You must now provide a turning word: "Before the Yellow Crane Tower."

Soaring alone beyond all peers—consult you, O Supervisor of the Monastery. Uphold both the manifest and the subtle; through diligence, frugality, and hard work, who but you could renounce these? Receive guests with propriety.
He harmonized and comforted the assembly, placing others before himself. He was a pillar and beam of the Dharma-gate.

Even a pinch of salt the size of a fingernail, or a benefit as fine as a tortoise hair—if there were a moment’s lapse, one would fall headlong into the earth. The ancient Master of Yangqi ultimately fulfilled the compassionate mandate; his pure radiance required no polishing.
The Lamp of the Dharma is perpetually recorded.
I address you, the kitchen steward: transforming the raw into the cooked, let it be in accord with the Dharma alone. Within the rice is the gruel; this is drawing the bow of Zhang Shigong.
Masters Laoan and Nanyue once entered the grass; they pulled back their noses and followed the words of the Tathāgata, believing the lion’s roar.
When the entire assembly received a single ladle of molten copper poured into their mouths, both sages and worthies were occupied with this labor. [But] one kicked over the pure pitcher.
He stepped out and hurried away.

*The Verse on the Pure Land (with Preface)* In the past, the Venerable Master Yunqi took the single phrase "Amitābha" and spread it throughout the world like the sound of a lute. People vied with one another to call him the "Ancient Amitābha."

I was reborn [in this life]. In my early twenties, my heart was deeply moved by the desire for refuge. Later, while traveling as a wandering monk, I was driven by adverse winds into the region of Min.

Having entered the threshold of the *zongcheng* (the Great Vehicle), I relegated the Buddha-remembrance practice to the high shelves. In the year Jihai, I returned after receiving full ordination at Mount Ehu.

I engaged in conversation with both monastics and laypeople regarding the "true nose" (the essential core) of the Patriarchs; finding no one with whom I could truly speak, I again recalled that the kindness and compassion of my late teacher were so great that they were difficult to repay.
Thereafter, I also frequently recited the six characters of Amitābha, forming a connection for one hundred thousand recitations toward the Western Pure Land.
Some raised an objection, saying: "The Master is a guest under the lineage of the Zen school; why do you carry about such mundane household furniture? I replied: "Alas! What words are these?
The Pure Land of Lotus Flowers is where all the Patriarchs have flocked. How would I dare conceal my affinity for it?
I have penned one hundred and eight verses with my brush to awaken both the monastic and the lay. Whether you call it Zen or call it Pure Land, let people do as they please."

This is a program for the vigorous practitioner. It has nothing to do with the affairs of an old monk. Recorded on the fifth day after the Buddha-bath ceremony in the summer of the Xinyou year of the Tianqi era:
"The pure mind is itself the land of the West; walking everywhere throughout the West without shifting a step, the shadowless tree-top is not a form."
Phenomena: the moment a thought stirs, one is immediately fragmented.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; when the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name fades, who am I?
Thoroughly overturning the den of the word "who," the living Amitābha dwells within the village of three families.
A pure mind is itself the Western Land; why need one rely on Gautama’s ten thousand scrolls? With a single clap of thunder, both ears go deaf;
the whole body is squeezed into Zhaozhou’s “No.”
The pure mind is the Western Land; it rends apart Jambudvīpa and causes one to go and return.
It makes the hours and seasons run in reverse, where golden sands and water surfaces open with wondrous lotuses.
The pure mind is the Western Land; when mountains topple and valleys overflow, who am I? Before Mount Shaoshi, I have personally crashed through;
amidst the fierce flames of the red furnace, snowflakes fly.
A pure mind is precisely the Western Land; yet being entangled by shared conditions brings calamity upon oneself. The five aggregates and six sense organs are reduced to dust;
left all alone, one’s laughter is both amusing and startling.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; only by arriving there in person can one discern one's own ancestors. Drink dry the clear river and cast your gaze far upward;
the sun shines red in the bottom of the mirror-clear water.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West. The metaphor of turning iron into gold is not uniform;
if you grind it finely, it becomes a trivial matter. Do not let it be to no avail, O monk!
A pure mind is the Western Land; with staff held level, one walks carrying a cloth bag. Bought at a high price, it is sold again cheaply;
the gate of compassion is priceless—there is no need to contend.

A pure mind is itself the land of the West; leaping across Kunlun, one enters the gate of the sea. Reaching the place where the water ends and the mountains exhaust themselves, there clearly emerges a distinct world of its own.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; a thousand sages have ascended together upon the bottomless boat.
Having smashed through sheer cliffs and crimson crags, only now do I realize my feet have been worn through.
A pure mind is the land of the West; sweeping the ground and burning incense are matters of practice. When two mouths do not open, white mold grows within;
of this state, only the wooden man knows.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; it is clear without being made so, and still without being stirred.
If you ask further where that Land of Bliss lies, take these words and teach them to your descendants.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; red dust from the ocean floor surges up as auspicious flowers. What has been accomplished through ten billion kalpas?
Today, for no other reason, this *kāṣāya* robe is offered.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; the waters of Chu and the roads of Qin are level and smooth. Zen practitioners, do not give rise to thoughts of high and low;
when the heels touch the ground, it is most clearly manifest.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the barefoot Persian enters the Great Tang. The priceless jewel suddenly emerges from within his robes;
this time, he shall not serve as a flower-seeking groom.
A pure mind is the Western Land; the embroidered universe is perfected through pure karma.
As soon as the single phrase "Namu Amitābha" is uttered, this lofty physical vessel becomes vast and clear.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; with one invocation of Amitābha, one Buddha is realized.
When the entire earth becomes a world of silver, where else could one look for the morning star?

The pure mind is itself the Western Land; it burns away the *kaṇṭaka* thorns of Jambudvīpa. Once the flesh-tight undershirt is completely cast off, the true master stands forth in majesty and solitary revelation.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the bright pearl atop the uṣṇīṣa need not be sought through personal effort.
Eighty thousand miles can be reached in a single snap of the fingers—do not let this auspicious moment go to waste.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; its brilliant rays of light are a springtime beyond the kalpas.
Even becoming a Buddha is still deemed too busy for this world—how could one find the leisure to follow the herd of deer?

The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the aggregates and elements are fundamentally empty, the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Among the myriad objects there is no person—whom can this be understood by?
A single bright moon shines upon the clear river.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; profound principles and esoteric discourses are all left unmentioned. Precious ducks vanish as the incense fades and the curtains roll up;
yet, in a place where there is no Buddha, one is proclaimed supreme.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the blue-eyed barbarian monk smiles and nods his head. To him, the *maṇi* gem that follows color is like a shard of tile;
who would speak of jeweled pavilions or towers of jade?
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the moon grows old and the ice withers as true pride arises.
Across the single band of clear sky lies infinite bliss; this manifest reality brooks no compromise.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; a single thought of non-arising cannot be called back. It is best to cut off both ends completely;
the spring breeze blows up the ashes from before the kalpa.
A pure mind is the Western Land; verbal claims have no foundation, for practice is what is most intimate.
When the worn wooden fish is struck lightly, how many flowers of rain fall in profuse confusion!
A pure mind is the Western Land; receiving guests and welcoming visitors as if they were never there.
Shaving the head with lightness and washing the bowl with purity—this is a solitary monk for whom heaven and earth are one.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; the *zhidu* robe originally weighed seven jin. One need only let the coarse hair grow until it forms a mat;
there is no need for prostrations or further earnestness.
A pure mind is the Western Land; in samādhi, worldly afflictions are entirely unknown. With wild greens and soup, one passes the days;
a single thought of non-arising transcends incalculable eons.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; one must know that even while snoring in sleep, one is already passing through it. Once awakened at dawn, there is nothing else:
the three meals and daily fare remain as they were before.

The pure mind is the land of the West; break the painted jar and return home. When you encounter the fire of the twelfth month beneath a shadowless tree, the spring breeze will favor the blossoming of the hundred flowers.
A pure mind is the land of the West; in the Ultimate Bliss, no sufferings whatsoever can invade. With a single utterance of Amitābha, light radiates brilliantly;
when the flower blooms, one beholds the Buddha—there is no need to seek further.
A pure mind is the Western Land; for six months, bitter frost covers the earth. At dawn, travelers on the road do not avoid it;
with an ice-cold heart, one’s spiritual resolve shines solitary and bright.
A pure mind is the Western Land; it protrudes the two eyes born of one's mother. It cuts off all four sages and six classes of beings;
its breast is cast of iron, devoid of worldly sentiment.
A pure mind is the Western Land; its rows of trees constantly bloom white jade flowers.
The elder leans against the gate, gazing all day long; why does the wanderer not return home?
A pure mind is the Western Land; the lotus leaf is not overturned by wind or waves. The golden fish that has passed through the net knows the currents of the water;
yet now, wherever one touches, there is only dullness and stubbornness.
A pure mind is the Western Land; rain falling and clouds rising are exceptionally wondrous. A single set of bones rings out clearly;
this resonant sound is intended for all to know.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; its waters of virtue are ever clear within the ponds of the seven treasures. From where does the essential Dharma enter?
It enters at the very moment a subtle breeze stirs the sound of thought.

The pure mind is itself the Western Land; the moon on the water, the pines, and the wind are thoroughly pure. Failing to recognize the true direction when facing [reality], what need is there for a Buddha to come welcome you at the moment of death?
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; transmitted through successive generations like flowers in a mirror.
If you can realize it is neither tree nor terrace, the original source has no ground from which the eternal sprout grows.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; when the tree falls and the vines wither, one is intimately present within the words. A great laugh—people do not understand it.
To come along with me is also a barrier and a checkpoint.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; its waters and birds constantly proclaim wondrous sounds. The Yellow-Faced Gautama’s compassion is truly boundless;
it all stems from a single heart of maternal concern.

The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the sacred traces upon the stone endure for ten thousand ages. If you can personally touch them with the tip of your staff, you are a great śramaṇa who clearly realizes there is nothing to do.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; vast and penetrating, it is without dependence and transcends both difference and sameness.
Clapping my hands and singing wildly for many kalpas, the blood splashing from my eyebrows has turned the Brahma Heaven red.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; treading upon and severing the bridge, one beholds the ancient village. In a mere flash, the constant radiance pierces through the skull;
wandering at ease through the three realms, one alone is called the Honored One.
A pure mind is the land of the West; in that Pure Land, one hears not the encroachment of cold or heat. Several gales of fragrant wind come across the waters;
boundless transformed birds all return to their forest.
The pure mind is the land of the West; a single phrase of Amitābha stands at the head of the path. When the house is ruined and the people gone, where can one go?
The gate of compassion requires no bait and needs no hook.

A pure mind is itself the Western Land; in chaos and confusion, nothing at all is formed. If one is willing to believe that Amitābha dwells within this turbid realm, one will hear only the sound of scattered flowers in the air.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; there, not even a needle may pass, yet chariots and horses traverse it freely.
Just as the cawing of crows upon the ancient tree has ceased, a single bright moon emerges, veiled in mist.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; the bright moon hangs in the sky, its light chilling the heart. An old man of a hundred years divides his night-torch;
he shakes his wooden clapper with vigor, laughing as the night draws to a close.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; wooden horses neighing in the wind pass through Han and Qin. Treading upon skulls, who is the master?
Old acquaintances from many years ago are all renewed at once.
A pure mind is the Western Land; it encompasses the void, whether dry or moist. Only the wildcat is truly ancient and strange;
he breaks into a smile two or three times.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land. When the monkey is squeezed to death, its head bursts forth. In ten billion kalpas, one arrives with a mere snap of the fingers;
there is a reason for Amitābha’s immeasurable presence.
A pure mind is the Western Land; the ancient stream and cold spring are difficult to swallow or spit out. To see Zhaozhou’s true face through and through:
he strides across and charges straight ahead, unconcerned with others.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the gosling within the jar is called forth. The master of oneself has long been lost in a dream;
with a single invocation of the Buddha’s name, there is no need for doubt.
A pure mind is the Western Land; filial piety fulfills Cao Shan’s fondness for wine and madness.
Having drunk dry the news of the Land of Bliss, one laughs to see the blue lotus bloom amidst the blazing flames.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; within the light of formlessness lies the body with form.
When the mind and its objects entangle one another, they become a ghostly play; who is the self, and who is the person?
A pure mind is itself the land of the West. Even the words of the upward-transmitted lamp are not it. Within the illusory painting, open a single eye;
what need is there to further inquire into the profound mystery?
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; how could it ever be expressed by opening one's mouth? Only the summit of Tongxuan Peak is permitted;
upon the Stone of Ten Thousand Years, green moss grows forever.
A pure mind is the land of the West; to whom does this refreshing breeze descend?
With profuse sweat flowing in thick, dripping streams, one gains nothing but a body grown fat from piling it up.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the pillar and the lantern laugh without ceasing.
Having exhausted all the bitter flavors of the world, a lingering fragrance floats upon the meditation cushion.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the lute and zither have no strings, yet they are the music of primordial antiquity. Their resonance brings forth the infinite meaning of the ocean tide;
their sublime principles forever transcend past, present, and future.
A pure mind is the land of the West; when meeting people on a narrow path, one speaks of their merits and faults. When both ears are deaf, hearing becomes all the better;
who can then distinguish the *gong* and *shang* scales with a local accent?
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; it cannot be depicted even with colored brushes. On the stone bed in the deep night, there is no companion;
with one deep snore, the dawn has already broken.

A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; dwelling alone on a solitary peak, the realm is even more remote. Before the ten-thousand-fathom cliff, one personally glimpses the ground of enlightenment;
a trace of it is carried upon the corner of the *kāṣāya*.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; one must know that beyond the teachings there is a separate path to tread.
If you are a guest in the school of the Patriarchs, a breaking smile is truly beyond the discussion of non-arising.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; there, *utpala* flowers bloom in profusion upon rootless trees. Do not permit the old barbarian to be so habituated to idleness;
the scenery of "tortoise-hair" is as chaotic as hemp.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; though the ancient melody exists, those who can harmonize with it are rare. In days of yore, Mount Gui personally entrusted this teaching;
the five characters were inscribed in large script upon a hide.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; wearing a woolen robe, he responds to the occasion with a basket of flowers and medicine. He further asks how many people are here:
"Three times three before, and three times three after."
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; who has ever dreamed of it being poured from a flask? The old man with missing teeth merely faced the wall;
the one flower and five petals bloom to this day.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; does the leather bag still know pain and itch? What realm is it that turns heaven and earth upside down?
Beyond the night-bright curtain lies the night-moon pearl.
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; there, one gazes upon immortal fruits and rare blossoms glistening with dew.
As soon as the golden-colored dhūta beholds them, the long sword leaning against the heavens strikes one with its chilling majesty.
A pure mind is precisely the land of the West. Turn the collar of the robe inside out and wear the leather boots upside down.
If you are a true child of Shao Yang, you may seize or release Xuefeng’s snake at will.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West. A turtle entering the water walks upon dry land;
having completely shed its skin, fur, and even its marrow, it is now particularly pitiable.
The pure mind is the Western Land; crushing the clay pellets poses no obstacle at all. The Amitābha of one’s own nature has neither front nor back;
from the broad and long tongue comes the wondrous fragrance of the lotus.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West. Great scholars, do you recognize this clenched fist? Herein, victory and defeat are never divided;
when the moment arrives, what need is there to brandish weapons?

A pure mind is the Western Land; it is difficult to set foot at the head of a steep, rushing rapids. Having personally traversed rough stones and deep pits, do not treat Amitābha with indifference when He stands face-to-face before you.
A pure mind is itself the Western Land; seizing food and driving oxen in farming is far too much toil.
How does this compare to the useless fellow Lan Can, who meets people with a smile and raises his empty fist?
A pure mind is the Western Land; even a three-year-old child would have his hair turned white.
After reading through the secular classics and histories, one sees clearly that nothing exists, and sleeps soundly with a deep snore.
A pure mind is the land of the West. At the end of the year, one burns many paper offerings; clapping hands, one encounters the new sun and moon once more.
Amidst a mass of myriad flowers, one beholds the dragon lying asleep.
A pure mind is the Western Land; meeting in form, a raised eyebrow yields two or three [realizations]. The ancient path no longer bears the traces of carts or horses;
a tongue without bone is surely the compass needle.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West. Wearing hair and keeping a beard signifies a man of integrity.
As soon as the crimson-tailed golden-scaled one leaps forth, the clear pool has no water, yet the waves are coarse.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West. When the realm of Māra is empty, the realm of the Buddha is empty.
When the drifting clouds of the world have been gathered in entirely, a single orb bursts forth, making the heavens and seas crimson.

A pure mind is itself the Western Land. A Persian man reading Sanskrit scriptures in the marketplace—Baizhang spoke with such great confidence in his day that he is still called "The Red-Bearded One" to this very day.
A pure mind is the Western Land; flowers dancing in the void, a head in a mirror.
Having seen through these two wondrous matters, one sits upright within the house peddling Yangzhou.

A pure mind is itself the land of the West. Joining the ranks and following the crowd, I provide gruel and rice for the Sangha; once satiated, there is no concern other than the healing of the wounds of hunger.
With earnest devotion, I offer lamps before the Buddha.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; in an ancient temple, serene and secluded, the moon shines through the window. At midnight, a mouse is caught beside the bed;
at dawn, it flies out as a pair of embroidered mandarin ducks.
A pure mind is the land of the West; the pupil in the eye strikes the embroidered ball. Fretting over worldly affairs is never finished;
let all be empty and at rest, and simply desist.
The pure mind is itself the land of the Western Paradise. Coral on the ocean floor gazes toward the moon; the Unicorn Dragon King opens his eyes to behold it.
On the rugged, ancient path, few people travel.
A pure mind is the Western Land; poison and nectar are held in a single vessel. From the beginning, the power to kill or give life has resided within me;
whether releasing or grasping, there is no need for alarm.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; the "Dark Pearl of the Unseen" is not worth mentioning. To truly understand this flavorless phrase of the Old Monk:
flies scurrying over the back of a broken donkey.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; calling out to drive away the "tortoise-nosed snake" of the Southern Mountain is nothing but idle chatter once the jest is over.
Upon the tree, there is no shadow, yet the crows cry out in confusion.
A pure mind is the land of the West; amidst the vast expanse of dust, one turns back from chasing the deer. Only those who follow the current do not receive the transmission;
in the Gate of Chan, there is no phrase, yet it resounds like thunder.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; it is like a brazier of cold ashes where all has been swept away.
There is no need to blow it red-hot nor douse it with water; three meals of tea and rice suffice for all.
A pure mind is the Western Land; a tattered cassock is worn in disarray. Do not say this old fellow lacks strength;
within his bag he harbors a red-spotted snake.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; the boulders have no roots, yet the bamboo shoots have not yet emerged. The great ocean remains undisturbed through the night rain;
the wooden man dances and sings upon the wondrous lotus boat.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; if one is born there, one does not move a step from where one stands. Break open the Great Tang Empire and look within:
you must know that beneath your feet there are heights and depths.
A pure mind is the Western Land; a cricket in the fire swallows a large insect. As soon as a single thread of discriminative thought arises, mountains upon mountains and waters upon waters appear.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West. With a brow-raised gaze toward the West for eighteen thousand miles, a single snap of the fingers suddenly opens the unobstructed eye.
To reach the Western Land, one need not expend a single coin.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; the sea of suffering is as flat as a palm, without a ripple. The three thousandfold world cannot be lifted up;
with the whole body cast down, the dream is finally awakened.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; returning empty-handed from the alms-round, the belly remains unfed. What is the point of washing rice and grains?
It is simply because the *maṇi* jewel is within one’s robe.
A pure mind is the Western Land. Raising one's eyebrows scares people to death. When Zen travelers meet, they depart with a snap of the fingers;
Danxia loses his tattered head-khafi.
A pure mind is itself the Western Land; transcending the world, one veils the light and goes wherever one wills. Exhaust all karmic conditions from beginningless time;
do not allow your fine fur to be traded away.

A pure mind is itself the land of the West; smoke rises from beneath the feet and light shines from behind the crown of the head. Long lost in the sea of suffering, one finds the Land of Peaceful Nurturing;
a single blade of reed shall serve as the Compassionate Vessel.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; one’s livelihood has always been as vast as heaven. Within this, there is fundamentally no written character to be found;
there is no need to bore into ancient parchments from a thousand years past.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; realization is identical to the state before awakening. Within this turbid and evil world there is no discrimination;
it is mostly because what lies beneath one’s feet is free from discrepancy.
A pure mind is the Western Land; it is a live sparrow within the throat of a fierce tiger. This ragged old monk has no concern for such things;
in my leisure, I write many poems of the Land of Bliss.
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Twenty.
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Twenty-One.
Compiled by Honghan, Dharma Grandson of [Chan Master Wuyi] at Boshan.
Compiled by the Chief Seat and Dharma Grandson, Hongyu, together with those who have gathered to respond to the teachings of the religious school;
Chapter One: A Single Session of Realization.

Liu Yinping, the Grand Astrologer Hongbing, asked: "Regarding the two gates of Zen and the Teachings, are they one or two? Now you say that 'investigation and awakening' (*cānwù*) is the primary meaning.
Should all the vehicles of the teachings then be completely discarded? Great doubt leads to great awakening; no doubt, no awakening."
For those who have no doubts, how can they be further developed? For those who ultimately do not awaken, how can they reach the final consummation?

Furthermore, there is another class who, having read the public cases (gong'an) extensively, mistakenly identify with the immediate occasion; this is called "realization" or "not"? Moreover, among those in the teachings, there are many who are clearly proficient [in these matters].
Regarding this gateway to awakening, is there a distinction or is there no distinction?

The Master said: "The Great Master Śākyamuni sat at the site of enlightenment for forty-nine years; at the very end, he held up a flower to show the assembly, and thus there arose the principle of the 'separate transmission outside the teachings.
Is it indeed the case that there is a separate transmission outside the teachings? The School (Zong) is the backbone of the Teachings (Jiao). As for the Teachings...
This is the very eye of the school. When one main cord is raised, all the eyes are opened.

To know only how to adjust the eyes while failing to recognize the cord is to be ignorant of the principle that the Way of Teaching (jiao) and the Way of Practice (zong) are one; this is what is meant by "a forked path within a forked path.
Those who are willing to take the direct route along the cord will find that every teaching has its own fundamental tenet (*zongzhi*). Having attained this...

The essential point is this: every single word and every single character constitutes the most supreme occasion for awakening. If one fails to recognize this essential point and becomes mired in the literal text, then even the school (zong) becomes nothing more than the teaching (jiao).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "It is like the sun suspended in the sky, shining everywhere; yet a child closes his eyes and says to himself, 'Why can I not see?
So it is with much learning. It further says: "It is like a poor man counting another's treasures; he himself has not even half a coin's share. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
They abandon what they have studied and recited; their memory fails and they no longer master the texts. Greedily attached to fame and profit, they frequent the households of the nobility.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Even if one could expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it would not equal practicing untainted karma for a single day."
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "To use the conceptualizing mind to measure the realm of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly;

it will never succeed. Thus, while one may use these teachings to examine and discern for oneself, if one does not know the fundamental source (*zong*), it is a matter of the person, not the teaching.
This is because the teachings have a thousand variations, whereas the source returns to a single consistency. The teachings require broad mastery of texts...
Regarding the meaning: our school prizes immediate, direct authentic practice (*shōsan*). Thorough mastery is not achieved through the effort of many days;

yet, authentic practice does not require even a moment’s interval. It is not a matter of the effort of many days. To seek its current, there is no need for even a moment’s interval; to reach its source, it is likewise so.
There are those who seek the current and thereby find the source, and there are also those who find the source and abandon the current. This, moreover—
It lies in the person, not in the teaching. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; having no gate is the dharma-gate. Furthermore, a verse therein says:
"Just as there is a skilled physician in the world who cures illness with wondrous medicines, so too do the Buddhas teach 'mind-only' for the sake of sentient beings.
Since the mind is thus taken as the essence, one must thoroughly penetrate through the literal text. The *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* speaks of "perfect luminosity."

To understand [this] is not to rely on mental activity. Generally speaking, for sentient beings prior to the stages of realization (*bhūmi*), there is nothing in their daily lives that is not mental activity.
If one does not engage in genuine inquiry and earnest investigation, how could one possibly comprehend such mental activity? Every movement, pause, and thought is nothing other than mental activity.
Ultimately firm and solid, it can never be attained [through mere study]. Therefore, one should know that the source (zōng) and its expansion (yǎn) within the teachings are one yet two;
the teachings return to the source, being two yet one. This shortcut for genuine inquiry and authentic investigation is called the "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha).

It is fully contained within the teachings; it does not involve the abandonment of the teachings. As the Great Master Gaofeng said: "The immeasurable, wondrous Dharma-gates are all the first step in Zen inquiry."

This is one meaning. If one is a true lion cub, they do not enter the herds of others. Before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* had yet opened its mouth, [the Buddha] entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings (*apramāṇārtha-samādhi*).
What is this "Immeasurable Meaning" if not the foremost? This continued until Śāriputra made his three requests for the Dharma to be preached.
The Buddha said, "I shall now explain the Dharma for you through its distinctions. Within that text, it says, "A single great cause and condition:
to open, reveal, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The original text subverts this by stating, "This Dharma cannot be understood through thought or discrimination.
Regarding these nine characters—"cannot be understood through thought"—how will you comprehend them? If you do not engage in genuine and earnest inquiry...
This is what is called "entering the sea to count its sands"; it is not the ultimate goal. Viewed from this perspective, the teachings cannot be discarded.

The essential point lies in grasping their fundamental principles. If one truly grasps the fundamental principles, then the teachings serve as a finger pointing the way, a raft for crossing over, a guide, an opening, and a supporting condition. How, then, could they ever be discarded?
Furthermore, it is said: "Great doubt leads to great awakening; without doubt, there is no awakening. Yet, for those who do not doubt, how can they be brought to realization?

If one truly possesses a pressing sense of urgency regarding birth and death, how could one help but doubt? If one does not doubt, it is simply because the urgency regarding birth and death is not keen enough.
It is like a cloud: when one’s breath ceases, where does one ultimately go? When one has not investigated the mind, one is led away by the karma of good and evil.
Since one no longer follows the lead of the karma of good and evil, where does one ultimately go?
Since you do not know where it has gone, how can you avoid doubting? If you do not doubt, you are a person with whom one cannot engage in discourse;
why then would you need to seek further awakening elsewhere? If you have indeed given rise to genuine doubt, even if you do not yet attain enlightenment, you will stand firm upon your own feet.
Do not give rise to a second thought; this is the very foundation for becoming a Buddha and founding a patriarchal lineage. To seek the ultimate elsewhere is not the ultimate at all.
If one reads the *gong'an* thoroughly yet mistakenly identifies with the immediate response (*dangji*), even if a thousand sages were to appear to save them, they could not do so.
