Chapter Six: The Power of Vows.

Question: Regarding the most supreme merit of generating the bodhicitta—the practice of a bodhisattva for the sake of both benefiting others and oneself—just as the bhikṣus made great vows before the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, for this purpose, those who hold official positions and have power and authority can easily accomplish everything.
However, for those who are humble and whose strength and resources are meager, what kind of vow-power should they cultivate to achieve merit?
"Virtue. The Master said: "The Dharma gates are immeasurable; may you serve as my guide. Whether mundane or supramundane dharmas, there is no aspiration that cannot be fulfilled.
'Aspiration' (praṇidhāna) means 'excellent' and it means 'desire. It is the desire to abandon all unwholesome dharmas, and the desire to shatter the fetters and afflictions of ignorance."
Because they wish to enter the profound dharma-gates of all bodhisattvas; because they wish to extensively practice wholesome dharmas to benefit sentient beings;

and because they wish to transform all living beings so that they may together attain the path of Buddhahood—if there were no aspiration, it would be like a painting without glue, like a horse without a bridle, or like a potter’s vessel:
though the raw clay has been formed, if it has not yet been fired in the kiln, it will ultimately be unfit for use. Therefore...
Beginner practitioners and all bodhisattvas take their vows as the foundation; therefore, they further strengthen them with great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). "Great" (*mahā*) means extensive;
"vow" (*praṇidhāna*) means to restrain. By means of these great vows, they extensively restrain their minds so that they do not fall back or regress.
When the Great Master Śākyamuni was on the path of practice, he made the Four Great Vows: "Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all.
Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all. Dharma gates are immeasurable; I vow to study them all. The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; I vow to realize it.
Now, by making the vow to deliver sentient beings, one will surely be able to deliver oneself. By entering this Dharma gate, afflictions will naturally be severed. This Dharma gate...
From this depth, the Buddha-way is spontaneously accomplished. To give rise to this vow, one must rely upon courageous wisdom and strength to empower oneself.
Like a person of great strength who possesses neither timidity nor weakness, and who never regresses, one enters directly into the Buddha-way;
such a vow is the most powerful. For this reason, at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha caused all the bodhisattvas...
He recalled his original vows, which universally and greatly benefit all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the gate of inconceivable wisdom.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas on the causal ground possess great power of wisdom and have made great vows.

This means that because one can crush enemies and adversaries, and because one cannot be bent or broken, one knows what is possible and what is impossible, as well as the absence of causes and evil causes.
The Confucian saying, "All day long striving diligently," is also an image of firmness and courage; for it is through self-exertion without ceasing that one enters the Way.
For a beginner, it refers to using courageous and powerful wisdom to subdue Māras and externalists, thereby entering the profound Dharma-gate. If one lacks this...
Regarding the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-bala*): it is like a seed that rots and decays in the absence of sunlight.

This power of aspiration is not something that only bhikṣus can generate; officials and ministers should also generate it. Furthermore, it is not only those with authority and rank who can generate it;
even all elders, lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), and even the most lowly and powerless, should all generate this vow. From oneself...
To deliver sentient beings: take all the merit one has cultivated and dedicate it entirely toward all beings in the great earth, so that they may together attain the Buddha-way.
This is the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). The awakened mind is precisely the bodhicitta. This mind cannot be generated partially; it must be generated in its entirety.

Furthermore, it cannot be generated intermittently; it should be generated at all times, generated repeatedly, generated in the presence of the Buddhas, and generated in the presence of the Bodhisattvas.

One should generate [this resolve] before the noble Saṃgha; one should also generate it before spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); and one should generate it before all monastic companions, all sentient beings, and the entire assembly of living beings.
By means of this great mind, one shall proceed until the attainment of Buddhahood, all due to the power of vows (praṇidhāna).
Therefore, know that the power of vows is the precursor to the Buddha-dharma. For example, if there is a person who thinks, "I wish to practice Chan meditation; I shall by no means fall back," then—
It is by the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). Not only virtuous aspirations, but even the desires of the world are all accomplished through the power of aspiration.
Long ago, there was a cart-pusher who did not believe in the Buddha-dharma. One day, while pushing his cart, he passed by the side of a stūpa and saw it being consumed by fire.
Unable to bear the destruction of its magnificent adornments, he stepped forward to save it. Having done so, he playfully made a vow, saying: "The Buddha has taught that..."
Regarding the law of karmic retribution: "I shall protect this precious stūpa; may I, in a future life, become one who is most tall, great, and powerful.
After casting off this body, may I be reborn in the realm of the asuras, with a body that is most tall, great, and powerful.
This vow made in play was fulfilled without fail; how much more so for a vow made with a true mind and a heart of utmost sincerity—there is no doubt it will be realized.
Regarding "fulfillment": just as one initially made a vow, one must carefully refrain from conceiving inferior thoughts and should instead resolve upon the bodhicitta.

Whatever roots of goodness—even the most minute—and whatever most sublime merits one cultivates, one should resolve that they all be dedicated toward all sentient beings so that they may together attain the Buddha-way.
Even if, in the midst of this, one should fall back or regress, one shall still rely upon the power of these vows.
It is like a person without sight who can move forward because they have someone to lead them. For those who cultivate the Pure Land, faith, practice, and vows serve as their provisions;
how could those who study Chan not take the power of vows as their guide?

If those living at home wish to abandon worldly toil, wish to leave the burning house, wish to transcend birth and death, and wish to escape the cycle of saṃsāra, it cannot be achieved without the strength of firm vows.
If that were so, one would be unable [to achieve it]. Therefore, one must give rise to great vows. How could one fail to resolve upon the Great Mind because of inferiority?
If one realizes the reality-mark of equality (*samata-lakṣaṇa*), then even a single minute sentient being is equal to Vairocana Buddha, without any difference.
The *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states: "The Tathāgata Vairocana enters into the body of a single minute sentient being and enters meditative concentration; entirely..."

The body is not dispersed. These sentient beings do not perceive or know this, because they believe the Buddha’s birth is of the same substance as theirs, and because, in principle, there are no boundaries.

As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "Making offerings to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha is equal to making offerings to the lowliest beggar. This reaches the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*), wherein there is no discrimination.

Viewed through this, although people have distinctions of noble and base, and ranks have distinctions of high and low, the mind— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

There is neither high nor low. Therefore, one should resolve to develop the Great Mind and sustain it through the power of aspiration, proceeding directly toward the Buddha-way without allowing even a moment’s interruption.
Chapter Seven: On Repentance. Question:

There are two meanings of repentance (*pāpadeśanā*). It generally encompasses the evil karma of sentient beings in both the past and the future; one should repent for all of these within one's own mind.
Now, such acts as inviting the Sangha, prostrating, and seeking repentance, or alternatively, upholding the various Prajñā-pāramitā sūtras, all constitute the meaning of repentance.
Furthermore, regarding the morning and evening repentance performed within one's own mind: in the Dharma, is this one thing or two? Is there a difference in depth? The Master said:
"The body, bound by karma, is oppressed by manifold sufferings; the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) blaze fiercely, and the six thieves (ṣaḍ-caura) invade from all sides.

The mental consciousness (citta-vijñāna) rushes about without a moment’s rest, giving rise to the causes of the ten unwholesome actions (daśākuśala-karma-hetu) and reaping the fruits of endless suffering (ananta-duḥkha-phala). Greed, anger..."

Delusion and craving are like a fierce fire; false speech and frivolous talk are swifter than a rushing torrent. Committing killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct is like falling into a bottomless and boundless abyss.
Attachment to views, pride, and sloth is like drowning in a shoreless sea of suffering.

One gives rise to sixty-two kinds of false views and establishes eighty-four thousand gates of obstruction, which hinder the bodhicitta, hinder the path to enlightenment, and hinder the practice of enlightenment.
Obstructing the vow for Bodhi, one wanders through the three realms of existence, failing to hear the sublime names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Sunk and submerged within the four modes of birth, how could one recognize the retributions of the past, present, and future? Little do they realize that the cause is linked to the fruit and the fruit reaches back to the cause;

cause and effect correspond to one another without the slightest deviation, even as fine as a hair. When the cause is minute yet the fruit is fierce, one must be cautious in one's conduct to avoid committing the transgressions of the ten habitual tendencies. Thus it is said: [the verse follows].
A small retribution may lead to a great one; thus, in the hells, there are sixfold reciprocal retributions.

If one does not earnestly apply oneself to repentance and reform past transgressions, then as one person commits and another repays, the cycle will have no end. Now, "repentance" (chàn) is the Sanskrit term *kṣamā*, which here means "to regret one's errors."
"Confession" (*chàn*) refers to the permanent severing of future transgressions; "repentance" (*huǐ*) refers to a sense of shame regarding past offenses. Thus it is said:

"I pray that you grant the elimination of sins already committed, and that I shall not dare to commit further transgressions in the future. Regarding the practice of washing the mind through confession, there are two meanings:

first, confession according to principle (*lǐ chàn*); second, confession according to phenomena (*shì chàn*). As for confession according to principle, it is as stated: "Since sin arises from the mind, one must take the mind..."
Repentance: When the mind is extinguished, transgressions also perish. When transgressions perish and the mind is extinguished, both are empty.
This is what is called true repentance. It is further said: "Those who wish to repent should sit upright and contemplate the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

All transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can eliminate them. As it is said: "Transgressions arise from karma, and karma arises from the mind. Since the mind is unborn, where will transgressions go?"
Peaceful repose. This is truly because the karmic burdens of sentient beings are so profound and heavy that, in a single moment of still contemplation, ten thousand distractions arise in an instant.

Unless one deeply penetrates the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is difficult to eliminate these [distractions]; unless one investigates the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), how can one extinguish transgressions?
Master Yongjia said: "Contemplating the true mark, one finds neither person nor phenomena; in a single instant, the karma of Avīci Hell is extinguished.
If one truly investigates the principle, the single gate of Chan meditation is the most certain and appropriate. Simply hold up a single phrase of the *huatou*;

if the Great Principle is not clarified, it should be as if one has lost one's parents. If one truly possesses such a heart as if losing one's parents, the waves of consciousness will naturally cease to arise.
Karma cannot bind them. Otherwise, one must suppress the deluded mind so that delusions do not arise; this is called the "extinction of the mind" and the "extinction of sin.

This is very much like scratching an itch through a thick leather boot. To wish to extinguish transgressions, to wish to resolve birth and death, and to wish to escape saṃsāra—there is no such possibility [without this].
Furthermore, it is like single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name while concurrently practicing the dharma-gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, deeply penetrating reality...

All such practices can extinguish transgressions; however, the single gate of Chan meditation is the most transcendent. It seems to extinguish transgressions more swiftly, and thus it cannot be compared with other dharma-gates.

Second is ritual repentance (*sāṃghāṭī-saṃvara*), which means facing the sacred countenances, extensively presenting offerings, scattering flowers, practicing the Way, reciting the great names of the Buddhas, prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground like a great mountain collapsing, and confessing [one's faults].

Lay out your grievances and seek mercy through repentance. One may perform the *Liáng-huáng Fǎhuá Chàn* (The Liang Emperor’s Lotus Repentance) or prostrate before the *Qīān fó míng jīng* (Sutra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas);

both are intended for repentance. Whether for seven days up to forty-nine days, a hundred days, or three years, when various auspicious signs appear, one will then be able to extinguish their transgressions.
This depends on one's own diligent practice; however, if one’s own virtue is thin and one’s conduct shallow, one should request the precepts.

Those of virtue are called the Saṃgha. Whether it be twenty-four positions, up to forty-eight positions, or one hundred and eight positions, when a vegetarian feast is prepared for them, it shall likewise extinguish transgressions.

For instance, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was unable to save his own mother; however, when the Buddha today, on the day of the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*, makes offerings to the assembly of monks and prostrates at the feet of the assembly of monks, his mother’s transgressions will be extinguished that very day, and she will be liberated from the suffering of the hungry ghosts.
By relying on the power of this practice, the confession master should regard the assembly of monks with reverence as if they were Buddhas; thus, one’s offenses will be extinguished.

One must not give rise to thoughts of indolence or contempt. If such thoughts arise, not only will the offenses fail to be extinguished, but one fears that, on the contrary, further offenses will be incurred.
This is like inviting a monk who lacks preceptual conduct to respond to an invitation to expound the teachings; such an act merely squanders the merit of one's offerings.
Even if a virtuous monk commits an offense, it is not that he can extinguish the transgressions of the confession master;
rather, this single gate of repentance involves contemplating the sufferings of the hells, giving rise to the bodhicitta, and engendering great fear and great shame.

One should reflect upon the boundless suffering of sentient beings in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, and for their sake, together seek repentance so that they may be liberated from the evil paths.
Suffering! Feast upon the bliss of the Buddha Vehicle and empty the hells, not merely for the sake of my own liberation. This is precisely the bodhicitta.
If one gives rise to this mind, the mountains of blades and trees of swords will all become fragrant groves; the glowing embers and boiling cauldrons will all become pure lands.
Then there is no evil that cannot be removed and no transgression that cannot be extinguished. Furthermore, as for repentance, it consists of contemplating birth and death.
Impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self: with a single breath not returning, one moment passes into another world. Should one fall into the evil realms, the suffering would be beyond description.
Fearing the suffering of the evil realms, one should resolve to attain Bodhicitta and perform profound repentance, just as that terrified king feared death.

Thus, there is no sin that is not extinguished. Regarding the King who was terrified: one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a king in the city of Pāṭaliputra named Aśoka, which in this language means "Sorrowless. He had profound faith in the Buddha-dharma.

He had a younger brother named Vitāśoka, which means "Remover of Sorrow," who was deeply attached to false views and believed in various non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas). Because King Aśoka took pity on his brother’s heterodoxy, he devised a stratagem.
He then said to the ministers, "I shall now bathe; enter that bathhouse and remove my celestial crown, robes, and other finery.
You must adorn my younger brother with my regalia and cause him to ascend the throne.

Once the ministers had carried out these instructions, the younger brother was just about to take his seat when the king came out, saw his brother, and immediately ordered him to be killed. The ministers addressed the king, saying, "This is the king's own brother; we pray—"
The king’s anger subsided and he forgave the offense. The king said, "He is my own younger brother. For seven days, I shall entrust him with the affairs of state and let him act as king.
When the seven days are complete, I shall kill him. He then provided him with various kinds of music, dancing girls, and attendants for his service and protection.
All the ministers and citizens went to offer their greetings. However, the executioner stood at the gate, sword in hand.
He stood and reported to the king every day: "One day has already passed; death shall come on the sixth day. This continued until six days had elapsed and only one day remained.
When the seventh day was completed, the ministers and others took the king’s younger brother and went together to King Aśoka.
They asked the brother: "For seven days you were king; all manner of music and entertainment were at your disposal as you wished. Was there anything lacking?"
A great multitude of people inquire after you and offer prayers for your well-being every day. Are you able to see and hear them?

Your younger brother replied, "Because I am terrified of death and my mind is filled with dread, I have not seen or heard anything at all. He further answered in verse: "For seven days I have neither seen nor heard sounds;
I have neither smelled nor tasted flavors, Nor have I perceived any tactile sensations. My body is adorned [with ornaments]."

Together with the various court ladies and others, because they contemplated the fear of death, they were unaware of such matters as the sounds of the courtesans' singing and dancing, the palaces, the bedding, or the various treasures of the great earth; they felt no joy at all.
This was because they saw the executioners standing outside the gate brandishing swords, heard the sound of ringing bells, and realized that the stake of death was being driven into them.

The mind, unaware of the wonders of the five desires, becomes attached to them and fears the disease of death; it cannot sleep in peace. Contemplating that death is approaching, one does not realize that the night has already passed.
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, whose face is like a lotus flower, the one in whom gods and humans take refuge, and in the Dharma and the Sangha which are free from outflows.
When the King saw his younger brother’s heart turn toward the Triple Gem, he was filled with great joy.

With various kinds of gentle words, he consoled his younger brother. If one repents, one possesses such a dread of death that the mind does not become greedily attached to the exquisite pleasures of the five desires within the realms of the world.
Furthermore, by contemplating the phenomena of dependent origination, one realizes that they are ultimately without self;
who is the creator, and who is the experiencer? Since the mind is fundamentally non-existent, the nature of sin is itself empty. This is what is meant by...

This is true repentance. Furthermore, one should overturn previous unwholesome conditions and sever the mind of continuity. Feeling self-reproach and self-rebuke, one shall disclose and lay bare the transgressions already committed, no longer concealing them.
Invoking the great names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, one contemplates the emptiness of the nature of sin.
No longer creating further evil karma within this field of illusion, one clearly understands cause and effect and guards the True Dharma.

In this way, there is no evil that is not eliminated and no transgression that is not extinguished. Whether one confesses for oneself or for others, whether it be the first or second [type], shallow or deep—none of these can be apprehended as distinct.
Chapter Eight: On the Retribution of Merit.
Question: To perform meritorious deeds in order to seek their reward is the most inferior faculty. Yet, if one does not perform meritorious deeds, what hope can there be for a reward?
Now, if both sin and merit arise from one’s own mind, are the various rewards not fixed and distinct?

The Master said: "The retribution of blessings and transgressions follows one like a shadow follows the body, like space responds to an echo, or like a person carrying a load where the heavier side falls first.
One cannot find even a hair’s breadth of distance from this; how then could one seek for retribution?

Nevertheless, all Buddhas are fully endowed with the two kinds of perfection—perfection in merit and perfection in wisdom—and thus, on the ground of practice, one must first cultivate the field of merit."

With the seeds of wisdom and merit deeply rooted in their conditions, they have spontaneously attained the opening of the mind; this is not for the sake of seeking recompense. The Buddha opened the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to initiate the myriad practices.
*Dāna-pāramitā* is here translated as "giving" (*śī*). As for the giver, they realize that the three spheres (*tri-maṇḍala*) are empty in essence;
thus, they do not hope for recompense, yet recompense follows of its own accord. *Śīla-pāramitā* is here translated as "precepts. *Kṣānti-pāramitā* is here...
Kṣānti is translated as "patience. Vīrya-pāramitā is translated as "diligence. In the teachings, it is said that these four [perfections] all cultivate merit.
The latter two perfections are called "wisdom," namely dhyāna and prajñā. The first four perfections all contain wisdom;
for if there were no wisdom, how could one be willing to practice generosity and diligence? Nevertheless, the Buddhas realize nirvāṇa by means of these.
The Bodhisattva practices the ten thousand deeds by means of this [giving], not seeking reward. It truly adorns the Dharma-body and nourishes the nature-ground (prakṛti-bhūmi).
Through this single dharma of giving alone, one proceeds directly to Bodhi; how much more so for the other perfections?

This is because a practitioner who extensively practices the six perfections must necessarily support them with the power of vows, dedicating them all toward unsurpassed Bodhi and seeking nothing else.
As for the fruit [of practice]: take the single dharma of giving as an example; throughout the stages of the ground (bhūmi) of all Buddhas, there is nothing that is not thus.

Subsequently, they attain pure Buddha-lands and become rich in the wealth of the Dharma, yet this is not for the sake of seeking karmic retribution. Formerly, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was a goldsmith;
he was well-versed in the nature of gold and knew how to temper and subdue it. The *Dharmapada-paramparā-śāstra* states: "Once, in the distant past eons, during the time of Vipaśyin..."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the fourfold assembly erected a stūpa. Within the stūpa, the golden color of the face of the image was damaged and incomplete.
At that time, there was a poor woman who took a gold bead to a goldsmith and requested that he adorn the Buddha’s face.

Subsequently, they both made a vow together: "May we two become husband and wife without being betrothed. By virtue of these causes and conditions, for ninety-one kalpas, their bodies were entirely golden. Later...

He was born in the Brahma Heaven. When his celestial lifespan ended, he was reborn in a Brahmin family in the central kingdom of Magadha, named Kāśyapa—translated here as "Drinking-Light Victorious Honored One"—a title derived from his golden complexion. Consequently, he resolved to seek renunciation, hoping to cross over the various realms of existence.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu! and his hair and beard fell away naturally, while the *kāṣāya* robe clothed his body. He remained [in the order] forever.
Among the assembly, he was praised as the foremost; eventually, through the transmission of the Dharma and the vestment, he became the First Patriarch of India.
This cause and effect is clearly evident. Because he adorned [the Buddha] with gold, his body came to possess a golden light. Through the mutual support of his vows, he realized the ultimate fruit.
This is not a seeking of retribution, yet retribution arrives of its own accord; it is not a matter of seeking reward. I have once appraised this: Bodhi...
The mind is like a seed; merit is like rain and dew upon a fertile field; while evil is like flames, firebrands, and axes.

For instance, when sprouts are beginning to grow, they must obtain rain, dew, water, and soil to reach fruition. If they were to encounter being scorched by fire or hacked by an axe, how could they ever take root?
It is like timber fit for a ridgepole or a beam; in such a case, firebrands and axes are both unsuitable, as is water and soil.
It would likewise be useless. A verse by the Seven Buddhas says: "The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; the commission of all unwholesome karmas is also an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam, the mind is like the wind; illusions produce that which has no root and no real nature.

The fool, claiming that both good and evil are illusions, commits various unwholesome karmas as if they were not mutually obstructive. Little does he know that illusory beings weave an illusory wheel for one another.
The enclosure. Illusory karma can summon that which is illusory and to be remedied. It is further said: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure;
from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished. This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.
Just as when constructing beams and pillars, one does not require axes, hatchets, water, or earth; so it was when the Buddha attained enlightenment, [manifesting] boundless lands and myriad virtues.
These adornments are all manifestations of one's own mind; they are entirely accomplished through roots of goodness cultivated since beginningless time.

Thus it is said that the fruition of the ultimate fruit is "retribution" (pāka); how could this not be retribution? It is simply that during the stage of the causal ground, there was no mind seeking retribution.

In the world, the consequences of the good and evil deeds performed by people do not deviate by even a hair's breadth. Formerly, in the Western Regions, there was a woodcutter who was selling firewood in the marketplace when he encountered...
A certain monk took the money he had intended to sell and gave it all away as an offering. Because of this act of giving, his heart was filled with immeasurable joy.

After traveling some twenty li, he cast off this physical body and was subsequently reborn in the human realm as a wealthy householder. Within those twenty li, stores of gold, silver, and precious treasures spontaneously welled up from the earth.
Although the benefit of the gift itself was very slight, because the intention behind the gift was supreme, the resulting retribution was likewise supreme.

Viewed in this light, although one does not seek karmic rewards for merit, one must nevertheless perform meritorious deeds. If one fails to perform such deeds, one will be born into poverty in this world and become a servant to others;
how truly lamentable this is! Some may cite the time when the Great Master Bodhidharma first met Emperor Wu, when the Emperor asked:
"Since my accession to the throne, the temples I have built, the scriptures I have transcribed, and the monks I have ordained are beyond counting."
"What merit is there? the Patriarch said. "There is no merit at all. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit?
The Patriarch replied, "This is merely a minor fruit of the human and celestial realms; it is a cause of outflows (*āsrava*). Like a shadow following a form, though it exists, it is not real.
The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merit does not depend on..."

These are all profound discourses on penetrating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and entering into principle. How could one discard the law of cause and effect merely because it pertains to the stage of cultivation?
For instance, when one has not yet attained Buddhahood, as for the minor fruits of humans and devas—if one does not cultivate them, is that wisdom or folly?
Kings and great ministers are the minor fruits of the human realm; Brahmā kings and Śakra Devendra are the minor fruits of the heavenly realms. This...
Without a specific cause, how could there be a superior retribution? One merely receives [retribution] according to karmic conditions; it is not sought after.

However, the cause is one's own mind and the fruit is one's own mind: greed leads to retribution as a hell-being, hatred leads to retribution as a hungry ghost, and delusion leads to retribution as an animal.

When good and evil are mixed, the retribution is that of an asura. The five precepts result in a human body, and the ten wholesome paths lead to the heavenly realms. As for the giving of wealth, one abandons stinginess.
Through greed one obtains wealth; through the gift of Dharma, one transmits the lamp according to the capacity and resonance of others.
These various conditions for retribution differ from one another, yet they are not objects external to the mind.
Chapter Nine: Dispelling Doubts. Question:
If one lacks the faculty of faith and is shrouded in great ignorance and darkness, yet begins to believe only recently, why does it ultimately end in ruin?
This is because the karmic consciousness is easily manifested. By what kind of perfuming can one plant roots of goodness? It is as stated above.
"Regarding the various meanings you have set forth, will you be able to practice them steadfastly so that they are never destroyed?
The Master said: "If one does not give rise to faith, it is because the conditions for obstruction are deep.

It is like those who dwell in the mundane world and say of themselves, 'I have attained the Dharma of securing the body,' without realizing they do not transcend the covering and supporting of heaven and earth, nor the operations of yin and yang. Are they not simply ignorant and dark?"
The Buddha presides over the Flower Treasury World (Avataṃsaka-lokadhātu), illuminating it like the sun and moon. The twelve classes of sentient beings are all born here and grow up here.

Because the Buddha illuminates sentient beings with the light of compassion, and because he reaches them with a heart of pity, yet they do not believe in the existence of the Buddha—is this repaying his kindness, or is it betraying it?
Even if one does not give rise to faith, and does not believe in the cause...

As for the result: those who do not believe in cause and effect, and do not believe in the existence of the Buddha, fall into the hells or are born as hungry ghosts within the realm of animals for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Even if they leap beyond inconceivable and ineffable worlds, how could they ever escape from within the sphere of the World-Honored One’s transformation and cultivation?
Those who initially believe do so by virtue of minor roots of goodness, while those who ultimately destroy their faith do so due to evil conditions.

Because of these hindrances, one who desires purity becomes biased toward defilement; one who desires progress becomes biased toward regression. It is not that the essence of the pure white mind possesses the quality of defilement or regression;

rather, these arise from the conditions of habitual hindrances that produce various false views. Because of these false views, regression and disparagement arise. There are two meanings to this regression and disparagement:
first, "regression by cause," which is the loss of faith, accompanied by self-reproach, self-remorse, and self-shame.

First, upon encountering those who practice the same Dharma-gate, one does not wish to see them. Second, due to a sense of shame and remorse, one conceals one's own disgrace and gives rise to slander.
Some say, "The Ultimate Way is vast and remote; there is nothing to be seen. Others say, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have long since passed away;
those who now turn toward them are practicing a mere fiction. Still others say, "Those who preside over the Dharma are not pure."
[He is] pure, yet he himself is not pure; how can he instruct others? Or it may be said: a person of integrity ought to encounter abundance, yet they are poor;
a person who practices goodness ought to encounter favorable circumstances, yet they meet with adversity;
a greedy person ought to encounter poverty, yet they are wealthy; and one who commits evil ought to encounter adversity, yet they enjoy favorable circumstances. Because...
These four types of people give rise to doubt and slander, causing unwholesome dharmas to circulate and the gates of goodness to be shut. They fail to realize that the Way is not distant from people;
rather, it is people who distance themselves from it. This is not because the Way is obscure or remote. Furthermore, one should know that every person possesses Buddha-nature.
Light is emitted from the gates of the six sense organs, shaking the earth. It is also said: "The cool moon of the Bodhisattva constantly traverses ultimate emptiness;
when the water of sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears within. A verse by Master Fu says: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep."
Morning after morning we rise together; whether sitting or moving, we are always in each other’s company. In speech and in silence, we dwell together, never parting throughout the entire day.
They are like a shadow following a body. If you wish to know where the Buddha has gone, it is simply this very sound of speech.

Viewed in this light, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are present now; they have not long since entered parinirvāṇa. It is because those who preside over the Dharma are themselves impure that [the teachings] are all rendered impure.
Because one perceives others as impure while being pure oneself. Do you not see what the Sixth Patriarch Master said?
"If one is a true practitioner of the Way, one does not see the faults of the world. He also said: "Their faults are not mine; my faulting them, however, is a mistake.
If one is truly a practitioner of the Way, it is like having the most virtuous and wise person among a hundred students as one's teacher. Thus it is.
If there is no one among your peers, take the Dharma-gate as your teacher. If there is no one to uphold the Dharma, take the good spiritual friends throughout the world as your teachers.
If there is no one among those good spiritual friends, take Śākyamuni Buddha as your teacher.
Śākyamuni Buddha is the master of the Dharma and is the one who is pure; you should have no doubts—reflect upon this.
This can be seen. Furthermore, those who are upright are poor, while those who are good suffer setbacks; those who are greedy are wealthy, while those who are wicked enjoy smooth success.

When inferred through the three periods of time, not even a hair’s breadth of this is ever off. Not only across these three periods, but throughout the vast expanse of millions of kalpas past and future, there is likewise retribution.

Formerly, when the Venerable Ānanda suffered from a carbuncle, the great assembly was struck with alarm and doubt. The Buddha commanded a physician to incise it and treat it by applying medicinal ointment.
He then recounted the causal conditions from many kalpas and revealed them through this verse: "Even if a hundred kalpas should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution must be experienced by oneself. Furthermore, there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers who...
The verse in response says: "Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the sea, nor by entering into mountain caves—there is no place on earth where one may escape retribution.
By this it is known that the upright suffer poverty because of excessive stinginess in previous lives;
the virtuous do not obtain what they desire because of many evil causes in previous lives; and the greedy receive wealth because of much giving to others in previous lives. As for the wicked...
One attains favorable conditions because in previous lives one associated harmoniously with many people. In this life, whether one is good or evil, greedy or modest, these are repaid in the future;
one should know that this spans many kalpas. As for those who withdraw of their own accord, even if they fall into hell, their transgression is still relatively light.

However, those who give rise to slander and thereby harm the Dharma-gate will be reborn in the Avīci Hell throughout the ten directions; when that world-system perishes, they shall again take refuge [in another].

"Furthermore, those suffering in the hells are deeply pitiable; how tragic! It is also said that while the consciousness of karma is easily manifested, by what kind of cultivation can one plant roots of goodness?
By turning toward the Dharma-gate with faith, one plants roots of goodness through the most swift and direct means, thereby abandoning the pleasures of the evil realms.
Because they possess great compassion, those who have faith and turn toward the Triple Gem cherish all sentient beings."

Out of compassion, one rescues and protects sentient beings and plants roots of goodness. Because one believes that the causes and effects of good and evil follow one another like a shadow follows a form and must inevitably be requited, one plants roots of goodness.
Believing that the various Mahāyāna sūtras will certainly cause one to escape the sea of suffering and reach the other shore, one plants roots of goodness.
Believing in the single gate of Buddha-recitation, one will certainly see the Buddha and certainly attain Buddhahood, just as in the analogy of planting seeds.
One plants roots of goodness because the true fruit truly exists and one will certainly be born in the Pure Land;

one plants roots of goodness because one believes that practicing Chan will inevitably lead to the realization of the Great Principle, the definitive understanding of birth and death, and liberation from the cycle of saṃsāra, such that one may preach the Dharma to deliver others without end, for there are many exemplary models among the various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Furthermore, one plants roots of goodness if one is indeed able to fully practice all the meanings set forth above.
This is the wheel of non-retrogression. In this very life, such a person is called a "flesh-body bodhisattva. All devas and benevolent spirits will constantly protect them;
all Buddhas and bodhisattvas will constantly grant them their grace. They serve as eyes for gods and humans, and as a helmsman for the sea of suffering.
Whenever they utter a single word or a single verse, it enters the eight consciousnesses of sentient beings like a diamond that cannot be digested.
For example, while the intestines may be pierced and destroyed, the diamond (vajra) is indestructible; how much more so, then, that which is inherently indestructible?

Regarding all those who harbor doubts, the scriptures employ the metaphor of "hesitation" (*yōu-yù*). This hesitant mind suspects both itself and others, and because it can obstruct the Path, to suspect oneself means:

This refers to those whose faculties are weak and inferior, making it difficult for them to enter the Path. Little do they realize that there is a treasure within their robes and a talisman behind their elbows.
"Since he is a great man, why should I not be so? Those who harbor such doubts should place faith in the teachings of all Buddhas, which are entirely words of truth.

Through seeing, hearing, and reflecting, they shall enter deeply into the realm of the Dharma. By means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they shall extensively deliver sentient beings and penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Emptiness. That there are no sentient beings to be saved is the entry into the Vajra Samādhi.
Chapter Ten: Dedication. Question:
The myriad dharmas return to the One; this is the Great Dhāraṇī. The above various gates represent the ultimate skillful means, ranging from shallow to deep.
"Is this not different from the 'Small' [Vehicle]? I beg for your compassionate instruction to explain the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The Master said: "The myriad dharmas returning to the One is the Great Dharani. This means that the One Dharma encompasses the entire Great Canon of teachings.
As the Buddha taught the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, one should seek to enter deeply through a single gate. Because of this single gate, all are subsumed."
Because it encompasses all dharmas, it is said: "The ocean of ink used to write this single-word Dharma-gate would never be exhausted.

Although these aforementioned gates differ in their skillful means, ultimate realization, depth, shallowness, greatness, or smallness, if one takes up a single phrase as a *hwadu* (critical phrase) for genuine investigation and earnest study, no Dharma-gate will fail to be subsumed within it.
Through Zen practice, one penetrates the truth of the *dharmakāya*. As for the principle of the *dharmakāya*:
Because there are no boundaries, if one wishes to be born in the Pure Land, does that Pure Land reside outside of the Dharmakāya?

If one wishes to investigate the matter beyond the ordinary, one must know that Vairocana has a teacher and the Dharmakāya has a master. To seek a teacher or a master apart from the Buddha is most certainly not so.
To recite the Buddha’s name and seek to see the Buddha is also a teaching given according to the capacity of the listener; yet they fail to realize that their entire being is [the Buddha].
"Buddha" refers to the ancient Buddha newly realized; thus, the principle of mindfulness of the Buddha and seeing the Buddha is made manifest.

Yet it is not called "mindfulness of the Buddha," for its intent lies in the path that transcends the ordinary. It cuts off the ten directions while sitting, yet it is not called "Pure Land," for its intent lies in taking a single step in secret movement.
For one who investigates the ultimate principle, mindfulness does not scatter; not only does it not scatter, but it presses forward until entry is achieved.

As for principle: because thoughts do not arise, all mental states fail to arise—is this not *śamatha*? With the entire body entering into principle, the mind and its objects are vast and open—is this not *vipaśyanā*?
To be fully endowed with the two dharmas of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, yet not to be designated as "śamatha-vipaśyanā," is intended to mean *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, when all thoughts do not arise, evil has no way to emerge; since evil does not arise, is this not *śīla*? With the entire body...

This is precept, yet it is not called "precept. This means that because there is nothing to transgress, one speaks of "maintaining" [the precepts]. This is like gouging a sore out of healthy flesh. The body is not "mine";
when one seeks its roots, sense-objects, and the realm of the vessel-world, they are utterly unobtainable. Who, then, can be the giver? Who can be the recipient?
Since there is neither subject nor object, there is likewise no sentient being outside the body who receives the gift. And yet, there comes one to beg.
Furthermore, it is said: seeing forms is not a matter of form; this is the giving of the eye. Hearing sounds is not a matter of sound;
this is the giving of the ear. Fragrance and stench do not intersect; this is the giving of the nose. Eating without perceiving taste; this is the giving of the tongue.

There is no distinction between male and female, nor any characteristic of roughness or smoothness; this is the giving of the body. When principle is clearly penetrating and the mind does not engage with external objects, this is the giving of the intellect.
This is giving (*dāna*). Forgetting sleep and losing appetite, not begrudging even one’s own body or life—this is the perfection of the *nirmāṇakāya* (retribution-body) giving.
Realizing that there are no objects external to the mind, and that the principle of the Dharma-precepts is established—this is the perfection of the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment-body) giving.

Yet, these are not called "giving" because the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of the dualistic mind of giver and recipient. One must arouse great courage and vigor, remaining unaffected by suffering or pleasure, and indifferent to cold or heat.
Advance directly to investigate the root source, aspiring toward great enlightenment. "Aspiring" refers to one's vow; "courage" refers to one's power.

As for that vow, even with hundreds or thousands of obstacles, one cannot be discouraged or cowed. As for that courage, even when maras or heretics invade and disturb, one cannot be broken or subdued.
Were it not for the firm persistence of the power of one’s vow, how could one become a man of bronze head and iron brow?
My son, that which is not called the power of aspiration is to abide in the True Dharma without displaying the banner of guidance.
If one is willing to investigate with a sincere mind, such a person possesses great merit; it cannot be compared to worldly blessings. It does not seek the pleasures of the heavens;
it cannot be compared to the merit of a Brahma King. This merit and its conditions pervade the entire being, surpassing the bliss of the Third Dhyāna Heaven, like one who has entered the great ocean.
One's entire being is water, yet one does not seek water elsewhere. For those who practice Zen, their entire being is sustained by blessings;
yet they do not seek blessings elsewhere. This is because the benefit and merit are vast and great. Yet, it is not called a "reward of fortune.

It is like one dwelling in leisure, who has forgotten emotions and severed all thoughts, such that they no longer perceive a body. Furthermore, how could this be called the "physical well-being" of a Zen practitioner? It is the person practicing Zen [who attains this].

This is a great karmic reward. Furthermore, how could it be called a "karmic reward" in any other sense? To have faith in this single phrase of the *huatou* is the pivotal point for escaping birth and death and the sharp weapon for shattering worldly afflictions;
thus, all doubts are completely resolved. How, then, could one wait for some separate explanation to dispel those doubts?

Taking this single character of the Dharma, do not seek it for oneself, but dedicate it all toward the sentient beings who are illusory transformations within the great earth, so that they may together [attain liberation].
To ascend to the shore of enlightenment—this is the true intent of this dhyāna. The *Pranidhānapatala* (Chapter on Vows) explains the intent of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). The Sūtra says:

"From the initial prostration, through all merits acquired in accordance with the practice, I dedicate them all to all sentient beings throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.
I vow that these sentient beings shall always attain peace and happiness, be free from all illness and suffering, and have no desire to commit unwholesome deeds."
All [unwholesome states] shall fail to be accomplished, while all wholesome dharmas one cultivates shall swiftly reach fulfillment.

One shall close the gates to all evil realms and reveal the correct path to humans, devas, and nirvāṇa. This power of dedication and aspiration is both horizontally pervasive and vertically exhaustive.
Fellow practitioners, you should be courageous; with the roots of goodness you have cultivated, dedicate them to all beings throughout the great earth, and do not give rise to indolence.

The thought of indolence: when Bodhisattvas see the suffering and affliction of sentient beings, they take it upon themselves to endure it in their own bodies; how much less would they begrudge their own roots of goodness?

As a sutra says: "If all sentient beings, because of the accumulation of various evil karmas, experience all manner of most grievous fruits of suffering, I shall take them all upon myself and cause those sentient beings to attain complete liberation, ultimately achieving [Buddhahood]."
Ascending to Bodhi, one acts as a substitute for others by serving as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for them;

or, by intentionally retaining delusions to sustain rebirth, one assumes a body of suffering to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them not to commit evil. When the cause perishes and the effect is extinguished, this is called "substitution.

This is because the Bodhisattva dedicates their roots of goodness for the benefit of sentient beings, enabling them to leave suffering and attain happiness; it does not mean substituting with one's own physical body.
Sentient beings undergo suffering; even if one were to substitute oneself for them, how could one truly benefit them universally?

If a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for sentient beings so that they realize the emptiness and quiescence of the aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus), evil has no way to arise. Even if one seeks the characteristic of its arising, it cannot be found.

They may suddenly enter perfect clarity and remain far removed from the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and so forth. Because the Bodhisattva possesses the power of great vows, this is called "Universal [Benefit]."
It is to take upon oneself the suffering of sentient beings. Furthermore, as for dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one must first have cultivated roots of goodness;

one then dedicates those roots of goodness that one has cultivated so that all sentient beings of the great earth may together leave the realms of suffering, together be born in the Pure Land, and together attain the path of Buddhahood.
If it concerns matters of self-benefit alone, it seems there would be no need for dedication. [If one thinks,] "I myself have not yet planted..."
Those with roots of goodness who wish to benefit sentient beings should likewise support one another through the power of vows. Vows and dedication are a unified path, free from discrimination.
Furthermore, this exchange between Layman Liupu and Master Boshan is entirely like a dream or an illusion, for there is neither subject nor object.
By means of these roots of goodness—devoid of subject and object—one should universally dedicate them all to the dream-like and illusory nature of the great earth.
Sentient beings all together attain the Buddha-way and together enter nirvana without remainder. When the ten classes of sentient beings have been fully liberated,
yet one perceives no one who has been liberated, only then does one enter this Samādhi of the Inexhaustible Treasury of the Srotāpanna Dharma-gate.

Compiled by Honghan, Dharma-grandson residing at Boshan.
The Chief Seat and Dharma-grandson, Hongyu, together with those gathered from the three Wu regions, responded to the inquiries of Grand Historian Guan Tai.
Guangyue stated: "In past lives, I planted a few roots of goodness and was thus able to hear the teachings that transcend the ordinary."

Throughout my journey, I have been unable to overcome the profound depth of obstructive conditions and the coarseness and restlessness of my mindfulness. Although I possess a spirit of inquiry, it cannot be sustained.

Furthermore, I lament being bound by the shackles of illness, which has prevented me from traveling to various regions to seek instruction and personally witness the inconceivable activities of great beings who transcend the ordinary.
Only Master Hanshan, with his clear vision, twice proclaimed the Way-Teacher’s name; he expended great compassion and graciously lowered the shadow of his whip to guide me at last.

This is merely counting the treasures of others; it does not rescue the hungry or the poor. Throughout the two periods of six hours [day and night], though one seeks even a small measure of correspondence with the Dharma, it is utterly impossible to find.
How fortunate that my ears have not yet been satiated, for from afar I have heard of the profound transformation at Bo Shan.

Upon finishing the reading of these admonitory words, my spirit involuntarily gallops forth, and I cannot help but sigh again: "How marvelous! Even among the Venerable Kāśyapa’s descendants, there still remain those of true bone and marrow who employ written words."
Liberation. Transmitting the Buddha’s seal of mind—though my body lacks wings, it cannot soar; lest I lose this in a single kṣaṇa, I harbor regret for eternal kalpas.
Taking advantage of the opportunity of Master Xiānkōng’s flying staff, I have burned incense, washed my hands, and inscribed these words on paper to respectfully inquire after your robe and flask.
I pray that the Great Master will cast the light from his brow toward my very marrow, and guide me in whatever ought to be done.
I commend these two minor works of yours; both are products of the mind, intellect, and consciousness, involving conjecture and conventional understanding rather than the actual realm of reality.

Nevertheless, even within them, there are moments where they leak through [into the truth], and therein lies no small measure of the Master’s application of the tongs and hammer. Gazing southward, my heart yearns for you; I look up to you with sorrowful longing, with sorrowful longing.
The Master said: "When I first traveled to Stonehead City (Shitou Cheng), I heard of the three great masters Han, Da, and Lang; my heart was filled with a yearning to take refuge in them.
I served as an attendant to my preceptor and, through traveling south to seek instruction, gained entry into the room of the late Venerable Shouchang.

He bestowed upon me the 'Pivot of the Boatman' (Chuanzi Gongan) kōan. For nearly six years, through bitter cold and scorching heat, I neglected sleep and forgot to eat. Thus did those three great masters purify my consciousness."
I was utterly unable to recall it. I took my leave of the former Master Xian and have resided at Boshan for twenty-five years now. For several years, seekers of Chan have come and gone like a stream.
Having obtained your layman’s verses on ancient cases (*gū*) as well as various biographical records, I read them with a sense of refreshing clarity.

Only then did I realize that there is a Bodhisattva manifesting in the body of a layman to preach the Dharma; my joy was immeasurable. My only regret is the slight sense of deficiency in not having met you in person to receive your instructions.
On the eighth day of the fifth month, at Kyoan Hermitage in Shinshū, I received the letter sent by the lay practitioner Kokuchi.

It was like encountering sweet rain in a drought; it greatly comforted my long-held longing to see him. I have read it three times with all my heart, unable to let go of it. This, too, is a rare opportunity in this world.
Your letter states that although you have doubts regarding the path beyond, they cannot continue to arise. Furthermore, you say: [The remainder of the text follows.]

He encourages them to act as they ought. Yet, remaining suspended between doubt and faith, you claim that while the layman embodies the Buddha-dharma throughout his entire being, you nevertheless seek words concerning what he "ought to do.
This is very much like one who dwells upon the sea yet goes to others to ask for water; it is something people find difficult to believe.
It is also like burying your troops and seeking battle, as if thinking that while the other cannot prevail, you yourself will surely be victorious. Furthermore...
"Householder, this is a manifestation of a bodhisattva. That he humbles himself and maintains an empty mind to request the Dharma from the assembly—is it not as it should be?
However, as for the path that leads upward, it is difficult to put into words. The moment one opens one's mouth, ten thousand miles of white clouds intervene.
Only the single matter of doubt can truly allow for entry; yet if one cannot maintain continuity therein, it is because the resolve for liberation from birth and death is not urgent enough. Its...
The single word "all" (一切) is exactly what ought to be done. This is why the layperson speaks of dreams when there are no dreams; it is like gouging a sore into healthy flesh.
Surely he does not intend to understand through the true Dharma, yet he cannot avoid plundering his own person by taking the realms of a dream as real.
It would not be amiss to analyze each point one by one, so that those who do not yet know may come to know, and for those who already know, what harm is there in further augmenting their Dharma-joy?
There are two types of awakening and understanding, with many gates of entry; these are fully detailed in my separate correspondence.

I hope you, Layman, will examine them and not reproach me for troubling you with such detail. As for discussing the path that transcends the ordinary, one need only let out a great shout like a blast of fire.
I shall incinerate them and cast [the ashes] toward other worlds, lest this pure and white ground be defiled by such dust, dregs, and impure soil.
This is merely a brief word; we shall have further opportunity to meet in person. With no further formalities. Sincerely yours, [Name]
The single word "awakening" (wu) is referred to as "poisonous medicine" by those within the lineage of the Patriarchs; since even its traces are not to be found, how much less is there any awakening?

Now, disregarding the taboo against such words, I rely upon them to speak, so that the wise and the ignorant may have something to discern and choose, and the various teachings and lineages may be clearly distinguished.
This is truly a companion on the journey, ensuring that practitioners do not fall into dangerous obstacles or deviant paths.
Furthermore, regarding the discourse on dhyāna, there are two gates of awakening. The first is to attain understanding through written characters and spoken language.
The second is to attain thorough penetration through investigation within one's own sphere of experience. Now, the power of understanding is weak, while the power of thorough penetration is strong.

One who understands is like hearing someone describe an object; one who penetrates thoroughly is like seeing the object with one's own eyes. Thus it is said: [The original Chinese text continues: "Hearing..."
Although the vision is one, there is a vast difference—like that between heaven and earth—between having doubt and being free from doubt.

Furthermore, for those who understand through words but have not yet attained thorough awakening, there are two kinds of obstacles: first, the obstacle of words; second, the obstacle of principle (*dharma*).
As for the obstacle of words, it is like a person eating honey: the more they eat, the sweeter it becomes. Regarding the twelve [links of dependent origination]...
Analytical Teaching: To seek the principle of truth deeply, yet find no point of intersection with the realm of birth and death—this is called an obstruction. As for the obstruction to principle:
although one may have a semblance of clear understanding regarding the ground of ultimate reality, as if one’s entire body were composed of jewels, one cannot derive practical utility from them;
likewise, there is no point of intersection with the realm of birth and death. This is called an obstruction.
Furthermore, for those who understand through the literal words but have not yet attained thorough awakening, there are two kinds of pride: first, the pride of self (*asmimāna*);
second, overweening pride (*adhimāna*). As for the pride of self, it means thinking, "I have now already awakened, while sentient beings remain in delusion;

my realization is such that others do not know it. From this, pride arises. As for overweening pride, it means thinking, "I have already entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*)," and so forth.
There is no Buddha to be sought, and below there are no sentient beings to be saved. As for the single word "Buddha," I do not even like to hear it.
From this, arrogance arises.
Furthermore, those who understand from within the words but have not yet attained thorough awakening harbor two kinds of timid and weak minds. The first is:
First, having seen that the principle is ultimate, one thinks, "My practice cannot reach it. Within the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), I have not yet personally traversed or realized them;

from this, a mind of cowardice arises. Second, having seen that my ground is already the same as the Buddha's, one thinks, "I truly do not possess the functional fruit of Buddhahood—how could supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and radiance belong to me? From this, a mind of cowardice arises.
Furthermore, regarding the understanding derived from the words, for those who have not yet attained thorough awakening, there are two kinds of notions of security.

The first is the notion that on the ground of the principle of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is received; mountains, rivers, and the great earth do not obstruct the eye-sight. It is further said:
"Perfectly identical to the great void, it is neither deficient nor redundant. Within this great perfect essence, if one seeks birth, death, coming, or going, they are utterly unfindable.
One attains it; from this, one gives rise to the thought of peace and security. Second, although the principle may be clearly understood through study, one cannot personally realize it.

Among the various vehicles of the teachings, it is most appropriate and secure to focus primarily on the Pure Land and the rebirth attained through mindfulness of the Buddha. From this, one gives rise to the thought of peace and security.
(The above are all considered "diseases of meditation.")
Furthermore, regarding the realization that penetrates the fruit and does not form interpretations based on words, there are two kinds of actual enjoyment:
first, attaining the transformative manifestations of all Buddhas; second, attaining the functional utility of the fruits of all Buddhas.

As for "transformative manifestations," this refers to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, as well as clouds of incense, flowers, banners, pennants, and precious parasols within the pure and impure lands of all Buddhas. And...

The eight classes of devas and nāgas are equal to me; they are neither two nor distinct. If it were otherwise, it would be because they have not yet attained thorough awakening, or because there would be a partiality in this principle.

Second, regarding the attainment of the functional power of the fruit of all Buddhas—namely, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, up to the ninety-seven [marks], as well as the pure *dharmakāya* and the supernatural powers and radiance—it is explained as follows.

The Dharma and so forth are equal to me; they are non-dual and without distinction. If it were otherwise, it would be because one has not yet attained thorough awakening, or because there would be a partiality in this principle.
Furthermore, as for "the fruit of thorough awakening, which does not form interpretations based on words":

this refers to the fulfillment of the wondrous, effortless conduct (*anabhisaṃskāra-caryā*) of all bodhisattvas—namely, the wondrous conduct practiced by all bodhisattvas of the past, the future, and the present throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas.
This means that they are identical in time, identical in place, identical in body, and identical in conduct; within a single [moment], they are...

In a single instant, even within the space of a single atom, everything is fully present. Were it otherwise, it would be because one has not yet attained thorough awakening, or because this principle possesses partiality and limitation.
Furthermore, when one’s realization is thorough and one does not form interpretations based on words and letters, one shares the same essential nature as the twelve classes of sentient beings.
One’s own body enters the bodies of others, and the bodies of others enter one’s own body. A single body enters many bodies, and many bodies enter a single body.
That world enters this world, and this world enters that world; worlds enter into themselves.
The body: one enters the world within one's own body, yet upon entering the body, no world is seen; one enters the world, yet no body is seen.
They mutually encompass and mutually merge, without destruction and without confusion. Furthermore, within the sphere of sentient beings, they share a single aspiration of compassionate longing.

Furthermore, within the realm of sentient beings, one gives rise to great compassion that identifies with them (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*). This means that both good and evil are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and are merely manifestations of one's own mind.
Since there are no objects external to the mind, and thus no [independent] activity, one exercises loving-kindness and compassion;

yet, this does not obstruct liberation from the state of being without intrinsic nature, even while within that very essence of non-nature. If it were otherwise, one would not have reached ultimate penetration.
Because of awakening. This principle possesses distinct divisions.
Furthermore, one who has attained thorough awakening and does not form interpretations based on words is identical in their illusory transformation to the twelve classes of sentient beings.

That is to say, that which arises through conditions has no intrinsic nature; arising is fundamentally non-arising. Since there is no intrinsic nature within conditioned arising, how could sentient beings exist?

It is real, yet like a magical illusion. I dwell with it as such; were it otherwise, it would be because one has not yet attained thorough awakening, for there would be a partiality in this principle.
(The above concerns the actual enjoyment of the awakened mind; it cannot be known by those who merely understand through intellectual interpretation.)
Furthermore, those who derive understanding from mere words but have not yet attained thorough awakening give rise to boundless deluded interpretations.

Some develop a deluded interpretation based on the notion that daily activities are no different [from the ultimate], thinking, "It is only my own spontaneous accord. Others develop a deluded interpretation based on the idea that by following the flow they have recognized their nature, thinking, "There is neither joy nor sorrow.
Still others develop a deluded interpretation based on the notion that supernatural powers and wondrous functions—such as carrying water...

Some give rise to a deluded understanding based on the lines, "Carrying firewood. Some give rise to a deluded understanding based on the lines, "Since from the beginning there has been nothing at all, where can dust and dirt cling?
Some give rise to a deluded understanding based on the lines, "When the mind arises in response to objects, how can Bodhi grow?

Some give rise to a deluded understanding based on the lines, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all fully reveal the body of the Dharma King. Some [give rise to a deluded understanding] based on the lines, "Ignorance is in truth..."
There are those who give rise to deluded understandings by asserting that "nature is itself Buddha-nature" or that "the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.

There are those who give rise to deluded understandings by striking [the student] as soon as they enter the gate. There are those who give rise to deluded understandings based on the expediency of verbal responses to questions and opportunities.

There are those who give rise to deluded understandings by claiming there is no need for investigation, but rather to directly assume realization. There are those who give rise to deluded understandings by scolding [the student] as soon as they enter the gate...
They give rise to delusory understandings. Some, through the study of poetry, prose, and literary compositions, or through mastery of arts and crafts, give rise to delusory understandings.

Others, through the practice of "letting go and letting go again," giving rise to the notion that "to open one's mouth is already an error," give rise to delusory understandings. Alas! This is the supreme flavor of clarified butter (amṛta).
They are treasures cherished by the world; yet when encountered by such people, they instead become poisonous drugs.
This is truly because the True Dharma has declined and fallen, while demons and delusions flourish, and their continuous lineages fill the world.

For those who set their minds upon the realm of birth and death, one must first illuminate and shatter these false and illusory states. Furthermore, there are three further complications that must not be left unaddressed.
The layman has spoken it through. An ancient worthy said: "What is Chan? A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind its head.
"What is Chan? A fierce fire frying oil. "What is Chan? A brick. These are precisely the entanglements transmitted by the Patriarchs.
Nevertheless, even so, I tell you clearly: continuity is also most difficult.
I asked Senior Official Jisheng Qiong about this, saying: "Since the time of Guishan, the Five Houses have been extremely strict in selecting their successors.

Consequently, the lineages of Weiyang and Fayen were cut off early on—was this truly the case? Furthermore, after several transmissions from Dongshan down to Taiyang, the Dharma was not bestowed lightly;
even when he was nearly eighty years old, he lamented that there was no one to succeed him, and thus sent his robe and sandals separately to Fushan."
He sought afar for those worthy of the Dharma-vessel and found only one person, Touzi. At that time, the lineage of the Dongxia school was as thin as a single thread;
yet once Touzi obtained Fuyong, the profound wind was revived and spread extensively to this day.

Those who today claim to follow Yunmen and Linji but have not yet reached their realization all turn over completely, abandoning their former ways to take him as their master. This is truly because what he is called for is taken with such strictness.
Those who attain it must do so with refinement; those who attain it with refinement will surely transmit it far and wide. Is this not so?

Now, the single lineage of Cao-Dong has become increasingly subtle yet has never been extinguished; how could it be that the single lineage of Linji, though ever more swift, is instead being lost in its transmission?

Lately, there has been a tendency to cultivate [the path] over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, while awakening is sought in a single night; this has become such a widespread custom that there are even those who, as soon as they don the *kāṣāya*...
"Sha! he then proceeded to administer blows and shouts. When asked about this, he replied, "This is the Linji School.
Is the Linji School truly like this? Su Shi once said, "I borrow your clappers and mallets; I too shall perform my play upon the stage.
To regard the tongs and hammer as mere theatrical performance—is this the fault of the student, or rather the fault of the teacher? I beg you, Master, to speak forthrightly.
The Master said: "Our school traces back to the Great Master Bodhidharma, who transmitted the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. Observing my land of Eastern Zhendan, I see the presence of the Mahayana spirit.
I received a prophecy from the twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, which says: 'Although Zhendan..."
There is no other path; one must simply tread upon the feet of the descendants.
He came specifically by sea, and from the very first moment he met with Emperor Wu of Liang for their dialogue, he did not yield even an inch to human sentiment, acting like a single iron broom.

He continued for nine years facing a wall, seeking a person for the sake of the Dharma. When Shen Guang stood in the snow until it reached his waist, [Huike] still rebuked him as having a frivolous and arrogant mind, saying that if he hoped for the True Vehicle, his diligent toil was in vain. This was truly because when the teacher is strict, the Way is honored;

and because the cause is true, the fruit is correct. Therefore, he severed his arm to find peace of mind and forgot his own body for the sake of the Dharma, even to the point of carrying grain to the mill and working at the troughs. Not...
Only by avoiding being submerged in the mud could the Great Dharma truly circulate and the "dragons and elephants" emerge in competition.
Although it was said that those who had attained the Way under the Sixth Patriarch were as numerous as a forest, his true lineage holders were only the two great sages of Qingyuan and Nanyue.
Master Mazu—whose single foot trampled the world and whose single mouth swallowed the Western River—possessed what kind of spiritual capacity and karmic practice? Yet he was... [seal certified].
After Xinxin, he served Master Yue for fifteen years, and his understanding of the profound mysteries deepened daily.

When the time came for him to open the hall for formal preaching, he still ordered a monk to test him, saying, "For thirty years, I have never lacked salt and sauce. Only then did Yue acknowledge his readiness. Such was the rigorous scrutiny of the ancients;
these matters are recorded in the historical records and can be clearly verified. How could I dare, out of fear that the lineage would die out, transmit the Dharma to those who are unworthy?

As for the lineage holders: although the *Chuan deng lu* and its various records state that the lineages of Guishan, Yangshan, and Yunmen have been severed, those who have inherited their branches and descendants still exist to this day.
As for the single school of Fayan, by the time of Great Master Yongming Yanshou, there were thirty-six successors in Goryeo;
the bounty of his virtue flourished and overflowed far and wide, such that it cannot be fathomed by the ordinary mind.
This refers to the succession and transmission [of the lineage]. Five generations after Dongshan, it reached Taiyang Xuan.
Xuan entrusted his monastic robe and leather sandals to Master Yuan, through whom he obtained Touzi Qing. Qing obtained Furong Kai; Kai obtained Danxia Chun;
Chun obtained Changlu Liao; Liao obtained Tiantong Jue; Jue obtained Xuedou Jian, continuing down to Wansong at the beginning of the dynasty.
Xiu; Xueting Yu; these were transmitted in succession until our late Master Shouchang, who was indeed the authentic successor of the Cao-Dong lineage.

Its source is thus deep and its stream far-reaching. As for the Linji lineage, it was on the verge of collapsing by the time of Fengxue, but through Shoushan Nian, and Nian obtaining Fenyang Zhao, and Zhao obtaining Shishuang Yuan, it was revived in the world, continuing down to the beginning of the present dynasty.
Tianru Ze and Chushi Qi possessed a brilliance so radiant that it reached the heights of Tianqi.

They provided exhaustive commentaries on the "Verses on Ancient Cases" (Sònggǔ) of the four masters, whereby the style of the school underwent a complete transformation; those who discerned this lamented it.

For in the vehicle of the *zong*, what is prized is the conformity of the core essence (*xīnmèi*), not merely the succession of the lineage gateways (*mén tíng*). Thus, when speaking of its ultimate severance, all five schools are [equally affected].

As for "severance": if one considers what remains, all five schools remain. If one encounters the right person, then whether it is through direct perception or inferential knowledge, the priority and sequence are identical;
how could there ever be severance? If it is not the right person, then adding water to milk thins its flavor, and writing "crow" three times results in "horse";
how could such "existence" be true existence? As for what the lay practitioner asks regarding taking the strictest approach, that which is attained will necessarily be refined.
Those who have attained the essence of it will surely transmit it far and wide; my own view is precisely this. I did not expect that you, Layman, would also see it in this light.

For this reason, it is better to fail to find a person than to bestow it upon one who is not a fit vessel. When one fails to find a person, although the lineage may be severed, the truth of the Way remains.
This does not harm the Great Dharma itself; however, to bestow [the teachings] upon those who are not fit vessels means that while the name is transmitted, the reality is false.
This deceives one’s own mind, deceives the Buddha, and deceives the world. It is like one blind person leading a multitude of blind people, pulling them together into a pit of fire.
As for the future—boiling cauldrons, fiery furnaces, sword-trees, and mountain-blades—who knows how many kalpas they will endure? A person of wisdom would rather shatter their own body than do so.

Like a mote of dust, he would never have been willing to commit such an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*). Yet now, as for the practice of striking with the staff or shouting the *he*, it is not merely those who have first donned the *kāṣāya* who do so;
