even laypeople (*avadātavasana*) follow this custom. What they fail to realize is that this was what was considered correct in antiquity.

This is precisely what is criticized today. Take, for example, Deshan, who would strike a student as soon as they entered the gate; according to the *Chuan Deng Lu*, how many people did he ever actually hit?

Or consider the Great Master Linji, whose single phrase contained the three mysteries, each mystery containing the three essentials, along with the four selections and the four guest-host relationships—all of which were used to test people within the context of spoken words. He never indiscriminately applied the staff. Moreover, regarding a single phrase:

Within this [teaching] are contained the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials; thus, every single blow of the staff and every shout must fully embody the principles of the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials.
Since a single shout can be divided into five teachings, a single blow must likewise possess the Three Mysteries. At the precise moment of application, there must necessarily be distinctions;

as for killing and enlivening, granting and taking away, the priority lies in responding to the immediate capacity of the student. How could one possibly go from door to door along the streets, treating everyone with blows and shouts?

Regarding its application: if one does not carefully examine the capacity of the student and applies the strike indiscriminately, this constitutes the arbitrary establishment of a sectarian school and becomes mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
It incites a class of arrogant practitioners who fall into the pit of their own conceptualizations and the trench of dogmatic views.

They stubbornly assume a position of mastery, mistakenly taking on responsibility, seeking only the "winter-gourd seal" of external recognition, and greedily coveting prostrations and offerings to delude the ignorant. Each...
Each claims to have achieved the retribution of the Unsurpassed Way, yet in the end they will surely sink into the bitter sea of birth and death.

This is precisely what is meant by "the error lies with the false teacher, not the fault of sentient beings. However, for those who truly seek liberation from birth and death and travel the world with discerning eyes, they will certainly not be deceived by such people.
Alas! We live in the final age; it is essential to distinguish between the orthodox and the heterodox, and to differentiate the true from the false. One must turn toward—
Within this fundamental section, the matter has been thoroughly deliberated. Do not engage in debates regarding the continuity or discontinuity of dharma-heirs.
When the Great Minister Liu Xin-cheng asked, "From a thousand miles away, we have partaken of the wind of your teaching and pressed you relentlessly through the night.

Master, in your great compassion, even the stone man sheds tears. Yet, alas, the clouds of delusion grow ever thicker; therefore, I shall forthwith express my wild thoughts in their entirety as a confession."

I repent. May my compassionate father, the Master, grant this wayward son his forbearance and, disregarding shame, respond point by point to my inquiries, so that I may awaken to the turning of the pivot on this very spot and suddenly sever the tangled web of complications.
How could I begrudge even flaying my skin and breaking my bones to repay this profound debt of grace for the Dharma-milk?
The Master said: "The Dharma-lineage has fallen into decline; one looks around and finds no one truly worthy of trust.

Today, among those in the world who call themselves 'men of knowledge' (jñānin), there are none who do not claim to uphold the direct transmission of the Great Master Bodhidharma. They brandish the staff and shout the 'hit' throughout the world;

this is not limited to monasteries, for even the laborers and commoners on the streets all falsely claim to have attained realization. All of this is the fault of false teachers and their errors, not the fault of sentient beings."

In the leisure time between my meditation sessions, my hair stands on end and my heart grows cold. I regret that I cannot use the blade of wisdom and the edge of insight to sweep away the factions of Māra, thereby repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
It is not that I dare, with a mind subject to birth and extinction, create the karmic causes for the hells by breaking the summer retreat to travel back and forth.

I am fortunate to have met with various officials and lay practitioners in Jinling who protect and uphold the True Dharma. Now that the retreat has concluded, I encountered a lay practitioner who questioned me regarding the Dharma-gate;
my heart was filled with great joy. Yet, while the paths of Chan (Zong) and Teaching (Jiao) differ, they both converge upon a single principle.
Those entering the capital do so at varying speeds; it is not that I dare to suppress the Teaching with Chan, nor Chan with the Teaching. If there were truly something to be suppressed, it would be—
These are demonic people. Furthermore, who is Dharma? Who is the wise one? How dare they recklessly engage in forced interpretation to distinguish between superior and inferior?
As for their objective, they claim to examine the beginner’s stage to provide guidance; yet they do not take the direct path.
I shall answer each question as it arises, for I do not wish to辜负 (disappoint) the layman’s intent. What is valued is responding beyond conventional bounds;
I hope you will not take my words as a fixed standard. If you can grasp the meaning before the question is even asked, then the layman has no question and Bo Shan has no answer.
Within the Great Perfect Enlightenment, not even a single character or trace remains. Layman, do you believe these words?
Question: I have received your master’s instruction that when the single breath does not return, where will one go?

This cuts off the path of words and thought; it is difficult to bite and difficult to chew. With a single "kiai" sound, empty space shatters to pieces. This is truly the most supreme and ultimate principle.
Although I, Xuan, am a lowly person, during the Wu-wu and Ji-wei years, I once set foot upon this path for two years. Yet in the Geng-shen year, I fell gravely ill and ultimately entered hell.
A single phrase of Amitābha is like hot water poured on snow; why then, until this day, have we instead wandered about beating ourselves?
This present karmic occasion is not a matter of mere recklessness; it seems that in past kalpas, I must have been among the descendants of Fulong (that is, Tiantai).

Whenever I read the *Miaozongchao*, its description of the ultimate point of taking and rejecting—that which is identical to being without taking or rejecting—feels truly capable of enabling rebirth in the West.
The staff: Truly, it does not hinder the ultimate pinnacle of the Zen school. "The streams and mountains differ; the clouds and moon are the same.
Indeed, the Tiantai teachings entirely employ entanglements to sweep away entanglements, and paths of understanding to cut off paths of understanding.

Yet, from the Four Teachings, the Six Identities, the Ten Vehicles, and the Four Great Vows—once a single phrase is raised, it instantly becomes more than two hundred and seventy-one thousand phrases. And as for the Zen school...

The essential point lies solely in the three contemplations within one mind. Yet, apart from the twenty-seven thousand one hundred and more phrases, this single phrase of "three contemplations within one mind" cannot be made clear.
Therefore, many phrases do not depart from this one phrase; even this single phrase has no name or appearance that can be grasped.
Without waiting for the tree to fall and the vines to wither, long ago the phrases have returned to nowhere. Profound!
It was as if three gentlemen from the past five or six years had returned, wearing conical caps and square robes, holding the Three Great Works in their hands.
They circumambulated the Buddha three times beneath the Boshan Hall, prostrated at the Master’s feet, and stood with palms joined,
looking only for the Great Master to extend his own hand and eye to graciously receive them.

The Master said: "Since you, Layman, have already been planting your feet within the School of the Patriarchs for two years, and have used a single phrase of Amitābha to dissolve the hells—like hot water poured on snow—this cannot be considered reckless.
Although there has been some inconsistency between earlier and later [practices], it is clear that your will truly aspires to the School of Emptiness."
Why not incinerate it with the fierce flames of the Vajra? It is evident from this that one still awaits a single phrase of Amitābha, failing to realize its practical utility.
Since you, Layman, possess complete intellectual understanding and are in secret accord with Fulong, it is unnecessary to ask;
you surely know that what the *Miaozong* says—that the ultimate of grasping and rejecting is identical to non-grasping and non-rejecting—is true. Yet, even now, you still have grasping and rejecting.
Is it without accepting or rejecting? If there is accepting or rejecting, then even the single word "identical" is a false statement.

Even if one stubbornly asserts mastery and claims it is unimpeded, what can that do against accepting and rejecting? Though one passes through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, one cannot escape this trap.
One may say of oneself, "I am pure," yet not form the thought of being pure. It is like a person dressed in white clothes entering into ink.

In the midst of the pond, he says of himself, "I am not stained by ink. This is not merely deceiving others; it is truly deceiving himself. The essential point for rebirth in the West lies in a single mind that is undisturbed.
Layman, are you now indeed free from such distraction? If you have not yet reached this ultimate state, the cycle of birth and death rages on.

Even if one grants that ten recitations can lead to rebirth, this is merely a provisional skillful means for beginners. Were there even a hair’s breadth of lingering attachment, [rebirth would be impossible].
Is this the ultimate Dharma? Or is it not the ultimate Dharma? If it were not the ultimate, then the staff would break;

one must not fail to understand this. If you say that the Tiantai teachings use entanglements to sweep away entanglements, then they are no different from those who are themselves not bound by entanglements.
As for their relative superiority or inferiority, one who is truly wise will naturally discern this for themselves. Many phrases do not depart from a single phrase;

can one enter many phrases by means of a single phrase? If this is possible—for example, like seeking water and first finding its source—then once the source is found, one need not worry that the branching streams and spreading currents will not reach their destination.
If, however, one seeks it among the branches and tendrils, although one may understand it in one's mind...
I have already understood. Others may preserve this for the rest of their lives and yet never arrive at it.
To recklessly claim that one has "already returned home" is like seeing an egg and demanding a rooster; is this not too premature a calculation?

Question: We have received the Great Master’s instruction that the single thought-moment of consciousness is itself the inconceivable realm, yet one must not hope to grasp this without realizing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Furthermore, he said that the locus of the Dharma Master Zhiyi’s wondrous awakening does not reside within the Three Great Works.
When paying homage to the Lotus Sūtra, how sublime is our Master! Who would say that the Great Master is not himself the Great Teacher?

As for those of us who are dark and ordinary, we have mistakenly relied upon what the Great Master Zhiyi said: that the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] first takes the true reality (bhūtakoṭi) as its object.
When objects are encountered, they are immediately the Middle; there is nothing that is not true reality. Bound to the Dharma-realm, every single thought is the Dharma-realm.
A single form, a single fragrance—none are not the Middle Way. Thus one gains firm conviction in the inconceivable realm. It is not merely that ordinary people and fools have a share in this;
even those who are intensely engaged in lust, killing, theft, and falsehood must, by the very nature of their actions, be subsumed within the single precept. And yet, it is precisely this lust...
Killing, stealing, and lying—in a single thought-moment, their very substance is simultaneously affliction and bodhi, birth-and-death and nirvana.
If one attains genuine faith and maintains firm grasp of this, practicing these perfect deeds according to this Perfect Teaching, yet still does not understand birth-and-death, [it is because...]
To say that the Great Master Zhi (Zhiyi) deceives or defrauds people—this is surely impossible.

The Master said: "I maintain that the single thought-moment of consciousness (*ekakṣaṇa-vijñāna-citta*) is itself the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). That the Great Master’s wondrous awakening does not reside solely within the Three Great Works is a true statement;
it is certainly not a mere speculative view. That a single thought-moment is endowed with the three thousand [dharmas] is the teaching of Zhi (Zhanran)."

The Master’s own realization did not arise from scholarly learning. Such statements as "emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle are identical," or "all phenomena produced by causes and conditions," as well as expressions such as "a single form or a single fragrance," derive from scholarly learning; they are certainly not the Great Master’s place of awakening.

Although you, Layman, have gained conviction in them, these are merely understood through the conscious mind. Since they do not constitute true entry into awakening, they remain within the realm of consciousness.
To resolve the obstructing mind is like oil mixed into flour; there will never be a time of escape. One must not fail to examine this carefully.

To claim that the nature of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying is itself the truth is utterly ignorant. Within the very essence of truth, there is no killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying. These are afflictions inherent to their own substance.

When one realizes that the essence is empty and quiescent, and that what arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature—being like flowers in the sky—then both "bodhi" and "nirvana" are merely superfluous words.

They do not exist because they are uncreated; rather, they do not exist because their fundamental nature is non-existent. To then say, "Based on this Perfect Teaching, one cultivates this Perfect Practice," is precisely what is called "speaking of a dream while in a dream.

It shows a failure to recognize that the Great Master’s [teaching of] sequential progression (*xingbu*) is not merely sequential, nor that his teaching of perfect integration (*yuanrong*) is not merely integrated.
This perfect interfusion lies in the fault of the student, not in the teaching. Within our school, it is not that we do not study the teachings;
we simply do not become stuck in such interpretations. It is like entering directly with a single blade, swiftly slaying Yan Liang for the sake of satisfaction.

Question: I have received your gracious instruction, Master, which states: "As soon as one opens a path of conceptual understanding, one immediately falls into birth and death. I truly submit to this.

However, regarding what you call the "inconceivable realm" (*acintya-viṣaya*), it is simultaneously emptiness, understanding, and the mean. These three truths reside solely within the single thought-moment of the present conscious mind.
This single thought-moment is the most inferior [of all phenomena], yet the three truths within this one mind are the most sudden, the most perfect, and the most noble.

It is unsurpassed. Although its realization and entry are extremely difficult, the Dharma-gate of the inherently evil nature involves taking the entire nature as cultivation and the entire cultivation as residing within the nature;
thus, cultivation and nature are non-dual. One directly cuts off ignorance, reaching even the delusions of views, thought, and the sands of Ganges.

It is like smelting iron: the coarse dross is removed first, not by deliberate intent, but because it naturally falls away first. This single thought-moment directly transcends the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Upon birth, one may immediately realize the stage of Perfect Abiding (*pariniṣpanna-vihāra*). This is a direct and sudden path where the levels of attainment are far transcendent;
it seems that this is not merely a matter of easily resolving the cycle of birth and death. Great Master, in your great compassion, please do not have any concerns.

The Master said: "As soon as one opens a path for intellectual understanding, one immediately falls into birth and death. As the Great Master Yongming said: 'All that is shown in the Perfect Teaching is yet not fully realized;
it is only when one realizes that the nature of words is detached from them that it is called liberation. Those who study the *Zongjing Lu*, who would dare claim that the nature is detached?
They all recognize consciousness upon consciousness and seek the mind within the mind; the more they produce and the more they seek, the further they wander in their search."
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To use the conceptualizing mind to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly;
it can never catch fire. If one does not engage in such conceptualization, by what Dharma-gate could this be called a 'shortcut'?"
Shaolin said: "The mind must be like a blank wall before one can enter the Way. One need not debate whether the nature is good or evil;

rather, through the complete integration of nature and cultivation, one should take up a single phrase of the *huatou* and pursue it with intense, relentless inquiry, as if mourning for one's deceased parents. How could conceptual understanding ever arise?"
Once the fruit is obtained and bursts open, its radiance shines forth like the fierce flames of a red furnace.

The dust and sands of views and thoughts dissolve instantly like ice, just as when a tree is cut at its root—it is impossible for branches and leaves to grow again. How much more so regarding the path above this, which exhausts the profound mysteries;
to remove the coarse while retaining the subtle seems to require an extra measure of mental effort. Even the most subtle sprouts... [are suddenly extinguished].
It is difficult to exhaust [the defilements] all at once; one must directly transcend the stages and ranks. Without practice, there is nothing with which to equalize [the teaching];

to claim that verbal understanding alone accords with reality—such a thing is impossible. Those who study the Tiantai teachings should not presume upon the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) to harbor pride, failing to seek wondrous awakening. How could the saying about "steaming sand" be deceiving me?

Question: Regarding the four teachings of the *Zang*, *Tong*, *Bie*, and *Yuan*, Master Zhi established them. These four teachings consist of five verses whose stages and positions are clearly defined and do not fall into superficiality.
Setting aside the latter four verses for now, the first verse alone states: "The seven worthies and seven stages are the initial capacity of the *Zang* teaching;
within the stages of the *Tong* teaching, the first and second are simultaneous; the *Bie* faith and the *Yuan* five-grade positions [overcome] view-delusion and thought-delusion."

The first subjugation occurs while dwelling as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). "Dwelling as an ordinary person" refers to the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages (*sādhāraṇāvāsa*), which is one of the four pure lands (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Regarding the seven stages of the worthy ones (*saptakalyāṇaka*): these consist of the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-viśrāma-citta*), the distinct applications of mindfulness (*prabheda-smṛtyupasthāna*), the general applications of mindfulness (*samasta-smṛtyupasthāna*), and the four stages of preparatory application (*catvāri prayoga-avasthā*).

Setting aside the stage of the four preparatory applications for now, within the context of the general and distinct applications of mindfulness alone—specifically, the first [application], the contemplation of the impurity of the body (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) among the five stages of mental abiding—[the subjugation occurs].

The single practice of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) opens up the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the six subtle gates, the sixteen special victories, and the methods of contemplation, refinement, perfuming, and cultivation—these wondrous keys to both mundane and supramundane dhyāna-gates.
Once these are opened and unified, every single one is nothing other than an inconceivable, perfectly wondrous Dharma-gate.
It is precise, direct, stable, and secure, ensuring that the single thought of the cognitive mind and the eye-sight remain steadfast.

Upon landing, there is absolutely no stumbling. How much more so when it comes to the gradual and the sudden, the esoteric and the exoteric, the distinct and the perfect—there is not a single tangle of trivialities to be grasped, nor a single thing to be discarded. This is what is called "the 'ya' and 'zhe' within the vast void.
If one errs, let one follow that error; the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is there. Great Master, with your great compassion, I pray you do not harbor any further concern.

The Master said: "Regarding such phrases as 'the stages and positions of the four teachings and five verses are clearly distinguished,' and even down to 'a single sutra’s opening and convergence,' every one of these is nothing other than an inconceivable, perfectly wondrous Dharma-gate, fully contained within the Three Great Works. I shall not cite them here at length.
Yet that which is described as 'precise, exact, stable, and fitting'—this is the vision of the Great Master Zhiyi, not the vision of ordinary students."

Furthermore, the layman said: "If one can preserve this single thought of the conscious mind, then when the light of the eyes falls to the ground [at death], one will certainly not lose one's footing.

But with which mind does the layman preserve it? If he uses the conscious mind, that conscious mind is obstructed by the "shadows" (the transition between lives) and thus cannot know past lives or possess supernormal penetration;

I fear such things cannot be accomplished in a single lifetime. At the moment of death, good and evil are like a person’s debts: whichever is stronger will first drag one away—not even a hair’s breadth of difference.
When thoughts arise, how could it be merely a matter of words? For instance, when Han and Shi saw Shoushan, they did not remember that matter at all;
even "the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss" is but the talk of one who is drowsing.

Question: Having received the Great Master’s instruction, a great lay practitioner asked: "If one simply maintains the *huatou*, can the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures be entirely discarded?
Answer: Why do you hold such a view? The Three Vehicles were taught specifically for those of the Three Vehicles.
Have you not seen what the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "Only those who have attained sudden awakening are exempt from following the Dharma"?
Following this profound teaching, how could one again harbor doubts, asking: "If one simply maintains the *huatou*, can the Three Great Works (*Sānbùdàoshǔ*) be entirely discarded?

Nevertheless, within the Three Great Works, all practitioners of the three vehicles are collectively subsumed as "perfect persons" (*yuánrén*) of sudden awakening; and the four teachings and ten vehicles are likewise [subsumed]. Six...

This refers to the Four Great Vows. Although they are precise and exact, not permitting even a single word to be distorted, in reality there is not a single dharma that can be accommodated or followed.
Thus, in the entirety of Jingxi’s *Vajra-Needle*, he relies entirely upon a dream, which perfectly accords with what my Master said during his formal address upon the conclusion of the retreat:
"Every single thing is a matter within a dream. Furthermore, at the end of the *Vajra-Needle*...
A single phrase says: "Suddenly awakening from a dream, neither the questioner nor the respondent, nor that which was asked or answered, can be found at all.
If this is so, then as for the *Zong* (the Essence) and the *Jiao* (the Teaching), who is not within a single dream?

Nevertheless, the *Three Great Works* and the *Vajra Needle* must ultimately not be discarded along with the *Triyāna* and the *Twelve Divisions of Scripture*. How could the Great Master have ever intended to discard the Three [Baskets]?
Riding upon the twelve divisions of the scriptures and the three great treatises— the *Vajra-needle* included— may I, while my breath has not yet ceased,
take these three great treatises and the *Vajra-needle* as a broad-foreheaded butcher’s single-handled pig-killing blade.
At the moment of death, one lets go. This is because one relies upon the empowerment of the Great Master. Yet, even before letting go, there is still the power of the ordinary person’s vows.
The Master said: "A single phrase of the *huatou* is difficult for the clever student to grasp, because their intellectual understanding is too great; they are like a monkey."
I leap and bound about without a moment’s rest, wishing to gather [these thoughts] into a perfected person and call myself one of sudden enlightenment.

This is like falsely claiming the title of Emperor; I dare not speak of it to others. In truth, there is not a single dharma that can be accommodated or followed. It is much like covering one's ears while stealing a bell.
If one were to let go of even a single word or phrase, it would be like eating a delicious delicacy—how could one forget it? How much more so for the teachings and principles!
Yes. Reflect upon this and it will become clear; there is no need for Boshan to add further annotations. As the ancients said:
"Without a crystal bead, it is difficult to clarify turbid water; without the wisdom-torch of the Zen school, it is truly difficult to shatter the profound darkness of ten million kalpas.
How much more so regarding the dream within a dream! I fear that the *Three Great Treatises on the Diamond Scalpel* may not be easily explained to you, Layman.
It is indeed a butcher’s blade.

[The Master] asked: "Setting aside for a moment that the Perfect and Sudden teaching of the Tiantai school is noble and unsurpassed—let us grant that even its subtle and intricate details are truly not as direct and penetrating as the Chan school.
Yet, for one like Huguang, whose past karma is so profound and heavy, would it not ultimately be better to abandon the easy?"
It is difficult. To speak with sweet words while enduring suffering—why is this? Allow me first to borrow the conditions of the world to reflect upon myself.
By nature, I am dull and inferior. At first, having received my degree, I declined the post of Librarian; when selected for the office of District Magistrate, I quickly moved to a cold mat.
Wherever I went, I was never free from the heavy encirclement of worldly burdens. Laughing, I have staked my very life, singing my own song amidst the constant tasting of bitterness and hardship.

From self-dancing to the Dharma-gate of the great matter of birth and death—how could these be the same as children’s play? Yet, regarding the timing and the person followed, one must still investigate the ultimate principle.
Since our Great Master has fully raised the standard of the true command, why need one merely follow the fashion of ordinary folk by discarding armor and rushing to the wind?
One should simply reflect that while Bodhidharma first opened the school of Shaoshi, Master Zhi was the one who initially established the lineage of Fulong. And...

The five schools of the lineage are like the blazing sun at midday, while the secret treasury of the three contemplations remains submerged in a dark chamber. One is scorching heat, the other is chilling cold;

they cannot be compared in the same breath. Consequently, those who abandon the heat to seek the cold—guarding the profound mystery through myriad hardships—unconsciously become addicted to its particularities and cast themselves into them.
I often lament that after the wondrous enlightenment of Dàsū, the likes of Jīngxī and Mìngyǎn stood alone.

The lamp’s cold flame barely persists as a single thread amidst the dark stream; the relationship between teacher and disciple is like that of an infant and a pestle—my heart is consumed and my countenance grows dark.
Holding fast to this King of Vows, I shall not avoid the hells; having no mind to seek ease, I am fated to toil on.
Whether like an ox following or a sheep resisting, I await the teacher’s decisive action.

The Master said: "The Tiantai school’s doctrine of perfect and sudden enlightenment is the most honored and unsurpassed. I venture to ask: what is it that makes the doctrine of the Tiantai school the most honored and unsurpassed?
If you say it is the principle of the perfect culmination of the one mind, then this should be sought within the mind itself, not through the teachings.
Our Great Master Bodhidharma transmitted the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; he came across the sea and rejected all names and forms. Therefore, he said:"
"Directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha. This resonance and awakening is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
Although one enters the inconceivable realm, the traces of mental activity cease. As for the path that leads upward, not a single sage has transmitted it.

To speak even the word "Buddha" is already superfluous. This is not like the schools of formal teaching, which inherently involve degrees of difficulty—possessing aspects of the Perfect, the Sudden, and the Provisional.
Those with discerning nature—who among them could not study the teachings? Yet, it is truly difficult to find such a person within the Gate of the Patriarchal Lineage (Zongmen).
Layman, why do you not reflect that the life-vein of the Patriarchs hangs by a thread? It is precisely at this moment that one must strive to penetrate deeply.

As for the "Teachings and Vehicles" (*jiaocheng*): to clearly comprehend the Great Dharma, to transmit the mind-seal of the patriarchs, and to open the eye of wisdom for sentient beings—this is truly the supreme aspiration of Mount Bo.

Question: "To practice by departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness. Since one has already departed from mind, intellect, and consciousness, with what does one practice? What is it that one practices?
The Master said: "As for the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*), how can one leave them behind?

Simply take up a single phrase of the *huatou* and investigate it with true diligence and earnestness, as if you had lost your parents. When the mind, intellect, and consciousness attempt to arise but cannot do so, what need is there to 'leave' them?

This very mind, intellect, and consciousness—how could they possibly be left behind? It is like adding snow to a red-hot furnace; though you seek their traces, they are utterly unfindable. Furthermore..."
"What is this that you have penetrated? The layman should immediately take up "What is this? and seek its ultimate resolution.

If one does not understand, it is best to harbor doubt. After a long silence, he said: "When idle clouds have dispersed and the wild ravines are clear, the vast sea and sky are bright with the shining moon."
Question: What is it that makes one a fool? Having been spared by my teacher from being cast aside, I have received his diligent answers to my questions;
yet he has analyzed and peeled away [my delusions] until they are difficult to respond to. Since I am but a fool and not one beyond the ordinary, how could I have grasped this before even asking?

The Great Master answers without answering; I, the fool, question and then question again. Only through your great compassion, I pray you, will you finally instruct me. Once I was shown: "If, right now, there is..."
To speak of "accepting and rejecting" with the single word "sameness" (tong) is itself a false statement. Xuán further doubts this:

if the fundamental principle of the *Miaozong* (Profound Pivot) truly consists in accepting and rejecting—wherein "increasing existence" and "increasing non-existence" constitute the perfect subtlety—then does this not mean that the initial state of non-existence falls into the Lesser Vehicle?
The Master said: "To have more by having less—this is what is called perfect subtlety. Yet he did not realize that Tiantai was merely borrowing a path to return home;

he ultimately did not fall into the conceptual trap of existence and non-existence. The two characters "existence" and "non-existence" are but echoes within perfect subtlety; they do not represent a state where there was originally nothing at all.
If one were to tune a lute by gluing its sounding board shut, this would not be the case only for those of the Small Vehicle;

even for ordinary beings whose mental activities are burning with passion, to attempt to match them to the perfect and subtle [Dharma] is much like feeling for empty space or striking a hollow sound. Even if they were to pass through many kalpas, there is ultimately no principle by which they could attain it.
Would a person of wisdom not feel deep pain upon reflecting on this?
Question: One has received your instruction. Regarding the use of "entanglements" to sweep away entanglements versus one who is not bound by entanglements, how do their merits compare?
I, Xuan, am further in doubt: Is not being unbound by entanglements the ultimate principle of the higher realm?

If we were to compare this with the Tiantai school’s doctrine of "two yet non-dual" and "non-dual yet two," we would be precisely disputing the presence or absence of these entanglements. Only our Great Master truly said: [The text here implies a citation of the Master's teaching on this point.]
I do not dare to suppress the School with the Teaching, nor the School with the Teaching; how could I again establish a distinction of superiority or inferiority?

If you claim that the deficiency lies in the person and not in the Teaching, then the fault of entanglement in doctrinal reasoning would not be avoided. How could it be that the fault lies solely in the person?
The Master said: "To be unentangled by the vines of conceptual proliferation truly depends on the person and not on the teachings. It is like being born into a royal house;

one’s natural nobility requires no external cultivation. If one were to compare this with [merely] functional efficacy, the difference in excellence would be as vast as that between heaven and earth."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Ānanda, even if you could expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it would not equal practicing untainted karma for a single day.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* further states: "It is like the sun hanging in the sky; a child closes his eyes and says, 'Why can I not see? So too is much learning.
This is the teaching school's method of discerning the relative superiority and inferiority between the teacher and the recipient. It does not depend on...

Through deliberation, [the doubts] were suddenly resolved like ice melting away. In the present age, those who study the teachings and principles—why do they not grasp the main framework and determine the fundamental rules?
Is this the fault of the scriptures, or the fault of the people?

Question: One received an instruction stating that many phrases do not depart from a single phrase; one must obtain the source of the water. If one pursues the branches and twigs, to claim falsely that "the phrases return to where?"—is this not premature?

I, Xuán, have heard that the Tiantai school exclusively employs the six consciousnesses, which is called "leaving the *zhàng* for the *chǐ*, leaving the *chǐ* for the *cùn*," and is also called "cutting down the tree to find the root" or "seeking the water to find the source. How could this be...?

This does not contradict the fundamental tenets of our Master; rather, it traces back to the source and sweeps away the tangled branches. Once the root is attained, the branches are themselves the root;
once the source is found, the stream is itself the source. A single phrase contains many phrases, and many phrases constitute a single phrase;
there seems to be no further distinction to be made between priority and sequence.

The Master said: "The Tiantai school exclusively employs the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). This is precisely like our own school’s practice of 'riding the thief’s horse to pursue the thief'—is it appropriate to take that horse as the root or the source?
If one takes the horse as the root and source, this is called being oblivious to the master;
it may be described as a servant who fails to distinguish [the master from the servant]. Guifeng said: 'Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream; it is merely...'"

The one mind and the eight consciousnesses are like a single blade; how much more so for the rest? If one discusses the principle of perfect ultimacy, one must grasp its root and not seek out its branches and leaves;
one must reach its source and not stagnate in the spreading current. To grasp the root is to see that every branch is wood;
to grasp the source is to see that every drop is water. If one takes the branches, leaves, and spreading currents as the fundamental, [one has missed the mark].

Regarding the source and flow [of the Huai and Si rivers]: how could it be merely a matter of relying on the Huai and Si? To claim they are the very same as Lake Anavatapta—is that not too premature a calculation?
Question: You have once instructed me, saying: "In a single thought-moment of the mind of consciousness, ensure there is no 'losing one's footing. Which mind is used to ensure this? If...

If one uses the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*), once that mind is separated from the physical body by the *pañca-skandha* (the "five-shade" barrier), one will be unable to know past lives or possess supernormal powers; thus, it may be feared that the goal of this lifetime will be difficult to achieve.

The Great Master, out of his great compassion, issued this admonition: at this point, can ordinary and ignorant people truly afford to claim they have attained what they have not attained, and treat hell as a mere child’s play?

Nevertheless, since the Tiantai School specifically employs the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) as its core tenet, this aligns perfectly with the principles of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calming and Insight).
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "By recollecting the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.
This implies that even the recollection and mindfulness [involved here] employ the six consciousnesses; there is certainly no error in this.

Although a person of the Perfect Teaching is most consummate and sudden, they must—regardless of what stage they reach, what delusions they sever, or what principle they realize—thoroughly penetrate all the various teachings and stages when making retrospective judgments. Within the specific capacity of such a student...

It is not necessary to rely on the supernormal power of knowing past lives; rather, the teachings clarify the application of the six consciousnesses. The six consciousnesses clearly reveal the stages and positions [of practice].
If one can cultivate according to the teachings, even if a practitioner is ultimately unable to protect themselves, the principles of the teaching can serve as their guarantor.
"An ordinary fool speaks with the straightforward speech of an ordinary fool, hoping only that the Great Master will take pity on him and accept him, and then instruct him accordingly.
The Master said: "The Tiantai school’s provisional use [of these terms] is as clear as the sun and stars; it is simply that you, Layman, have misunderstood them. Have you not heard?"
To contemplate emptiness as real is to contemplate birth as non-birth. If one takes the six consciousnesses as the sovereign, it is like steaming sand to make rice;
the sand is not rice. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha refutes that which performs the act of discernment as being the mind, and further commands a subtle investigation.

That you, Layman, identify the six consciousnesses [as the mind] without waiting to seek the nature of the mind that is quiescent and eternal is precisely analogous to mistaking a thief for one's own son.

Is this not erroneous? Regarding the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*: first, one takes the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as the object; the created realm is itself the Middle Way, wherein nothing is not real.

Emerging from within this true reality, the two meanings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are explained: the quiescence of the dharma-nature is called *śamatha*, while its constant illumination is called *vipaśyanā*.
The essence of *vipaśyanā* lies in initiating practice rather than lingering in the gate of mere intellectual understanding. As the Great Master of Nanyue [Huisi] did for ninety days...
Constant sitting leads to simultaneous, perfect realization; it is not a matter of intellectual understanding. Furthermore, as the *Dharmatā-sūtra* states:
"Cessation is not the ultimate truth; one meets the truth through cessation. If even cessation is not the truth, how much less so is the conscious mind (*manovijñāna*)?

Regarding the cited phrases such as "recalling the Buddha" and "mindfulness of the Buddha," when one mindfully contemplates emptiness and attains the opening of the self-realized mind, does the conscious mind still persist? If one judges this by means of the intellect, [one will fail to see].
If one takes this teaching as the ultimate, then there is no need for Tiantai’s contemplation of the mind, nor the laborious constant sitting of Nanyue.

Delusions would never be severed, and how could the principle ever enter the Perfect [Teaching]? Even if one were to practice for many kalpas, one would merely be a person speaking of the mind and nature;
the fire of the Way has never burned one's mouth. How can talking about food satisfy hunger? Do not deceive yourself; reflect upon this and it will become clear.
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Twenty-three;
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Twenty-four.
Compiled by Honghan, Dharma Grandson residing at Boshan.
The Head Seat and Dharma-grandson Hongyu, together with Jijiao Daxiang, Sizhuo Fashi, and Wenwen, asked:
"Within the Huayan assembly, those of the Two Vehicles are like the blind and the deaf; nevertheless, they are also inclusively gathered therein."

The Śrāvakas [are included here] because this scripture encompasses immeasurable vehicles. Although this sutra states that those of the two-vehicle lineage do not arise [in that land], the factors of the path (mārga-dharma) it proclaims are mutually accessible to both the Great and Small Vehicles; thus, it is no different from the "Four Noble Truths" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
As for those who must spend kalpas in that sutra before realizing the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Amitābha likewise employs the three vehicles.
Regarding the salvation of sentient beings, [this teaching] should naturally encompass both the Two Pitakas and the Five Teachings. Why, then, do you say it does not include the Hīnayāna?
Furthermore, if it already encompasses the *Avataṃsaka*, how could it fail to encompass the infinite vehicles subsumed within the *Avataṃsaka*?

The Master said: "Since you, Layman, already know that the *Avataṃsaka* subsumes immeasurable vehicles, how could it be that noble śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—who at times closed their eyes and silenced their hearing—were not all acting through the Tathāgata’s supreme power of skillful means?

It was for the purpose of guiding a certain class of those with limited capacity to give rise to profound faith and believe in the One Vehicle. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: 'The Buddha, by means of countless skillful means...'"

They guide sentient beings because, in reality, all are for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. This sutra states that those of the two vehicles who do not produce [the roots of goodness] are specifically intended to convert and guide those of the two vehicles who cling to emptiness and do not cultivate the Pure Land. The Commentary says: "How could this apply only to ordinary beings?"
It also delivers the noble ones of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). If even those of the two vehicles are born [in that land], how much more so will Bodhisattvas not be born?

One should have no doubt that Amitābha delivers beings through the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Since he guides and transforms them by means of the three vehicles, he also encompasses immeasurable vehicles (*apramāṇayāna*);

the two sutras are mutually consistent, and their meaning is self-evident. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "The icchantikas do not enter [nirvāṇa]," which does not mean that icchantikas cannot enter nirvāṇa.

Question: Practicing the Way through other gates is called "ascending out of the three realms," whereas mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land is called "transversely exiting the three realms.

This is because the so-called "other gates" are taught as the correct instruction for the practice of the Middle Way (Madhyamaka), while Zen meditation is termed the "separate transmission," and the Pure Land is likewise described [as such].
Since all paths involve transcending through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), why does he now say that "contemplation is itself mindfulness" and "mindfulness is itself contemplation"?
By directly equating this with the Tiantai contemplation, does he not, conversely, render the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection) dull and neglected?

The Master said: "Regarding the discourse on 'horizontal' and 'vertical,' the *Chao* states: 'It is like a worm inside a bamboo stalk; if it moves vertically, it is difficult to pass through the nodes, but if it moves horizontally, it is liberated all at once.
This means that because the Land of Bliss and the realm of suffering stand side by side, it is called 'horizontal.

However, this is merely a preliminary explanation. When discussing the One Mind, both the horizontal and vertical are all-pervasive. It is only in the case of the Pure Land that the vertical is not fully present, which is why it is referred to as merely 'horizontal.'"

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "The light of that Buddha is immeasurable; it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without obstruction. The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "This mind creates the Buddha;
because the mind is itself the Buddha, the Pure Land is but the mind. Since the realms are described as being horizontal [in extent], how could the mind not be perfectly complete?
Other approaches do not refer exclusively to meditative visualization (*vipaśyanā*); rather, they truly encompass all dharma-gates. As for Chan meditation...
That which is called the "Separate Tradition" (biezhuan) is not that which is expounded by the five teachings. Pure Land is also termed the "Direct Path";

how could it be reached through the three contemplations? Now, it is said that contemplation is itself mindfulness, and mindfulness is itself contemplation; raising a single thought instantaneously fulfills the practice of contemplation.

Because one attains rebirth through the transcendence of a single thought-moment, rather than being born only after the completion of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), we know that mindfulness does not obstruct the inclusion of contemplation;
nor can contemplative practice dull or hinder the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

Question: The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* (*Guanjing shu*) explains that the sixteen contemplations encompass the three truths (*tisatyāni*). Now, if this sutra is used to supplement the *Contemplation Sutra*, one enters the gateway of the Tiantai contemplative system;
if this sutra is categorized as belonging to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one enters the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai fajie*).
However, while the Tiantai school uniquely attributes the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the fourth dharma-realm (fajie) exists only in the *Avataṃsaka*.

It is unknown whether the three contemplations (sanguan) of the Tiantai school can encompass the contemplation of the dharma-realm; this is a point of distinction between the Tiantai and Xianshou schools.
If for the purpose of a synoptic comparison, the Master said:

"The Commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Guānjīng Shù) explains that the sixteen contemplations encompass the three truths; now, by means of this sūtra, we shall cross-reference it with the *Amitābha Sūtra*."
This is also not an obstacle, for the sixteen contemplations provide a lateral connection to this sutra. Why is this?
The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that the jeweled nets, walking trees, lotus ponds, and stairways are all composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
that the light of that Buddha is immeasurable, and that the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas are innumerable. Furthermore, by including the Western Land, how could the suspended drum not be complete? One.

The sixteen contemplations seem not necessarily to belong to the gateway of the Tiantai teachings; rather, it is more appropriate that the Tiantai teachings enter into my own single thought-moment as the path among paths.
This is because this sutra is categorized as belonging to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), and Tiantai [classifies] the Perfect Teaching [as such].
[The teaching] returns exclusively to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The *Jiyao* (Essential Excerpts) states: "The non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena exists only in the *Avataṃsaka*.

Since it is called the 'Perfect Teaching' (*yuanjiao*), how could it not encompass the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena? Using the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena as the title for the 'Contemplation of the Dharma-realm,' how could it not encompass the Perfect [Teaching] and the partial [teachings] of Amitābha?
It is like a single drop taken from the ocean; it does not hinder its being identical to the entire tide. Thus say Tiantai and Xianshou.
Is this not what is meant by the phrase: "Distinct yet not distinct, not distinct yet distinct," as applied to this sutra’s commentaries and sub-commentaries? Question:

The *Jiejing lun* (Treatise on the Combined Sutras) judges that Amitābha’s Pure Land is provisional (*upāya*) rather than ultimate (*paramārtha*), whereas the Pure Land of Mind-only (*cittamātra*) described in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* is the ultimate Pure Land.

However, the *Vimalakīrti* states: "When a bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who possess a straightforward mind and so forth will come to be born in his land. How is this to be reconciled?
This clearly states that the matter of gathering in sentient beings—dying here and being born there—is no different from [the land of] Amitābha;
it directly points to the phenomena of rebirth. Why, then, does the treatise divide this into two separate parts? The Commentary states:
"This refers to 'one-pointedness of practice' (shishixin). But how could one-pointedness of practice not be called "mind-only" (weixin)?
The Master said: The *He lun* states that Amitābha’s Pure Land is provisional (*upāya*). As it says, "A single thought-moment" and "one mind undistracted" refer to the provisional and the real.
The Pure Land of Vimalakīrti is the real; as it says, "According to the purity of one's mind, the Buddha-land is pure.
When a bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, as it says, "With a straightforward mind... sentient beings come to be born in that land," this is the provisional within the real. As for... [text continues].

Pointing to the gate necessarily implies entering the room; as entering the room necessarily implies passing through the gate, the general purport of these two sutras does not preclude their mutual citation, for they are not two separate fragments.
Regarding the "single-mindedness directed toward phenomena" (*shishi yixin*) mentioned in the Commentary, it emphasizes the practice of recitation.

It states: "If one penetrates this mind, the four natures do not arise, and it accords with the wisdom of emptiness; this is called 'single-mindedness in principle' (*li yixin*). This is principle within the phenomenon. How could this be?
If this were attained, it could not be called "mind-only.
Question: This sutra states that among those born as sentient beings, many are those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). However, the Great Version says:
Those born in that land shall all, in a single lifetime, succeed to the position of a Buddha. This meaning of "all" is not merely that there are many;

rather, it implies that even those who do not undergo birth from a womb and so forth are all in the state of succession to Buddhahood, and are all Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi).

The Master said: "This sutra states that among those born as sentient beings, many are 'in their final birth before Buddhahood' (*ekajātipratibaddha*). This word 'many' is spoken from a proximate perspective.
The Great Version says, 'All shall, in one lifetime, succeed to the position of Buddha. This word 'all' is spoken from a remote perspective."
This sutra states: "Those born in that land are all *avaivartika*—in the language of China, 'non-retrogressive.
Are they not, therefore, destined to eventually succeed to the rank of Buddhahood? That is to say, they will immediately succeed to the Buddha’s position upon being conceived in the womb.

This makes it even clearer that they are not bodhisattvas currently designated as 'Equal Enlightenment' (*samyaksambodhi*). For the extended and the abbreviated are simultaneous; this is what is meant by the 'path within the path,' which is further clarified herein."
This is true. Question:
A person who practices *nienfo* (recitation of the Buddha’s name) alone does not cultivate auxiliary causes; it is said that "if one obtains the root, need not worry about the branches.

Therefore, it is stated that by not cultivating other practices, one attains *pāramitā*. It is also said that this constitutes a great deal of goodness and merit, such that all Buddhas, with their myriad...

The causal flowers of practice adorn the Dharma-body. Now, when we contemplate what the Buddha has realized, can it be said that he possesses only the "plain" (or unadorned) Dharma-body, or is it rather that he is already fully endowed with the adornments of the myriad practices?

The Master said: "For those who practice the single method of reciting the Buddha's name alone without cultivating auxiliary causes—consider that in the ancients' Pure Land practices, when spiritual friends diligently exhorted others to recite the Buddha's name so they might be born together in the Pure Land, was this not an auxiliary cause? By not practicing other deeds and solely reciting the Buddha's name, one reaches the other shore;
thus, to have faith in this one gate is itself a multitude of good roots, and to transform those of a similar kind is itself a multitude of blessings. Furthermore,
Having long possessed the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) constitutes "abundant goodness" (*puṇya*); having long cultivated other practices constitutes "abundant merit" (*bhāga*).
This is the adornment of the myriad practices already perfected; it is not the primordial *dharmakāya*.
Question: The teachings of the Zen school instruct people to investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? This seems no different from other *gong'an* (public cases).

Yet, there has never been mention of dedicating the merit toward rebirth in the Western Pure Land. The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "Investigating the essence of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) is identical to the method of venerable masters who instruct people to take up a *huatou* (critical phrase)."
The mental state of doubt (*vicikitsā*) is extremely similar [to this]. This is merely a similarity; it is still a matter of directly investigating the word "Who? (*shui*).

The teachings categorize four types of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection), yet they do not list the method of "investigating the essence" (*ti-jiu*) as one of them. Now, although it is included under the name "holding fast," it seems that the original scriptures did not intend for it to be so.
One should not use this to enter the gateway of the Pure Land practice. If one says that by investigating this *huatou* (critical phrase), awakening will occur, then the mind—
"Even if one does not awaken, one will still not fail to attain rebirth. This is a retreatary step left behind for the Chan school; it is merely falling into a 'thieving mind.
If you say that unless this doubt is resolved, one cannot attain rebirth, then you are actually worse off than those who simply recite the name directly without giving rise to such doubts.
Although they do not attain awakening, they still manage to attain rebirth. Thus did Master Zhiche speak directly.
This constitutes the correct practice for purifying the Buddha-land. Ci-zhao, Tian-qi, and Du-feng all taught people to investigate the "Buddha-recitation" (nianfo).
Upon what basis did these masters rely? As for the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the Patriarch Yunqi and other masters, why did they not directly point to the word "Who"?
If it is merely similar [to the method of investigating the mind], are there further differences? Regarding the points where they are not entirely identical, why...

[The Master] pierced through [the questioner's intent]. The Master said: "In the Chan school, we teach people to investigate and study; what is valued is the aspiration for great enlightenment. There is no further turning toward the Western Paradise.
How can you speak of 'leaving behind one step' so as not to lose the opportunity for rebirth? This is merely the commentary of a layperson; it is not the intent of the Chan school."
The *Chao* (Commentary) states: Regarding the practice of "investigating the essence through nianfo" (*ti-jiu nianfo*), it cannot be left unexplained.

"Investigate" (*can*) means to penetrate through; "essence" (*ti*) means to apply oneself closely. This close application also carries the sense of pausing in contemplation, which the Chan school would certainly not employ.

As Shaolin said: "The mind must be like a wall before one can enter the Way. Furthermore, this is not the same as proceeding with direct recitation. To compare their respective merits, Yunqi [said]:...
The various masters of our school are likewise one gate to the Pure Land; they gather in this class of practitioners by opening up a single thread.
When the Way is thus revealed, how can one distinguish between what is similar and what is not?

Question: Since all lands are sustained solely by perception (*saṃjñā*), one should replace deluded perceptions with pure perceptions. Just as a child remembers its mother, there must be wholesome perceptions; her countenance and deportment can be clearly visualized.
Now, regarding the single gate of holding the Name, one merely ensures that the sound of the recitation continues uninterruptedly without grasping at appearances.
This is no different from reading and reciting [scriptures]. Because the mind is easily distracted, invoking the Name serves as a skillful means (*upāya*).
Alternatively, some rely on the inhalation and exhalation of breath, using it as a support to bind the mind.

Such methods as those for collecting the mind and regulating the breath found in the *dhyāna-sūtras* appear to belong to the Hīnayāna and do not constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Might they not, then, be practices intended for ordinary persons of great resolve?

The Master said: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "Recalling the Buddha and mindful of the Buddha" means that when mindfulness and recollection are continuous, one naturally attains the opening of the mind.

This is not comparable to the mere holding of the name until reaching the state of "single-mindedness without distraction. For those who read and recite, they merely seek to memorize and understand; for those who hold the name, they simply desire rebirth in the Pure Land.
It is like carrying a heavy burden and desiring only to reach home—how could there be any scattering or distraction? This continues even unto single-mindedness.
It is not chaotic; it is not a matter of binding the mind by means of the vital breath (prāṇa).

To be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the time it takes to snap one's fingers is as swift as the wind, similar to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. How could a bodhisattva of great resolve abandon this shortcut dharma-gate to seek elsewhere?
Question: The *Great Sutra* states: "If there are sentient beings who give rise to even a single thought-moment and mindfully recollect Amitāyus, they will certainly be born in that land.
Yet, the commentary specifies a fixed period of only ten recitations and does not mention a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, the nature of mindfulness arises and ceases moment by moment (*kṣaṇika*), whereas according to this sutra, one is born through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) after seven days. If this is so, then those who have not attained dhyāna-concentration would have no share [in this practice]. If it is as you say...

Regarding "a single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*): if it were interpreted as "attaining Buddhahood upon a single recitation," then Huiyuan’s gloss as "taking refuge with a single-minded heart" would not logically follow after the mention of the "ten recitations.

Conversely, if one follows the literal wording of the sutra and takes it to mean "a single thought-moment of a heart of love and joy," then there is a discrepancy between this and the statement in the *Transformed Sutra* (*Kuan-wu-liang-shou-fo-ching*) that one reaches the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya without a heart of attachment; thus, the difficulty and ease of the two accounts differ.
"In this case, even those who possess no meditative concentration at all can attain rebirth. Furthermore, does not this superior expedient surpass that of the *Shorter Sutra*?

The Master said: "Since the ten recitations and this version [of the *Longer Sutra*] are mutually compatible, how can one distinguish between their superiority or inferiority? For a single thought-moment possesses..."
Because all thoughts are fundamentally one, a single thought is not necessarily superior; since ten thoughts are identical to one thought, it is not necessarily inferior.
Therefore, to speak of a single thought does not preclude ten thoughts, and to speak of ten thoughts does not preclude a single thought.
Furthermore, a single kṣaṇa does not preclude seven days, and seven days do not preclude a single kṣaṇa. As the Sūtra says: "In a single thought, universally contemplate immeasurable kalpas."
There is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Whether it is said to be one thought-moment, ten thought-moments, seven days, or many kalpas, all are the supreme skillful means of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one need not deliberate over whether [the practice] is fixed or unfixed, nor pleasant or unpleasant;
simply recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind, and nothing will remain unaccomplished. It is like a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold. Moreover—
There is no room for doubt. Furthermore, why must one compare their transcendence by means of difficulty or ease?
Question: If these seven days are set aside as ordinary times and one waits until the moment of death to practice mindfulness, this has already been rebuked by Tianru.
Regarding the statement that "now, as it belongs to a period of peace," does this mean that after seven days, for the remainder of one's life, one will never again fall into disorder?

Or does it mean that even if one falls into disorder thereafter, one will ultimately attain rebirth? If one were never again to fall into disorder, it would not be appropriate to designate the period as merely "seven days.
If one were to fall into disorder again, then one has already regressed; how then could one cause the Buddha to manifest before one?
The Master said: "The sutras state that from one day up to seven days is a fixed period for rebirth. This does not distinguish between the time of death and ordinary times;
it means that upon hearing the Buddha's name even once, one should immediately exert fierce diligence for seven days. For those who do attain rebirth, this is clear.

However, as for those who have not yet attained rebirth, they must maintain an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness moment after moment. How could they possibly stop reciting the Buddha's name after seven days?"

Regarding the two characters "grasping" (執) and "maintaining" (持): how are they explained in the text? The commentary states: "Grasping" means hearing the name and receiving it with courage and decisiveness, so that it cannot be shaken or taken away.
"Maintaining" means having received it, one guards it, remaining forever constant and firm so as not to forget it.
How then can one speak of [only] seven days, or of following after distraction? The practitioner should maintain single-minded right mindfulness, making it even more intense and sharp.
If one continues for a lifetime with the same intensity as the initial moment of generating the aspiration, why worry that the Buddha will not respond with grace?

Question: The *Chao* (Commentary) clarifies that "single-mindedness of principle" constitutes the achievement of the power of contemplation; thus, thorough investigation belongs entirely to the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*).

Yet, while it was previously stated that wondrous contemplation is difficult to achieve and thus the superiority of holding the name was revealed, it now appears that this [method] again accords with the methods of contemplation. Is this not so?

Meditative contemplation (*samādhi-vipaśyanā*) is superior to the recitation of names. If one claims that "investigating the word 'Who' (*shui*)" constitutes thorough inquiry (*ti-jiu*), then this would entirely belong to the School of the Patriarchs (*zongmen*).

Furthermore, when investigating a *huatou*, there should be no discursive thought; yet [if one relies on the text], how many rational paths could one possibly resort to—such as "knowing non-duality" or "quiescent illumination beyond thought"?
One cannot avoid falling into error in both respects. How can this meaning be reconciled?

The Master said: "The previous statement that 'wondrous contemplation is difficult to accomplish' was intended to manifest the extraordinary excellence of holding the Name. This is because the minds of beings in this Sahā world are largely distracted;

thus, holding the Name to gather the mind is superior to the gate of contemplation. Now, however, we again incorporate the methods of contemplation, for the method of contemplation is itself a Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
Just as holding even a single thought-moment does not preclude the full possession of all contemplations, so it is when reciting the name of Amitābha."
As for the sutras, they are the sublime realms of the West; who would not find a profound resonance with them?

However, because the practice of upholding [the name] emphasizes manifest excellence, and because the object of contemplation is so sublime, it does not hinder the swiftness of name-holding. Because the path of name-holding is direct and expedient, it does not hinder the transcendence found in the methods of contemplation.

Since both approaches are established in their own right, how can one say that [name-holding] falls short? As for the investigation of the Gate of the Patriarchs (Chán), it is a method tailored to specific capacities; it seems unnecessary [to apply this critique here].
To harmonize this with the Pure Land teachings: when one investigates, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? this immediately belongs to the Chan (Zen) school.
Here, the path of words and language is cut off; thus, one must not rely upon intellectual reasoning as a support.

Question: Throughout this entire commentary, the primary emphasis is placed on the maintenance of principle (*li*). Thus, the method of maintenance explained therein is considered the most vital point.

Now, since this practice is the recitation of the Name (*nienming*), why is it further described as the contemplation of principle (*liguan*)? And since it is already the contemplation of principle, why is it further presented as a "critical phrase" (*huatou*)?

If Chan, Pure Land, and *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) are thus conflated into three methods, then although the underlying principles may be perfectly harmonious, the practitioner’s mind will fail to settle upon a single focus. What then [should be done]?
This constitutes our fundamental tenet. How could this not be identical in principle to the method of entering deeply and practicing with uninterrupted dedication through a single gate?

The Master said: "Although the entire *Shuchao* (Commentary on the Commentary) returns fully to the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), according to the 'Profound Discourse' (*Xuantan*), when adhering to brevity, one simply maintains the name (*ming*).
The text states: 'To raise its name is to simultaneously possess all virtues; by focusing solely on maintaining it, one unifies the hundred [virtues].'"

Practice it without omission. By this, one knows that while single-mindedly valuing the holding of the name (*nāmadheya-dhāraṇa*), it does not hinder the illumination of contemplation of principle (*li-guan*).
When the contemplation of principle is clear and penetrating, it is like adding oil to a fire; the blaze will become even more fierce and intense.

If one merely raises the doubt for investigation or discusses the contemplation of principle alone, it is like the great *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which encompasses immeasurable vehicles (*yāna*); for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, every single path is a way forward. Yet, it is also not...
This is called a "confusion. However, it is simply because their capacities are compatible; it is also the skillful means (upāya) of our venerable teacher. Question:

The Commentary states that "one mind" is precisely the Chan of Bodhidharma’s direct pointing. It further says that the Sixth Patriarch rejected [the invocation of Amitābha] as being "without [reliance].

Thus, the pedagogical arrangements (mencan shishe) differ. Even if one were to propagate the direct pointing and yet simultaneously praise the Western Paradise, what would become of the meaning of direct pointing?
In the end, there is no way to clarify this. Since you say it is "direct pointing," why do you further state that the gates are different?
Is it then that the Shaolin and Caoxi traditions are also not the same?
The Master said: "The *Śāstra* states that 'one mind' does not merely refer to the Chan of direct pointing; rather, the entire Great Canon is fully encompassed within it.

As for attributing this to the Chan of direct pointing, this is intended for those who investigate through the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), not for those who merely engage in the mechanical holding of the name.
That the pedagogical methods differ is precisely what accords with the Way of direct pointing."

No. This is for those who take up the practice of reciting the name to trigger their spiritual capacity. Yunqi [Zhuhong] subsumes the method of investigating through mindfulness of the Buddha under the single gate of the Pure Land.
This is intended to widely accommodate various capacities. Those who study the commentaries and sub-commentaries may, without hindrance, seek to enter deeply into one particular gate.

It is like a person entering the ocean, yet demanding that it be compared in depth and breadth with the Huai, Ji, Yangtze, and Yellow Rivers, or further analyzing their similarities and differences—is this not so?
How foolish! Question:
The Commentary points out that reciting the Buddha’s name with utmost sincerity (zhìxīn) extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death from eighty billion kalpas;

this refers to the "principle single-mindedness" (lǐ yīxīn). As for "phenomenal single-mindedness" (shì yīxīn), many recitations merely extinguish minor transgressions. Furthermore, it cites the *Sutra of the Names of the Buddhas* (*Buddhanāmasamgiti-sūtra*) as saying:

"Upon hearing the Buddha’s name even once, one extinguishes the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas. The commentary explains: "Hearing it 'once' means not waiting for repeated recollection;
'immeasurable' means not limited to eighty billion kalpas. Thus, why must one point exclusively to the single-mindedness of principle?"
Within this context, there is an internal contradiction. Furthermore, this sutra also states that by hearing the sutra or hearing the name, one attains non-retrogression in all cases.
If so, would it then follow that everyone who makes a casual vow or calls upon the name while distracted also attains non-retrogression?
The Master said: "If one truly attains single-mindedness, then it matters not whether one is concerned with principle or phenomena.
As for the commentaries stating that many recitations can extinguish minor transgressions, this is spoken from the perspective of those who rely on single-mindedness while still amidst distraction.

When it is heard that hearing the Name extinguishes sin, sentient beings remain in delusion and likewise do not understand. For example, those in hell who hear the Name immediately attain ultimate realization and also achieve rebirth—how could this be otherwise?"
Cessation extinguishes transgressions; it is merely a matter of whether the sentient being’s mental power is diligent or lax.

Generally speaking, within the teachings, the discussion of phenomena and principles, and of meditative concentration and distraction, is like the regulations for military operations. In deciding victory on the battlefield, the priority lies with the individual;
one must not regard that which is fixed by formal rules as the definitive correct teaching.
Question: Zao Bo stated that the Great Way of the One Vehicle of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is not within the realm of bodhisattvas who seek rebirth [in a pure land].
For what reason, then, does the "Elder Son" of the Avataṃsaka [Śākyamuni] lead [beings] back to Ultimate Bliss by means of the Ten Vows?

As Master Daosheng said, if icchantikas possess Buddha-nature, then the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is cited as proof for their subsequent emergence. Now, since these practices and vows do not at all accord with those of Zao Bo, which treatise’s school [should this be considered]?
If one asks where the ultimate intent finally returns, Yunqi merely extracts the passage concerning "guiding back," yet this still cannot rectify the error of Daoxuan and Fazang.
One should know that Daoxuan and Fazang are not easily subject to disparagement. Now, if one wishes to harmonize these two meanings, what would the explanation be?

The Master said: Zao Bo (Zhiyan) stated that the *Avataṃsaka* is not the realm of bodhisattvas who aspire for rebirth [in Sukhāvatī], yet in order to manifest the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), he did not hesitate to suppress that [teaching] and exalt this one.
That Samantabhadra leads [beings] back to the Ultimate Bliss is precisely because it encompasses the infinite vehicles (*anantayāna*).

Zao Bo acted thus to transform ordinary beings of great resolve so they might enter the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) directly. Samantabhadra is a bodhisattva within the Flower Treasury World; by means of the ten...
The Vow to guide those returning to Sukhāvatī is for the sake of universal benefit for those of the three faculties.

Just as by observing one direction, one enters a single corner, yet the ten directions appear everywhere, so too, because the Great Mind is difficult to arouse while rebirth in Sukhāvatī is easy to achieve, their ultimate aim and destination coincide.
By this, we know that Zao Bo was not at all mistaken; how could Yunqi possibly consider him wrong?
Yes. Question:

Since concentration arises from precepts and wisdom arises from concentration, then for one of single mind, self-restraint of the mind begins at this point. Within this state, wisdom will naturally arise;
there is no need for further expedient means, as one will spontaneously attain the opening of the mind. (The Five Gates of Tiantai Buddha-Recitation)

The sequence is likewise. Now, the maintenance of phenomena (śamatha) is subsumed under the gate of concentration (*samādhi*), while the maintenance of principle (*prajñā*) is subsumed under the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Yet, one might ask: if the maintenance of phenomena is unable to destroy delusion, and those of sharp faculties proceed directly to the maintenance of principle—attaining wisdom without relying on concentration—would it not be possible for them to reach the path of awakening through the clear illumination of all rational paths?
The Master said: "From precepts arises concentration," and so forth, up to the gradual stages of Tiantai; this is the methodological rule of the Exegetical School (*jiao-jia*).

However, there are also cases where wisdom comes first and concentration follows. For instance, the teaching that by single-mindedly holding the Name one immediately attains rebirth [in the Pure Land] could not be believed unless one’s roots of wisdom were deeply awakened.
Yunqi [Jian] categorized "factual holding" (*shi-chi*) as belonging to the gate of concentration, while "principle holding" (*li-chi*) he classified as wisdom.

Regarding the inclusion within the gates: this is also the methodological principle of our school. However, phenomena (*dharma*) are not sustained without wisdom, and principles (*tattva*) do not manifest without meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Since phenomena sustain [the mind] and can thus give rise to wisdom, how could one fail to shatter delusion?

Furthermore, one must know that a single phrase of Amitābha possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom; this is because it penetrates deeply into the principle. Why is this? It is because it exclusively upholds the myriad virtues.
To bear this great name and not give rise to any evil—is this not the precepts? To reach the state of "one mind undistracted"—is this not concentration?
