To spontaneously attain the opening of the mind—is this not wisdom? To contemplate the emptiness of reality and the non-arising of dependent origination—is this not the principle?

To penetrate deeply into the ultimate principle where the Pure Land is but the mind, such that being born there is not separate from being born here—this is the ground of perfect enlightenment. Why must one abandon it?
To enter into understanding by means of the objective support (ālambana) may it be called the path of awakening?
Question: Although there are sixteen contemplations, speaking of the Buddha alone suffices. As stated in the sūtra: "By contemplating the body of the Buddha, one perceives the mind of the Buddha."

Regarding the contemplation of the Buddha’s body, one enters through a single mark or excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), such as the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between the eyebrows, which can subsume the *nienfo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).

For what reason does Ciyun merely instruct people to visualize the opening and closing of a lotus flower? Furthermore, why does the *Chao* (Commentary) also limit this to being a supportive cause for the "Universal Contemplation" (*puguān*)?
The Master said: "As for the statement in the *Contemplation Sūtra* that 'the Buddha is immediately all-pervasive,' it is because the Buddha takes the Dharma-realm as his body.

Regarding the statement that 'by contemplating the Buddha's body, one also sees the Buddha's mind,' this means that by taking the sublime object as a condition, one enters the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Since one enters through a single physical mark,"

Regardless of whether the white tuft between the eyebrows and the lotus flower are open or closed, any single contemplation according to one's conditions among the sixteen gates of visualization serves as an auxiliary cause.
Thus, the designation of "Universal Contemplation" as an auxiliary cause in the *Chao* (Commentary) remains most accurate and appropriate.
Question: Many sutras state that practitioners who practice mindfulness of the Buddha see the Buddha appear before them, such as the Elder Huiyuan’s three visions of the Sage’s marks and so forth.

This refers to the practitioner being able to bring the Buddha to dwell upon their crown. When ancient masters instructed others to resolve their will to seek such a sign, they meant it during their ordinary life.
Why does this present sutra speak only of the Buddha appearing at the moment of death? Is it that the merit of seven days is not yet sufficient for a vision to manifest?
Is it that one merely feels [the presence of the Buddha] at the moment of death? Or must one necessarily see him manifest before oneself before being able to see him at the time of death?
The Master said: "Many sutras state that the practitioner sees the Buddha manifest before them; there are also passages concerning seeing the Buddha in the future."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one recollects the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha both in the present and in the future.

These two characters, "certainly" (*bingding*), possess profound significance. It is like sowing grain and obtaining grain; there is never any labor that goes to waste. Master Huiyuan beheld the sacred image three times—this was seeing the Buddha in the present.
The masters of the Pure Land school experience the Buddha coming to welcome them at the time of death—this is seeing [the Buddha] in the future.
The Buddha is indeed present. Viewed from this perspective, one need only fear not reciting the Buddha’s name; one need not fear that the practitioner will fail to see the Buddha.

Whether for a full seven days or at any other time, simply maintain single-mindedness without distraction and single-pointedly uphold the Name, thereby awakening the Amitābha of one's own inherent nature.
The images of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are reflected therein. Question:
Because the minds of Bodhisattvas who have attained rebirth are not inverted, they are able to know in advance when the time has arrived, in accordance with their original vows.

If this is so, then those who "shed their bodies while sitting" or "perish while standing," who are nearly able to come and go with freedom, and who can recognize from where death departs—why did the masters of old not use this as a means of examination?
Why do they instead say that one must wait until the moment of death to know what it is like, as if one could not know it beforehand?

The Master said: "The Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land and those of the Chan school who achieve 'sitting-transcendence' or 'standing-extinction'—those who have realized where death goes—are fundamentally not comparable.

It is appropriate that practitioners of Pure Land karma know when the time for rebirth has arrived; they fix a date for their departure. For those in the Chan school, it matters not whether they know [the time of death] or not;
having penetrated the Great Principle, they regard birth and death as being like a dream or an illusion. How could they be anxious?"
Having gained a foothold within the midst of dreams and illusions, how could one regard birth and death as substantial realities?

Furthermore, you should know that once the transformative ritual is completed, coming and going are free and spontaneous. Such inconceivable liberations are known only by those who share the same path;
how, then, could they be compared for similarities or differences with the cultivation of pure karma?

Question: The *Amitābha-sūtra* (Guānjīng) speaks of ten recitations, while the treatise clarifies that at the time of death, the power of the mind is so fierce and sharp that it can surpass the power of practice accumulated throughout one's entire life;

this refers to the "ten recitations" of the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra]. Since that text does not mention the time of death, are these two accounts the same or different? What if these seven days [of practice] are considered?
It is not necessarily the case that this must occur at the moment of death; rather, these ten recitations may also pertain to one's ordinary life.

Since they do not constitute the "great mind" of the final moment, how could they possibly transform one to go to the Treasure King (Amitābha)? Your treatise, on the contrary, takes a single thought-moment as the correct standard. Where does this principle reside?

The Master said: "The *Daben* [Great Canon] speaks of ten recitations for the purpose of attaining rebirth through ten recitations. As for those who do not attain rebirth, it refers to the daily ten recitations;
although the end of life is not explicitly mentioned, it is clearly implied by the time of death. This treatise clarifies that at the moment of death, the power of the mind is fierce and sharp.
This constitutes one type of hesitation: practitioners may say they fear that their karmic obstructions will be too heavy at the time of death to achieve rebirth."
The fierce and sharp [resolve] prevails over it; it can overcome even the power of lifelong practice. This is the meaning of "exerting effort," which enables the practitioner to achieve rebirth.
For example, if one is normally fierce and sharp and has already accomplished the great task, then even ten recitations or seven days do not exceed a single thought-moment.
Why, then, should one spontaneously give rise to doubts and difficulties?

Question: Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta serve Amitābha together as the Three Sages of the Western Paradise. Since Avalokiteśvara’s “turning the hearing back toward one’s own nature” and the present practice of “single-mindedly holding the name” both take sound and hearing as their teaching essence (*dharma-kāya*), they should properly belong to the same Ear-organ Perfect Penetration (*karṇendriya-pariśuddhi*). Furthermore, Mañjuśrī also made a vow to be reborn there; why, then, was he excluded? The *Shizhi Chao* states that the ear-organ... [text fragment] ...is not [the path]. Answer: The reason for excluding Mañjuśrī is that his primary function lies in the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*) rather than the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). Although he aspires for rebirth in the West, his essential teaching does not focus on the auditory organ. As for Avalokiteśvara, although the principle of the Ear-organ Perfect Penetration is indeed applicable here, the specific method of "holding the Buddha's name" (*nāmadheya-dhāraṇa*) is categorized under the Mind-organ Perfect Penetration (*manas-indriya-pariśuddhi*). This is because the mind is the sovereign master that governs all six faculties. When the mind is concentrated and single-mindedly focused on the Buddha’s name, it naturally encompasses the other five organs. Therefore, while the Ear-organ Perfect Penetration provides the theoretical foundation, the actual practice of the Name-recitation Samādhi belongs to the Mind-organ Perfect Penetration. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the statement in the *Shizhi Chao* that the ear-organ is not [the path], this refers to the fact that for those of dull faculties who cannot achieve penetration through the ears, other methods must be employed. It does not negate the general applicability of the Ear-organ Perfect Penetration to the Pure Land path. As for the inclusion of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, it is because they are the two great Bodhisattvas who specifically manifest as the attendants of Amitābha to guide sentient beings to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Their presence is indispensable for the fulfillment of the Buddha’s vows. Therefore, they are included among the Three Sages. The exclusion of Mañjuśrī is based on the distinction of his primary pedagogical function. There is no error in this.

Regarding the inclusion of mindfulness of the Buddha: mindfulness of the Buddha can include the faculty of hearing, which is Śrī-Ābhāsvara (Poti). Śrī-Ābhāsvara can include Avalokiteśvara (Guanyin), yet Avalokiteśvara does not include him.

Since Śrī-Ābhāsvara maintains the practice of holding the name—which does not belong to the hearing of sound—does this mean that Avalokiteśvara does not serve as a substitute for Amitābha as the presiding teacher of Sukhāvatī?
The Master said: "The ear-faculty takes sound-objects as its basis; revolving inward, it enters into mindfulness of the Buddha, while the tongue praises [the name] aloud. Yet both belong to sound.
While the meanings of 'hearing' and 'entering' differ, Mañjuśrī selected one faculty for deep penetration—how could he have failed to choose this?

Yunqi’s judgment regarding the similarities and differences between faculties and objects cannot be used to claim that Avalokiteśvara does not include Śrāvakaprabha. This is also the case when discussing the practices for rebirth."

If one does not adopt the Ear-organ Perfect Penetration, does this mean that Śrī-Ābhāsvara does not encompass Avalokiteśvara? This is precisely what is meant by "beating the drum while playing the lute";
it is not a matter of comparing the spheres of practice of the various sages based on their external traces through the various Dharma-gates.

Question: The World-Honored One has said that for those practitioners who take the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the mind of grasping at objects) as their own nature, it is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal.
Now, is this mind of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo xīn*) the攀緣心? Or is it not the攀緣心?
If it is the攀緣心, then all discernment, observation, and conceptualization (*jue-guan siwei*) are the very root of birth and death. If it is not...
Regarding the mind that takes conditions as its object: why do you say that the nature of mindfulness arises and perishes, and that causes and effects have distinct responses?

If you claim that this arising-and-perishing mind is itself the non-arising-and-non-perishing mind, then why speak of "cooking sand"? This would be as incongruous as the principle of waves and water; for while waves are indeed water, sand is not food.
When the Great Awakened One establishes metaphors, he would surely not make them so redundant. This is precisely what is meant in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
If a person with a distracted mind recites "Namo Buddha" even once— what is called "the name" by Nan Neng—
if they do not sever the hundred thoughts that arise in the mind when encountering objects, is this not simply using this very mind of arising and ceasing?

Question: At the end of the sutra, it first speaks of non-retrogression and subsequently of rebirth in the Pure Land; this is precisely because one achieves completion in the present life, surpassing all other teachings.
Yet, in the *Chao*, you instead open up the possibility of failing to achieve rebirth due to a short lifespan or many obstacles, stating that one will attain birth in a future life.
This falls into what Master Cizhao said: "That person does not know for themselves that they shall be born in the Pure Land, yet they insist on [waiting for] the future."
In future generations, when one is reborn among humans once again, they cite the Chan school’s "just as the head emerges" and "ready-made" expressions as proof.
Why, then, did Yongming exclude them? Is it because there is a faction that claims "Chan without Pure Land," while another clarifies the truth of pure karma within the School of the Patriarchs?
This must be addressed regarding the Zen tradition.
The Master said: "In the sutra, the term 'non-retrogression' is mentioned first, followed by 'rebirth.

This means that having first spoken of those already born in the Pure Land, it subsequently states that through mindfulness of the Buddha one will certainly attain rebirth; it does not refer to attaining realization in the present life.

The *Commentary* (Chao) opens up the possibility of short lifespans and many obstacles for practitioners with many obstacles who do not believe in their certain rebirth; however, for those who have faith, there are no such obstacles."
Regarding "being born in a future life," this refers to those who lack faith; even if they hear the Name, they plant only inferior seeds.
Hearing the Name is supreme because it transcends all other teachings. This does not fall into the category of mere "compassionate illumination" rhetoric or Yongming’s polemical discourse.
To single-mindedly support the path of Pure Land while pushing the Chan school toward a ten-thousand-fathom abyss is not considered an overstep in the practice of Chan.
There is a gateway; because one has thoroughly penetrated it through three lifetimes, as soon as one emerges, it is already fully realized and available for use. Why then labor over each phrase?
It is in perfect accord with the Pure Land path.

The Head Seat and Dharma-grandson, Hongyu, together with Jiao Zong, compiled the *Dahxiang* (Echoes of the Teaching) in response to the questions posed by Master Xueguan.
Regarding the inquiry on the "Investigation of the Head-Phrase": "If it is not genuine, one falls into the demons and outsiders of the five aggregates of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*," and so forth.
The Master said: "Examine the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* closely; the fifty kinds of demonic activities do not go beyond a single word: 'attachment.

For instance, when the physical aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) becomes clear and all discursive thoughts fall away, such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Observe the cause of this."
Solid delusion serves as its foundation. Because this solid delusion cannot be dissolved, one scrutinizes it within the midst of delusion;

upon seeing something extraordinary, one immediately forms a conception of it as sacred. Is this not attachment? If one does not form such a conception of it as sacred, it is called a "wholesome state.
Not forming it means simply being without attachment. Furthermore, within the five aggregates, all are collectively based on delusion.
Bind it with the two characters "xiang" (thought/phantasy). If this first point is not broken from the outset, then these very deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) are the root and stem of Māra.
If their root is not eradicated, how can one merely prune their branches and leaves to prevent them from arising?

They even exploit one's empty clarity and consume one's vital essence; all are produced by the conjunction of deluded thoughts. It is not that Māra comes from without; if one is involved [in such thoughts], [Māra follows].

To guard and protect [the mind] at such a time is truly what is called "adding frost to snow" or "pouring oil onto fire. For instance, within the *śukla-ābhāsa-skandha* (receptivity to impressions), there is the deluded thought of "empty luminosity";
yet this empty luminosity is itself a deluded thought. This is because one has not yet reached the ground where the seeking mind is absent; how could it be anything other than delusion?
Similarly, within the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception), there is the deluded thought of "interpenetration. As the first chapter states: "The mind loves perfect luminosity. This is precisely...
The preceding was a delusion. When the faculties and their objects interpenetrate, one immediately gives rise to attachment; thus, all ten types are said to be "mental attachments" and so forth.
This is because the celestial demons emerge from within the perfect realm and couple with the loving heart to produce boundless demonic karmas; how could they ever be saved?
This is because the practitioner must first decisively sever this single thought. When there is no mind, there is no attachment; when there is no attachment, how could the word "clinging" even exist?
As it says in Chapter Nine: "The mind’s love enters extinction; craving for profound emptiness and the like are all demonic activities.
This is precisely because the initial deluded mind has not been broken. It is truly what is called "steaming sand to make rice"—the sand [remains sand].

This is not the fundamental meal. It is like the subtle and hidden deluded thoughts within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Since the nature of the aggregate of formations is constant flux and movement, it is called the "root-source of arising and ceasing.

From this point, it is revealed that with the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), one thoroughly perceives the root-source within the aggregate of formations to be entirely subject to arising and ceasing, with every thought-moment failing to remain still. Because the practitioner does not follow along with this flux of arising and ceasing, [this stage is reached].

One attains a concentrated, luminous, and upright mind. At that time, the celestial Māra cannot find an opportunity, because one merely gives rise to conceptual calculations within the perfect and primordial source.
One exhaustively investigates its beginning and end—whether there is a cause or no cause—and since such calculations exist, one loses right and universal knowledge.
The single character "calculation" (ji) emerges from the depths of the obscure; as the text says: "Observing that profound clarity, one cannot see through to its very source."

It is as in the section on the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*): inverted false conceptualization refers to the vital impulse of the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*) suddenly collapsing and splitting apart.

When the six sense faculties become empty and still, they no longer run wild. This emptiness and stillness resulting in the absence of wild running is precisely the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Once the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted, because seeing and hearing have become mutually accessible and their functions are purified, one says: "The emptiness of all formations is thoroughly realized. Yet, one still relies upon the source of consciousness;
as long as the essence remains unperfected, one gives rise to superior resolve (*adhimukti*). These ten types [of practitioners] all give rise to superior resolve based on the mind of consciousness.
Having formed such superior resolves, they deviate from perfect penetration and give rise to various categories [of rebirth]. Within the Chan school, those who are...

Those who apply their minds [to these matters] find that neither of them has any bearing [on the ultimate truth]. Zhi Da said: "The Buddhas of the ten directions have all been swallowed by me in a single gulp;

where else could there be any sentient beings left to save? This is the station of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, from which they cannot dislodge him. As for demons, heterodox spirits, and externalist seeds—what can they do to you?
If you wish not to be consumed by them, simply enter the principle with your whole being; there is no need to wait for them to be expelled.
There is no need to wait for protection; when deluded thoughts are exhausted, the activities of Māra will naturally cease. As the ancient masters said:
"It is best to strike a single blow at the very root, so that branches do not sprout beyond the joints."
Question: "One does not cling to cultivation or realization, yet one does not abandon cultivation or realization" (and so forth).
The Master said: "In my school, we do not distinguish between those who are sharp or dull, wise or foolish; one simply enters through faith.

Once the fierce and keen resolve has been aroused, it is as if one were sitting before an iron wall and a silver mountain, seeking only to break through and emerge. All deluded thoughts are entirely [extinguished]."
One is able to enter. As for the practice of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*), where shall it find rest?

Once one attains the sudden opening of a single thought—like seeing the sky after parting the clouds, or recovering a long-lost object—what further use is there for the practice of contemplative observation?
It is simply valued that the intent of inquiry is most earnest; yet this inquiry itself involves practice, though it is not defined by such practice. It is like seeing through the world.
The conditions for investigating the ultimate Way also involve contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*); however, it does not establish its name based on such observation.
As the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith* states: "Except for those who have attained sudden awakening, who do not follow after dharmas.

If one takes contemplative observation as one's primary practice, then there will be a mind that observes and illuminates, and necessarily an object that is observed and illuminated. With the duality of subject and object established, this is nothing other than delusion.
Why is this? Therefore, the Chan school says: "Walking alone upon the Great Way; there is no objective realm outside the mind.
One must merge the ten directions of the world, along with one's own body and mind, into a single entity. Only by cutting off both extremes does one find the entrance.

As for the path that leads upward, you must investigate it yourself; otherwise, it is all merely the livelihood of ghosts. How can such things be equated with the practice and realization of the Buddhas?
If one speaks thus, yet the result remains vague and fails to reach this ground, it is called self-deception;
such people are truly pitiable and hardly worthy of being mentioned. Nanyue said: "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet defilement is not attained.
This very cultivation that is undefiled—can one say that this perfect cultivation still retains the character for "cultivation"? This very... [text ends]

Regarding the evidence of defilement, one might ask: "Can one who has attained perfect realization still attach to the word 'realization'? If this is so, then although one practices all day long, there is no practice;
sweeping the floor and burning incense are entirely the infinite Buddha-activities—how could these ever be abandoned? It is simply that one does not attach to practice or realization.

Even in the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*) there is no longer effortful action (*anābhoga-prayoga*); how much less so in the tenth stage? This is stated even up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Dharma is like rain or like clouds; yet even this was rebuked by Nanquan as being entirely at odds with the Way.
How much more so, then, can one compare the contemplative insight of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) with the Gate of the Patriarchs to determine which is superior?

Question: When Bodhidharma came from the West, he overturned the old molds all at once, teaching only the Dharma-gate of the single mind-ground, directly pointing to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Subsequently, the five schools emerged, each with various different approaches, such as the "Five Ranks" and the "Three Mysteries."

Regarding the four roles of host and guest, up to the four types of discernment (*liao-jian*): is this because the Dharma itself is thus, or is it because the capacities of sentient beings (*qun-ji*) differ?
If one claims that the Dharma is inherently thus, then according to the teachings which state, "This alone is the one reality;

all else is expedient means" (*upāya*), there should be no room for expedient means within the teaching of direct pointing (*zhizhi*). If, however, one claims that because capacities differ in a thousand ways, the Dharma must adapt to those capacities...
If that were so, then the twenty-five methods of perfect penetration in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—which were taught to suit the capacities of various practitioners—would already be complete;
why then create these redundant and superfluous methods? If this were the case, the First Patriarch would have undergone all this arduous travel from the East for no purpose.
The Master said: "When Bodhidharma came from the West, he overturned the old molds all at once. At the moment of transmission, there was truly no duality of dharmas.
Why, then, speak of 'five'? It is because there are five masters of the Dharma that one cannot help but speak of the 'Five Houses.
How could these Five Houses obstruct the Dharma-gate of the single mind-ground? Even such expressions as the Three Mysteries, the Five Ranks, and the Guest-Master [relationship] are entirely..."

Names and phrases are merely footnotes to the direct transmission. If one truly attains the Way not transmitted by the thousand sages, then the Three Mysteries, the Five Ranks, the Guest and Host, and the Ruler and Minister will be as clear as pointing at one's own palm;
for such is the nature of the Dharma. It is not a matter of making distinctions to accommodate various capacities.
If one seeks to certify the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground within the framework of the Three Mysteries and Five Ranks, it is much like searching for the roots and trunk by following the branches.
As for its root: it is neither identical to nor separate from the branches and trunk. If one were identical to the branches and trunk, one would not have attained the root;

if one were separate from the branches and trunk, one likewise would not have attained the root. If there is a root, it is the root of the branches and trunk; if there are branches and trunk, they are the branches and trunk of the root. This can be seen by a wise person who reflects upon it.
Within the teaching, it is said: "This alone is the single reality; the other two are not true. They are not true.

This is what is meant by "expedient means" (*upāya*). Without expedient means, there is no way to guide others. Although its reality is not [limited to] reality, without it there is no way to open up those expedients.

Thus, while it is said that expedient means return to reality, what harm is there in expedient means and reality being manifested together? Within the teachings, expedient means each lead along divergent paths;

within the school (*zong*), the characteristics are based solely on the fundamental inquiry (*ben can*). When the fundamental inquiry is shattered, it is like the moon reflecting in a thousand rivers; when the divergent paths are penetrated, they all flow back to the source.
If the wind whistles through ten thousand apertures, it seems as though the Dharma of universal penetration and differentiation cannot be discussed on the same day as the profound station.
Yet, since the arrival of the First Patriarch, this Dharma-gate has been most venerable; how could it be called superfluous?
Question: Entering *samādhi* through hearing, reflection, and cultivation is the natural law of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles;
it seems impossible to dispense with this. Indeed, ancient masters have also said: "I have a rough knowledge of the Three Piṭakas and the twelve divisions of the teachings," and further:

"First enter through the realization of understanding derived from hearing, and later accord with the truth through non-conceptualization. Thus we know that one must first hear the teachings before practicing Chan; this has been the way of all sages.

This is an unchanging rule. Alas, how is it that the venerable masters of recent times do not examine whether a student has ever heard the teachings, but instead uniformly present them with "tasteless" koans, commanding them to engage in intellectual excavation morning and evening?
Rather than avoiding deluded thoughts, they thus fall into a state of non-discrimination (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, Guishan said, "This one study is most wondrous and most profound. He also said, "If there are those of middling capacity who cannot yet transcend suddenly, they should for now set their minds upon the teachings.
This was still so during Guishan’s time, which was the flourishing era of the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma.
If we distinguish between the eras, how much more so is this the case in the present age, which coincides with the decline and decay of the Final Dharma? How could it not be so?

Since all those encountered possess sharp faculties, one may uniformly employ the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle to guide them. Moreover, it seems that adapting the teaching to the capacity of the recipient and administering the medicine according to the illness cannot be dispensed with.
The Master said: "In my response to the question of Layman Liu, I stated that the *zong* (essence) is the framework of the *jiao* (teachings), and the *jiao* are the details of the *zong*.
If one practices according to the teachings, one should realize and enter into accord with them to be considered a true heir of the lineage.

While hearing and understanding seem easy, thoughtless sincerity is difficult. Only under our ancestral masters is there the subtlety of 'thinking without thinking,' as it is also said: 'The mind is like a wall.'"
Only then can one enter the Way. Furthermore, whether one has heard the teachings or not does not constitute an immutable rule.

For instance, it is said that by reciting a single verse from the teachings, one may suddenly attain great enlightenment; again, it is said that beneath a single word, the ground of the mind opens and flows through.

How could one wait until having traversed all names and phrases before claiming to have attained awakening and entry? For those who engage in investigation, this does not involve forced interpretation;

indeed, the two words "forced interpretation" (chuàn-záo) are a great harm to the Dharma-gate. While they may occasionally appear in the Scriptural Teachings (*yìshè*), they truly do not exist in the School of the Lineage (*zōngmén*).

This single study is most wondrous and most profound; everyone ought to aspire to its immediate transcendence. How could one willingly settle for the methods of the middle or lower capacities? Not so.
In discussing people of the age of semblance and decline, it matters not whether they are wise or foolish; if they simply possess a resolute mind, this constitutes superior wisdom.
To transform the Dharma of the final age into the True Dharma, and to turn those of middling and inferior capacities into those of superior faculties—this seems not at all difficult.

Question: Regarding the three trainings in the outflows-free state (*anāsrava-śikṣā*), it is the sincere word of our Buddha that concentration arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) is brought forth by concentration.
Yet Miaoxi says, "Others have concentration first and wisdom later; this old man has wisdom first and concentration later. This greatly contradicts the Buddhist scriptures.
If we verify this through contemporary experience, it is like a person intoxicated by wine: their nature of wisdom becomes deranged and confused, but when the intoxication subsides...
Then the nature of madness will naturally subside, and wisdom will be preceded by meditative concentration. Thus, the words of Miaoxi become all the more reasonable.
How does the Great Master synthesize and harmonize these with the Buddha’s sutras and the ancestral teachings?
The Master said: "First concentration and then wisdom" is the sincere word of the Buddha. "First wisdom and then concentration" is the compassionate instruction of the Patriarchs.
To omit both is not a definitive treatise. For instance, when a person cultivates concentration, if there is no wisdom as a precursor, they cannot cultivate it;
thus, wisdom may well come first. When wisdom exists, precepts are established; when precepts are established, concentration arises; and when concentration arises...

Yet, as for wisdom’s brilliance, it is like seeking the beginning and end of a wheel by tracing its rim; they are utterly unobtainable. Viewed in this light, even the term "Great Wisdom" (Mahāprajñā) is but superfluous speech.
In truth, the Buddhas and patriarchs are already in perfect accord; what need is there to seek further reconciliation?
Question: Yongjia said, "If one realizes it, karmic obstacles are originally empty. This is a statement regarding the realization of the Way.

Yet, both the Venerable Siṃha of the Western Land and the Great Master here in China were people who had attained full realization; why then did their karmic obstacles not become empty? They necessarily had to undergo retribution before it was over.

If you claim that the very point of undergoing retribution is the meaning of karmic obstacles being empty, then consider a person who has committed the ten evil deeds and subsequently recites the Buddha's name.
Even those who attain rebirth while carrying their karmic burdens must inevitably return to this Sahā world to repay their past karma before they can achieve liberation.

If one who has attained such great realization fails to exhaust their karmic obstructions upon rebirth, then those of great realization would actually fall short of those who merely practice nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name).

If you claim that those of great realization have truly emptied their karmic obstacles and can surpass practitioners of nianfo tenfold, then even a lion could be taken as a teacher—yet it remains that [such a being] has not yet fully realized the ultimate.
Regarding this category [of karmic obstacles], how does the Master synthesize and reconcile it?

The Master says: "Karmic obstacles are empty"—this is not easily understood. To claim that encountering royal peril is merely repaying past debts is truly a failure to realize that karmic obstacles are empty;
it is not the correct doctrine. Does one not recognize that the site of practice is like the moon in water and the myriad practices are like flowers in the sky?
The demonic armies are within a mirror; the Buddha’s activities are within a dream. If you take that which is within a dream to be a reality, it is not empty.

If one realizes this meaning of emptiness, then both "repaying" and "not repaying" are merely words from a dream. Reciting the Buddha's name while committing the ten evils and attaining rebirth while carrying one's karma results in the immediate release of all evils;
as one hastens toward the fruit, one forgets the cause—this is not "returning to repay. In the lowest of the low grades of rebirth, even seeing the Buddha is still distant; one must pass through...

Once the fetus has been long gestated, it finally attains the blossoming of the flower; this is not a failure to repay [the debt]. Would it not be foolish to compare its excellence or inferiority with that of the *Zongmen* (School of the Lineage)?
Question: The circumstances regarding Yunmen’s request for instruction and Muzhou’s realization of the Way are recorded in great detail in the *Chuan Deng Lu* and the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*. Its...
Upon meeting Xuefeng, he immediately recognized him as his teacher. There were no words of formal inquiry; everything consisted of a continuous exchange of questions and answers.
Later, when he appeared in the world [as a master], why did he not succeed Muzhou, but instead succeed Xuefeng? Could it be that his mind was swayed by the rise and fall of people’s reputations?

If so, that would not be the way of the Patriarchs; how could one take such a person as a model? As for succeeding to the Dharma in later generations, those who obscure their own minds are truly pitiable.

"Va. [The Master] added the *vajra* to this. If one were to claim that there was an omission in the recorded words, then at the moment of transmission—wherein the source of the lineage of wisdom for a thousand ages is bound up—how could one dare to arbitrarily edit them? Surely there must be a reason;
I beg the Master to supplement it, so as to avoid confusing future generations who inherit the Dharma.
The Master said: "When Yunmen saw Muzhou, he was cut off at one leg and immediately attained realization; yet this was not yet a great penetration.
When he first saw Xuefeng, Xuefeng commanded the assembly to welcome him as a 'man of knowledge' among five hundred. This was because Xuefeng had certified him with the Dharma-eye."
The next day, they went up Xuefeng Peak. As soon as the Master saw him, he said, "For what reason have you come to such a state?
Yunmen then bowed his head. From this point on, they were in accord. Furthermore, these two words, "from this point on" (cóngzī), are not merely borrowed phrases.

Moreover, they subsequently refined their practice together for many years, using them to seal the Mind School (Xinzong). This was not done out of a desire to change their resolve according to prosperity or decline. People of the present day, however, [use] jade...
One regards one’s teacher as an enemy, yet seals that very teacher as a benefactor.

Little do they realize that the one who stamps them may not necessarily be right, and the one who polishes them may not necessarily be wrong. To take what is wrong as wrong does not lose the primary cause for attaining the Dharma assembly;
however, to take what is wrong as right ultimately leads to the evil retribution of the hells. It would be better to remain unenlightened for a thousand lifetimes than to...
Could it be that [the truth] is manifest in a single day? How could the words regarding the "dropping of blood" deceive me? You must examine them thoroughly; do not allow yourself to be negligent.
A Zen practitioner from Shan asked: "Chan is the 'separate transmission outside the teachings. Master Jingyin, with a single shout—"
[This] encompasses the five teachings. Now, if all five teachings are outside the scope of Chan teaching, what does this mean?
The Master said: "Jingyin [Zhaozhou] encompassed the five teachings in their entirety with a single shout, thereby resolving the delusions of those who lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Have you not heard that 'a single shout does not function as a single shout'? Even if ancient Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas were to arrive here, they too would have to withdraw."

This is already the case for those of ordinary capacity; how much more so for those who are keen-witted and possessed of quick intelligence? Thus it is said: "A single shout can encompass the five teachings;
that which the five teachings cannot encompass is Chan."
Question: Chan is not external to the teachings, and the teachings are not external to Chan. There are only words and sounds; in reality, they possess no dual nature.
What, then, is meant by the "separate transmission"?

The Master said: "What is called 'Chan outside the teachings' is not the Chan enumerated within the teachings; it is truly that which the World-Honored One indicated by holding up a flower—a reality not conveyed by words or sounds.
At that time, the hundred thousand devas and humans were all at a loss. If one were to discuss what is explained by the teachings of sound, why would it have been necessary for Kāśyapa to smile?
It was the World-Honored One who certified this as the distinct transmission outside the teachings."
For this reason, it is known that for forty-nine years [the Buddha] never once revealed this message; indeed, it is something that cannot be expressed by the teachings.
Thus it is said that what is "outside the teachings" is actually the very backbone of the teachings.

It is called "outside the texts" and "beyond the characteristics of speech" because its value lies in thorough awakening. If it is truly outside the teachings, does there exist a separate transmission?
Question: The Great Master Qingliang (Zongmi) took Chan as the sudden teaching, seemingly based on his interpretation of the Sixth Patriarch’s *Platform Sūtra*.
If he were wrong, then all would be wrong; yet if it is not sudden, it must be perfect (*yuan*). Likewise, if the teaching is not perfect, it must be sudden.

To treat Chan as merely Chan—claiming that not only does one not encompass the five, but the five likewise cannot enter the one—is to explain things through circularity and only increase one's confusion. I pray you, clarify this.
I hope that your compassionate voice will spread forth and provide instruction.
The Master said: "To claim that Qingliang [Zongmi] took Chan as the sudden teaching is to suppress Chan while exalting the doctrinal teachings.

When the Sixth Patriarch spoke of 'revealing and instructing the sudden Mahayana teachings,' he was merely taking a shortcut across the road; it was specifically intended for those within the ancestral school who are called 'sudden awakeners.'"
If one says that it is not sudden but perfect (*yuan*), then as for this single word "perfect," it is not even established within our own school.

If one were to establish "perfection," then it would no longer be perfect. If one says that "Great, Square, and Vast" (*Dafangguang*) also reveals the characteristics of the fruit-virtue, then regarding the principle of the *dharmakāya*, since that principle transcends all opposition, how could "greatness" be established? All phenomena arise through conditions and respond through transformation.
It is infinite. Its ultimate substance has no exterior; it rolls up and unfolds with sovereign ease. As for the two characters "fang" (vast) and "guang" (broad), they are merely borrowed terms:

"fang" refers to the Great Vehicle, while "guang" is used in contrast to worldly discourse. Furthermore, the phrase "marking the school to enter the inconceivable directly" is itself superfluous speech;
how much more so when considering the five teachings? Our Buddha’s designation of Chan as being "outside the teachings" makes this even clearer. It is like a person being born...
Within the royal house, one does not speak of noble signs. Furthermore, as for those ranging from the ninth grade to the first grade, each grade may be gathered;
however, how could one who is born in the palace of the heir apparent be gathered by mere rank? Zen stands outside the teachings; it cannot be described through metaphors.
