If a lay practitioner wishes to accomplish this matter, they must develop deep faith in the gate of the Patriarchs and swiftly resolve the issue of birth and death.
There is no other method that surpasses this one; such a thing is impossible.

This single phrase of the *huatou* is the elixir for transforming the bones, the wondrous medicine for restoring the soul, and the sharp axe for felling the dense forest of birth and death. As it is said:
Regarding the immeasurable Dharma gates, the hundreds of thousands of thorns of views, all conceptual attachments, and the demonic adversaries of the five aggregates:

as soon as one touches upon this single phrase, they dissolve like crumbling walls or melting ice, and a second thought never arises. Why is this? It is because one is free from all discursive thoughts.
It is like observing a single breath that does not return; where, ultimately, does it go? That very place of departure is [the truth].
It is unclear. It is like sitting amidst the flames of a raging fire; one only wishes to rush out.

From this, one knows that delusion need not be suppressed, the mind need not be observed, concentration need not be practiced, wisdom need not be produced, views need not be severed, and demons need not be subdued.
Then, one naturally becomes settled and composed. This is because the mind is fierce and sharp, like a blazing fire, capable of consuming everything. As it is said:
Because it flows swiftly, it can sweep away all things; because it is like a fierce wind, it can clear away all things;

because it is like a divine arrow, it can pierce through all things—just as when one shoots at a stone tiger, if one hesitates for even a moment, not only will the feathers sink, but the arrowhead itself will break.
Therefore it is said: "The place where the Way-person acts is like fire melting ice; once the arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to return.
Xuansha may truly be called one who has found the shortcut to the Dharma-gate and reached the target of the Dharma-gate. If you investigate in this manner, [you will attain it].
Suddenly, one morning, he performed a somersault. Having passed away and returned to life, he immediately established new regulations and issued new edicts.

With a single glance, high and low were seen at once, and the myriad phenomena were simultaneously revealed. He cut off all streams, allowing passage neither to the mundane nor to the holy. As Master Foyin said:
From one gate, one arrives at another gate; clearly, the Universal Eye illuminates heaven and earth.

Even if one were to gather Mount Sumeru into a brush and take the vast ocean as ink, one could not write even a small fraction of it; therefore, it is said that the Great Canon and the Small Canon flow forth from this very source.

This is no mere boastful claim. If one has not yet reached this level of the "ground" (the fundamental state), their spoken words will arise like clouds and their verses will pour out like water from a jar;

yet all of it will result in inverted views and understanding. This is like those of recent times who falsely claim to be "men of knowledge" (jñānin), taking the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients and providing commentaries for each line, matching them all with intellectual paths of meaning.
When a person of true discernment sees this, they know that the ancestral style (zongfeng) has been swept away from the ground. It is said:
Is it not fitting that one should weep bitterly with flowing tears? When I arrived in my native village, I saw the Imperial Historian Wu’s *Eulogies on Ancient Cases*.
Their prose was so ornate and elegant that few contemporary eulogizers could rival them.
One day, the Historian asked me, "Has the Great Master ever seen the disciple’s eulogies on ancient cases? I replied, "I have. The Historian asked, "What do you think of them? I said, "Layman..."
"This is an intellectual understanding, not the gate of awakening. The Grand Historian asked, "How do you know this?

I replied, "When the Layman [Zhaozhou] praised the old woman burning the hermitage, saying, 'A withered tree on a cold cliff gives birth to a great monk,' was that not an instance of such understanding? Is that not the case for the monk who refused [to leave]?

The Grand Historian said, "Indeed. I said, "Is that not what you call 'understanding'? At these words, the Grand Historian felt as though he were being released from a wooden barrel箍 (gū). He was enlightened.
This was a person who had long cultivated the mind; at a single word, he immediately recognized his error.

As for those pseudo-knowledgeable ones of recent times who discuss this *kōan*, it is unlikely they have even dreamed of it. Alas! The ancestral hall is in autumn’s twilight, and the winds of Mara blow fiercely.
Amidst the clamor of all saying they are practicing Zen, everyone has fallen into the net of demonic delusions; has there ever been a single person capable of leaping free?
Whether or not one attains this depends on whether the clergy and laity can distinguish clearly and remain untainted by such demonic influences.
If they do, I shall cover them with my patched robe; this may be called repaying the profound kindness of the Buddha.
In the late autumn of the Patriarchal Hall, there is only the wise person who remains. Throughout the world, the winds of Mara blow; who rejoices and who resents?
They rush about with staffs and shouts, inflicting them upon the blind. Hands are severed and feet are broken, all while claiming this is "responding to the occasion.
Their entire bodies bleed, yet they know neither pain nor itchiness. Laughing wildly and recklessly—what kind of appearance is this?
This means failing to comprehend; it is merely a matter of suppressing the eyes with words. How bitter! How painful!
The gods cry out and the ghosts weep—three thousand seven hundred instances of this great pattern. To seize one’s food and drive away one’s oxen: there is absolutely no such principle.
These spoken words and verses are for those who merely parrot others; they are the very root of birth and death. Are you willing to let them rest by themselves?
I have written these words; may the lay practitioner exert himself. Set the mind in one place—now is precisely the time.

To those who are practitioners, I show this as for a Chan student: your parents gave birth to you and endowed you with a set of spiritual bones, forged like pure gold; it requires only that you [polish] them deeply.

They give rise to right faith and deeply awaken the great potential. Yet, regarding the teachings of the Buddha throughout his lifetime, they do not seek wondrous realization but instead pursue nothing but empty sounds;
though they possess much learning, it is equal to having heard nothing at all, like an elephant sinking in the mud, which, despite its full strength, cannot extricate itself.
Unable to leap out [of this state], they are truly pitiable. As for you, sir, you were born into a great clan;
from childhood you were a noble young gentleman, and you have further emerged from the ranks of the imperial examinations.

When you entered official service, you made offerings to Dharma masters and earnestly requested their instruction, becoming thoroughly proficient in the teachings of the scriptures. Yet, when questioned regarding the matter of your own fundamental nature, you are utterly helpless.
Why is this? Because names, phrases, and numerical categories are not the ultimate Dharma;

it is only under the gate of our ancestral masters that one does not give rise to intellectual understanding but directly probes the source. Thus it is said: "Only when the mind is like a wall can one enter the Way.
This is truly because all sentient beings employ the conscious mind (*vijñāna*) for discrimination and conceptualization. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The ālayavijñāna, at all times..."

There is interruption. Regarding the characteristics of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), it is like the flame of a lamp: when it arises, it internally grasps the oil and wick while externally emitting light.
Depending on this internal grasping and maintenance, the seven evolving consciousnesses arise, with the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) being the most powerful.

Depending on the external characteristics of the vessel-world, they give rise to the apprehension of the five sensory objects (*viṣaya*). This assistance and arousal proceed without ceasing; the mind arises following objects and matures through conditions, manifesting in active operation (*samudācāra*).

They act as mutual causes and effects; they serve as reciprocal bases for clarity; and through their successive arising, burning, and ceasing, they continue without interruption until the very beginning.

Thus, the conventional designation of "seeds" is established from time immemorial. When viewed from this perspective, the resultant phenomena of active manifestations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arise boundlessly and exist simultaneously;
how could they depend on new perfuming? As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "All seeds are fundamentally..."

The nature of existence does not arise from perfuming (*vāsanā*). The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "O Mahāmati, inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).
Grasping at various sense objects and the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) are the causes of the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*nirūpaṇa-vijñāna*)."

By this, one knows that there are both the original (intrinsic) and the newly perfumed (adventitious), which together produce the active manifestations and increase the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

This is because ignorance perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness). Pure dharmas are likewise; know this by analogy with the above. If one takes the correct meaning, *tathatā* itself does not receive perfuming.
*Tathatā* is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is not the cause of the mind; nor is it a seed capable of producing resultant dharmas, as [is the case with seeds].
Because it is equal to space, the nature of the mind is not defiled; it is untainted and is called "naturally pure. Why is this?

If a dharma were eternally abiding, it could not constitute a seed, because it would be without differentiation at all times. From the perspective of its purity, it is also designated by the name "seed.
The four virtues of *nirvāṇa* are the seeds of the four great elements; they arise from original enlightenment and permeate [the mind].
Explanation: The four virtues are inherently present from the beginning; they do not arise from seeds. They are designated as "seeds" because they are names derived from their causes.

Because they can erode and damage the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), practitioners who have faith and delight in the Mahāyāna employ the samādhi of the Greatly Wise Person’s Vast Space-like Vessel to carry out the practice of great compassion.
By means of the resultant virtues of Vairocana, they serve as the cause to perfume the state of causal development.

For this reason, it should further be understood that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is extremely weak and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and is therefore not a perfuming agent (*vāsaka*).

Only the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and a portion of their associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta*) are capable of cognitive reflection; because their power is most superior, they have the capacity to self-perfume this ignorance (*avidyā*).
When fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) arises from the absence of substantiality, it purely accomplishes the four virtues.

Because it utterly illuminates and exhausts ignorance (avidyā), it is said that when the four virtues are perfected, the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna) perceives its own exhaustion—how much more so, then, regarding ignorance? It is like a thousand-year-old dark room where a single lamp can destroy the gloom;

thus, within the pervasive purity, nothing else can be admitted. Since the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) of the ten realms is entirely transformed into pure function, it is called the "small and large scales."

"Ma" refers to the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Physical Body. If one can take this single step into the fruit, then in every atom and every world-system, one will universally enter them all.

Thus, it is well to tread the gate of the Patriarchs and seek the matter that transcends the ordinary. One must simply wait for the cord at one's heels to snap and the tip of the nose to be twisted around;
only when a separate path for the breath is opened is it truly the time of arriving home. Otherwise, even if you reach the ultimate limit of the profound, it is still not it.
Subtle! These are all the livelihoods of other schools; they are not the "grass for the master of the house.
With a complete skeleton of golden bone, Generate profound right faith. Deeply awaken the great functional capacity To penetrate the teachings spoken by the Buddha;
One should seek the gate of wondrous enlightenment. If you stagnate in names, numbers, and phrases, [you will miss it].
Whether heard or unheard, it is all but the Zen of our ancestral masters; Truly, one does not dwell in intellectual understanding but directly probes the original source.
The mind enters like a blank wall; Within the *ālayavijñāna*, the grasping is firm in its active manifestation.
It gives rise to successive signs of burning, Recurring again and again without interval.

The pure dharmas are likewise thus: through the marks of the Buddha’s fruition-merit, they perfume the fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) of the practitioner at the causal stage, just as boiling water melts snow.
When the four virtues are perfectly complete and round, from where could consciousness and perception arise? Being pure and excluding nothing else, the functioning of the ten realms never ceases.
Having waited for the fundamental causes and conditions, I shall once again explain and demonstrate the Chan of realization for you, O benevolent one.
For a student, one must thoroughly digest the sacred scriptures; every single word and character must be integrated back into oneself. As it is said:
The Buddha has already fully realized and perceived this; what need is there for further opening? It is said that he merely opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for sentient beings.
It is like a hidden treasure in a poor person's house: once that treasure is obtained, one is no longer poor. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says: "The Tathāgata’s Great Treasury of Radiance."
This is the ground of the pure awakening of sentient beings. Since it is called "pure," how can there be sentient beings? The subsequent text states:

"Only by permanently severing ignorance does one attain the Buddha-way. It further states: "This ignorance has no real substance. If one knows that it has no substance, [then there are no sentient beings].

In the Great Luminous Treasury (*Mahā-ābhāsagarbha*), the essence is fully manifest. Thus, it is said that when a Tathāgata cultivates *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* on the causal ground, he knows these [phenomena] to be like flowers in the sky;
thereupon, there is no cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Zhuan (Zhuan Daokai) stated: "They are non-existent not because they are produced [as such], but because their fundamental nature is non-existent.

This reaches its conclusion in the Chapter on Samantabhadra, which says: "To know the illusory is to be detached from it; no expedient means are required. To be detached from the illusory is awakening itself; there is likewise no gradual progression. —Zhongfeng Da.
The Master said: "These two chapters clearly possess the air of a patch-robed monk. As for using illusion to cultivate illusion, these were all spoken by our Buddha out of necessity;
they were not his fundamental intent. If one says that principle is thoroughly pervasive and interfused, what harm is there in its sequential manifestation?
One simply fails to realize that a single thought-moment contains the three thousand realms, and a single mind fuses the myriad practices, leaving no trace of coming or going."

Lengthening and shortening occur simultaneously, dissolving the distinction between far and near; distant and proximate become one and the same. In this very moment, the principle of the non-dual realm of self and phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is realized as the eight aspects of enlightenment.

Though one attains the Way in diverse lands, the principle knows no partiality or limitation. The myriad practices are perfected in cultivation; within this single thought-moment, all matters are fulfilled without seeking them elsewhere.
To contemplate that which is remote and ancient is like looking upon it today. Having obtained the great precious chariot, one’s steps are level and upright. Its...
It is as swift as the wind. That is to say, while being perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*), it does not obstruct sequential manifestation (*xingbu*);
thus every matter is accomplished. While being sequentially manifested, it does not obstruct perfect interfusion; thus every mind is without interval.

By this one may know that, upon merely hearing the name, contemplative practice arises, ignorance is severed, the six sense faculties are purified, and ultimate perfection is achieved. To speak of the word "Buddha" is already superfluous talk.
If one seeks the traces of the three vehicles’ practice, clarifies the right and wrong of the six stages of realization, and thereby cuts off the three delusions,
accomplishes the three wisdoms, and realizes the three virtues— extending even to adorning the buddha-lands and transforming sentient beings—

then I shall not be counted among their ranks; I shall likewise keep my mouth shut and wait for another three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to once again associate with my fellow practitioners on different peaks.
It is seen. By means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he transforms all sentient beings;
yet when sentient beings receive this transformation, the Buddha cannot be apprehended. One knows that ignorance has no substance, being like flowers in the sky.
While on the stage of the causal ground, the Tathāgata thoroughly understood birth and death; knowing that illusion is itself departure, and departing from illusion is itself awakening.
Having awakened to this reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), he knew that even knowledge cannot be established within the unestablishable.
Thus, he gave rise to the mind of great compassion, wherein a single thought-instant encompasses all practices.
In a single moment, one perfectly completes many kalpas, as numerous as the atoms within worlds as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Because the principle is without division or limitation, this is called "perfect realization. To realize this is termed "true knowledge. This refers to the fruit of realization;
it is not a realization that stands in opposition to the causal stage. Since the "revealing cause" does not establish a separate realization, this is called "Great Perfect Enlightenment."
The most supreme sūtras are all commentaries on the vehicle of the ultimate school; If you wish to seek the Zen of the Patriarchs, arouse great courage and valor.
Like a lion cub, leaping through the air with somersaults and roaring inconceivably, All the beasts have their heads split open; wait until you realize the fundamental causes and conditions.
I shall further explain this for the sake of the virtuous one, the Zen practitioner Xiangxian:

For those who study, the wisdom derived from hearing becomes increasingly manifest, giving rise to all kinds of realized wisdom; therefore, it is said that one does not depart from words and letters, yet one does not cling to them.
Letters serve as the means for the Way. The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra states: "To achieve boundless wisdom, one first relies upon extensive learning;

the teachings of the Buddha-treasury declare that entering the gate of Nirvāṇa swiftly is entirely due to hearing the Dharma. For those who have thoroughly investigated the mind, even the singing of birds and the blooming of flowers can trigger the awakening;
how much more so when the golden mouth of the Buddha personally proclaims it—how could this fail to nourish the sprouts of wisdom in the field of the mind?
Yes. You should know that the Buddha within the minds of sentient beings preaches the Dharma for the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind.

The sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind listen to the Dharma preached by the Buddha within their own minds. Furthermore, you should know that among the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind, there is no one who listens.
Within the minds of sentient beings, there is no Buddha who speaks; both are simultaneously elucidated, and their two aspects are instantly empty. As the Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma, nor does he deliver sentient beings. In the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, that which transcends verbal expression is termed "inconceivable" (acintya).

It is truly because practitioners do not realize their own minds, clinging instead to various names and signs, seeking the state of the Buddha’s wondrous adornment as a fruit while remaining oblivious to the conditions of the causal mind’s true wisdom.
Therefore, Master Daruma dispelled their attachments and stagnations by pointing directly to the human mind;
he condensed three kalpas of cultivation into the present moment and opened the eye of wisdom for those born blind, its marvel residing in a single instant. He raised [the banner]...
The pearl within the hem of the robe is suddenly revealed as the family treasure; the suffering of wandering in hardship ceases without the need for seeking.

One enters the gate of benefit and salvation, extensively inviting all to practice and cross over. There is no tree of Bodhi, and the mirror is not a stand; it serves as the true refuge for sentient beings and acts as the mother of wisdom for Bodhisattvas.
When the duality of subject and object dissolves and the mind severs attachment to right and wrong, it is as stated in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*: "One does not wait for adornment..."
Yan thoroughly understands all dharmas because by attaining one, he attains them all. Thus it is said: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the world;
when a single speck of dust rises, the great earth is gathered. Riding this precious vehicle, to roam the four quarters in playful joy—is this not fitting?
Some say that the sequential arrangement of stages is clearly set forth in the teachings; why then do you obstinately hold to your own views and utterly discard this?
The Commentary says: What words are these! One should know that the stages and positions are inexhaustible because the mind is inexhaustible.

If one can comprehend this principle of the inexhaustibility of True Suchness and the single mind, then all the six perfections, the four means of integration, and the myriad practices will likewise be inexhaustible.
To turn and show this to the minds of others is also equally inexhaustible, just as when one lamp ignites hundreds of thousands of lamps, all who were in darkness become illuminated.
Because all things are inexhaustible, the First Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted the inexhaustible lamp through the principle of inexhaustibility.

It illuminates the dark and deluded paths of ten thousand kalpas, accomplishing the Buddha-work of radiance for a single moment. One must enter this through awakening; it does not rely on verbal explanations.
Once the Great Principle is revealed, it is like a blazing fire or boiling water that admits not even a speck of snow; ignorance does not wait [to be dispelled].

It is severed by itself; the state of fruition is not achieved through external effort, but is realized spontaneously. It is like being under the guidance of a patriarch, who presents a single phrase as a *huatou*:
"When the breath does not come again, where will you ultimately go? It is as if one were in a pit ten thousand fathoms deep, desiring only to leap out;
even if the eight sensory objects were to converge before one, there would be no leisure to look back. If for even a single moment—
If you do not seek the way out within, you will lose your body and forfeit your life. Therefore it is said: "It is like one man facing ten thousand enemies;
when face-to-face, how can there be time for even a blink of an eye? If you apply yourself with such earnestness, then with a single "clatter," the bottom of the bucket falls away.
It is still the same person as before; it is not that the person is different. At the place where one practiced in the past, even the Buddha-dharma does not exist.
I leave behind these few traces of my imperial legacy; how much more so, then, regarding human relations and worldly conditions—matters of whether one practices or does not practice.
The Dharani is without words, yet words manifest the Dharani.
By not departing from the conditions of words, one employs the Way to accomplish boundless wisdom and swiftly enter the gate of Nirvana.
Even the waterfowl and the forest trees discourse upon the true nature of reality;
how much more so the words spoken by the Buddha—how could they not nourish the seeds of wisdom?
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings discourse with one another without interruption, yet there is no speaker and no audience who listens; it is utterly free from verbal expression.
This is called the inconceivable. If one does not recognize one’s own mind, how can one seek the wondrously adorned land of the Buddha-fruit?
Could it exist apart from one’s own mind? The three great kalpas of long duration are all perfectly accomplished in a single thought;
the jewels are inherently complete, so there is no need to seek them elsewhere.
He widely opens the gate of benefit and salvation, Flowing on incessantly without exhaustion. Realizing this Dharma of the One Mind, he wanders through the four quarters;
The lamp of wisdom destroys the deep darkness, So that all who were in obscurity become fully enlightened.
Like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, He cuts through the current straight to the bottom, And in an instant ascends to the other shore.
Without further discussion of sequence, One cut, all is cut; One perfected, all is perfected.
When the principles of teaching and realization are unimpeded, One should delight in the Zen of the Patriarchs.
When the single breath does not return, where ultimately does one go? It is like being in a ten-thousand-fathom pit; One simply must personally leap out.
Though the eight objects of sense intersect before one, do not give rise to a moment’s distraction.
It is like a man breaking a great enemy force—how could he afford to blink his eyes? Use your mind with such urgency that suddenly the bucket slips from your hands;
you are no longer the person you were. Where would worldly conditions then exist? Do not give rise to the mind of the world.
This is indeed a favorable occasion; having waited for this fundamental cause and condition, I shall once again explain it for you, O practitioner of the Chan of Transcendence.
Now, for those who study, the very first requirement is to possess the eye that discerns the Dharma, so as to thoroughly penetrate the entire Great Canon of the Tathāgata.
The principle is fundamental. Thoroughly investigate the conditions of practice until the mind is free from doubt and this matter is accomplished. Master Yongming said:
"Only by preparing the foundation of the One Vehicle and strengthening the walls of the myriad practices can one begin to construct the lofty and realize the substantial.

It is not enough merely to seek a thorough understanding under our ancestral masters; otherwise, one will only plunder empty reputations, which has nothing to do with ultimate realization. You must...
Know that the single character "Principle" (zong) is the mainstay of the net of the teachings. As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "Cessation (zhi) means to cease all marks;
even to the point where the mind cannot be apprehended, this is cessation. To contemplate the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions is contemplation (guan). Yongming said:

Alternatively, one may use contemplation of principle to counteract the cessation of phenomena; this means that when one accords with principle, delusion subsides. Alternatively, one may use contemplation of phenomena to counteract the stillness of principle;

this means that through non-conceptual awareness, one knows the objective realm. One should know that for those who practice Chan meditation, as soon as they raise a single phrase of the *huatou*, the mind of discursive thought subsides of its own accord without waiting to be stilled—is this not "cessation" (*śamatha*)? What need is there to speak of "cessation"? It is great!

Principle does not depend on illumination; it is self-illuminating. Is this not contemplation? What contemplation can be described? As soon as a thought arises, one falls into mental activity (*manas*).

Once discrimination begins to sprout, one immediately commits a "medicinal taboo" (a fundamental error). When the Second Patriarch searched for his mind and could not find it, he attained immediate peace of mind.
Thus, he knew the principle of no-mind, the gateway to all wonders. If one realizes no-mind, there is no obstruction encountered anywhere.
Stagnation. To cut off even a single speck of dust as an object of opposition, what need is there for the labor of dispelling it?

To give rise to no single thought of emotion, one does not rely on the power of forgetting external conditions. By this, we know that when the mind is free from concern for affairs, ten thousand emergencies may arrive at once without disturbing the spirit;
when the mind is free from concern for affairs, a thousand difficulties may present themselves individually without troubling the deliberations. How could one wait for eternity...?
This clearly exhorts and admonishes the student: if one returns home by way of the path, one will gain great advantage.

However, as for exhausting the ultimate limit of the vehicle of the school and investigating the profound subtleties of the ancestral Way, it requires only letting go completely from the edge of a precipice and personally accepting the responsibility.

Only after death can one return to life; this cannot be faked before the eyes of the Master. Therefore it is said: "Only after the life-root is severed does one finally attain the power of verbal expression. Not so.
Alas! All have fallen into the present age and are forever submerged in the sea of suffering.

Countless billions of heterodox views take root in the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, while hundreds of thousands of kinds of deviant paths arise from emotional conceptualizations. Only the Way of our Patriarchs is most profoundly profound;

it accords with the One Way to encompass all perfectly and unites a thousand paths under a single track. It does not involve the gradual stages of the Three Vehicles, for cause and effect are simultaneous.
How could this interfere with the disparities of the Five Teachings? In the Buddha’s birth, all is suddenly extinguished; in a single kṣaṇa, one penetrates many kalpas;

the entire dharma-realm enters into the tip of a hair. Yet even such [attainments] remain but the second tally, and have not yet fulfilled the intent of the Plucking of the Flower. As the Great Master Linji said:
Following the current without ceasing, one asks: "How is it? True illumination is boundless; explain it to him as such. Detached from characteristics and detached from names, no one can receive it.

Once the "whiskered blade" has been used, it must be sharpened immediately. When the principle is thoroughly penetrated within the world and vision transcends all things, having realized the sharpness of the whiskered blade, be careful not to hesitate.
Having expanded the mechanism of illuminating function, do not allow yourself to stop short. How could this be for those of shallow roots and inferior understanding?
This is what can be known; it is not something that those who cling to old stumps or harbor ignorance can ever reach.
Those who possess deep faith in the "separate transmission outside the teachings" should, whenever they encounter objects or circumstances, exert themselves with this very intent.
If one wishes to understand the source of birth and death, First, one must possess the eye of discernment (*pravicaya*).
When both practice and principle are thoroughly penetrated, And one no longer falls into doubt, Possessing such a pure and white mind, One may then seek the Unsurpassed Way.
It is like constructing a multi-storied pavilion: One must first lay a firm foundation; Or like a lapis lazuli flask—

Able to contain the milk of the lion, Unimpeded in mastery of the teachings and their principles, Acting as a supportive condition for the vehicle of the school, one who desires to investigate the matter beyond:
Simply uphold a single phrase, Without giving rise to conceptual discrimination—this is called true *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Within the five hundred gates of settling the mind, One transcends suddenly through non-mind.
Not involving oneself in the Three Vehicles, what concern is there with the Five Teachings?
When the fruit is severed and one revives again, the essence itself is free from mental conceptions. Because mental conceptions are far removed, false views have no way to arise.
A single kṣaṇa enters many kalpas; the Dharma-realm is condensed within the tip of a hair—this is still but the second tally.
The intent of the unfulfilled plucking of the flower—when the "blow-to-the-hair" blade has been used, do not harbor hesitation;

enter suddenly into the inconceivable. Only then is it called the Extinction of Ambrosia. Wait until the fundamental causes and conditions are exhausted, and I shall speak further for you, O Benevolent One.
To the Chan practitioner Zhuyu:

For one who studies, it is essential to thoroughly investigate the fundamental source; there is no need for the branches and leaves. What is meant by the "source"? It is that the three realms are but mind alone.
What is meant by the "source"? All phenomena are but consciousness. Thus it is said: "Before one has realized that objects are but mind, various conceptual discriminations arise;
once one has realized that objects are but mind, discrimination no longer arises. The Patriarch said: "If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not a single inch of earth in the great world.
This is because those who merely listen and study recite names and characteristics, providing intellectual interpretations that match the words, yet the eye of their mind does not [awaken].
[The Master] said: "To practice exclusively through contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) is entirely irrational. Those who cultivate meditation (*chan*) value only the contemplation of principle;

their minds are harmonized with everything they encounter, yet they are ignorant of names and marks (*nāma-rūpa*). These two [approaches] are mutually deficient. Some forget conditions and seek the gate of liberation;

others cling to delusions and grasp at the fruit of ultimate realization. They strike away the waves while seeking the water, or take the mud itself to be the jar. Failing to understand that all is but mind, they give rise to false attachments. Failing to understand that all is but...

Regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*), people falsely speculate whether it exists or does not exist. Master Yongming said: "The *ālayavijñāna* is vast, all-encompassing, and the root-source of the myriad dharmas.
This essence cannot be described; it is subtle and most difficult to conceive. It pervades the entire dharma-realm yet has no abiding mind;
it sustains all things without manifesting any signs. Entering the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Consciousness-Only, one destroys false attachments."
[Regarding] the "Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of the *Śūraṅgama* through the Erroneous Mind," Maitreya said:

"From the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I cultivated the samādhi of mind-only consciousness (*cittamātra-vijñapti-samādhi*) and entered into *samādhi*. Thereupon, I attained the supreme, wondrous, and perfect *samādhi* of the conscious mind.

All the lands of the Tathāgatas throughout space—whether pure or impure, existent or non-existent—are all manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind. World-Honored One, I have understood this clearly."

It is so. Because it is solely mind and consciousness (*vijñāna*). From the nature of consciousness, immeasurable Tathāgatas flow forth. It concludes by saying: "The mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous;

it enters the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), remaining far removed from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one suddenly enters the limit of perfect luminosity.

Immeasurable Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, flow forth from me; there is neither self nor other. The conditions for defilement and purity, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [flow forth] from..."
This arising is beyond thought and beyond deliberation; like a magnet that moves without consciousness, it revolves through the six realms of existence.
Like a *maṇi* jewel that rains down treasures without intention, it extensively saves all sentient beings. It is called the source of sentient beings, which is the *tathāgatagarbha*.

From the state of an ordinary person one enters the state of a sage, with distinct stages at each level. Through the sage, the ordinary person is illuminated, layer upon layer, penetrating through to the ultimate clarity. The Sage—
Whenever both are extinguished, the single path is simultaneously revealed; when mind and consciousness mutually merge, the thousand paths are collectively saved.

Thus, Mañjuśrī seals practice with principle, so that the path of differentiation remains unimpaired; Samantabhadra unites principle with practice, so that the gateway of the fundamental source is not abandoned.

Cause and effect are employed interchangeably, yet this is not a calculation that the fruit exists within the cause. Cause and effect are simultaneous, yet this is not a calculation that [the cause exists within] the fruit.
There is a cause. It admits of no calculation or deliberation and does not belong to discursive thought. Its essence and function contain one another; mind and phenomena penetrate each other.
Emptiness possesses all virtues and transcends the realm of the myriad existents; phenomena are unimpeded and are fully contained within the single principle.
Only then can one enter the gate of the Patriarchs and seek the path that goes beyond. Where the body is hidden, there is no trace; shake the void to pieces and vanish.
No trace remains; the body cannot be hidden. Turning over the great earth—truly, molten iron flows like liquid gold. It is well to take this very body and bury it alive.
Ultimately, as for the root source, there is no need for branches and leaves: it is simply Consciousness-Only and Mind-Only.
Without giving rise to conceptual discrimination, one recites the texts while still contemplating their principles;
by practicing dhyāna to comprehend names and signs, these two aspects mutually penetrate one another—this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Liberation does not consist in forgetting conditions, for in the ultimate state there is no false grasping; the essence of consciousness is most subtle and profound, secret, and inconceivable.
The mind that abides nowhere throughout the entire realm Sustains itself without manifesting images. It accomplishes the unsurpassed, wondrous, perfect purity;

impurity and purity are transformations of mind alone. By realizing this nature of consciousness-only, one enters the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), thereby departing from the dependent (*paratantra*) and the imagined (*parikalpita*). It is like a magnet attracting a needle.
Like a mani-jewel raining down treasures, Principle and practice penetrate one another; Practice and principle together provide salvation.
In the place where mind and object are both fused, One enters this gate of non-obstruction. The hidden body vanishes its traces, shaking out the very marrow of space;
With no traces left, there is no need to hide the body— It overturns the great earth and its marshes.
Relying on the walls of the Dharma-realm, there is no need to discuss the Middle Way. When molten iron flows as liquid gold, Zen and the Way flash forth from this.
Once you have realized your original causes and conditions, I shall again explain the standard for the Way to you, O practitioner of Zen.

Now, for those who study, this is the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden, the definitive exposition of the ultimate meaning. It is vast and profound, thoroughly investigated, exhausting the source and reaching the limit of all phenomena.

One must grasp each and every point in its actual application; be careful not to cling to names, marks, stages, or levels, nor to the provisional and the definitive, or the literal and the symbolic characters.

Do not allow these to obstruct the radiance of the Buddhas or cloud the wisdom-eye of sentient beings. Do not cling to practices and positions, for to do so is to distance oneself from perfect penetration and remain ignorant.
The explanations of skillful means all fall within the realm of words used merely to stop a child's crying. You should know that when our Buddha pointed directly to the arising mind, he meant:

this mind acts as the cause; this mind produces the fruit; this mind establishes its station; and this mind receives its name. Within the state of no-name and no-station, it establishes names and stations;
without departing even a single step, it is naturally so. Within the absence of cause and effect, it constructs cause and effect.
How could it depend upon external conditions for its retribution? Rather, it is fully present according to one's own mindfulness. As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"If one perceives the Teacher of Men through his majestic power, physical appearance, or lineage, this is the root of illness and a perverted view; such a person cannot know the most supreme Dharma.
This is because sentient beings spontaneously give rise to thoughts of inferiority, obscuring their fundamental superior conditions and failing to recognize the Dharma manifested as the fruit.
The body is the fundamental awakening that is the basis for causes; it is not that the wisdom of other Buddhas pervades oneself, but rather that one’s own Buddha-wisdom pervades others.
It is not that one's own cause proceeds toward another's fruit; fundamentally, that which is the fruit of others is utterly sustained by my own cause.

By this, one knows that cause and fruit are simultaneous, and that the path of the sage and the ordinary person is one and the same, entirely devoid of dual characteristics. Thus, one immediately transcends the various demons and directly penetrates the pure and perfect—how could there be any gradualism?
Next, one must not abide in even a single dharma within the Buddha Vehicle. When the One Path is indeed level and uniform, then the ten thousand differences are simultaneously extinguished.

An ancient verse says: "At the bottom of the azure sea ten thousand fathoms deep, atop the emerald peaks ten thousand cubits high; the sun rises at the very heart of midnight, and flowers bloom in the ninth month of autumn.
If it were otherwise, all would be turning one's back on awakening to merge with the dust, abandoning the self to follow external objects. — *Huayan Lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
It is said: "If one clings to names, names arise; if one abandons explanations, words are produced. To point at a deer and call it a horse is to expect awakening and instead encounter delusion.
To grasp at shadows as real and take sickness for the Dharma is to misinterpret the Buddha’s intent and erroneously cling to the conditions of birth.

Is it not fitting that the Tathāgata called such people 'those who are to be pitied'? Only within our ancestral teachers’ school does a single phrase of the *huatou* blunt the spearhead and shatter [delusion].
It is like fathoming the vast ocean; one must reach the very bottom before coming to rest. When you observe that a single breath does not return, where exactly will you go?
This is not something that can be known through discursive thought, nor can it be understood by the ordinary intellect. When the four marks are transcended, the life-root is suddenly severed;
when the four ailments are cured, the nature of wisdom becomes purely clear. It is like the sun shining upon autumn frost, or like an arrow piercing a stone drum.
The power of this *huatou* cannot be compared even by a fraction to the hundreds of thousands of various methods for cultivation and realization.
Therefore, among the three thousand and seven hundred patriarchs, there was no way to escape [the cycle] except through this gate.
For example, when the Sixth Patriarch asked Master Nanyue, "From where have you come? he replied, "I have come from Mount Song. The Patriarch then asked, "What thing comes in such a manner?"
Yue Wudui remained thus for eight years until he suddenly attained awakening, saying: "To describe it as a single thing is immediately off the mark.
The Patriarch asked, "Do you still require cultivation and realization? He replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet defilement is inadmissible.

Observe this man of realization: when he opens his mouth and utters words, he does not incur even a hair’s breadth of censure; he may truly be called a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net.

It is like watching for the moment when a single breath does not return; this should be treated as being of one essence with this case. If you truly know the place of departure, then you will know the place of arrival.
If the place of departure is not clear, then doubt must suddenly arise, such that a needle cannot pierce it and water cannot moisten it.

The entire great earth is a pitch-black void; one cannot penetrate it. If you wish to find a point of entry, and once you have found a point of entry, you wish to find a point of exit, you must believe that there is a principle not transmitted by the thousand sages.
It is like the case of Deshan blowing out an oil lamp, or when the Master Fu heard the sound of drums and horns and suddenly realized his former faults. This is not merely—
He pinched his own nostrils and said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like grasping at the tip of a hair;
to encompass the Great Void is like a single drop cast into a vast abyss. Furthermore, in ascending to the hall, he said: "Holy names and mundane titles are all empty sounds;
extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not only bring about entanglement?"

When one eventually grows weary of this, it conversely becomes a great affliction. From this, we know that to set foot upon the stages and positions of the gate of merit is much like scratching an itch through a boot.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching of definitive meaning is vast and profound, exhausting its very source. Each and every point attains practical utility;
be careful not to cling to names and forms. Although it speaks of stages of practice and realization, the mind’s inherent completeness leaves nothing out.
If thoughts of superiority or inferiority arise, they are but the distorted visions of those with diseased eyes—yet the Dharma-body is the fruition that is manifest.
Because this cause obscures original enlightenment, cause and effect are simultaneous.
One who does not give rise to perceptions of distance or proximity and realizes there is no duality of characteristics, has already transcended the realm of Māra.

If one does not know this single Dharma, one cannot yet be called a follower of the Buddha-vehicle. To be stuck in names is for names to arise; to abandon speech and yet further engage in discourse is delusion.
Though destined for enlightenment, one encounters delusion again; One fails to comprehend the Buddha’s intent.
Only our ancestral teachers of Chan single-handedly uphold a single phrase. It is like one who exhausts the depths of the ocean, Only reaching the bottom that they finally rest.
This practice is not a matter of deliberate effort; Cessation and extinction are both left behind, As are the notions of self, person, and sentient being.
When the life-faculty is severed, how can the hundreds of thousands of gates of cultivation and realization arise? One cannot describe even a small fraction of the fruit;
where does one know it has gone? It is precisely when meeting suchness that it comes. The mind of the Way transcends all obstruction; the sacred measure is free from entanglement.
A single movement of thought belongs to defilement; the arising of emotion is immediately a taboo for the medicine.
If one breath does not come again, the doubt-mind must suddenly arise. The vast earth is pitch black;
there truly is a path that goes upward. This is the track of all the patriarchs. When this path is not attained, thoughts and feelings will never flicker.
How could a man of ambition and resolve ever be willing to rest for even a moment?
Having waited for the fundamental causes and conditions, I shall once again provide an exposition for you,
my fellow practitioner of Zen, Tongshui. For a student,

there is no text among the words of the Tripitaka— the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma— nor among the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, nor the partial and the perfect, that has not been extensively traversed.
Master Qingliang said: "Take the holy teachings as a clear mirror to illuminate one's own mind; take one's own mind as a lamp of wisdom to shed light upon the profound meaning of the sutras.
Like a king of swans selecting milk from water, or like the sun shining upon high mountains, the great mind of perfect faith enters deeply through this.
One must by no means hold the sacred realm aloft while deprecating oneself as inferior. As the sutra says: 'If one hears this sutra...'"
"One who is neither startled nor terrified should be known as one who has not planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five buddhas;
rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
When the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: "How marvelous! How marvelous! All sentient beings are fully endowed with the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata.
This is precisely the fact that ordinary beings and sages share the same source; it is exactly analogous to the Lotus Sūtra’s revelation of the Buddha's knowledge and vision to all sentient beings.
Those who hear this and give rise to perfect faith accord with the fundamental intention of all Buddhas and realize the intent of all the scriptures.
The Sublime Meaning. The following text states: "It is solely because of deluded thoughts and attachments that one is unable to realize it.

This means that ordinary beings are deluded by false thoughts, while those of the Two Vehicles are attached; neither reaches this source. If one realizes that false thoughts are fundamentally empty, then all is perfectly interfused and unimpeded—how could there be any attachment?

One should know that the principle of the One Mind establishes teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings; though the paths differ, they lead to the same destination. —From *Haihui Chan* (Sea-Wisdom Chan).

The Master said: "The myriad phenomena of the forest and the ten thousand images reach their ultimate limit in emptiness; the hundred rivers and all tributaries reach their ultimate limit in the ocean;
