Third, the dedication and aspiration, which the *Awakening of Faith* calls the "Mahāyāna mind," meaning to carry all under heaven together, leaving no one behind.
These three minds are the essential practices for those beginning their cultivation. As the Sūtra says:
"If one does not give rise to the bodhicitta while cultivating all wholesome dharmas, they are entirely under the influence of Māra. However, the bodhicitta is not merely to be generated once;
it must be generated in every thought-moment and repeatedly generated. At all times, one should recollect the Buddha and dedicate [merit], and therein one should generate this mind. [End of] Mi[tsu].
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and upholding his name, one immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
One should know that in this Sahā world, the minds of people are turbid and evil; the karmas of body, speech, and mind arise in every thought-moment.
To single-mindedly uphold even one phrase of Amitābha Buddha’s majestic name of myriad virtues is like casting a bright pearl into turbid water;
the turbid water cannot fail to become clear. When mindfulness of the Buddha is cast into a distracted mind, that distracted mind cannot fail to become the Buddha.
Thus, did not the Venerable Master Yunqi rightly call this the "miraculous elixir for transforming the bones"? If one cultivates this method of mindfulness of the Buddha...

Furthermore, it is not necessary to place excessive emphasis on contemplation of principle (*li*). If one practices contemplation of principle, the moment the mind slightly stirs with thought, the contemplation fails.
Simply take up one phrase of "Amitābha" and recite it like flowing water. Let the recitation proceed until, without conscious effort, it becomes spontaneous;

when you ultimately reach the state of "one-pointedness without distraction," the Pure Land of Principle will be attained. This is precisely the time to make the vow for rebirth across ten quadrillion lands. It is not...
Beyond the single mind, it is further said: "The light of that Buddha is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction.
One should know that by being born in this one land, one is born in immeasurable lands; by recollecting this one Buddha, one recollects immeasurable Buddhas.
Why is this? Because the principle is without division or limit. If one realizes this meaning, one attains the perfect cultivation of the single-minded recollection."

The Buddha is good in the beginning, middle, and end, increasing with every thought-moment. When one contemplates emptiness as true contemplation, then the intersection of the Buddha and the path arises.
When one is purely of a single mind, then both the Buddha and birth are extinguished together. To know that the single mind is fully endowed with myriad virtues is called "goodness in the beginning.
To fully practice myriad virtues is called "goodness in the middle. To immediately perfect myriad fruits is called "goodness in the end. By this, one knows Amitābha.
The Buddha-land is not far from here; one can be reborn there in the mere snap of a finger. Why, then, should you not aspire to go?

Not only is it not far, but within the minds of sentient beings, in every thought-moment, there is the appearance of a Buddha in the world, and in every thought-moment, there is the nirvana of a Buddha. Thus, in every thought-moment, there is both the appearance in the world and the entry into nirvana.
All these are merely provisional names. To know them as provisional names is to realize that their very substance is free from conceptual thought.
If one is free from conceptual thought, one perceives the eternally abiding Dharmakāya; thus, both the land and the Buddha become manifest. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

"If there are sentient beings who say that the Buddha is eternally abiding, unchanging, and undifferentiated, you should know that in their household there is a Buddha. Why is this? Because 'Buddha' means awakening."
Regarding the meaning: because one awakens to the fact that this rational nature (*dharmatā*) is pure, no evil whatsoever can destroy it; therefore, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*).

Because its essence is without arising or ceasing, it is called "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*). One should develop deep faith and aspiration toward this land and this Buddha, swiftly vowing to be reborn there and entering with a fixed deadline;
one must not be dilatory. If you say that the purport of the Pure Land has already been revealed to you:
Regarding the sublime secret of Zen meditation, what is its meaning? It is said: Did we not say before that one should simply seek to enter deeply through a single gate?

Who is there to compare their relative merits? As for the single word "Zen," the Buddhas of the three periods have been unable to utter it from their mouths, let alone exhaust it upon paper and brush.
Wait until you have performed a somersault within the Pure Land, and then I shall ask you.
When you do not draw another breath for even a single moment, where will you ultimately go? As soon as you conceive a thought of deliberation, the ancient Buddhas have long since passed away.
"Three pounds of flax," "a dried piece of dung"—if you cannot resolve these through discussion, leave them aside for another time.
I shall reveal this further for you; it is not too late.
Among the immeasurable and wondrous Dharma gates, Chan and Pure Land are the most direct paths.
If you seek to enter deeply through one gate to achieve swift accomplishment, first give rise to the Bodhicitta to moisten the seeds of great compassion.
Benefiting both oneself and others, One should never seek for one's own sake alone.
If one does not give rise to this great resolve, it is because one is under the influence of Māra. Therefore, single-mindedly uphold the vast name of Amitābha Buddha;
It is like casting a bright pearl That can purify turbid water, Or like an elixir that transforms the bones.
Transforming from the mundane to enter the sacred, The fruit is the state of single-minded non-distraction. This is called the Pure Land of Principle;
It is perfectly interfused and mutually unobstructed. Its radiance shines throughout the ten directions; One land is all lands, one Buddha is all Buddhas.
Virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, In every thought-moment, it grows to full perfection.
A snap of the fingers and one is reborn; In its very essence, it is free from all thoughts.
To see the eternally abiding Buddha is called being born into the Buddha’s family. Because the nature is fundamentally pure, No evil can destroy it.
The ultimate reality is free from arising and ceasing; This is called Amitāyus (Immeasurable Life). Forever departing from the evil realms is called [liberation].
Having been reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one further inquires into the Patriarchal Chan. Though the mouth is full, there is nothing to utter;
"there is both Chan and Pure Land" is like a tiger with horns. Neither written words nor spoken language can proclaim even a small fraction of it.
As soon as one speaks of the Path Above, the lips and teeth immediately clench shut.
Having waited for this fundamental cause and condition, I shall further explain it for you, O Benevolent One.

The ocean of the Zen person’s nature is fundamentally boundless; purity and defilement interpenetrate one another. It is only according to the functioning of karma that they are perceived, such that each attains their own self-enjoyment.
During Amitābha’s stage of practice as a bodhisattva, he extensively manifested the power of his great vows and revealed the appearance of a pure land to transform those who recite his name.
If a person focuses their mind with single-minded intent, like a child yearning for its mother, and their thoughts remain unwavering, they will attain a degree of purity in both mind and environment.
Or by contemplating wondrous forms and images, with all their various ornaments, and by recollecting these contemplations until they are fully accomplished, one attains rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
Or, in a single kṣaṇa, one may attain non-retrogression in mindfulness; through mindfulness of emptiness, one beholds the Buddha and is reborn there upon the snap of a finger.
By reciting the name of this one Buddha, all three faculties are universally benefited. Just as a *maṇi* jewel can rain down all manner of treasures, so too is the name of this one Buddha:
it accomplishes all wisdom. When the mind is pure, the land is pure; for the Buddha’s birth is clearly manifest.
One Buddha is all Buddhas; all lands are one land. Outside the mind, there are fundamentally no lands; every realm appears solely as the manifestation of the mind.
If one realizes that lands are nothing but mind, then to be born in those lands is to be born here. There is neither birth nor non-birth; there is neither non-birth nor the birth of birth.
There is no non-arising that gives rise to arising; there is no arising that gives rise to non-arising. If one realizes this non-arising, then dependent origination is mutually unimpeded:
what arises necessarily arises, and what departs truly does not depart. The pure lands and wondrous lotus flowers all arise from one's own mind.
The pure mind is itself the Buddha; it is inconceivable. To recite "Namo Buddha" even once, all together shall attain the Way of the Buddhas.
[This was written] in response to the inquiry of the practitioner Bi Ru.

Someone asked: "The Avataṃsaka is the fundamental gateway of Vairocana Buddha. Its principles, phenomena, and practices are perfectly complete, manifesting the marks of wisdom, compassion, and virtue within the stage of Buddhahood, as it fully possesses immeasurable vehicles.

Since there is nothing not subsumed within these immeasurable vehicles, I do not understand why the Chan school is called 'Sudden Enlightenment. Under which teaching is it categorized? Is it not because Qingliang [Xuanzang] judged it to be Sudden?"
Is this included within the teachings? Or is it that which has not yet reached the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao)? It is said:

"The *Avataṃsaka* possesses immeasurable vehicles" because it universally reveals the marks of the Buddha’s fruition-merit to all sentient beings, thereby serving as the cause for their stages of practice.

It enables those of great resolve to enter [the path] suddenly, just as a single drop of water is identical to the great ocean. Thus, the sudden awakening of the perfect capacity is fully present within the minds of sentient beings.
The wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata represent the ultimate pinnacle of the Teaching School (Jiao-jia). This is not comparable to the gate of awakening in the Chan school.

Regarding that which can be encompassed by the Teaching School, there is no single sublime Dharma spoken by our Buddha over the forty-nine years of his ministry that has not been fully included by the classifiers of the teachings.
For what reason, then, did he further pluck a flower and show it to the assembly at the Vulture Peak, where hundreds of thousands of humans and devas were all—
All were at a loss for words. Within this assembly of humans and devas, could there not have been those with the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden [teachings]?

Why, then, wait for Mahākāśyapa alone to break into a smile? Therefore, the World-Honored One confirmed the principle of the separate transmission outside the teachings and entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa.
By this, one knows that what the five teachings cannot encompass, only the Chan gate can encompass—indeed, it encompasses all five.

Regarding the teachings: as Master Jingyin was able to distinguish the five teachings within a single shout, how much more so for a single word, a single verse, or even a single movement or stillness—all of these embody the principle of the Pure and Perfect.
Unless one has attained realization, it is impossible to even vaguely approximate this in the slightest degree.
Furthermore, when the Chan school speaks of "sudden," it refers to the suddenness of sudden awakening, not the "sudden" used in the classification of the teachings. This is indeed so.
As for teaching, its value lies in leading sentient beings toward awakening and entry [into the truth]. Once awakening is attained, how could it be encompassed by the teachings?
One should know that within the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), there is a distinct excellence. An ancient worthy said: "This matter does not accord with the vehicle of the teachings."
Only those who have arrived can know this; it is not a matter of contentious discourse.
Someone asked: "The Avataṃsaka is the Dharma-gate of the Arising of Nature. When sentient beings awaken and enter it, within a single atom they see through to the boundless Dharma-realm.

They realize that the substance of the mind is unified with it, reaching the source and forgetting all emotions, penetrating the fundamental origin of all Buddhas and thoroughly understanding the multitude [of phenomena]."
This is the fundamental limit of birth. Thus, the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka) says: "That which constitutes the foundation cannot be accomplished through effort;
that which constitutes the source cannot be attained through practice. It is like being born into a royal family—this is natural nobility.

Is there any further excellence beyond this, apart from what the Chan school calls "sudden enlightenment" and "a separate transmission outside the teachings"? It does not involve this Great... [text truncated]
"Is there some other superior point in the teaching? He replied, "What kind of talk is this? The Sūtras have clearly told you:
the Tathāgata has manifested these marks and qualities of the fruit-stage so that beings of great resolve may aspire to awaken and enter it.

How could the two words 'awakening and entering' possibly be as far apart from the characteristics of verbal expression as heaven and earth? If they were identical to the characteristics of verbal expression," [the teaching would be in vain].
Regarding those who do not expect wondrous enlightenment, does the Sūtra not say: "It is like a poor man counting another's treasures; he has no share of even half a coin.
Even if one knows of the Tathāgata’s boundless treasury of Dharma-jewels, one remains like a destitute son still staying outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut;
it is not one's own portion. Even if one were to suddenly enter perfect clarity and enter the inconceivable Dharma-realm, [it would still not be one's own].
Regarding the Gate of Enlightenment, one must know that above the Dharmakāya, there is yet another matter. Thus it is said: "The path leading upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages.
For instance, when Chan Master Shushan Ren asked Muzhou Daowu: "The principle of the Dharmakāya is a principle beyond the subtle and profound;
even 'not grasping at the realm of right and wrong' is still merely a matter pertaining to the side of the Dharmakāya. What, then, is the Dharmakāya itself?"
Regarding the matter above: Guishan held up his whisk. The Master said, "This is still a matter on the level of the Dharma-body. Guishan asked, "What is the matter beyond the Dharma-body?
The Master snatched the whisk away, snapped it in two, threw it to the ground, and returned to the assembly.
Guishan said, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes, but difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk. This was still at a time when he had not yet awakened," and then there was [a sound].

This is merely a summary; it is not a matter of leaping out of the conceptual traps of the teaching schools. How else could one attain such expedient benefit? Later, he asked Mingzhao, "When the tree falls and the vines wither, where do the words return?
Mingzhao said, "It simply makes Miaoxi’s laughter even fresher. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "So, it turns out there was a blade within Miaoxi’s laughter!

One should know that in the School of the Patriarchs, a single phrase— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The final sentence fragment, "One should know that in the School of the Patriarchs, a single phrase," has been translated as requested.*
Transcending verbal explanations—this single phrase alone cannot be refuted even by the commentaries of the entire Great Canon of Teachings.
That which does not accord with the vehicles of the teachings becomes all the more clear. Is it not therefore fitting that this is called the distinctive excellence of the separate transmission?
Someone asked: "In the Chan school, the two terms 'awakening' (wu) and 'entry' (ru) are held to transcend the vehicles of the teachings.

Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* already contains these very terms in the phrase 'opening, showing, awakening, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,' why wait for the Chan school to take 'awakening and entry' as its primary objective?

The reply was: "In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings and emitted light from the mark of the white tuft between his eyebrows. From this..."
The heavens rained down four kinds of flowers. Having thus completed the certification of the teaching of the Lotus Sūtra, the great assembly in that gathering neither understood nor knew it;

this was not only true for those who had awakened and entered [the truth]. As I stated in the *Origins of the Pure Land*, the Lotus Sūtra is the "great matter of cause and condition" (*mahā-kāraṇa*) within the context of "opening and revealing," whereas the plucking of the flower and the smile are the "great matter of cause and condition" within the context of "awakening and entering. Therefore...
The World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi. Upon his third request, he spoke again, saying: "I shall now, for your sake, expound the Dharma in detail.
I shall first speak of the single great cause and condition, revealing, instructing, awakening, and leading others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As the text says:
This Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or conceptual discrimination. This is because if the teachings were not beyond deliberation and discrimination, they would be inexpressible.
Therefore, Śākyamuni closed his room in Magadha, and Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī.
It cannot be known by wisdom nor recognized by consciousness; without the gate of great awakening, there is no way to achieve accord. Thus, our school...
Within the gateway [of the Dharma], wondrous awakening does not reside in verbal explanations. That single word "awakening" is like a dragon obtaining water or a tiger relying on a mountain;
it is also like a sea vessel that, upon encountering a favorable wind, suddenly covers a thousand *li* in an instant.

This is not comparable to those of the scholastic schools who spend their days speaking of "awakening and entry" without seeking wondrous awakening. If one can truly contemplate the profound meanings within the sutras and enter through such contemplation, [one will attain it].
Those who awaken and enter into this state without conceptual thought cannot be bound by the net of the perfected teachings of the Three Vehicles;
furthermore, from within their own minds, they are able to manifest a great treasury of the teachings, such as the Master Zhizhe of Tiantai and the Great Master Guifeng.
This is precisely the School of the Gate (Zongmen), not the followers of the Scriptural Teachings (Jiaoren). It was within the *Lotus Sūtra* that [the Master] attained sudden and great enlightenment;

under a single word of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, his mind-ground was opened and he achieved wondrous realization. This wondrous realization lies in the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, and not in the Three Great Works or the various commentaries and sub-commentaries.
For one among us in the School of the Gate, how could it be limited merely to the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* and the *Lotus Sūtra*?

Thus, whether it be the barking of a dog, the crowing of a rooster, the singing of a bird, or the blooming of flowers—encountering conditions wherever one turns, one is able to awaken and enter [the Way].
It is like when Master Linji asked Huangbo about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma;
though he failed to grasp it on three occasions, at the banks of Dayu, he saw through Huangbo’s method and exclaimed, “So, there isn’t much to Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma after all!”
This is precisely the superior quality within the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), which cannot be contained by the Vehicle of Teachings (Jiaosheng).
Someone may ask: "As the Master says, knowing that ignorance has no substance is simply to say it is fundamentally non-existent;

furthermore, pointing out that it is non-existent because it is not created, and that its original nature is non-existent—then citing such phrases as 'knowing illusion is itself liberation,' one need not rely on cultivation or realization. As in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*...

Yan said: "In principle, there is sudden enlightenment; through this awakening, all is simultaneously dissolved. In phenomena, however, there is no sudden elimination; they are exhausted only through a gradual process.
Why, then, do you say that once one enters the principle, cultivation is no longer required? He replied: "If one speaks in such a manner, it is not only the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* that does so.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) even says: 'Using illusion to cultivate illusion. Have you not heard the Great Master Zhongfeng say: 'Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra...'"
The second chapter possesses the full bearing of a Zen monk. It is like the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where the mind is sought through the "seven locations" and found to be ungraspable;

even down to the earth, water, fire, wind, space, views, and consciousness—the principle of the perfect fusion of the seven elements reveals that every sense organ and every object is the manifestation of the wondrously luminous true body.
For a man of resolve who takes up this burden with his whole being right here, what further need is there to wait?
Through diligent toil, one attains realization through the refinement of the subtlest points. Thus our Ancestor said: "To speak of cultivation and non-cultivation is dualistic talk. He also said:
"Realization through cultivation is not non-existent, yet defilement is not permitted. This very state of non-defilement is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind;
it does not compare to the fixed rules and regulations of the scholastic schools. It is the true illumination of the Great Principle—the single word "Awakening" (wu).
One must also spit it all out. How much more so regarding its cultivation and realization—can even a hair’s breadth of trace be retained?
This has already been clarified for those who understand the Great Principle. If one cannot leave behind views and transcend the realm of emotion, one is entirely falling into pits and ravines.

Thus it is said: "The Great Principle is already clear; it is like mourning for one's deceased parents. Master Zhongfeng’s verse says: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are as level as the palm of a hand;
A single official road is as straight as a bowstring. People of this age do not understand the meaning of integration; Iron walls and silver mountains stand before them.
This single word "awakening" (wu) is like an iron wall or a silver mountain. If one speaks of cultivation or non-cultivation...
Xiu: This is much like seeking out one’s own bondage within a state that is essentially free from bondage.
Therefore, the excellence of the Chan school—how could it be compared with the doctrinal schools to determine its superiority or inferiority?

If one is truly a person who has attained thorough enlightenment, they will not hesitate to burn incense and sweep the ground, perfecting all manner of practices; yet even wholesome thoughts do not arise, let alone various unwholesome ones.

Someone asked: "Regarding the study that transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) and cuts off the paths of ordinary beings and sages—how does one transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness?

The single word 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*) is not necessarily a bad thing. As it is said in the teachings, the Hīnayāna seeks realization by extinguishing consciousness; yet in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, the eighth seed-consciousness is identified as the *tathāgatagarbha*.
If one says that the seeds of karma are eternally true, people will feel fear and find it difficult to believe. All of this is for [the sake of... "
It is not expounded for the sake of ordinary, ignorant people. As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the eighth consciousness, the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is the Tathāgatagarbha.

The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* also says that the host of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes the seeds of the Tathāgata. It further states that those who have not yet perfected the Buddha-nature do not realize enlightenment by extinguishing sensation (*vedanā*).
Since sensation is not extinguished, perception (*saṃjñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise so. This is as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: the nature of consciousness is all-pervasive.
The *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra], by means of the practice of great compassion, arises from the fundamental wisdom of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*). It does not belong within the five stages;
its aspects of practice and cause-and-effect are dedicated solely to revealing and awakening sentient beings to the Buddha-fruit, clarifying that the Buddha-fruit is free from the two delusions.

How could it be separated from mind, intellect, and consciousness? Although the gates of dharma concerning the aspects of practice are established, the Buddha does not speak of them, for he intends to lead them directly to their respective stations.

The Bodhisattva himself declares that the Buddha merely emits light to signify this. Nevertheless, in order to lead sentient beings of great capacity to awakening, he establishes the stages and positions of the Buddha-fruit;
thus, he directly bestows the Buddha-fruit as the cause. In this way, the cause takes the fruit as its cause, and the fruit takes the cause as its fruit.
Therefore, without departing from its original location, it fills the entire Dharma-realm—within every single physical mark and every pore of the body.
The lands and realms are layered upon one another; the bodies of Bodhisattvas and Buddhas mutually encompass and enter one another;

and beings of various classes have their bodies and environments interpenetrate—all without any obstruction. By this, it is known that in the fruit of Buddhahood, there are certainly no two delusions to be severed for those of great capacity.

Taking the fruit as the cause makes it even clearer that there is no delusion to be severed; how much more so for the extinction of consciousness? Those within the Chan school investigate the path beyond the ordinary.
They have already transcended this fundamental dharma-gate by one step; how can it be said that they depart from mind, intellect, and consciousness?

It is said that when the Chan school speaks of departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness, the principle is extremely profound and mysterious; it does not mean the extinction of consciousness. This refers to being single-mindedly...

Bring up this *huatou*. If you do not understand it clearly, it will be as if facing a great enemy; the mind, intellect, and consciousness must arise, yet they cannot arise. For this reason, it is called "detachment" (*li*).
This is not a detachment through severance. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says: "To know that things are illusory is itself detachment.
It is also not a detachment where there is something to be detached from. This single phrase of the *huatou* alone can transcend the countless skillful means within the teachings. As...

In the Tiantai school’s single mind and threefold contemplation, inherent evil is itself the truth; cultivation arises entirely from nature, such that even a single form or a single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way.
Were it not for wondrous awakening, all would merely belong to the realm of conceptual consciousness—like using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying, ultimately failing to attain the principle.
Even if one contemplates and achieves realization of the principle, one cannot avoid defining the distinctions of the six stages of attainment. Take, for instance, the Great Master Zhiyi himself.
Even those with the capacity for sudden enlightenment may only attain the five stages; how much more so for those who have not yet awakened?

Therefore, the enduring strength of our school is that as soon as one first resolves their intention, they do not fall into a hierarchy of stages. This single dharma-gate alone is the most swift and direct path, such that it cannot even be compared to the teachings of the scriptures.
How much more so for those who, having passed away, are revived once more to illuminate the Great Principle, and further leap beyond that principle itself.
Regarding the term "nest" (kōjū): it is said that it is like a fine, sturdy tree; as soon as it emerges from the earth, it utterly outshadows the shadows of all other trees.

It is like the *pingga* bird; though still within its egg, its cry already surpasses that of all other birds. Therefore, when those of the Zen school preach the Dharma, every word and every phrase is like a thunderclap or a flash of lightning;
the followers of the Three Vehicles tremble with fear, and those on the Ten Stages are startled in spirit. These are words of truth; they are real.
Regarding "words," as the Great Master of Dongshan said in verse: "Like the taste of the *kṣīra* grass; like a vajra-pestle.
The sublime grasp at the very center; striking and singing raised together. He also said: "The principle is pervasive and the path is pervasive; grasping and carrying, grasping and following the way.

If one errs, it is auspicious; one must not offend or oppose it. It is spontaneously true and wondrous, belonging neither to delusion nor enlightenment. Thus, even the single word 'enlightenment' is a defilement."
It cannot be attained. How much less could the teachings and principles of the Three Vehicles leave behind even a trace?

Therefore, the entryway of the Patriarchal School overturns the world and turns heaven and earth upside down; it is most profoundly mysterious. Thus it is said: "The entire Tripitaka of commentaries cannot break through it. Master Fayan said:

"When principle reaches its ultimate limit, emotional conceptualization vanishes. How could there be any analogy to equal it? In the end, it is like the moon on a frosty night, left to its own course."
It fell into the stream before me. One should know that the initial aspiration is itself able to transcend all dharma-gates;
it is the preeminent excellence of all those who attain awakening—how could brush and paper ever suffice to exhaust its description?
The Buddha points to the mind as the cause of birth; this is the fruit-virtue of all Buddhas. Furthermore, he shows that the fruit-virtue of the Buddha is the causal mind of sentient beings.
Because cause and effect interpenetrate and are mutually pervasive, the Buddha’s realization is perfectly clear;
thus, the nature of the dharma-realm is缘起 (dependent origination). One enters suddenly into the inconceivable, and does not take this [nature] as a cause.
How could one obtain the fruit of eternal abiding? Even if one practices for many kalpas, one is not called "born into the Buddha-family.
Therefore, he speaks of the wondrous lotus flower, which reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Those who cling to the marks of fruition and virtuous conduct cannot understand this;
because the gap between the ordinary and the sage is vast, they naturally conceive thoughts of superiority and inferiority.
Only through the Zen of our ancestral teachers Is awakening and entry expected;
That which the vehicles of teaching cannot encompass, Yet can encompass within those very teachings, Transcends the measure of the dharma-realm And stands far apart from words and concepts.
The three thousand and seven hundred patriarchs Successively transmitted and received it one another, So that the lamp of the Dharma has never been extinguished.
Moving amidst those of different kinds, his head and horns stand out with brilliant clarity;

his coughs and the swinging of his arms respond to circumstances without equal—this is the long-standing excellence of our school. O wise ones, seeking wondrous awakening, be careful not to harbor any hesitation.
To Layman Jiang Yuechuan:
For one who wishes to transcend birth and death, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is foremost. That Buddha’s name is Amitābha;
he extensively made forty-eight great vows. If one can recite his name, one will certainly be reborn in peace.

Later, turning toward the Buddha, one reaches the place where Māra cannot go. One unravels the armor and spears of the Three Mysteries and shatters the banners and lances of the Five Ranks.

Within the black-lacquered bucket, one discerns countenances and distinguishes colors; beneath the shadowless tree, one whistles at the moon and chants with the wind. With every step taken from the very base of one’s feet, one meets Boshan face-to-face in his true essence.
If you have not yet attained such realization, you must not fail to chew these words of Chan warning thoroughly, one time after another.
Take up a single koan that is devoid of meaning; engage in a matter that is utterly groundless.
One day, when it suddenly bursts forth, your entire being will encompass the universe. If you seek even a single mark of a sentient being, it is entirely unobtainable.
What thing is in delusion? What person is in awakening? Layman, your long sighs with Boshan are all merely superfluous words. This poor monk sweeps them away.
On this single *kaṭhina* (seating mat) of ground, I have created an immovable pavilion for the lay devotee. I do not know how the lay devotee perceives it.
His Highness Prince Wang of Fanshan is of noble, natural lineage; having come to wander this Sahā world by the power of his vows, he guides all living beings.

However, as the oceans of practice unfold in successive layers, one must maintain the intention to benefit both self and others. Through mutual integration and penetration, one becomes in accord with the Dharma. Furthermore, the ultimate principle is profound and mysterious;

To thus perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas—how vast is its benefit! Your Highness is a person of transcendent capacity who has already entered the Secret Seal (*guhyamudrā*).
As for this samādhi, there is no need for this poor monk’s superfluous words. My humble disciple has returned bearing the precious gift of Your Highness’s letter;

I know that you share a karmic affinity from past lives. If the spring waters rise high, there is no harm in boarding a boat and dancing the oars toward the Dragon Pond at Boshan, playing as the occasion demands.
This poor monk has instructed his attendant to prepare incense in a separate steamer; let the waterbirds and the forest trees [be the witnesses].
To speak of the true nature (*dharmatā*) for Your Highness,
yet for Censor-in-Chief Chen Xitang his doubts do not arise—
this suggests his resolve regarding birth and death is not urgent, and thus it appears inconsistent with what was previously instructed. Is this truly so?
The urgency of birth and death is so profound that if these two characters—"Who is it?"—are not clarified, how can one avoid doubt?

When the spirit of doubt suddenly arises, even the functions of mind, intellect, and consciousness do not stir, let alone the paths of intellectual interpretation. Although the Pure Land is practiced concurrently, one must by no means harbor thoughts of self-sufficiency or thoughts of security;
these two are the great maladies of those who investigate the mind. Layman, you must know this. Once you have recognized this...
As for illness, I shall never tread upon these two paths. Did not the Patriarch say: "I swear I will not rest until I have struck down this dark-skinned slave"?
Since he was already a great man, why should I not be so? These two characters—"Is it? (*shì shuí*)—are the sharp axe that severs the mind, intellect, and consciousness;

they are the wall that cuts through the path of worldly ways; they are the essential ford for escaping birth and death. To investigate this Dharma-gate of these two characters is like Han Xin [crossing the river].
Only by forming an array with one's back to the water, disregarding peril and ruin, can one finally achieve resonance.

Within this single lifetime, one must resolve the public case that has remained unresolved for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes. A person of wisdom should treat days as years; their body may freeze and their belly may hunger.
One must not allow the *huatou* (critical phrase) to have any interruption; one need only shatter the mass of doubt.

When the mind, consciousness, and intellect, along with all paths of intellectual understanding, melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress, only then will one attain great peace and bliss. Such a person has gained a benefit a hundred thousand million times greater than anything else—nothing could possibly compare to it. How is this?
Furthermore, regarding the gathering of lay practitioners (with an appended letter of invitation):

Throughout the ages, there have been periods of prosperity and decline; yet, regarding the extensive offerings at Buddhist assemblies and the compilation of the Chan school’s records, it was through these means that the compassionate intent of the kings who entrusted [the Dharma] was not betrayed.

This began with our late Emperor Ming and the Second Patriarch, and at that time, figures such as the Hanlin Academician Shen and the Court Gentleman Huang—who were among those who followed the dragon [to serve the dynasty]—all resolutely took up this task.
To take up the great protection [of the Dharma] as one’s own responsibility is a precedent that can be found in the historical records of Jianye.

For this reason, the drum of poison has not resounded, and many have perished from afar within the imperial capital. The Wheel of the Dharma has not turned, for both king and ministers have for half their lives belonged to the capacity of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Yet the Upādhyāya is the teacher of the entire nation and the eye of devas and humans; yet for thirty years past, it was as if he were about to...

as an old man emerging from the mountains, I utterly lack the bearing of a true man of spirit. Though a sharp blade is swift, it does not strike the innocent.

For a hundred years, this magnificent undertaking has been neglected. How is this different from a skilled butcher joyfully beholding a fat sacrificial beast?

For two years, I have been exhausted by the task of ferrying others across; it is like a frail man gazing longingly at a massive cauldron. Furthermore, the reputation of Fushan’s two paths has already reached us, and those in charge fear they will be too late to follow.
This year, I shall certainly not leave the mountain. These words were spoken previously, yet my intention is now to fulfill them. Should...

Behold this physical body of the four elements as being like an illusion or a conjuration; when the single breath does not return, what ultimate purpose will it serve?
This is the most urgent matter for us. If one does not attend to it with urgency, then beyond mere warmth and satiety, everything is for others.

It is busy. Even securing mere warmth and fullness is an extraordinary matter; how much more so other concerns? I hope that you, Layman Hui-fa, will respond to the occasion with wisdom and allow no moment’s rest.
Regarding the single phrase: "When this one breath does not return, after all, where will one go?"

If you find the proper place and broaden your compassionate vows, this is the ultimate hope of this poor monk.

A sick person should first realize that this body is entirely composed of provisional conditions and lacks any real master; it is like a dream and like an illusion. Thus, the illness can be cured of itself.
This is because [the body] exists due to karma; karma arises from delusion; delusion arises from the mind; and the mind is itself unborn (*anutpanna*). Where, then, can the illness take refuge?
If one contemplates this truth throughout the twelve periods of the day, the illness will not require medicine to be resolved.

This is self-healing. One who nourishes [the mind] well does not perceive the existence of a body, nor do they see the existence of a world. When encountering objects or meeting conditions, they are like wood or stone.
One should simply observe that which existed before one’s parents were born: what is this original face of mine?
Taking this single phrase as a *huatou*, examine it with earnest persistence; do not allow a second thought to arise. This is called skillful cultivation and treatment.

like a wind sweeping away dust, not even a trace remains. If, however, one attempts to grasp it within the realm of existence and non-existence, it is no different from feeling for something in empty space while debating its size.
Is it a matter of distance from the Yang? "Having horns but no whiskers"—this is a translation of two types of speech. Zhaozhou’s two-layered public case can be seen by reflecting upon it;

The second question states: "If the essence of wondrous clarity is exhausted, one falls directly into a state of inert emptiness. This is because the layman has misunderstood the essential meaning of the fundamental principle (*gangzong*).

To know existence is like the speech of one asleep; how could such a person recognize its source? This is precisely the lifeblood of Caodong.
It is like holding a numinous pearl in one's palm, or like a mute man eating honey—the heart and mouth are both sweet.
I cannot reveal this to others. If one were to explain it using "stolid emptiness" (*wankong*), it would truly be a case of black and white being diametrically opposed.

whether you can attain liberation amidst the conditions of worldly truth; and whether wealth, beauty, fame, and profit can move your mind.

Then you will have missed a timely opportunity; the Great Principle will remain obscure. Would you truly wish to follow along with external conditions and act as a foolish person?
However, in investigating this single thought-moment, one must rely on the assistance of karmic merit and favorable conditions.

In practicing these deeds, whenever one cultivates a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), it is only the Triple Gem that is most supreme;
therefore, it cannot be compared to other gates of goodness. Recently, there has been a class of people who merely say, "Practicing goodness need not be restricted solely to the Buddhist gate.

Let these words of Zen warning serve as a talisman to spur yourself on, distancing you from all transgressions and aspiring toward great enlightenment. With carriages and horses thronging together and the people leaping like scales, there is no need for a response beyond the conventional; what is most joyful is to find it amidst the dust of the world.

Nevertheless, this Great Chapter may be circulated without hindrance; it serves as an eye-opening medicine for all people under heaven. It is not mere text.

Regarding the inquiries made by Yu Rong and Zi Xun regarding the fundamental tenets of the Cao-Dong school: this study is most wondrous and most profound, like drawing a fine gold needle from its socket.

I am determined to clarify and illuminate this matter; it would not be improper to assist it with manifold virtues, just as rain and dew nourish the auspicious sprouts.
This is my hope for you and your brothers.

That you, my noble brother, have deeply entered the path of the Dharma and been born into this virtuous family is no small matter; it is all obtained through the power of vows made over many lifetimes, taking the Dharma as one’s kin.
What is valued is that the mind is as suchness and the environment is as suchness. As for the mind being as suchness, there is no environment outside the mind.
As for the environment being as suchness, there is no mind outside the environment. Abiding in the world as if in empty space, like a lotus flower unsullied by water—only then...
One might say that one dwells in the dust yet transcends the dust, and engages with phenomena yet remains detached from them;

however, if this were not so, one would be no different from those who abide in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). Do you brothers not recognize this? This matter must be verified within the context of actual circumstances.
If one remains idle and free from affairs, claiming that one does not see worldly dharmas engaging the mind, this is called self-deception; it cannot be otherwise.
Examine truth and falsehood. Whenever you encounter circumstances, thoughts will arise; do not attempt to suppress the mind with the mind.
Simply maintain the original *huatou* (critical phrase) of your inquiry, and it will naturally dissolve like ice melting or a fortress crumbling, without expending even a fraction of effort.
Even if you experience a great awakening, do not immediately claim it to be the "gate of enlightenment. In our Dharma, there is no greater fault than regarding awakening as non-awakening.
Only those who have not attained awakening yet claim to have attained it commit the great falsehood of *mahā-mṛṣāvāda*. You, my brother, already understand this deeply;
it seems you do not require the redundant words of this poor monk. If one has awakened but does not claim to have awakened, one will certainly never again fall into delusion.
If one has not awakened yet claims to have awakened, one will certainly regress and fall. You may see this clearly by carefully reading the *Recorded Sayings of Gaofeng* and Dahui’s reply letter.

Furthermore, there are masters of the Way who are preeminent in the Great Learning and whose understanding of the Dao is profound and deep; yet those who secretly investigate its mysteries—I have seen such a person in you, Layman.

Your letter states: "I deeply admonish myself; I dare not deceive myself, nor do I dare to yield to myself. These three phrases are most pleasing to my humble mind.
If you truly apply your mind in this way, earnestly maintaining the *huatou* of your primary inquiry, you will certainly reach the level of the ancients.
This field of practice—though you have not yet attained the gate of great enlightenment—is precisely the foundation for becoming a Buddha or an Ancestor.
It is like planting grain: if one plows it and weeds it, how could it fail to ripen and yield a harvest? Layman, believe this deeply and with full conviction.

Do not harbor doubt or hesitation. Suddenly, by chance, when you strike against or collide with something, you will finally realize that rice is made from grain; thereafter, you will no longer run about seeking it elsewhere.

However, the depth of one’s capacity cannot be generalized by comparing it to the gateways of awakening (*bodhimukha*). I have recorded one chapter of the preface here, praising it with all my might.

Why is this? Because it is all the mind of the six consciousnesses. The essential point lies in adding 'more earnest' to what is already earnest. It is like losing a precious treasure and being determined to recover it; how could it be merely a matter of reading books?"
Amidst all circumstances and conditions, one neither lets go nor pursues. Why is this? It is because this single thought-moment is heavy.
When Lord Zhao Qingxian was still a youth in scholar’s robes, he began his investigation; upon reaching the rank of official, he attained great enlightenment upon hearing the sound of thunder.

This concerns not only your parents of this single lifetime, but all parents—both those who gave birth to you and those you gave birth to—throughout hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes.
They shall all receive the benefits of this Dharma. Compared to worldly filial piety, this is more than a difference between heaven and earth.
Furthermore, you should encourage your mother to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name, so that she may eliminate the karmic burdens of many lifetimes and serve as a bridge for the present life.

In doing so, you, Layman, will achieve both worldly and world-transcending forms of filial piety. Written hastily amidst busy affairs, I respectfully offer this reply. Other matters await further opportunity.
Wu! It is not that I have failed you.

Within the scriptural teachings, one is not without careful attention; it is known that [the mind] functions within the sphere of consciousness and perception. As a sutra says:

It is like the sun shining in the sky while a child closes his eyes and says, "Why can I not see it? So it is with much learning:

one knows that the more knowledge and understanding one has, not only does one fail to realize the Way, but such knowledge actually becomes a condition that obstructs the Way. Consequently, he shook out his sleeves and departed to seek instruction elsewhere.

Later, for another six years upon the "Fishing Boat" kōan, I finally attained a fleeting glimpse.

To wish to employ this mind by using the mind is something that would not only take a single lifetime, but even through kalpas upon kalpas, one might seem unable to complete it. Why is this? Because of the very mind that is capable of stillness and capable of illumination.
Because it is the root. Furthermore, since no thoughts or deliberations arise from this mind, its fundamental substance is revealed alone; how could one wait for even a brief moment?
Even if one were to remain entirely without thought from birth until old age, has the root of this very thought ever flickered even once?

It is similar; even within the primary substance (*dharmatā*), there is no mutual interaction, let alone during the intervals of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) and meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

that is, within the field of the eight consciousnesses, you have identified [the mind] as the fundamental essence. Therefore it is said: "Vague and dim, as if walking in the shadow of a lamp.
This is my sincere confession, not a falsehood. Last year, while sitting in the shade of pines with your honorable younger brother, we heard the calls of birds and discussed this in the hall.

If you had truly reached the stage of non-doubt, you would have attained practical utility at that very moment; why wait until after an illness?
