Setting aside the matter of finding a middle way for now, worthy brother, do you still recognize it? You must simply be the Buddha within your daily activities, yet you must also spit it out.
Xinghua said: "I have never scattered real pearls from within a purple silk curtain for you people. Why do you shout and clamor so recklessly? If you do not [act thus]...

To pass through and descend from within a purple silk curtain inevitably invites the censure of "confusing red with purple"; it is not a phrase that captures the vital power of the Gate of the Patriarchs.
He further applied his mind, saying: "When there is no activity, one need not fear a lack of clarity; one only needs to guard against the arising of discursive thoughts.
If one knows that a single thought arises through conditions yet is unborn, it is immediately transformed. This is taking "arising through conditions yet being unborn" as the means of transformation.
"Regarding 'thoughts and deliberations' (niàn-lǜ): can such talk as this be tolerated within the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zōngmén)? Who shall receive the thirty blows? It is further said:
'When responding to objects, one does not fear the arising of thoughts and deliberations; one only fears a lack of clarity.

When there is clarity, there are thoughts and deliberations, yet there is also manifest illumination. This, again, uses clarity to remedy thoughts and deliberations. Can the Gate of the Patriarchs tolerate such things?"
"If one speaks, who shall eat the thirty blows? It is also said: "The fundamental substance is inherently present; it is illumination within stillness.
Within the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), can such talk as this be tolerated? "Who shall eat the thirty blows? This is merely the grandmotherly tongue of the Teaching School (Jiaojia);
it is not the Gate of Awakening (Wumen). It is also said: "There is no need for effort," and again: "Thus one protects [it]."
Ren said: "Do not forget, do not assist. All such [injunctions] are but inverted and conceptualizing minds;
they are not true investigation. This is what was previously explained to you, my worthy brother: it is merely "as if" (似), not the reality. Even this word "as if" is itself a skillful expedient.

This is for the sake of consolation. If it were truly so, one would not need to wait for this kind of realization; as soon as one moves, one is liberated, and as soon as one presses down, one turns away from delusion.
There is no need to cite scriptures or teachings, for doing so only leads further and further away and is irrelevant. Why is this?

It is because you have never engaged in genuine investigation from the beginning, but instead have used a mind of intellectual understanding to seal everything. This is precisely what is meant by "mistaking a servant for a master" or "mistaking a thief for a son."
An ancient worthy said: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know 'there is'; the tabby cat and the white ox, however, do know 'there is.
A monk asked Jiufeng, "What is the head? He replied, "One need only know that there is. The monk pressed further, "What is the tail? He replied, "Exhausting the present moment.
These two characters, "knowing that there is," are by no means a matter of intellectual speculation or conceptual consciousness; they take one's daily activities as "knowing that there is."
Yes. I once remarked: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know its existence; they scoop up the bright moon atop the shadowless tree.
Yet the cat and the white ox do know its existence; they shear the white clouds within the valleys where no response is due. Who can understand this meaning?

Aside from this "one who knows there is," what is the same and what is different? Furthermore, it is said that among the words and phrases of the Zen school, not a single one of these strange and wondrous expressions is anything other than a means to cause people to know this matter. Look only at the point where your worthy brother has attained realization.
If you were to form such conceptual understandings, the Zen school would be swept away and utterly destroyed. As for the two characters "knowing there is," when have you ever even dreamed of them?
Indeed! If you simply have this realization, my worthy brother, you may apply your mind directly to see through to the profound and hidden depths of the ancients.
Therefore it is said: "If you wish to know this matter, you must stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk upon the bottom of the deepest sea;
turn your body beyond the limit of Vipaśyin, and sleep soundly at the crossroads. Furthermore, you must experience the profuse flow of cold sweat.

Only by undergoing the "whipping of the staff" can one attain it. Otherwise, though one may maintain that illumination is stillness and stillness is illumination, guarding this state all day long and never giving rise to a single thought—remaining uninvolved with the mind and the mind uninvolved with phenomena—even to fully comprehend this intent does not yet constitute a true realization.
With you, Zen practitioner Shan-lai, we have been separated by three thousand li for twelve hours. You have wandered all over China; what is the point of this treading of your own heels?
The moment you entered the gate, I already knew you. Running east and west, colliding with everything—what do you hope to achieve? If it were...

A man with blood beneath his skin will naturally choose a master of the fundamental school for twenty or thirty years, carrying firewood, drawing water, tilling the soil, and digging the earth—not considering these tasks beyond his duty. Nowadays, there is a certain class of false teachers who bewitch the men and women of families;
as soon as they open their mouths, they say, "What Chan is there to investigate? What practice or effort is there?"
It can be done. To directly take it up is already eight *ke* (two hours) too late. For this reason, it is called "swift and nimble," "heroic spirit," "natural," and "transcendent.
Since one does not apply the mind to one's own fundamental share (*fen*), those traces of karmic consciousness (*ye-shi*) cannot be worn away.
Having consumed the food provided by the donors, one merely studies poetry, studies characters, studies ancient verses, and studies [the records of] the ancients.

To reveal and instruct: even if one manages to master verbal facility—to surpass Li Bai and Du Fu in poetry, to outshine Zhong Yao and Wang Xizhi in calligraphy, to produce ancient verses like rising clouds, and to deliver instructions like pouring from a jar—it is merely called the activity-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) in its vast confusion.

Even if one succeeds in deceiving others so that they believe, take refuge, prostrate, and make offerings, it only serves to adorn a single leather bag. When this bag collapses in a single day, the hands—
In a state of frantic confusion, the Lord King Yama will not let him pass.

In the boiling cauldrons, the glowing coals, the sword-trees, and the knife-mountains, he shall have no end to his days for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes. Even when he emerges from there, one knows not how many more kalpas remain.
With the eye of purity, observe such false spiritual friends as they are: like worms in a latrine, or like thorns upon clean ground.
A stinking crow in the clear breeze; it is also called a person without shame, a person without integrity. Do you know this yet? Can you discern this yet?
If you possess the eye of a student of the Way, you will be able to distinguish the true from the false right here.
Then you may well shake out a few ribs beneath your patched robe. This conglomeration of the four elements—just so, beat those two pieces of skin!
You may be able to lecture and speak eloquently, but when the breath ceases for a moment, where will you go? Do not rest content merely by taking up this matter;
do not seek to verify it through the scriptures; do not let yourself be led away by good or evil karma;
and do not claim that the entirety of the ten directions is simply this self, fundamentally without coming or going. If you hold such a view—
"In the future, you will surely have your share of drinking molten copper and swallowing hot iron.
Since this is not the case, how else can one attain what is appropriate? When the single breath does not come again, where will you ultimately go?
It is as if sitting amidst silver mountains and iron walls, seeking only to burst through them; can a second thought possibly arise there? Can it be tolerated?"
If you are still engaging in conceptual thought and discrimination, you have not yet reached such a state. At this point, you need only let out a single shout of "Hūṃ!
and perform a somersault beyond the realm of Vipaśyin and even further than that; only then may you come here to Mount Boshan to receive my severe blows.
Otherwise, you had better go among the thousands of crags and myriad valleys to gather firewood and pass your days—this has nothing at all to do with me, the old monk.
Matter. The verse says: Those who study the Way are as numerous as cow hairs; those who achieve enlightenment are like the horns of a rabbit.
Everyone delights in what is easy and plain; who would be willing to peer into the mountain peaks? The accumulated emerald greens and the layered cliffs are ultimately difficult to depict.

With conventional names and clever phrases, emotional thoughts perversely engage in carving and boring. Upon encountering the Black-Faced Old Man, one cannot avoid being subjected to his stripping away. A man of will and resolve should seize the moment.
One must awaken early and break through the barrier of birth and death; only then can one be called a master of ultimate learning.
*The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi*, Volume Thirty;
*The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi*, Volume Thirty-One.
Compiled by the Dharma-grandson of Boshan, Honghan;
and jointly assembled by the Dharma-grandson of the Head Seat, Hongyu. Opening Preface.

Furthermore, what humble growth could compare to the Great Minister of Justice, who planted his grass to communicate his sincerity? The entire earth is without fault; the fragrant dust of the southern ridges connects [to this land], yet the Central Heaven alone yields precedence to Minnan.
This inscription records the name of the Buddha’s land. From of old there has been this lineage, continuing the flame of the ancestral lamp so that its light extends infinitely.

We respectfully acknowledge Your Excellency, who has revealed the pearl within his robe and once again donned the mirror of wisdom. Appearing as a high official, you serve as a leader; acting as a lord of the land, you protect the golden ramparts.
You are as alert as a peacock at the sound of thunder and as unstartled as a tiger. Who could surpass you when entering the gates of Yang and Li? This stele text is inscribed in white.
I, [Name], venture to say that when Ciming paid his visit, he was planting pine trees along the path and playing with a spiritual serpent on the snowy ridge;

listening to the deep waters of Yanxi, he captured them alive, making no distinction between monk and layman. When the fruit ripens and its fragrance wafts, the holy and the mundane are of one measure.

Having hung my staff in the mountain crags, I have not followed worldly sentiments in polishing my waxed sandals; now that I am sailing upon the mountains and waters, I feel ashamed to wipe away tears at the mud-sealed gate. Haste! Haste!
Having crossed the ridges to plan for the monastic grove, I venture to board the boat to ascend the patriarch’s seat. I now decline your lofty courtesy and hope you will examine my humble sentiments.
Again, Zhang Zhongcheng.
The jewel trees emit smoke, perfuming the fragrance of the precepts across the fields; the gate of compassion reflects back, beautifying the sun of wisdom in the midst of heaven.

Relying upon a singular heart of supreme pity, you celebrate the power of vows from many lifetimes. We respectfully venerate you,阁下 (Your Excellency): entrusted with the sacred Mount Ling-shan, you encompass the mundane world;
smelling the osmanthus, you leave nothing hidden, while Hui-tang’s “living word” startles the world. Through the realization that things are fully known, you have attained awakening.

The wondrous and subtle words of [Amitābha] remain in our ears. Since it was so in antiquity, why should it not be so now? To penetrate the causes and conditions of ten thousand kalpas and accomplish the Buddha-work of a single moment;
to churn the milk and cream of the long river and restore it to the pure Brahma-heavenly beings; to transform the great earth into gold.
I, [Name], am merely concerned with securing warmth and food; I know nothing of the affairs of the mountain gate.

Having long since severed ties with the world, I find great satisfaction in the mist and clouds beyond the mundane realm. Recently, having received your gracious letter, I have been hesitant and perplexed regarding my conduct;
I regret that I lack the leisure for further delay, as I truly find myself at variance with your command.

Furthermore, Huang Xiaolian’s blessed ground, Zhulin, relies upon the gentry to flourish as a jewel-like society; the Buddhist land of Quannan depends upon both clergy and laity to fan the breeze of compassion.
To manifest the True Vehicle within the *ārāma* and to bind together vows for Bodhi—our humble thoughts reach you, Honorable Minister, who stands as a keystone pillar for the Confucian gate.
The Dharma moat serves as a golden fortress; the eminent monks are displayed high upon the wall, while the worldly eyes are but specks of dust within it.

A single call receives an immediate response—there has always been someone within the sound. A second offense will not be tolerated—who among those wearing robes lacks the treasure? He drives the three chariots to entice his children.

Reining in the white ox, he employs the four means of integration to transform beings into a single stream. Raising high the crimson banner, the elephant and dragon trample on; the ordinary and the sage are harmoniously unified.

(I, so-and-so), have long been enamored with hills and valleys and am unacquainted with the marketplace. Stubbornly, I have only gathered withered firewood; flickering, it is difficult to tame the wild horse.
The time to cross the ridge has already been fixed; the staff that shakes the void shall not turn back. To go against your compassionate command—this is my communication.
Perspiration flows from the body.
Furthermore, golden cords demarcate the paths; lotuses bloom in ponds of eight virtues; jeweled nets radiate light; and the music of joy resounds through the sevenfold rows of trees.

The Confucian and Buddhist traditions flourish together in this Buddha-land; humans and devas mingle within this grove of pearls. We respectfully consider your station: with half a verse, you attained the emptiness of mind; through the convergence of three lifetimes, you met your karmic conditions.

Having awakened to the Way upon hearing a clap of thunder, what prevents you from embracing your children and grandchildren? Transmitting the mind by pointing at snow, it does not hinder the marriage of sons and daughters.
To engage with phenomena while remaining detached from them, to dwell amidst the dust of the world while transcending it—you summon the goose from within the jar and release [the wild geese].
A crane among the clouds, I am accustomed to a diet of mugwort soup. At times I doubt the Sanskrit script; hearing the warbling of the oriole, I am ashamed of my own speech;
receiving your elegant letter, I feel deeply embarrassed. I hope you will forgive my singular ignorance and spare me the trouble of further verbal elaboration.
Furthermore, it is clarified that the mirror is not the stand; it reflects clearly through the state of no-mind. Bodhi has its seeds, which truly sprout through sincere faith.

Relying on the golden ropes of the power of vows, one moves the pivot and serves as a protective bulwark. I respectfully consider that beneath your station, the source of spiritual power is pure and bright, and the tree of the Way...
In full bloom, the entire Dharma-realm is gathered within the tip of a hair; with a single thread of silk upon the palm, the profound non-duality is expounded.

One must know that the Golden Grain has returned; as the great trichiliocosm is gathered together, we joyfully behold the *tāmarasa* flower manifest once more. Branch after branch of coral bears the moonlight.
My practice has been like a balustrade reaching into the clouds, treading upon the fragrant dust of past sages. I have penetrated the jewel-treasury for the sake of the deluded masses;

having cast myself at the Deer Park, I have unworthily received the precepts of a "wax-man. Entrusting my traces to the gate of Chan, I am ashamed that the lamp was transmitted from the Patriarchal Ancestor.

Hastening to turn my staff, I am startled by my own tardiness; how could I dare to cling to conditions and respond to this summons? As I take up the brush, I tremble with awe, finding no leisure for abiding ease.

Furthermore, the Great Layman Chen, a preeminent minister of the Heavenly King and a Bodhisattva official, has sealed the True Vehicle of Vaiśālī; his subtle realization accords perfectly with its refined traditions, and he follows in the footsteps of Taiqiu’s virtuous achievements, vying for eminence as a peerless arbiter of character.
With the weight of his rank and the prestige of his banner, he commands the respect of the provincial governors along the Yangtze. Screened—

His literary achievements are as eminent as those in the *Dharmayāna*, and his investigations into the patriarchal lamp occupy half the registers. Among the monks, most are the "scales and dragons" of the Min Sea; he has grasped a single shaft of the holy arrows.
You, sir, have truly acted as the ramparts and moats for the city of Gumsan, reviving the dharma-lineage of Master Yan.

All may awaken to the Chan that does not cross the Stone Gate; you have pulled back the numinous wind of Xueqiao, joyfully beholding once more the excellence of the "drinking water" of former times. Treading [upon this path]...

A divine steed treads upon a fierce tiger; how could one seek only the clamor of a bustling courtyard? To beat the Dharma drum and erect the banner of compassion, what is prized is the leaping of dragons and elephants.
This poor monk has not yet beheld the clear radiance, yet first looks up to the stars and clouds.

Such is the nature of things. I think of Zishao’s verse on the sound of frogs under a moonlit night: "I have nothing hidden. I rejoice in Huangbo hearing the fragrance of the osmanthus; I receive deeply your [kind] guidance.

Jian: I still look forward to the occasion of drawing near to your robes. Although your transmission of the Dharma to Minnan does not emulate the "back-touching" or "front-touching" dialogue regarding the bamboo whisk, you have found a connoisseur in the Grand Tutor.
As for the karmic conditions concerning overturning the tea kettle, though it may be late for us to clasp arms together, my spirit is not far from you.
Furthermore, the lay practitioner Huang Xingyuan and others (2) envied Huangmei for carrying the mortar;

they marveled that his wondrous realization was that the mind is neither the stand nor the tree. They laughed at Jingu [Zhiyi] for wearing his hair, seeing him as one who transcended the mundane world with a refined character.

He demonstrated how one can dwell in a household while practicing the Brahma-conduct, and how one can discourse on the Truth without destroying the conventional. Whether it be "no questioning" or "muddying the earth," all are...

One may produce the petals of a blue lotus; there is no distinction between brass and stone, for all are materials for gilding gold. One polishes the jewel of the precepts amidst the five turbidities—this water can indeed be made clear.
One hastens toward the path of goodness through the eight prohibitions; all sentient beings are Buddhas. The marvel lies in turning one's head to reach the shore;

it is not hindered by returning home along the very road one travels. Carrying staff and wooden block, one wanders through the marketplace; meeting the occasion, one performs the play. One merely inserts a stalk of grass.
To establish a monastery is like blowing fire with the wind. When Gan-zhi prepared an offering, Nanquan smashed the rice-pot;
when Pang Gong was struck down, Lingzhao fell over from the side. To speak words of non-arising while sitting in a circle requires a true adept.
To pick up a priceless jewel from a heap of refuse belongs to a hero. It is my hope that you lay practitioners will, with a free hand, pull back your robes.
The inner treasure: lift your head and recognize the person within the house. Not only do you possess the stone drums and golden ramparts, but you also understand the holy arrow of Master Yan.
The blue waters flow backward; with one shout, the trust of those years is verified. Having found the path through the azure clouds, all worthy gentlemen here shall ascend to the heavens.

A numinous mind makes the flowers beneath the brush flourish; a refined countenance grasps the purple peaks at their tips. These startling, living phrases have descended from the piercing of the holy arrow;
these ears-tipting sounds of Dharma flow forth amidst words as clear as melting ice. The archetypes of the past are not yet distant, and for the heroes of today, there is no difficulty.
Strength lies in taking up the burden; the Way is found in personal practice. Moreover, the Eight Min Regions excel in this regard.

In this land of heroic talent and refined character, there have been those who vie in praise of the *Shujing* (Tiger Histories) and the *Lunjing* (Qilin Classics). Throughout the successive generations of the Patriarchs who have maintained the lamp illuminating the world, there has never been a lack of monks who provide profound exegesis as treasures of the Sangha.

Our meeting with the Dharma is like the meeting of a needle and its eye; the flourishing of the Dharma relies upon it as a golden rampart and moat. I prostrate myself and pray: [The remainder of the prayer follows.]
The jewel within his robes shines brilliantly; the Dharma-eye beneath his brows suddenly opens. The precious mirror hangs high, illuminating the true light within without obscuration.

If you do not fail the appointment at this famous mountain, you shall directly stride like a wild crane soaring into the void. I still hope to behold your extraordinary radiance, though for now I must bid farewell with these words as swift as a soaring wild goose.
Though the streams and mountains differ, the clouds and moon are the same. With these eight lines of respectful writing, I decline your offer of the seat on the left.
Furthermore, the lay practitioner Xu Liuyue of Weiguo (Appended: A Letter of Invitation).

I humbly consider that the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle has been upheld as the sole transmission throughout China. May the ancient capital within a thousand *li* deign to hear the resonant sound of the gavel being struck.
I venture to present this short letter to convey my innermost thoughts from afar. I reflect reverently upon the Great Master Wuxi of the Five Indias...
He ascends to the heavens; a single flower distinguishes his uniqueness. With a compassionate heart he saves the world, manifesting in the forms of a bhikṣu and a bodhisattva.
With the Buddha’s hand he heals humanity, acting as a master of vast edification. Every person relies on him as a protector, and everywhere he is depended upon as a bridge across the stream.

The Dharma assembly towers over the Western River; its fundamental tenet, "Mind is Buddha," resounds throughout the East. Your illustrious name rings out across the land, and those who take refuge in you fill both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

(Hongji) I am ashamed that I have fallen into the dust and vapors of the world; I long to hear your voice. Yet, considering the vast distance between our borders, my sincere devotion remains stifled and distressed.
I prostrate myself before this auspicious connection; how could I dare to be late in seeking your protection? Recently, due to the local magistrate...
The official layman [Hongji], rubbing his eyes and shaking his staff, has humbly employed the brush of Mao Ying to bow his head and offer these words:
I pray that you will come southward upon a single boat; the treasury of the True Dharma Eye must surely be transmitted.

Looking westward from the twin banners, the roar of the golden-haired lion is certainly not from another. (Hongji), as I prepare to send this letter, how can I overcome my longing and yearning? In the second month of spring.
On the first day of the month, Hongji again prostrated himself with his head to the ground.

He humbly reflects that the Celestial King’s eminent ministers possess a reputation for meritorious service that outweighs that of the eight barbarian tribes, while the Bodhisattva retainers serve as a bulwark whose achievements surpass those of the Five Monasteries.
By unfolding the *Karunāpuṣpa* Sūtra, they propagate the Great Teaching; by beholding the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa, their sincere hearts are brought into harmony. At the Jetavana Grove...

It is not far off; our reliance upon the golden ramparts and moats is secure. We respectfully venerate you, the Great Layman, the Sixth Elder: with the talisman suspended from your elbow, you demonstrate dwelling amidst the dust without being defiled;

with the treasure revealed within your robes, you believe that the mundane is fundamentally identical to the True. You form a flourishing grove of compassion and radiate light across the ocean of enlightenment.
The *udumbara* flower has its seed; the Buddha’s illumination is impartial. Chasing the blind tortoise and whipping the lame turtle, you strive for the sake of the Dharma.
The Sea God’s Dragon plots to release a swift falcon and let loose a noble hawk; yet how could it be for the sake of a wild sparrow in the woods? Throughout the world, purple-gold light is emitted;
throughout the city, the fragrance of blue lotus petals is wafted. Not yielding to the profound models of the Golden Grain (Śākyamuni), we joyfully behold the Great Achievements of Your Excellency.
You illuminate the light of the mind within the five aggregates, practicing dhyāna amidst desire; you shake the ancestral Way at the four crossroads—what living being would not [rejoice]?
The Buddha’s flower-rain once again moistens Mount Zhong; his floating cup shall surely leap upon the riverbanks. His traces may be sought, for the conditions for the Dharma are near.
I respectfully compose these words of thanks, unable to fully express my devotion and reliance.
Furthermore, [I address] the various lay practitioners currently residing in the Southern Capital (attached is the invitation letter).

It is held that when ten thousand streams return to their source, the jade-like liquid serves as the essence of the entire tide; and when the five capitals arrange their markets, the golden balance becomes the sovereign of all stalls.
Thus, those who turn toward the summit must necessarily honor the King of the Dharma, while those who extend their hands [in compassion] regard the earth [as their field of action].
He likewise divined his victory. From afar, Xiangsong gazed with reverence; Kongxi looked on with joy. We respectfully contemplate the Great Master Wuyi:

clouds parting over kalpas past, dew moistening the present day. He continued the lamp of Caodong; through his compassion, he raised up all beings and universally tamed the nature of birds. He succeeded Shouchang’s bowl;
as the mirror of wisdom hung suspended, he suddenly uprooted the weeds from the human heart. Among guests, he is the host; within the host, [he is the master].
Guest: The eye of the patch-robed monk has undergone many transformations. "The ox is not an ox; the horse is not a horse. Even the mouth of an ancient Buddha finds it difficult to open here.
Where the mist retreats from the peaks of Chu, the Qilin rests within the Flower World; where the frost clears over the waters of Rao, the Lion roams and manifests the Golden Lamp.
The banner flutters across the field of those who aspire to transformation; the rain falls upon the seeds that hear the sound.
With its tip leaning upon the jeweled canopy, it now resides in Jinling. The Way-drum has long resounded like a deep thunderclap, fortunately protected by the Great August Emperor;
the lamp of righteousness shines ever bright through the thin night, commemorating the distant arrival of the First Patriarch.
Yet, as the skin and marrow are difficult to distinguish, who shall brandish the "blowing-hair" sword? As the elephant and oxen jostle together, how can one regulate the imperial chariot?
From two thousand *li* away, we contemplate the Buddha-sun rising once more; a million people gaze in hope for the rare appearance of the *udumbara* flower.

(We, the undersigned), while our red karmic ties remain intense and our dark obstructions have not yet vanished, prostrate ourselves in homage to Your Majesty’s grace and grasp a single fly-whisk to pledge our hearts to the Buddha’s entrustment.
For this reason, we have prepared offerings of flowers and water, arranged our mats and seats, and come from afar to welcome you.
This subtle and wondrous hall is a realm first purified and adorned. As a thousand clouds pay homage to the seat, the peaks of Wu may rival the Twin Śāla Trees.
When one sage responds to the occasion, the waters of the Huai River together become the five flavors. How can we, [Name et al.], bear not lifting our heads in anticipation?
We respectfully submit this letter on the first day of the second lunar month. Disciples protecting the Dharma: Ren Zhen, Zhu Kui, Yuan Kai, and Wang Yong.
Ji Chengce, Yan’er Gui, Pang Chengchong, Cao Yingqiu, Zeng Hualong, Chen Yuanmou, Wang Weixin,
Zhou Guangxia, Wu Guomo, Lin Yuyu, and Zhou Yunzhong, etc., again prostrate themselves.

I humbly submit that on Vulture Peak, the Great Minister alone excelled in receiving the final entrustment; and as the lineage branched out from Eagle’s Peak, many renowned scholars were recorded in the *Lamp of the Dharma*.
Like a seal impression appearing upon the surface of the water, they awakened the elders within this realm, widely propagating these sublime tracks.

Erecting the wondrous banner on high, I respectfully address the esteemed members of the assembly of Great Laymen (Mahā-upāsaka). Your minds harbor the principles of governance and statecraft; you have directly ascended to the celestial palace of the Heavenly King.
Gazing upon your towering pillars and bedrock-like stability, may you not forget the great causal conditions (*nidāna*). Without relying on the divine blade, the clouds manifest in five colors;
without beating the poisonous drum, the heavens rain down fourfold flowers. At the mere touch of a fingertip, one encounters the Master everywhere; passing through the City of Transformation...

As one proceeds toward the site of the Jewel, ten thousand realms shine with the splendor of a flourishing era; the monasteries of distant lands reflect its radiance, and all living beings are bathed in the grace of its cultivation.
At ancient shrines, clouds of incense form colorful canopies. While the sounds of the Dharma have not yet spread far, the Way of the Patriarchs flourishes here.
If you should follow conditions by taking up your staff, let the flower in your flask serve as a silent messenger. Though the streams and mountains differ, the clouds and moon remain the same.
This is the same. We respectfully request that you accept these eight lines of verse and decline the seat to your left.
Furthermore, we address the assembly of local gentry and lay practitioners of the Southern Capital (attached is the invitation).

We humbly observe that as the *Avataṃsaka* flowers part like rain, they spread across the ocean’s droplets to provide a vast exegesis; as the numinous leaves fill the heavens, the wondrous sun shines forth its radiance.

Yet, as for universal virtue: may the whale-bell and tortoise-drum resound greatly through the celestial thoroughfares; may the jeweled raft and golden ropes surely gallop high upon the solar carriage.
Do not lament that the path to enlightenment is not broad, nor feel sorrow for the sages of former awakening.
I secretly grieve that there are none to protect the Dharma, and that those who inquire after the Dharma are easily obstructed. To the left of the Yangtze and to the right of the Xiang...
Together we board this wondrous and pure vessel; here there is neither kin nor stranger.

As the broad and long tongue manifests, those who offer their devotion with uplifted sincerity occupy half of the *pūrṇākṣara* (the full syllable), while those who receive it face-to-face propagate the causes for the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
With all our hearts we reverently proclaim our faith, accumulating red offerings and taking refuge. We respectfully venerate Master Boshan, whose marrow flows from the Cao-Dong lineage.
The needle was applied to the crown of the head; the eight flavors of Lake Anavatapta were poured forth across many regions. The moon of precepts clarified this land through the three emptinesses.
From time immemorial, the flower was plucked and offered; pointing at the cypress tree, it was all entrusted to the novice Mokṣa. In the ordinary view, one sees only the trap for tigers.
He tames the wild monkeys and pierces the nostrils of those who struggle in the mud; his brandishing of the blade is like the moon, such that his numinous staff could fly.

it is like turning a mirror upside down and seeking its reflection. How utterly ignorant this is! Indeed, our Śākyamuni Buddha does not speak falsely.

Regarding "not speaking otherwise": The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that if one recites the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction for as long as seven days, one will immediately attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that if a person, even with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and once utters "Namo Buddha," they shall all together attain the Buddha-way.
These words reveal his heart and soul, showing his thoroughgoing concern for others. This is what he meant.
If you do not believe this, who can be trusted? These words are trustworthy; why then doubt the gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) in the Pure Land?
To speak briefly: what kind of mind is it that remains undistracted for seven days? And what kind of mind is it when one enters a stupa or temple and chants "Namu Butsu"?
Those capable will attain it. The Way of Chan is simply this. If this is the true teacher [of the Way].
A single roar from a lion causes the heads of all beasts to split asunder. One may speak of the Pure Land, and one may also speak of Chan.
It is permissible to say that the Pure Land is Chan, and that Chan is the Pure Land. It is permissible for both to be affirmed, and it is permissible for both to be negated.

Throughout the day, though one recites, there is never anything being recited; throughout the day, though one gives rise [to thoughts], there is never anything being produced. Throughout the day, while being without thought, it does not hinder one from speaking of thought. Throughout the day...
Non-arising does not preclude speaking of arising; it is perfectly round like a mani jewel. If one seeks its place of abiding, it is utterly unfindable.
What "meditation" and what "pure land" are there to bifurcate? Nevertheless, there is yet one further phrase: Amitābha.
I have never spoken of it before; I wish to exhaust my feelings and reveal it all, yet alas, my tongue is too short. Alas! This lightning-fast mechanism is reserved for the wise.
Preface to the *Hongshi Lu* of Jianzhou.
When I was serving as the "Crow-Scaring Official" (Quwu), I once traveled through Min Province. I learned that Jianzhou was a reservoir for the School of Principle (Lixue).

Later, upon reading various texts of the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp), I further learned that Jianzhou was also a reservoir for Chan Buddhism. Whenever I encountered a monk from Jianzhou, I invariably inquired about the local worthies of their home province;
yet, they often failed to provide an answer. Consequently, I remained despondent for a long time. In the spring of the Ding-si year, I...
My younger brother, Master Yongjue, initially abandoned Confucianism to enter the Buddhist path and studied "withered Chan" under the late Master Shouchang.

Because he was extremely familiar with the former worthies of his own region—men as pure as polished jade and as noble as phoenixes and peacocks—he possessed qualities that exceed what I myself have been able to know.
I was greatly delighted and pointed to his chest, saying, "This is a complete history of the monastic community. My brother replied, "I..."
I intended to record and transmit this account. Not long after, my late teacher passed away. Later, the Master came to Boshan, where we lived together for five years.

During that time, I occasionally sought to fulfill his previous promise, to which he replied, "Wait until you can recognize your own nostrils, and then I shall do it. Subsequently, he returned to Min Province and lived in seclusion in the mountains, and no news of him reached us.
In the spring of the Wuchen year, I was returning to Boshan from Gushan; while traveling through Jianzhou, the Master came out to meet me.
At Kaiyuan Temple, I recognized him at first sight and said, "Now you may consider yourself a monk of Jianzhou.
The Master smiled but did not answer. I then asked, "Have you swept the pagoda of Shouchang yet? The Master said, "I have not neglected the sweeping;
it is simply that I do not permit others to know of it. I said, "Then you have been sweeping it in secret. The Master asked, "And what about you, Preceptor? I—

[The author] said, "Sweeping has not been neglected; it is simply that [the floor] has never been disturbed. The Master said, "It seems you, Reverend, have never swept either. They laughed at each other and parted ways.
In the winter of the Jisi year, a letter arrived at Boshan from the monk Zhicheng of Jianzhou, who sent this work for my inspection and requested a preface.

Upon reading his compilation, I find it divided into four sections, the first of which is titled: [...]* *(Note: The original text ends mid-sentence with "首曰" (firstly titled), indicating the subsequent titles of the sections would follow.)*

"Reaching the Source" (Daben) re-illuminates the fundamental tenet. Second is "Manifesting Transformation" (Xianhua), which clarifies the responsive manifestations. Third is "Exalting Virtue" (Chongde), which records various deeds.

Fourth is "Assisting the Teaching" (Fujiao), which serves as a golden wall and moat for its protection. Taken together, they are titled "Extending the Śāsanā" (Hongshi), thereby exalting the transformation of the Dharma.
Their discernment is correct, their arguments are definitive, their research is extensive, and their classifications are rigorous; are these not the work of a worthy historian?

In the past, Daoxuan compiled the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha) during the Tang dynasty; he was not proficient in literary composition and was moreover unaware of the existence of the *Bielfzhuan* (Separate Biographies).

His treatment of the Dharma-tradition of Bodhidharma reflects how dark the understanding must have been among those of such arid and desolate disposition. Later, Zanning compiled the *Sengshi* during the Song dynasty;

though his learning was vast, his talent was sparse. Furthermore, he categorized Huangbo within the "Responsive Miracles" (*Gantong*) section and listed Yantou under "Relinquishing the Body" (*Yishen*).
To place Yongming on the same level as Xingfu, yet to exclude Yunmen—who was a preeminent figure among the monastics—would be an even greater error.
Juefan followed with his own encomiums and commentary; his work is lofty, elegant, refined, and brilliant, ascending to the ranks of the masters.
However, it merely transmits the lineages of the various worthies of the Chan school; can this truly be called a "complete history"? As for the present Master’s ambition, although...
It is a single province alone; yet Xuan-ning deems it elegant and fitting, while Juefan praises its perfection. It stands far apart and unique, with no prior works to compare it to.
From this alone, one can glimpse a portion of the Master’s caliber—how much more so when considering those of a thousand years past!
It is through the Master that [the teachings] are transmitted; for a thousand years to come, it is through the Master that they shall be known.
Thus, the Master’s merit truly extends both before and after this millennium. When the Jianzhou region speaks of those who propagate Buddhism, who could it be other than the Master?

Therefore, I joyfully observed the fulfillment of his work and did not decline to compose this preface. Furthermore, I have heard that the Master’s writings are exceedingly numerous; I shall certainly abridge them all.
If this is transmitted by Qing, then future generations throughout the world will receive great benefit from it—not merely the people of Jianzhou alone.
I beg to request that you wipe your eyes and await it with anticipation.

Preface to Sending My Elder Father Back to His Hometown The Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind. Sentient beings likewise preach the Dharma according to their own kind, and thus they too attain understanding according to their own kind.
When I, this unworthy one, recalled the time of my renunciation, I traveled downstream to Shicheng and heard [the teachings] at Waguan Monastery.

There was a lecture hall for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and his heart deeply yearned to attend it. He encountered an acquaintance who pressured him to return home; at that time, he used expedient words to escape.
Three months later, he met another person who suddenly said to him, "Your father has met with misfortune; the funeral pyre is about to be prepared.
Reminded of his boundless filial debt, he fell to the ground in great grief, nearly fainting away. He then reflected upon his previous encounter with the Dharma.
Huā said: "The eight sons all took Miaoguang as their teacher. Furthermore, they witnessed Jingcang and Jingyan transforming their father so that he left the household life;

this is the filial piety of world-transcendence, which cannot be compared to worldly filial piety. Consequently, they resolved to leave the household life like an arrow released from a bowstring, with no power to turn back.
To this day, for more than thirty years, they have not sent a single letter home. In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Tiānqī era, Yǒngfēng..."
The Assistant Prefect, Master Wang, learned that this unworthy one was from the same village and came to visit.

Since the time I left the household life, I have avoided mentioning my surname and clan, fearing it might stir up worldly attachments. Yang Chunchi, a man of talent, was a fellow traveler with Master Wang;
he questioned me repeatedly, so I offered him this verse: "If you wish to know where I dwell, It is in a humble lane where worldly passions are still. [He then] crossed the water.
He knew my surname; seeking the city, he recognized his old tomb. Turning his body toward the altars of the state, he opened his eyes to witness the passing of the seasons.

Familiar with his former leisurely wanderings, he was atop the Golden Cock Mound. He first remembered that his uncle might still be there, hoping yet to see him and thereby inspire in him a superior resolve.
When Chunzhi brought the verse back and inquired, he learned that his late uncle had already passed away shortly after the unworthy one had left the household life.
Yet my aged father remained healthy, sound, and free from ailment; those former friends and acquaintances had merely sent me empty words.
As soon as my father heard that his unworthy son was dwelling at Mount Boshan, he traveled from more than a thousand li away by boat.

When we finally met face-to-face, it was as if waking from a dream; grief and joy mingled within him, and he felt as though he were being born again. This was because of my late grandfather and his ancestors...
None of them could even hope to equal one-fifth [of his]. My old father is now seventy-three years of age; yet he remains vigorous and eats well.

When compared by the measure of longevity, is this not a second birth? That in my declining years I am able to behold his compassionate countenance is due to a stroke of divine fortune, beyond what the mind can conceive.

Reflecting on that kinsman and friend who skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma, I realize he was none other than my own guide, the humble disciple. This— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "This—" and lacks a concluding clause. The translation reflects the available fragment.)

Because my aged father yearned to return home, I calculated that I would be unable to provide for him until the end of his life. The sin of this separation is such that its instances could not be counted even by plucking out one's hair.
I respectfully record these circumstances of my birth to mark the beginning and the end [of this matter]. Thus it is said.
The Preface to the Eight Precepts:

When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas. Having attained a rank identical to that of Great Enlightenment, they are truly the children of the Buddhas.

This is the Bodhisattva precept; it is not merely the eightfold precept. Nevertheless, while there are great and small precepts, their essence is neither different nor the same. As for the precepts...
Whether extensive or concise, the principle is indivisible; yet the precepts have their interruptions and continuities, and their nature is beyond both opening and closing.

Were it not for the Great Being who benefits sentient beings, there would be no avoiding transgressions amidst the dust and toil of the world. For a practitioner with power, how could these be difficult to practice for even a moment?

To ascend the shore of the path of dependent origination, a single day’s fast serves as a bridge across kalpas of accumulated karma. As for the precepts of a single day, do not dismiss them as trivial.
One fully attains the complete merit; regardless of its duration, it is immediately equivalent to the full precepts.

It is like drinking a single drop of the ocean—the flavor is identical to that of the entire sea—or like casting a single drop into the ocean, which becomes one with all the waves of the sea. One must know that while the precepts may seem shallow, their merit is profound;

from a subtle cause comes a thoroughgoing fruit. This is the skillful means (*upāya*) devised by the Sage, the compassionate provisional teaching that leads toward reality, and the ultimate destination indicated by the Great Being.
Xijian [revealed] the reality underlying provisional means; Master Qingshan summarized their essentials; and Grand Historian Wu verified their commonality.

Thus, the perfect practice was gathered in a single moment, while extraordinary causes were planted for eternal kalpas. This does not discriminate between noble and base, nor does it distinguish between the wise and the foolish.
Simply cultivate a firm and resolute heart, and you will certainly enter the ocean-treasury of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.

The preface to the *Shengsheng She Jisha Fangsheng* (The Vow to Refrain from Killing and Release Living Beings in Every Life) states: "To protect living beings, one must kill; only when killing is exhausted does one find true peace. This is the determined resolve of a courageous man.
Indeed, it is because sentient beings indulge themselves in the cave of ignorance, nourishing this decaying body; they only know how to kill others, yet do not realize they are killing themselves.
The five māras blaze fiercely, the six thieves inflict harm, the four snakes attack with poison, and two rats gnaw at one another.
From kalpa to kalpa, they slaughter my life of wisdom and plunder my Dharma-wealth. They may truly be called great enemies and bitter adversaries, yet they are also our kin.

They cherish and nurture [the body], subsequently binding themselves to it; they slaughter all sentient beings and consume their flesh and blood, indulging at will in the nourishment of the four great elements.
Yet when a single breath does not return, it turns entirely to ash and soil. Because of this finite body, they commit infinite sins; their fundamental nature is thus narrow and inferior.

When delusion reaches its extreme and there is no turning back, the retributions of the three miserable realms arrive; who then could take their place? If one can reflect back upon oneself, this is truly so.

One should don the armor of firm resolve and wield the vajra sword to slay the mara-thieves within the forest of the five aggregates and chase away the snakes and rats upon the ground where neither sun nor moon exists.
One should expand the compassion and forbearance of the Dharma-body and give rise to the great pity of shared essence. Upon seeing...

To regard all sentient beings as one’s only child, to be free from the notions of "self" and "other," and to transform formless beings through unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*)—this is how the Elder Yunqi profoundly mastered the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The Venerable Zhan took up this spirit of compassion and cultivated loving-kindness, entirely following the model of Yunqi to propagate it at Tongji.
Thus, these various superior persons encouraged and guided one another, and the establishment of the society originated from this.
[The practice] flourishes. The karma of killing is severed from this point on. It is not merely a matter of abstaining from killing, but also of releasing living beings.
It is not merely saving the lives of sentient beings, but truly continuing the life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas, and extending the life-force of wisdom for all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they share the same essence (*tongti*). This is the merit of no-merit, the virtue of no-virtue—what is called "taking killing as life. I do not...
It is by means of brush and tongue that these things are given names.

In the Preface to the "Chapter on Repaying Kindness," I have heard that the ocean of suffering is boundless and the compassionate favors are manifold; yet sentient emotions are restricted by limits, and the nature of consciousness is deluded.
Ignorance leads to the clear existence of intimacy and estrangement within limits; yet when there is no knowledge, one falsely discriminates between "self" and "other.

Thus, one revolves through birth and death, where the karmic retributions of the three miserable realms are inexhaustible. As a traveler lodging among humans and devas, the rising and sinking within the nine states of existence never ceases.
Changing heads and faces, parents from many lifetimes settle the grievances of bandits; wearing horns and shrouded in fur, kinsmen through kalpas repay the debts of children and grandchildren.
The Great Master gave rise to thoughts of compassion and expounded the Dharma-gift that is difficult to repay fourfold;
the Elder, appearing in his declining years, instructed a single son of evil nature. [The child] slept upon his chest and frolicked upon his knees.
True compassion is universal. Men are compassionate fathers; women are sorrowful mothers. Their affection is boundless.
They take the world as their hall and its people as their foundation. The profound kindness of the sovereign cannot be repaid.

Taking supernatural powers as their benefit and joy, and taking the practice of deliverance as their cause for cultivation, the compassionate virtue of all Buddhas never ceases. They renounce illusory wealth and plant [the seeds of merit].
The blessings of humans and devas are surpassed in an instant; one casts off the outflowing body and severs the notion of solidity. To transmit the mind is supreme;

by understanding the meaning of the Dharma, one causes the Dharma and its meaning to circulate. One returns to the wise ones of the triple world, who recognize profound kindness and repay that profound kindness.
This must be the task of the Layman Jiutao; without declining this prolixity, he vows to enter this vehicle.

Preface for the Seventieth Birthday of the Layman Zhao Zhanxu In the past, while reading the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, I encountered the passage: "The host of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) are the seeds of the Tathāgata. It further states:
"Lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land; they grow instead in low-lying, marshy mud. From this, one knows that the Buddha-dharma does not consist solely of [abstract] discourse.

Regarding *tathatā* (suchness), it is spoken of alone as being without birth (*anutpāda*). This is because people are intoxicated in a realm where emotions are forgotten and consciousness is obliterated, causing their intellects—like those of lame donkeys—to become self-imprisoned within a state of ash and withered wood.
Indeed, the Buddha manifested leaving the household life to clarify that the ultimate truth is not something conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

He did so to shatter the attachment of ordinary beings to the home and to lead them out from the cage-like confinement of the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms. Thus was the pure manifestation revealed.

By dwelling at home, one clarifies that the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). This refutes the two vehicles’ transcendence of the mundane, preventing them from falling into the pit and trench of nihilistic emptiness and extinction.
Since these are called "manifestations," each has its own prescribed ritual; how could Śākyamuni have been unable to escape his position in the imperial palace?
Or how could Vimalakīrti—who delighted in fine things and craved scabs—have stayed in Vaiśālī? Observe how Mañjuśrī knocked at his door, competing [with him].
When discussing the non-dual, Vimalakīrti merely set out a single empty chair and removed all other furnishings;

thus, although this elder appeared to have a household, his refined character was so serene that he was truly nothing more than a shaven-headed layman. The Buddha, however, manifested residence within the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha*), where the rules of Dharma were strictly observed;
yet, while not destroying the mundane world, he fervently expounded upon the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), precisely demonstrating that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.
How can the pure and the defiled be different? Who says that worldly dharmas divide and fracture boundaries? It is merely like drawing scratches and claw-marks upon empty space.
When I first arrived at Dongyan, I immediately formed a bond of *dharmaprīti* with Master Zhao Zhanxu. His father was known as Layman Yuzhai;
a man of lofty talent and profound virtue, he was a leading figure among the elite of Jianxi and was deeply versed in [the teachings].
The Buddha-dharma takes the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* as its dwelling and the *Zongcheng* (the Patriarchal Vehicle) as its sustenance.
Thus, the Master held firm faith in this Way, possessing a singular and profound affinity for these two teachings.

Furthermore, he cherished them as his family precepts through successive generations, hoping that his descendants would all row together in a single boat and ride side by side to roam within the ocean of Dharma and the garden of enlightenment. His countenance was serene and his heart harmonious; his spirit—
His flavor was like the spring wind that nurtures all things; his virtuous conduct was like sweet syrup, and his reputation for virtue spread far and wide.

Moreover, he was able to transform worldly afflictions into Buddhist practice and sit upon the realm of desire as if it were a meditation seat. In his view, the monastic assembly at Dongyan was as urgent as attending to one's own household affairs.
Furthermore, whenever there were vacancies among the administrative duties and monastic offices, he never failed to attend to them with his whole heart and provide for them through manifold means.

Now, at Dongyan, a thousand disciples have gathered like the finest of the auspicious and the wise, soaring like phoenixes; everyone regards this place as a grove of *campaka* flowers, all of which is due to the power of your broad protection.
If this is so, it would be appropriate to say that you are Vimalakīrti returned from the beyond, manifesting in the form of a householder.
He took filial piety and fraternal kindness as his model for conduct, and the *Shi* and *Li* as his ceremonial robes.
Thus his noble descendants have transmitted his fragrance, standing in dense rows like jade branches encircling the steps or emerald trees leaning in the wind.

Although you, sir, have not yet unfurled your wings that reach the heavens to present your treasures at the imperial court, I know that your innate nature accords with the Dao; you surely regard official rank as but floating clouds. Nevertheless, [your virtue] has accumulated.
How profound! The Creator who flows forth his light cannot further aspire to surpass you, O Sage of the Future. Why do you thus consider yourself so superior?
In my view, your contemplation of the body, mind, and world is like bubbles and flowers upon the water; your domestic ties and kin are but a single theatrical stage;
and the extension or brevity of your lifespan is but a mere speck on the dust of kalpas. Such is the vastness of your breast and the magnitude of your mental scope.
How brilliant! You wish to grasp and mold the Great Thousandfold World as if merely tossing aside your shoes and sandals, letting them strike the ground with a sound of playful laughter.

Now, as you measure the seasons and calculate the years, it is precisely a time when one must not overstep the boundaries of propriety. I, for my part, am honored by our friendship in the Way beyond the mundane.

Unable to present the peach of Du-suo or pour the refined wine of pepper flowers, I have instead composed this brief verse to serve as a single branch of the udumbara flower, offering my congratulations on your longevity.
The verse says: "There is a beautiful person whose conduct is pure and simple; The radiance of wisdom shines brightly, yet remains entirely unmanifest.
When hungry they eat, when thirsty they drink—what else need be done? In speech they follow one another, in silence they dwell together. [He] leaned upon his staff.
Reaching toward heaven, it is yet higher still; across the vast blue ocean, one spans stones to form a bridge. The sixteen-foot golden body becomes a mere blade of grass;
the great trichiliocosm is looked down upon as a peach held in the palm. The worldly waves all claim to wash away human nature, yet fish and dragons instead take water as their very life.

Moving upstream against the current and following the flow downstream, one grasps the true nature of things. Karmic streams wind and turn as the wind carries the boat. The mustard-seed city and the kalpa-stone endure for many autumns;
yet in a single glance, all is traversed in an instant. If someone asks about the matter of long life in the present, raise your eyebrows and laugh with ease.
Preface to the Fiftieth Birthday of the Layman Huang Xinjing:

As for practitioners, they do not dwell upon signs, nor upon the sign of a "life-span. A hundred years are equal to empty flowers; only by attaining accord with reality does one realize eternal abiding.
If one clings to a lifespan of a hundred years, one merely obtains those hundred years, being entirely subject to the shifting transformations of the two realms of light and darkness.
It is not a phenomenon that is eternally abiding. Master Fu Daoshi said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast.
It is able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither with the four seasons. What is called the "lord of the myriad phenomena" is precisely the eternally abiding dharma.
Like clouds arising from a golden treasury, it is not formed; like being blown by the Vairambha wind, it is not destroyed. Even when the kalpa-fire blazes fiercely, my land remains blissful.
Yin said: "As soon as one realizes this principle, awakening occurs without depending on a teacher. To refer to this principle as 'longevity' (壽) does not mean it is subject to the cycles of kalpas;
to refer to it as 'life-force' (命) does not mean it is subject to birth and death; to refer to it as 'permanence' (常) does not mean it is subject to interruption;
to refer to it as 'abiding' (住) does not mean it is subject to coming and going. The cycles of kalpas, birth and death, interruptions, and comings and goings are all reflected within it."

Regarding the mark of the central flower: within the ground of the principle of *tathatā* (the suchness of reality), if one seeks even the slightest trace of substantiality, nothing at all can be found.

Within this state of non-attainment, the unique illumination of the Sage’s merit is revealed; thus, terms such as "life-span," "vitality," "permanence," and "abiding" are all merely superfluous words.

For this reason, I address the Layman Shou as follows: he is the One of Immeasurable Life, the One of Supreme Life, the One of Unequaled Life, and the One of Life Equal to the Peerless. He grinds away...

A speck of dust or a drop of ink is insufficient to compare their relative merits. A verse says: "If you recognize the indestructible diamond body, The child in your own eyes is the person before you.
In vain do you speak of peach fruits after three thousand years; There remains the numinous branch with spring beyond the kalpas."
Preface to the Garden Hermitage and Refectory of Layman Gu Xingweng:
In the past, the Layman Vimalakīrti resided in the city of Vaiśālī and propagated the Great Teaching; now, the Elder Layman Xing resides at [the] Stone... [Mountain].
Tou-cheng. Upholding the Great Dharma. The world of antiquity is the world of today; the heaven and earth of antiquity are the heaven and earth of today;
the sun and moon of antiquity are the sun and moon of today; the people and things of antiquity are the people and things of today.
Vimalakīrti is precisely Xinglao, and Xinglao is precisely Vimalakīrti. In propagating the True Dharma and illuminating this final age, they are non-dual and without distinction.

Therefore, Master Xing named his hermitage "Jin-su" (Golden Grain). Although the youth Sudhana visited fifty-three teachers and traversed a hundred cities like layers of silk cocoons, Master Xing never strayed even a step from his own place;
he silently investigated this Way within. Thus, he named his pavilion "Nan-xun" (Southern Inquiry).
He beheld ten trillion lands of the Pure Land from within this Sahā world, all of which were marked by lotuses.

Before the layman’s eyes, a precious pond surged forth, its *padma* blossoms in full bloom; thus he named his pavilion "The Land of Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*). This layman hailed from a distinguished family of noble lineage.
His reputation flourishes throughout both the court and the commoners; eminent talents have emerged in succession, and those who passed the imperial examinations have appeared in an unbroken lineage.

For this reason, the library is named "Jiaxiu" (Excellence in Literature). The Layman burns incense and sits in tranquil meditation, focusing his mind on *dhyāna* (Chan practice); he follows in the fragrant dust of the successive patriarchs and awakens the wisdom-mirror of people today.

For this reason, the hall is named "Jingxin" (Mirror of the Mind). The Layman’s breast is expansive and open, such that the mundane world cannot intrude upon him. For this reason, the shrine is named "Danyan" (Serene Tranquility).
The layman’s hundred affairs were in chaotic confusion, yet his mind was empty, clear, and serene; thus he named the hall *Chunyi* (Pure Unity).
The groves and springs reflected one another, and the bamboos and trees intermingled in purity; thus he named the pavilion *Yici* (Gathering the Verdant).

In this garden, the myriad conditions of worldly dust are dissolved, and the single consistency of past and present is harmonized. Entering Jin-su Temple, he discussed the discourse of non-duality; ascending Nan-xun Pavilion, he awakened to Bodhi.
The mind rests at the Pavilion of the Land of Bliss, fixing its gaze upon the realm of the West; it reads at the Hall of Jiaxiu, giving rise to the brilliance of the dream-pen;
it sits in the Hall of Mirror-Mind, turning over the volumes from the land of India. Its model is pure and singular, and its mental ground is serene.

It draws in the verdant hues of the deep forest and partakes of the fragrance of bamboo among the noble trees. The joy of the layman’s secluded refinement and the interest of dhyāna-pleasure transcend the ordinary by ten thousandfold.
When I reached this point in my writing, my heart was refreshed and my spirit delighted; it was as if I were standing within the garden itself.
I imagine that when you, Layman, read these words, although I, this poor monk, am separated by a thousand li, I shall surely not be far from your side, morning and evening.
Postscript to the Blood-inked Copying of the Avataṃsaka Sūtras by the Chan Practitioner Bazhenguan.
The Great Dharma is difficult to encounter, and the True Vehicle is rarely met. When offering a thousand lamps to the Buddha, how could one decline to repay even half a verse? (4)

The phrases moisten the heart; one would not begrudge giving up even one's entire body, let alone this most precious jewel that shatters the dust of ignorance—the complete scripture of the Dharma-realm, the gateway to the Great Being’s cause, and the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruition.
It fills the treasuries of the Dragon Palace yet resides within a single mote of dust; it proclaims the wonders of Vulture Peak and pervades the myriad phenomena.
Were it not for having planted the ground of Bodhi over kalpas of vast time, how could one hold it in the palms of one's hands?
Behold with your own eyes! How rare is this supreme condition! The Chan practitioner Zhengguan has long cultivated the seeds of omniscience and practiced manifold expedient means.
