Laughing, I gaze upon the thousand-tiered *stūpa*; its covering belongs to the universe itself. I bow my head to my brothers, who together established this merit.
Fundraising Appeal for the Society for Protecting Living Beings:

The true mind pervades all things; how could there be any distinction between the various forms of the six realms? Yet, as deluded thoughts follow conditions, one consequently experiences the diverse natures of many lifetimes.
The Great Radiant Treasury of the Tathāgata is the fundamental source of sentient beings' pure awakening. Sentient beings are most deluded...

The Root of Darkness. It contains the wondrous luminosity of all Buddhas in their stage of causal practice. Although the conditions of retribution may range from the most acute intelligence to the most dull and insentient, the nature of awakening remains perfectly complete.
When a spider weaves its web, its mechanical skill is evident; when a magpie builds its nest, its spiritual mind is even more ingenious.

A loach understands how to burrow into the mud to hide, while a louse seeks only to flee toward the dark. Observing these wriggling creatures, one sees they all instinctively crave life, even when subjected to injury or mutilation.
Yet they still cling to their physical forms: the "Sweet Child" remains amidst the dust, weeping until his bowels break; the "phantom-sack" insect dies while its body encircles its old burrow;
one who has recovered from nursing a child abandons the turtle about to be cooked; and one throws a pearl to heal a snake that is not yet dead.

How can one bear to have their skin flayed and bones stripped away, as they writhe alive within the boiling cauldrons; to have their bellies split open and hearts gouged out, as their souls flutter in terror amidst the furnace coals?
Their tears have not yet dried when their hair and skin fall away; their flesh still quivers as the kitchen hearths roar with clamor.
Piteous, in a mere instant it passes down their throats; who recognizes that gods cry out and ghosts weep? Who would believe they are being roasted for no reason?
One must know that every cause is repaid by its fruit: the karmic retribution of the three miserable realms knows no rest, and the shackles of ten thousand kalpas never cease.
How can one indulge one's passions and violate reason, selecting the fattest among the fresh and tender to slaughter?

To forget the Great Sage’s true compassion for sentient beings while indulging in the evil habits of the common and ignorant—devoid of even a trace of the desire to cherish life—merely using the excuse that "all things nourish humanity."

Arise and abandon the mind that creates karma of ruin and misery. Furthermore, how could you not know that the three miserable realms lie within yourself, unfailing by even a hair’s breadth, following you like a shadow follows its form?
I announce this universally to the Elder Daguan: Greatly rouse your compassionate heart and emulate the benevolence of one who unties the net.

Convene an assembly for the release of living beings. Do not begrudge the *qingqu* coins on the end of your staff; why be stingy with the old notes in your purse? Release them from their cages and enclosures as...
Emerging from the prison cell, one may joyfully attend to grooming one's feathers; escaping the cutting block and board is like leaving a butcher’s stall.

Clearly manifesting the spiritual consciousness of this illusory body, one beats its wings in the air, appearing in yellow robes to pay homage to its master; with head held high above the water’s surface, it gazes upward.

I turn this seal-knot to repay your grace; the retribution for such deeds is unfailing and cycles on without ceasing. Do not reproach me for my prolixity; I pray you will grant me a place upon the register.
Petition for the Fundraising of the Śarīra Hall at Aśoka Monastery.
Spiritual radiance flies forth in brilliant hues; throughout Jambudvīpa, his infinite bodies appear. Like an echo transmitted through a hollow valley, a five-tiered stupa surges from the seashore.
The white-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) is beheld by the seven assemblies, manifesting diverse forms according to their determined karma.

Merit is distributed across many lifetimes, giving rise to extraordinary retributions through the conditions of worldly dust. Truly, this is a verification of the Dharma-gate, since the golden coffin was sealed in its splendor.
At that time, how marvelous was the spring of the Bodhi tree! It spanned the harmonious radiance of the Azure Emperor (the God of Spring).

The True Body rained down eighty-four *bushels*, whereby the net of the karma of afflictions could be overturned. His compassionate vows fashioned eighty-four thousand [images], existing throughout both heaven and the human realm.
His light pervades the ocean of enlightenment, and his excellence blossoms within the grove of compassion. The stūpa shall never shift through all eternity; it is the adornment of the world.
Dependent origination is subject to decay. Old Yunmen, wishing to respond to the karmic resonance of sentient beings, erected the great Dharma banner upon his eyebrows and eyelashes.
May all virtuous people awaken the numinous knowledge of their own nature and vie to plant the seeds of Buddhahood on the shores of the Fragrant Water Sea.
Delighting in the study of geography, he purifies and breaks open the pouch of stinginess. I pray that you will grant me the brush to join in perfecting holy wisdom.

This draft for soliciting fields for feeding monks at Tianxin Monastery proclaims the True Vehicle from within the forest retreat (*araṇya*); though it stands amidst the marketplace, it is as majestic as a Buddha-land. There is no path other than Nirvana; even within the bustling city wards, there remains abundance.

In the monastic garden, one opens the mind and its objects within the single suchness; one merges past and present within the present moment. In brothels and taverns, Maitreya’s cloth bag drags across the ground;
among hunters and woodcutters, Nanquan’s wind-blown banner points directly. This breaking of conventions does not concern those of shallow understanding;
even a hair’s breadth of deviation leads straight into the land of pestilence. To transcend and be liberated requires a person of wisdom. This is the Way.

One truly attains a flavor resembling that of drinking the *amṛta* (clarified butter). Entering the state of sainthood from the ordinary mind, one first adorns and purifies the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*) and expels the hosts of Māra to cultivate purity.
This necessarily relies upon material resources to provide assistance; may one beg for even a drop of the rain and dew from donors, so that it may fortunately irrigate the heart-mind.
May the root-stump of the *bodhi* of one's own nature be planted, so that it surely flourishes upon the ground of Buddhahood.
The Sangha-field relies upon you; the retribution of karmic fruit never errs. We lament that you have bestowed true compassion, vastly expanding the sacred realm.
Long live the Master Shangshou Chang on his seventieth birthday!
A single plot of idle land at Shouchang; thorns were cleared away and trees were planted. Jade leaves and golden stalks spread throughout the world;
auspicious clouds of five colors are woven like fine silk. A vast radiance of light extends through the ten directions;
the flavor of white milk and fragrant gruel is long-lasting. Once it touches the lips, a white film forms; those with iron brows and copper heads can indeed withstand it. Fifty years ago...
Created by one who is intimately familiar with the aggregates; within the mountains of emerald mist, one exhausts all that is magnificent.

He says of himself, "I have reached out and grasped a crimson coral," yet it was originally but grass upon the ground of Mount Emei. I once busied myself intimately within this very place, handling it like brocade and like clouds.

These mountain shrubs were not merely casual acquaintances; only then did I believe that there is a distinct springtime on the cold crags. Dragons and elephants trample about, while phoenixes and qilin circle. How brilliant!
A hawk and a celestial steed are not of the Śākya clan; in the rear garden, one alone envies the braying of an old donkey. Gnawing at grass and clattering its hooves, it refuses all control.
With a single sound of the *ghanṭā*, the Dharma-gate opens; monks like clouds converge from every direction. A jade lock and golden key cannot pick it open;
the great ocean and Mount Sumeru are but a speck of dust. This year, at seventy, he spans the arc of the heavens; alone he sits upon the white [elephant] at the crossroads.

The ox-cart: beckoning with the hand and raising the voice cannot bring it back. How could the hidden treasures of the house be counted? Wherever one touches, mountains open up; there is no need to gather provisions.
On steep ridges and level plains, all are sites of jewels. Amidst the groves, the scent of gold and silver abounds; throughout the Dharma-realm, only the fragrance of the *utpala* lily is heard.
At the summit of Mount Ehu, Master Shangfeng celebrates his seventieth year;
high clouds blaze forth like canopies and banners, the color of golden blossoms. A bright lamp illuminating the world, he sits within the site of enlightenment.
A single ray of numinous light pierces the northern heavens; walking alone within the realm, his intent is extraordinary, far surpassing the teachers of the South.
A fine model. He pushed open the mortar before Old Master Bian; he snatched away the talisman from behind Lan Gong’s elbow.
On the plum branches, the news was revealed; he rode backward upon the divine steed of the Yan capital. With a golden hook, he dangled the leviathan from the bottom of the sea;

at the peak of Tianmu, silver waves surged. Returning, he monopolized the spring of the white clouds; eating parched grain and cooking sorrel, he was cut off from all neighbors. His virtue is comparable to—

Huangmei personally brought provisions to his mother; his poetry, like that of Cijue, exhorted his elders and kin. Since his innate filial piety was such as this, he regards all sentient beings as his only child.
Opening the hall, the Dharma-milk moistens the withered pines; preaching the precepts, the golden-scaled fish leap upon the fragrant islets.
The eminent monks of Yingbiao vie to gaze upon his radiance; with his three-foot black serpent-whip, he lashes the four quarters. Has he yet crossed the Huanglong Pass?

He knows beforehand whether a horse is black or yellow, like the master Bole. This year at seventy, he traverses the stage of "following the heart"; his age is double that of Zhaozhou’s hexagenary cycle.
If he could command the hour, the pearl would roll across the platter; he would swallow up sun and moon, and hang the cauldron from a tree. His eyebrows are like snow.
A painting is difficult to transmit; ten-thousand-fathom Sumeru towers above the vast river. I intend to follow the fragrant traces of Songxiao and Shaoshan;
I laugh as I compare this with the Great Thousand Worlds of China.
Written for the Chan practitioner Baishou.
A breast and mind pure and white—this is the style of the Buddha-household. The depths of the vessel-world are profound; the scenery and phenomena are one. A band of clear mists brings infinite joy;
colored clouds slantingly shroud Mount Sumeru. Shattering the colors atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, the numinous source is sucked back until the Yellow River runs dry.
Brightness and darkness intersect as they exchange their functions; clearly there are two mouths, yet neither has a tongue. When spring arrives, all things are released.

Ordinary flowers bloom everywhere throughout the world, their sprouts of wisdom fully unfurled. Do not say that the road beyond the pass is perilous; at the mountain peak, his feet were worn through by Xuan Sha.
Since ancient times, the karmic affinity for the Buddha has resided in Min; the bright moonlight contains the lion’s roar.
If you wish to recognize the old bhikṣu of Vulture Peak, you must also perform a somersault beyond the ordinary. When the Chan practitioner joyfully encounters this age of non-delusion, the nose...

I am too weary to wipe my head before worldly people; throughout my life, I have only known how well it is to dwell in the mountains. One should know that the Buddha-dharma lies at the edge of the mattock.
When the hoe is raised, one knows its weight; the sound of the hoe shatters the dream of dwelling in the mountains. Upon waking, one is no longer like the person of former times;
as soon as the eyebrows are raised, there is pain. I offer these words as a blessing for long life: the road from the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven.
Level and smooth. In the arena of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the spear is not raised. The Lamp of Transmission forever bears the name of this man of integrity.
Longevity! Layman Qingxi’s jar and bowl have entered the city of Qiaoyang. Upon entering the territory, I heard early of the Layman’s fame; the Layman’s wind of wisdom sweeps over all people.
Face to face, upon meeting, his brow first relaxed over his forehead. I have already told you the essentials of practice: the profound source is not to be sought from others.
Look with your own eyes at the gateway of the faculties and their objects; snatch out the family treasure from within your robes.
You are accustomed to driving the great white ox of Mt. Mui; roam freely south and north of the stream. Having plowed through every field of the household, there remains only the mist.

A single band of clouds across the autumn sky. Last year, at the age of seventy, I celebrated my birthday; immortals came from across the sea to praise my stride, yet I felt ashamed that I had not been invited to the Dharma assembly.
For your sake, I shall once more proclaim the Universal Gate of Yunmen: he carved open the primordial chaos to reveal the azure void, and with both hands, he reverently grasped the radiant sun.
He gathered the pearls within his skin-sack; who would say that mountains and rivers can obstruct the eyes?

Others celebrate ten, while I celebrate one; I celebrate eighty, while others celebrate seven. I await you for a hundred years to compose this long treatise, so that we may once again penetrate the secret meaning of the True Exposition.
Long-lived Layman Donghu: The waters flow and gather in the east of Jambudvīpa; the lake’s radiance surges, swallowing the azure heavens. Throughout the day, clouds and vapors rise to the Milky Way;
auspicious suns and favorable breezes open the Great Obscurity. Layman, you have long partaken of the dew from the Immortal’s Palms; you love to listen at the gates of Chan.
Dharma Words. My beard and whiskers are still white and dry; my dream-like body and mind are now at ease. A single sound of the Buddha’s name thunders like a clap of lightning;
the realms of consciousness, objects, faculties, and sense-fields collapse in an instant. One need not inquire whether it be the Sahā world or a Pure Land;
what does it matter if one is in a city or at the edge of a mountain? This year I am eighty-one; leaning on my staff, I traverse the days. When meeting people...
Much has been said regarding the cause of gathering sand; both the palm leaves and the *kumuda* flowers are fully prepared. For this layperson, I pray for long life:

may the paths through the snowy peaks and clouded mountains be level and smooth. May the adamantine eye protrude from the crown of the head, and may one walk with hands cast free atop ten-thousand-fathom cliffs.
The heels do not tread upon the weeds of ignorance; turning the body, one first realizes that empty space is small. The boundless oceans of lands reside on the tip of a single hair;
coral beneath the water is as bright as the moon.
Master Kong Zhiweng of Zhiquan in Shoucheng was my neighbor’s elder brother.
In over thirty years, a mere snap of the fingers has separated us. Since ancient times, the homeland and the distant frontier have been sources of sorrow;
how could one remember pure joys when one is but a traveler? Having happened upon news from a fellow villager, I first asked after my old friend whenever I met someone.

The venerable elder; counting on his fingers, barely a year or two has passed. Suddenly, it is as if I am facing the countenance of Master Zhi. At eighty years of age, your form is like a hanging arc;

your virtuous influence nourishes all like springtime rain and dew. I am originally a monk who dwells by mountains and waters; I have toiled to write this letter from a thousand miles away to visit you.
Having finished reading your letter, auspicious clouds unfold; within the clouds, an immortal comes from Du-suo. I join my palms in reverence.

With earnest sincerity, you requested my words; thus, I shall not decline to compose these humble verses for you, Elder. May you live long and remain ever vigorous—like a ridge, like a mound, and again like a mountain.
With staff in hand, picking through the clouds, you enjoy a life of leisure; with white hair yet a youthful countenance, who could possibly emulate you?
I have divined that the limit for my return shall be ten years; at ninety, you, O Elder, will precede me in death.
Should other matters cause us to deviate from this agreement, it is certain that I shall return to you when you reach the age of one hundred.
Master Yin Xin of Mount Lu has long been hailed as a Dharma cave throughout Jiangzhe.
An elephant and dragon are born with golden bones; he unfurls the *palm-leaf* scriptures like falling celestial flowers.
The flashing light from his brow is not to be overlooked. By the side of Lingxiao Rock, his fame is passed down through all time; he has nurtured the majestic power of a golden-maned lion.
Power complete; what business is it to stride across Mount Kuanglu? A thousand-fathom waterfall pours into the sacred source. Born by conditions, I have reached the age of sixty;
counting from the beginning, one full cycle of the sexagenary calendar has passed. When the measure of atoms is exhausted, the inconceivable is revealed;

suddenly, mountains and rivers leave not a square inch of earth behind. View this body as a phantom image or a bubble on the flower; the luminous faculties and their objects remain unstained by dust. Yue Mountain.
The waters of Wu present pure offerings; may you forever celebrate long life as one who does not age.

For the Layman Yu Wentai: above the three terraces, purple clouds swirl; auspicious mists and radiant light pervade the great trichiliocosm. Dewdrops nourish the City of Transformation. May your forbearance flourish.
Grass. The wind arises in the burning house, where blue lotuses bloom; the ox-cart is overturned as one sits upon the broad thoroughfare.
Worldly attachments pass before the eyes like drifting clouds. Walking at ease, one’s practice accords with the rustic spirit; taking meals at their appointed times fulfills the daily discipline.

This year I am sixty, the years suspended like a rainbow; day by day, the grand path of Great Enlightenment unfolds. A piercing wind through the very bones, a chill that penetrates the gallbladder—this is the clarity of *yongyi* (as one wishes).

The jewel is fully revealed; worldly thoughts are vast and empty, cold as ashes. The myriad phenomena of the universe vie to attend it. Raising one’s head, one joyfully beholds the moon over the Three Peaks;
beneath the dark trees, the secluded birds fold their wings and return. With beautiful whiskers and a ruddy countenance, he speaks much with laughter;
the mist and clouds withdraw toward his brow. Whether in the mundane or the sublime, he speaks of non-arising; what harm is there in presenting the two truths even in reverse?
In vain do I record the years upon the long star; though the sands of time are exhausted, the Way becomes ever more clear. Today I shall personally reveal it to you:
the ancient road from whence we came is broad and level.

Longevity! At this very moment, Layman Sheng, I once personally traveled to the kingdom of Tóngzǐ. There, auspicious radiance was pervasive and men of great virtue were numerous. The lineages of those wearing the ceremonial hairpins and robes have extended for ten thousand autumns and a thousand springs;
their hidden merits and literary achievements have been passed down in succession. I recall that my own footsteps once ascended to Yuèshàng Ān, and it is said that I there encountered you.
For the sake of *dāna*, with the profound conditions of courageous strength and the bliss of *samādhi*, what hindrance could there be to abandoning sleep and forgetting to eat?
This year, having reached the age of forty, I have completed the arc of my journey; shaking off the dust, I joyfully behold the path of Longmen (Dragon Sleep).

Upon the path of Longmen, the grasses grow lush and green; atop Jizhu Peak, years are no longer counted. Before one’s eyes, the green mountains rise in many steep cliffs; beneath one’s feet, the flowing waters are all murmuring and cascading. Murmuring...
Lord Liu-shui constantly performs [this music]. Longevity should correspond to the profound mystery within the body.

May the Lady of Longevity be foremost among the five blessings of the great categories; the True Man has no fixed station and must personally investigate it. Within the realm of sense-faculties and objects, one perceives their differentiation.
Luminous. Pervading heaven and earth without leakage, a single ray of spiritual light leaves ten thousand realms at ease. Returning from a dream, this is truly not the human world.
The frost is clear, the moon is cold, and the incense smoke in the burner is fragrant; there remain lotus flowers, dewy and chill. This year, at fifty, I encounter my birthday;
I dwell in the pure Vinaya, abiding by both vehicle and precepts. There is no need for a celestial mother to celebrate long life; the family home has been transformed.
He creates a treasury of bright pearls; this precious storehouse of luminous gems is inexhaustible. When the conditions of the occasion arise, his spiritual resonance penetrates everywhere.
Who can measure the span of his life in terms of sexagenary cycles? The Fusang tree originally stands to the east of the Sea Gate.
Long-lived Mother Hongchou, may you first be blessed with the five virtues; may your vast years be perfected by ten thousand merits. There is no need to offer prayers for longevity on the Jade Isles;
a single invocation of Amitābha makes the day pure and bright. With one recitation of Amitābha, the Land of Bliss is realized; even the water-birds and wind-tossed branches chant it forth.

With a wondrous voice, he snaps his fingers and smiles as he gazes upon the flowers of the highest grade; only then does one know that the Great Way is broad and level. At the first crossing of the *udumbara* flower, it accords with the age of sixty;

yet he further praises the purity of the earth as being nothing other than the purity of the mind. Amidst the chaotic bustle of a hundred affairs, matters as tangled as hemp, one must know how to dwell forever in the *nāga-samādhi*.
This is naturally a superior condition for one's descendants; they seek neither the heavenly realms nor the path of the immortals. *Borilī*.
The ground was the color of gold. There remained vermilion and the inscription of the Great Year.

Among the various offerings made by the Layman Tianyi for the construction of a stupa for his late mother, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. Even those who gather soil and sand to form groups and assemblies—such as our great layman—[attain merit].

Wishing to extend my filial thoughts, I have erected this banner-pole. To prolong the life of my venerable and compassionate mother and to bring her joy, I, though but a child in colorful robes, recognize that the worldly and the world-transcending are different and cannot be compared.
Indeed, it is not for the sake of adornment that I create this adornment, yet it serves to grace this small patch of ground.

For ten million years and more, I have heard that the ancient venerable masters, having paid homage at stupas to repay their mothers, were addressed by spirits in the air wearing crimson crowns and robes;
they emerged from the earth and personally bore witness to these events. You should joyfully preach the Lotus Sūtra; now is precisely the right time.

I recall the Elder of Shouzhiquan from our former neighborhood; his voice and countenance remain vividly present before me. The sound of his chess pieces enters my dreams, and the fragrance of his incense lingers on my robes. I often heard his instructions for the household, which brought joy to my countenance and submission to my heart.
Amidst the criticisms and reproaches of this mundane world, he remained entirely unaffected by anything. I have come here to study the Way for more than thirty years.

The virtue and achievements of our Elder are ever more radiant and vast. Now that he has reached eighty, on this great occasion of his arch-bowing birthday, his fragrant legacy shines upon his descendants, and the elixir of immortality blazes forth.
This causes me to dwell in reverie; though I cannot attend his banquet of longevity, I recall having entered his gate long before any signs of his future eminence appeared.

May the elder heed my words; I offer this blessing for your longevity. The dragon’s nature has long been tamed, and your aged teeth grow ever firmer. To analyze a single speck of dust or a drop of ink is like comparing it to the sands of the Ganges;

yet when measured against the elder’s lifespan, it falls short by more than the distance between heaven and earth. May the elder’s life be as the Great Mountains—not merely comparable to their towering heights, but beyond all such analogy.
The Master’s longevity is like the ocean; it cannot be compared to mere waves. Firm, upright, clear, and profound—none in the world can fathom it.

From past to present, from ancient times to now, the present is precisely the right moment. Who composed this verse? Who offers this felicitations? I follow the ancients, yet I am not merely an ancient.

In praise of the lay practitioner Li Yuangu: His mastery of worldly pivot-points is rarely known by the world. Sixty years since birth, he has not paused for a moment; wherever he encounters the stage, he takes up the bamboo staff to traverse the three periods of time.
Amidst the weeds, a *dharma-flower* puts forth a single branch. Without asking about ultimate emptiness, he discourses on the supreme principle; with joy, he speaks of conventional truth.
Li Wei. This mountain monk wishes to offer congratulations, having no other gift at hand; I have exhausted my brush and written only this poem of auspicious blessings.
On the Sixtieth Birthday of the Venerable Zhi-fei (Three Poems):

For thirty years you have followed me, Your refined spirit never conforming to the vulgar stream. You take up your staff to prevent slipping on moss, And delight in walking meditation amidst the dense trees.
Three strikes of the board in the hall; a single cry of the cuckoo from beyond the clouds. Today I meet my birthday; suddenly I am startled to find half my hair turned white.
For thirty years following me, you have traveled through cold and heat without weariness. The *kṣānti*-grass flourishes with the clouds; the *dharma*-flower blooms everywhere upon the earth.

Your light of precepts remains ever pure and bright; your daily recitations are redoubled in clarity. Whether it be matters of the Way or the affairs of worldly dust, they are all as light as a goose feather.
For thirty years following me, your pure conduct has been a model for the Sangha. You have remained indifferent to worldly trappings; why would you entangle yourself in withered vines?

Though the Dharma banner may fall, your mind remains pure; though the Flower Treasury World may equal your own body, it is ever-present. When you held the whisk, your words offered direct transmission; yet when the wheel of the mechanism turns, it seems as if nothing was ever done.

My dharma-brother Shouqian has for many years attended my master with his staff and almsbowl. Today, his years are precisely at their prime. Though he jests that his surname is "Cold," he fulfills the seasonal rites;
let us laugh as we behold this auspicious fortune blossom like a jade branch.
**Two Poems on the Completion of the "Life-Mirror" by Chengzong** From ancient times, the Chan gate has known no years or months; Who transmitted these idle words of "fifty years"?
If you wish to know the true message beyond kalpas, The sun shines upon the clear river—a single ball of brocade.
The sun, moon, and stars discourse on the true aspect; the mountains, rivers, and great earth proclaim the perfect sound. Within the flames of the red furnace, more fire is added;
its blazing heat cooks and steams the heart of the ancient Buddha.
Elder Wanrong and I met;
for me, the new year’s retreat has just begun. Yet in the blink of an eye, the bright spring has already brought gray hairs.
Unaware in my dreams that the frosty moon has grown old, I shall take up my bowl and enjoy the tides of the Zhejiang River.
The life of Layman Huang Xinjing has reached one hundred years;
half of the light and shadow of time has already passed. Though darkness and brightness shift and change, what can be done about it? I once heard the earnest words of Vimalakīrti in days of old:
"All kalpas of dust and time are but a single kṣaṇa."
The Chan practitioner Shouzhi spent fifty years amidst the illusory transformations of the human world. He lived with childlike simplicity in the mountain valleys, tilling the mountain fields;
white clouds and bright moons he has plowed through entirely, yet his spiritual horns remain only faintly visible, not yet fully formed.
The handle of the hoe is one’s entire life. In autumn it withers, in winter it dries, and in spring it blooms. When years and months have run their course, it undergoes change.
Do not let the clouds and mist dampen your *kāṣāya*.
At eighty, Zhaozhou was still diligent; he examined the haughty airs of the various quarters.
If you wish to recognize the true state of the ancients, do not seek ease and comfort as your final liberation.

The *Lotus Sūtra* analyzes the lifespan [of the Buddha] into atoms; having analyzed them all until the atoms exhaust their obstruction of the eyes, it teaches only that Mount Sumeru turns into white waves.
The Buddha’s birth within the realm of dust has no concern for worldly sentiment.
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Thirty-three;
The Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi, Volume Thirty-four.
Compiled by Honghan, Dharma Grandson residing at Boshan.
The Head Seat and Dharma Grandson, Hongyu,
together compiled these elegies for the funeral rites at the stupa of the late Master Shouchang (four poems).
On this day of last year, I paid my respects at the Master’s countenance; today I come again, but the stupa is already closed. In vain do you say that he has hidden his body beyond seeking;
thin clouds and sparse rain fill the human world.
A hundred feet reaching toward the heavens, a night’s frost; a claw-shaped water jar still hangs from a tattered wicker bed. When he came, the ancient path was surely wordless;
the incense smoke of Cao Yuan flows as a single, long thread.
The emanated body strides southward as he returns west; the five-colored radiance of his brush illuminates the night.
May the stupa of the Dharma-treasury, free from seams, not allow the pair of cranes to soar into the heavens.
I prostrate nine times before the shrine, tears falling incessantly. How can I ever again behold your compassionate countenance?
The white clouds and flowing waters remain as they were, yet I no longer see the One who expounded the Dharma on Vulture Peak.

In Commemoration of Master Chan (Four Poems) The tracks of the Elephant King portend the blossoming of auspicious lotuses; atop Wuyufeng Peak, his roar is like thunder. Today, what dense and dark smoke hangs from the trees?
Purple clouds swirl into the mass of white clouds.
The Dharma-treasure within the Sangha, a hero among men—its jade dew and golden stem are twice as precious. The sound of the bell in the still night cannot be contained;
it follows the clouds and waters through the new year.
The entire body remains enshrined in the stupa at the auspicious site of Nanhua; even now, the five-nipple clouds still cloak his feet. With his staff, he stirs the turbid and clear worlds;
one knows not how many have attained the Dharma through him.
For many years the Dharma rain has pervaded the realm; where does this illusory manifestation dwell?
Upon the moon over Poyang Lake, ancient and modern, its pure light shines brightly upon Mount Kuanglu.
Eulogy for Liu Hehe, the Meritorious Graduate (Four Poems) The breeze is gentle over the clear river as ripples part;
Once, a golden-scaled fish was caught upon the hook. Now, it does not vanish with the mist and rain;
Through many layers of evening clouds, it beckons me back at night.
Victory and defeat, honor and grief, are bound up in worldly sentiments; how vast is the Way of Heaven—how could it not be impartial? Now he does not know how to conceal his person;
throughout the entire world, all know the name of the Boatman.
The fragrance of the orchid and the iris is extraordinary; in the secluded valley where no one dwells, it blooms of its own accord. Do not say that the bitter frost will crush the trunk of the state;
for a thousand years, the pure wind shall cause the capes and robes to flutter.
In the cold of winter, how many know my heart? In the sixth month, the wutong trees wither—this is not the season. Yet I recall our promise upon the Sutra-Preaching Terrace;
now I have already composed this elegy for you.
Eulogy for the Governor of Qunyu, Qi (Six Poems) The carriage fills the road to Mount Fushan;
I linger about, yet cannot see you. My heart follows the swift current of the flowing stream; My gaze is cut off by the clouds of my native land.
The snowy wind soaks my bones with cold as it sees me off to Nanshu. My lingering feelings at this parting—upon whom can they be entrusted to enter a painting?

You have turned your staff toward Shengsheng Monastery; I feel pity that we shall rarely meet again. For now, I am barely able to bathe and groom myself; dragging along my illness, I speak of our subtle parting.

Since then, we have seldom met; yet you still presented me with your verses on medicine and illness. I am ashamed that my inquiries after your health were so infrequent, failing to live up to the spirit of Vimalakīrti.
Suddenly the autumn wind grew fierce, and the golden wutong trees withered prematurely. When the mournful news arrived, I struck the desk in inconsolable grief.
I have intended to paint your likeness, yet I cannot cease my longing for you from afar. Grasping my brush with tears upon it, I have written out this elegy for you.
"Poems Written at Heishuiyan, Moved by Sentiment" (Wuyan gu).

Cloud-stairs are like scales piled in tiers; leaning on my staff, I stroll at will. Water flows from the dragon’s mouth; pines lean against the traces of ancient stones. Ancient trees conceal beautiful birds;
layered mountains form a stack of emerald screens. Zen meditation has been entrusted here for a thousand ages; fame and profit are but a single light body.

Suddenly vast, it is no realm for wandering; Tranquil and carefree, one delights in the spirit of the Way. To further exhaust the meaning of the Western Patriarchs— The sky is clear, and the distant river shines bright.
**Sending Off My Father Home (Four Heptasyllabic Regulated Verses)** After more than thirty years, we meet once again;
The local accent remains the same, yet our countenances have changed. Our feelings of affection seem as if they still entwine our bodies.
Seeking fame? Honor and disgrace pass by like the wind over one's ears. Green robes of dyed hemp rely on the laughter of guests; who can truly share these *tamdala*-flower cotton rags?
In vain do you say that worldly affairs are full of reversals; clap your hands together—they all fall within a single dream.
Leaving my staff in the mountain forests, my mind is naturally clear; amidst the dust of the world, not a sound of rooster or dog is heard. Beyond the gate, the moon hovers over the stream;
at the head of the willow embankment, a lute hangs from a tree. All former vanity is but a dream; these present hair and beard merely purchase empty fame.
If my fellow villagers ask about my practice, I am simply that man who once stumbled through life.
I eat three meals a day and stop when full; after eating, with nothing to do, I delight in ascending the tower. The mountain scenery before me shifts and changes with the passing moments;
the clouds and mists at my feet come and go as they please. I regard the Dharma as my kin and distance myself from worldly appearances;
I view this body as a mere lodging, equal to a floating bubble. How many "Yellow Beam" dreams are there in the dusty world? To them, I yield the prize for resting upon a stone by the deep mountains.
No longer stained by the sweat of former days, I have shaved my beard and hair and donned the *kāṣāya*. My spirit is startled awake from the darkness of this fleeting life;

my original vow is to bring myself into alignment with the Buddha-way. How could one’s own flesh and bone endure the burdens of many kalpas? One knows that through karmic conditions, one has been lost in delusion for countless lifetimes.
Now, having won a measure of leisure, I let my mind roam as I lean on my staff and walk along the willow-lined embankment.

Spontaneous Compositions (Seven Poems) Dwelling deep in the mountains, I deeply admire the traces of Mount Huxi. Many guests I have encountered through smiles. With my staff, I carry the shadows of the setting sun;
My straw sandals tread upon the seals of purple clouds. Striking the table with chopsticks while brewing tea, I repay Maitreya; Drinking wildly and singing madly, I revile the world.
Master Zhigong: A gentle breeze begins to stir at the mouth of the valley; The pines and cypresses comb through the air like soaring dragons.
My robes are tattered and my bags are worn—let others laugh; Unstained by even a speck of dust, what cause for doubt? The water of desire plunges off the cliff with a frantic roar;
The clouds of craving emerge from the peaks with slow, lingering grace. This luminous, wondrous essence is ever thus: Profound and still, it is the principle beyond words.
Thus it is: swallowing up all the lands of the ten directions, who else could have achieved Buddhahood?

Life and death, emptiness and form—these two heavy barriers; one should skillfully employ the *Śūraṅgama* to discern the eight returns. When the cataracts before the eyes clear, the Milky Way is pure;

when obstructions in the breast are shed, objects and conditions are at ease. Beneath the pines, a hundred feet of shade seem like a fragrant pond; the water from the conduit flows through three bends.
Bamboo Mountain: Tired, I lay down beneath the green willow branches; how many rains of flowers fall upon the human world? Right and wrong, warmth and cold—none can constrain me;
for many years I have been bound to my thatched hut amidst the emerald peaks. Beyond the railing, the red flowers look like wild fire;
before the crags, the green moss locks in the cold ice. Three poles of bamboo shadow the phoenix of Mount Qi; ten thousand miles of wind strike the Zhuangzi.
The Sea Eagle: After several times the evening clouds have dispersed, a single bright moon ascends the ridges of the plum trees.
Having discerned the creative mechanism of grinding a brick [to make a mirror], the first light of day shines beneath Mount Daxiong. The wooden horse neighing in the wind rides upon the clouds away;
the mud ox drinking from the sea returns with the mist. Within these words there is a blade that pierces through the gallbladder; before one’s eyes there is nothing to pursue.
Dust flies; joyfully he shatters the mirror of the Qin dynasty. He does not don the robe transmitted from the Tathāgata.
The precious mirror is limpid and bright, the Dharma-realm is pure. Within this, one must discern the name of Samantabhadra.
Nirvāṇa has awakening, yet it is not awakening; Prajñā is non-arising, yet it benefits living beings. To break through delusion and awaken, exert no effort; to reveal the true and the false—
My heart is moved. Now, by chance, I have come to know the Elder Zhongfeng; the great earth and its mountains and rivers are leveled within the palm of his hand.
Who can recognize the landscape of this mountain realm? Dwelling here aids me in my joyous practice of mental fasting (*xinzhai*).

When bamboo shoots first emerge, I gather them with the clouds; when bean pods grow tall, I plant them amidst the rain. Forgetting all conditions, I sleep upon an ancient mat with a stone for a pillow; leaning on my staff, I walk at my leisure.
Fresh Moss. Tired of walking, I refrain from plucking the willows by the pond, Leaving them for the yellow orioles to fly to and fro.
Two Poems on Sheshan (畬山):
Having finished singing the song of the purple *zhī* fungi upon Sheshan, A few wisps of mist and cloud hang from the green *luó* vines. In the bamboo path, an old woman steals the bamboo shoots.
Departing, I see monkeys crossing the dry stream; Pine blossoms with their stamens brew fresh tea. Lotus leaves with their attached fibers mend my tattered straw raincoat.
It is simply that the practitioner’s vision is distinct: Ten thousand years and a single thought are left to dissolve as they may.
On Sheshan, I hew through the clouds atop the ridge; years and months are all forgotten, leaving nothing divided. Suddenly unrolling, suddenly unfolding, the dragon reveals its form;

drawing near and approaching one another, the birds call out in flocks. Knowing only that the price of the pearl spans the three thousand worlds, who cares for the radiance of ten thousand eight hundred leagues?
Having penetrated the barrier of Chan beyond measure, let the vast blue sea sink and submerge itself as it will.
In the Rhyme of the Magistrate of Chengyi (Two Poems) Hand in hand we proceed together in deer-drawn carriages;
the dense scenery naturally delights the heart. Bells chime from the halls and pavilions, beckoning the cranes to return;
Clerical staffs hang from the roots of clouds, while warblers warble around them. The sound of the pine paths is fit for hearing the Dharma; The stone gate is without seams, as if—

As a standard for conduct, the pure breeze does not diminish the guest who frowned; today, his name is once again added to the Lotus Society. Ascending high upon the flat rock, he halts his celestial carriage;
lightly waving the fly-whisk, he expresses his rustic sentiments. He once listened to the birds roosting in the pines amidst the wind;
returning now, he walks through the willow shadows where the orioles sing. Turning his body, he still seeks traces within the Flower Treasury; taking steps at ease, he has finished his journey home.
I ask you to examine the matter; you must recognize the true significance within it. How could one who is serenely detached allow the name "Buddha" to arise?

While traveling with the Judicial Commissioner Jian Dingzhai to Bailongdong (White Dragon Cave), we passed through three cities like layers of silk before reaching Xifeng (Western Peak). Upon arriving at Western Peak, we rejoiced that there was a spring within Bailong Cave, flowing from a thousand gullies.
Green. The treetops are unstained, yet the entire mountain is red. How can the mind differ between past and present? As rewards follow rise and fall, the realm remains the same.
Entrust this to all you noble practitioners who come and go: do not seek the tracks of fish at the bottom of the water.
In Reply to Grand Historian Zheng Songmen (Two Poems) Entering the gate, there is no need to ask for the winding path;
The colors of the herbs, trees, and groves unfold before me. You are willing to preserve my old calligraphy upon the beams;

We have already agreed to discuss the sutras by the branches east of the ridge. Fate has brought us together, fulfilling the prophecy of the non-sewn robe; There are no words worthy of being inscribed upon the wall.
The Inscription Stone. Those who dwell on this mountain do not yet understand this matter. When De-yun meets you, it will be late at another peak.

Throughout the great thousandfold world-system, there is nowhere that is not a meditation hall. All that meets the eye is emptiness; the wisdom-sword is like frost. As crows pass, they leave a sound in the azure void;
when guests arrive, one lacks the strength to descend from the rope-cot. Linji’s three punches have washed away all karmic mechanisms; a single handful of Caoxi’s water.
Even more fragrant. The fruit upon the staff’s tip opens the True Eye; what harm is there in letting out a long啸 (shout of joy) on the eastern marsh?

Answer: The Mountain Man Li from Yue Dong has spent these years finding delight in secluded forests with his alms-bowl and staff. In his meditative stillness, he has never engaged in bitter chanting. He scoops up water to lead the fish, and at times ascends [to the heights].
Down below. Piercing the clouds to gather medicinal herbs through many days of sun and shade. The cauldron has been smashed—no need to wash it.
The tree has no roots; I am too weary to seek it out. As soon as I hear someone speaking by the stream, I follow the deer back into the deep mountains.

In the rhyme of Great Minister Cao Nengshi: The ancient traces of the Sage Monk rely on your eminence; The Buddhist monasteries are all brought under your command. Suddenly, the various temples take on the hue of a flourishing community;
No living being fails to look up to your lofty character. The Spirit Spring Cave inhales the distant surges of the river; The Dew-of-Ambrosia pines swirl around the rocks.
Wall-onions: In vain do I conjure the image of Master Yan coming and going. How boundless is the flourishing of Mount Gu’s Jia-yun!
In response to the verse by Layman Chen □□:
By what cause do I take up my staff on Mount Gu? Drinking water and sleeping amidst the clouds, I divined a bountiful year. There is going and there is coming from the heavens.

A day without form or shadow; the wind from the tip of the staff. Holding incense, I offer this eulogy, rejoicing in this new attainment; waving the whisk to the sound [of the chant], I am ashamed that my skill remains unrefined.
If you wish to know the direct intent of the Patriarch, the land of Fusang originally lies to the east of the sea gate.

In the style of Layman He’an □□: A wooden horse soars into the void, neighing in the night wind; I know there is a man of high attainment whose verses are skillfully wrought. The oar enters the clear waves as the sandy shore recedes;
The poetic couplet matches the "white snow," our pure hearts in accord. Drifting clouds, piece by piece, float across the northern sky; The flowing stream murmurs as I gaze afar.

East of the Sea: from this point on, it is no longer possible to distinguish between staying and going; lightly gathered within the fibers of the lotus, it resonates with the rhyme of the layman of Helin.
That one arrow of the Sage pierces the heavens—let there be no distinction between north, south, east, or west. Before crossing the Stone Gate, one already knows the delusion.
Awakening. As soon as he grasps his staff, he examines form and emptiness. A letter arrives from across the sea, inviting him to go; a cup is raised by the river, entering the clouds to the east.
Now, let us not speak of the traces of divine monks; flower-rain falls profusely, turning both banks crimson.
In the Rhyme of Layman Li □□:

A clear radiance extends ten thousand *li* within this painted landscape; Wherever the eye turns, returning clouds allow the bird-path to pass. Azure banyan trees line both banks, concealing the shadows of oars;
White cranes piercing the heavens cry out in the autumn wind. If even the state of *dhyāna* permits the entry of worldly ties, Then liberation must surely involve these profound mysteries.
The meaning is exhausted. Within this lump of red flesh, do not let it pass by; clearly recognize your own true nature.

Following the rhyme of the Layman Wúyòng of Héxióng, there are now tens of thousands of koans; one knows not who can truly realize the Zen of the Patriarchs. The cypress tree in the courtyard—how pure and refreshing!

All-pervading: On the mountain peak, pine branches reach toward the hanging white moon; for ten thousand ages, the emerald pool reflects a slender clarity; in the living waters of the single stream, the sound of the waves is profound.
When people of this age further inquire about the meaning of the Westward Journey, do not trouble yourself with coughs or fists beneath the ribs.

In the Rhyme of Layman □□□ Vast and boundless, worldly thoughts are cold as ice; A flash of lightning across the clear sky, the ancestral lamp is transmitted. Through kalpas I have realized that mind is Buddha;
Several times I have awakened from the dream of being a monk. To say that foam and flowers conceal my traces is but idle talk; How could a phantom image possess any reality?
Love and Hatred. Waiting for guests and welcoming visitors, idly pointing and remarking; After three meals of fullness, there is nothing more one can do.
Written in the style of Sima Ruru of the Wu Dynasty (Five-Syllable Verse):
The misty waters of Xiangtan are vast; Taking hands, we return home at once. We enter directly through the gates of the Heavenly King; Who would have known of the Elder’s carriage?
All that has mind is but a dream; without cataracts, there are no empty flowers. I am most pleased with Layman Pang, who came to boil tea by striking the ice.
Following the rhyme of Layman Zhongyin Xie:

Gourd-bowl and bamboo hat startle at wind and rain; Satchel-bag fastened, he travels alone. Listening to conditions, he tires of being a guest; Wherever he is, he delights in dwelling among the mountains.

The waters are vast and the light of the clouds stretches afar; the pines are deep and the crane’s dream is idle. Fortunate to share the refined air of a layman, I have shattered the barrier of the Patriarch.

Fishing at the Terrace, I pass the year until the end of winter, when I hear the news of my parents’ passing. I urge my lone boat back home through the night. On the level sands there are no bird tracks; in the deep trees, the monkeys wail.
When shall I reach the riverbank? Few guests come to my home. Long have I contemplated these two rows of tears, which first fell upon the Fishing Terrace.

Amidst the snow at night, I weep for my father’s grave, which lies but a few feet away; why must I suffer such lingering captivity? The night snow falls without ceasing, and the cold rooster cries out without rest.

Not thinking of the startle of sitting or sleeping, blood and tears stain the mountain streams. Heaven questions the filial piety of the dark-robed one; the green mountains are now filled with white-haired elders.
Having reached Shucheng, thousands of li away, it is as if I were in my youth again. I halt my steps to seek the old path; touching my heart, I am moved by what I think of.
The new trees along the sandy embankment grow thick; old friends in the city are few. Alas for this realm of impermanence—who among us aspires to transcend it?

The river below flows white as a silken ribbon; mist and clouds reflect upon its shallow currents. Birds near the city walls seem to understand human speech; travelers arriving at their lodgings give rise to sorrow.
Flesh and bone have no blue eyes; half the children have white hair. In the desolate wilderness, high mounds rise one after another; they are all the burial hills of old friends.
The Zen friend Bitan followed me back to my native village. Amidst deep snow, he was unaware of spring. He wiped away cold tears by the stream; pulling at my robes, he stirred the morning clouds.
The ice layers pity the traveler’s horse; a fallen tree reveals a woodcutter. Mistakenly becoming a guest for many years, the language of my hometown feels even more intimate.
Seeking Master Huìtái of Dōngyuán, I took up my staff and climbed Mount Dōng. I traced the source to visit an old acquaintance. Where strange pines block the path, fine rain wets my robes.

The stone steps are as clean as if washed; the thatched gate winds around with slow turns. Meeting one another, neither grows weary; we sip tea and chant new poems. Parting from the Layman Huang Xingyuan:
I recall the day I first came to these mountains, yet I still think back to the time of our parting. Though we traveled thousands of miles apart, in the blink of an eye half a year has passed.
The Dharma teaching has no other instruction: the jewel in the robe must bring you joy yourself. Look closely at it in your daily life; there is no need to ask those you know.

To the Layman Balinghengting, who bears the power of great vows upon his shoulders and perceives the mind of the Way-man through and through: the precious sword must be sharpened, yet the jewel in the robe requires no seeking.
Mundane ties are entirely a dream; the Buddha-dharma is not merely a warning. I recall our appointment in the mountains: let us play the zither hanging on the wall.
Parting at the Forest of Virtue, Layman Youde:
beyond the boundaries of heaven and earth, one sees no end to the road’s length. The painted swan parts from the flowing water; cold gulls scatter in confusion upon the sand.

The white tuft brushes away the dust of the world; its clear shadow draws in the celestial raft. I am most delighted by the scenery along the riverbank: the branches are full and the flowers bloom upon the trees.

In parting from Layman Lu [Name], who can compare him to one who cultivates virtue? I envy you for your generosity; your mutual sincerity reveals that you possess the Way. Your excellence is far more than mere hearsay.
The staff strikes the empty sky; the straw sandals tread upon the mountain clouds. With a pair of clear and blind eyes, every hair and fiber is naturally distinguished.
Following the rhyme of Great Censor Cao Nengshi, he shows this to his fellow practitioners:

To climb the mountain, one must reach the summit; stride forth without delaying for even a moment. On perilous paths, rely solely on the staff; when the forked ways divide, you must surely ask the Master.
The clouds are deep; I hastened my way. The light fades; I regret my tardiness. Where strength is spent and artifice forgotten—who, indeed, is this majestic one?
Upon first entering Mount Gu, seeing the plum blossoms, I composed this spontaneously:
A rugged path of a thousand miles, I spare no thought for this aging body. My feet have truly lost their strength; Before my eyes, there is only cloud.

I frequently encounter birds seeking lodging, yet rarely see a traveler asking for directions. Do not be surprised that the plum blossoms laugh; another spring has slipped away in vain. In the same rhyme, I answer Mr.
Ruan Yuanhai, Minister of Works (Jiǎngqīng). (Preface to a Seven-Character Quatrain) The Great Master Ma sucked the lion’s cub dry with a single gulp.
Where could Hezang hide his body? The "Nine Bands" (Jiùdài) public case has been so from the beginning.
Not a single hair’s breadth was transgressed. The porridge and soup of the five flavors remain sweet and fragrant even now.

Having emerged from the tip of the cypress, he walks upon the summit of the seamless stupa. If you wish to know that the flower and fruit arise simultaneously, do not inquire about the news of a "return.
Before the time of Vipaśyin, the Old Stone took a single step; thereafter, he entered the community of Boshan, where he conducts further business within the fire.
As for "measure," there is no hindrance to putting him in a cloth bag. You must believe that the barking dog with many voices is right here at this very moment;
where is it? He further says, "Look under your feet."
River moon and mountain clouds reflect the azure sky; the profound mystery within is not called "mysterious.
The Lord of the East understands human intent and specifically uses the plum blossom to verify the separate transmission.
The yellow leaves and mountain flowers are matters for others to debate; yet when the mountain flowers and yellow leaves appear, the eye of the Way opens.
If one is willing to follow the shifting fashions of crimson and purple, one must know that spring arrives beyond the kalpas.
In Response to Layman Liu Yin-zhen, Following His Rhymes (with Preface) "To see form as not-form is to see the Tathāgata.

This is a discourse on shattering appearances to enter into principle; unless one’s practice has brought about the cessation of conceptual understanding, one cannot arrive there through direct experience.
You, Layman, are currently situated within the realm of conceptual understanding. If you were to mistake this understanding for awakening, you would not merely fail to perceive the Truth.

It is not true. I fear that masters and disciples may fail to distinguish the genuine from the false; therefore, under the Gate of the Patriarchs, what is valued is authentic inquiry and earnest investigation.
When the single breath does not return, and one knows not where one has gone, it is clear that one’s former views were not real. How then could one not harbor doubt?
If true doubt suddenly arises, one reaches the ground of great peace and bliss. Looking back at the path of intellectual understanding, how could it be anything less than worlds apart?

Scratching an itch with a leather pad. Three poems in the same rhyme. These are not intended as explanations of the mind through words; they are merely to avoid辜负 (failing to respond to) your kind intent.
Seven cushions worn through, the sky of views is shattered; even before the curtain is lifted, it is already profound and mysterious. The plum blossoms open unintentionally upon the branches;
their profusion on the branches verifies the authentic transmission.
Spring flowers and autumn leaves are but ordinary matters; spring leaves and autumn flowers also bloom.
Yet I laugh at the personal entrustment on Vulture Peak, which came forth with a voice atop the flagpole.

Clouds and sky are vainly sought in the midst of space; in that space, clouds and sky are the eternal mind. The color of the grass and the sound of the rain—one’s own direct glimpse—Pang’s children and grandchildren are the true connoisseurs.
In the same rhyme, I reply to Layman Qi Yuandai:

From of old, you have delighted in dwelling among the mountains with your staff and bowl; You take up your cane first to prevent the hardships of taking a step. For what reason today do we discuss the talk of snow?
This pure joy spreads throughout the ranks of the gentry.
Xieshan on Poyu Lake (Two Poems) Fish leap and kites soar amidst white waves;
beneath my feet, flowing waters leave the Wayfarer at leisure. Shao Yang’s mind does not follow the wind-blown sails;
the clouds rise from the Southern Mountain while the rain falls upon the Northern Mountain.
Treading through the spring across the waters of Poyang Lake, the pattern on his shoes is clearly brand new. Shaolin Monastery had no reason to alarm the mundane world;
that he returned to the West in a single shoe—how strange this man is!
In the company of Layman Wu Gongliang, as cold flakes struck our faces, we conversed at ease. Who could share such earnestness in the aspiration for the Way?
Recalling the ancestral hall deep within the snow, today, wherever we go, we uphold the family tradition.
Driving a hundred li with the layman Jiang Yige—what other mind could there be? The jeweled nets and fragrant clouds are not to be sought elsewhere.
Once you recognize that our family is utterly destitute to the bone, even the sand and soil picked up are all pure gold.
Having met with the lay practitioner Wu Shisheng for a brief moment, we have exchanged words on the Way. Though the muddy road ahead stretches for a hundred li, I do not decline the toil.
What worldly affairs could I offer you in return? There is only this single path leading home.
With Layman Liu Yanxian, we wade deeply through flying snow;
what reliance can there be? Clear water and freezing ice cover our faces. Suddenly, the spring sky unfolds its transformative sun;
may you first seize the branch of the southern hills.
Staying at Xita in Shaowu for early morning congee, the congee was hot and my teeth ached;
I knew that old age had arrived. The wind and cold made my bones shiver with a sense of fragmentation; the fleeting light of time could not fulfill my攀缘 (pān-yuan) desires.
I speak this so that the elders of all quarters may know.
Passing through the Zixia Pass, for what reason do I lean my staff at the Zixia Barrier? Upon the stone steps I sit in *paryaṅka*, old and fearing the cold.
Without resorting to the couch of an immortal to sleep, how many times have clear dreams entered Mount Fushan?
The Four Scenic Views of Baiguan Hermitage:
Washing-Ears Spring.
Amidst the mountains, one heeds not the affairs of the human world; after the meal, the smoke from the tea stove rises once more. One loathes to hear the wind in the pines and the cries of birds.

Speech. Cupping both ears to drink the clear spring, the *Sūtra of the Earth, Mountains, and Rivers*—one fascicle—is most clearly manifest, without characters or words. Sometimes it is spoken toward the pines.
Stone. Squatting with legs apart beside Mount Kongtong, I listen intently.

The bird-path gate winds and meanders, piercing through the layered peaks in a single thread. As I enter the layered peaks, the trees grow ever more numerous. Since there are no diverging paths from here, who could distinguish them?
Truly so. Do not mock the true traces of non-duality.
My drunken brushstrokes on the banana leaf have used this as paper; since then, no one has used you again. Entrust it to be planted in abundance—three or two more.
The trees bear inscriptions of insects and bird-script, their patterns formed spontaneously.
A Six-Word Verse in the Manner of Walking Beneath Pines:
My body turns upon the jagged stone steps; my eyes shift at the crimson and green atop the trees. This solitary mendicant, having nowhere to rely, laughs at himself.
Neither true nor conventional.

Beneath the bamboo, drinking several cups of clear tea to dispel fatigue; leaning on a staff, there is no need to exert effort. Fortunately, there are thousands and tens of thousands of stalks. It is not...
Maitreya crouches in contemplation;
the golden carp of the放生池 (liberation pond) cast their shadows upon the treetops. Their emerald feathers hold a frown beneath the water. Upon the path of inverted saṃsāra, they remain unaware.
Who is the True Man? (Six Poems on Wild Chanting) Whirling leaves, frosty winds, and withered stumps;
Clear sands, cold waters, and crystalline purity. Sitting alone in the public hall, leaning on my armrest, I am wide awake and alert.

Delighting in listening to the sound of thunder, I gaze upon the long-drawn carriages and horses of Chang’an; traveling along the riverbanks of Wu and Yue, I have beheld all the myriad hues of red and purple.
Meeting people along the way, I briefly discuss the subtle and the profound.
A few wisps of thin clouds rest upon the phoenix; a thousand layers of fine ripples bathe the dragon. When guests pass by, there is no hindrance to joining hands;
gazing at the reflection in the pond, one beholds the monk.
A cool breeze rises from the west; a bright moon ascends from the east. How laughable is the profound meaning of the Chan gate—a broken donkey!
Flies alight upon the ridge;

sparse and dense, duckweed floats upon the green water. High and low, cassias unfurl their exquisite blossoms. Leaning my staff on the peak, I gaze afar: before me lie the houses of the village, shrouded in mist and rain.
Moss coins stack upon the stone steps; Layers of scarlet curtains drape the mountain peaks. After the midday meal, I stroll idly along the pond’s edge, Picking lotus flowers with nine petals.
Passing the water, I reach the abbot’s quarters— A Five-Character Quatrain.

The mass of clouds pierces the mountain valleys; the sound of pines falls upon the streamlets. Leaning on the railing, I inquire after the signs of rain, and it is precisely the season of the apricot blossoms.

Moored by the Mei River, the waters are so vast that the boat seems small. Amidst the deep clouds, the trees appear low-hanging. Raising the sail-curtain, I ask the ferryman his name; he says, "This is Little Mei River."
The superior man of Bingshi gazes upon the water from his boat;

as the compassionate boat’s oars glide across the surface, the stillness of his mind extends infinitely. The entire world is a ground of lapis lazuli; there is no need to laboriously inquire about the moonlight.
A Song for Ruyi Hermitage, Presented to Master Zhi Along the winding and undulating mountain paths,
purple vapors rise from the roots of the rocks, pervading the forest and springs. The green pines and azure bamboos embrace the clouds.
Smoke. The colors of the landscape are as clear and serene as the mind; mountain streams swirl and flow throughout the three thousand worlds.
Within them dwells a man of high character whose years are unknown. He has come specifically to inquire about the Way before me. His wisdom is the gateway, and his insight is complete.

His heroic spirit shines forth, and his countenance is profound. He has stirred me to compose new verses on the Dharma. I have written these few words to establish this karmic connection. Infinite Dharmas...

Disciple Zhida Liu Rigao composed this. As for Master Boshan, he was a native of Shucheng.

He was then nursed by the wives of others who had children, but after several women were tried, none were willing to feed him. Duke Tai (Taigong) daily provided him with acorns and chestnuts for his wet nurse, and thus the monk did not die.
He was truly a divine anomaly. When he grew up, he was able to consume food and drink normally, yet thereafter he never drank again.
He abstained from wine and meat. Once, while playing with a neighbor’s child, he was knocked down by one of them and his teeth were broken.
His father, Master Gong, was naturally stern and severe; fearing his father’s reproaches, the monk spat out blood.

Upon returning home, he explained the circumstances in detail, so that his father did not become angry. His compassion and kindness were indeed innate. At the age of sixteen, he resolved to leave the household life.
He went to the Waguan Temple in Jinling to listen to lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Moved by a sense of urgency, he exclaimed, "The pursuit lies within myself;

He cultivated the path of Zhiyi’s *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). Once, while sitting outdoors beneath a pine tree, he was unaware of the passage of day and night as swarms of mosquitoes gathered upon his body.
He gnawed on withered wood; inwardly he was unaware of having blood, flesh, body, or mind, and outwardly he saw no mountains, rivers, or the great earth.
Thus five years passed without ceasing, even through cold and heat. He then went to Mount Chao-hua to receive the Bhikṣu Vinaya from Master Hong.
At that time, Master Shouchang Jing was residing at Mount E-peak, propagating the Dharma of the Cao-dong school.

When the Master heard of his reputation, he went to visit him. Upon seeing Shouchang, who was carrying a hoe and wearing a bamboo hat, appearing like a common farmer, the Master immediately harbored doubts in his heart.
He subsequently entered Guangze in Min Province and resided at Baiyun Peak for three years. He then presented a book written based on what he had attained to Shouchang.
Shouchang sent a letter back to him, stating that it was not the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Only then did the Master feel a sense of disillusionment.

He realized his error. He then burned incense and prostrated himself, destroyed the draft, and never showed it to others again. He applied himself even more deeply to the teachings of the *zong* (the Dharma-vehicle), reading the words of Chuanshi on "concealing the body.
Doubt suddenly arose within him, leading him to forget both sleep and food. After more than a year had passed, he suddenly saw the words of Zhaozhou instructing a monk;

Tracing the waters of Dong back to Caoxi, the source is deep and the current far-reaching. Dragon Peak connects with Phoenix Ridge; the mountains are beautiful and the winds are lofty.

Section. I pray that the former renown may not decline and that future students may have a path to follow. I humbly entreat all donors to join with their dharma-relatives in contributing funds for this collective printing.
This will not only cause the torch of wisdom to shine once more and be included in the Tripitaka for wide circulation, but will also cause those in spiritual darkness to suddenly awaken.
Its benefit to the world will be great indeed—how magnificent is its merit! Written by the dharma-grandson residing at Boshan, Honghan, with prostrations.
